text:
However, final passage now hinges on a small group of Democrats seeking tribal protections and assurances that President Donald Trump will not block wind and solar projects.

Trump cast doubt on those assurances hours before the vote. At a White House briefing, he said he supported the bill, then rejected a question about approving wind turbines.

“No, I will not approve wind turbines,” Trump said. He had called the bill “a great bill” and said, “We are behind it 100 percent.”

The vote on a procedural measure advances the legislation to an amendment process; it does not make the bill law.

Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., said supporters expected a “very healthy amendment process.”

The bill would make it harder to challenge projects in court on environmental grounds and limit the ability of states and the Environmental Protection Agency to block them before construction. Its supporters also point to provisions intended to make it easier to build power lines and add electricity — including renewable power — to the grid.

Whitehouse argued before the vote that the bill would benefit consumers and cut emissions.

He said it could save consumers $60 to $80 a month and prevent 1.5 billion to 1.8 billion metric tons of greenhouse gas emissions.

Whitehouse also said the measure would increase U.S. wind capacity by 25%, solar capacity by 28% and battery-storage capacity by 70%, though he did not mention the source of his numbers.

“This is a climate and clean energy bill,” Whitehouse said, adding that its effect on the power sector could exceed that of the Inflation Reduction Act, which he said had been weakened by Republicans.

Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., opposed advancing the bill.

He argued that its renewable-energy provisions would not offset measures he said could encourage more fossil-fuel use, including gas-fired power for data centers and expanded natural-gas pipelines and liquefied natural gas exports.

He said climate estimates that exclude gas burned overseas leave out emissions that still affect the global climate.

The bill’s project-certainty provisions are intended to prevent administrations from revoking existing permits and allow developers to sue over what the legislation calls “disparate treatment” of energy sources.

That could protect renewable projects from one administration and fossil-fuel projects from another.

The legislation also includes a provision requiring data centers to pay at least their fair share for the electricity and infrastructure they use, supporters say. The bill has support from industry groups in fossil fuels, renewable energy, chemicals, construction and manufacturing.

If the Senate passes the bill, it would move to the House, where it has support from Republicans and some Democrats but is expected to face opposition from progressive lawmakers. The schedule for amendments and a final Senate vote was not provided.

Whitehouse said the bill would be “the floor, not the ceiling” of Democrats’ climate and environmental ambitions.

text:
This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback.

The Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission recently approved AES Indiana’s plan to serve a Google data center in a contested case that highlights the complex challenges regulators and utilities face in allocating system costs for large computational loads.

According to the Oct. 7 order, AES will acquire or build new generation, storage and grid infrastructure for a 390-MW data center planned for Monrovia, a town Southwest of Indianapolis, at an estimated project cost of about $737 million.

The new generation, storage and transmission assets included in the Monrovia Project will go into the utility’s rate base.

AES says its electric service agreement with Google is designed to ensure the revenues will be sufficient to “reimburse at least 100%” of the project’s incremental direct costs. But the contract itself is heavily redacted, and an estimated $74 million in network upgrades has been explicitly allocated to all customers as a reliability need, prompting criticism from consumer advocates that the arrangement is shifting costs onto other ratepayers.

What are ‘reasonably allocable’ costs?

Indiana state law requires large load customers to reimburse at least 80% of project costs “reasonably allocable” to them.

Claire Wayner, a senior associate at the clean energy nonprofit RMI, said in an interview that while local projects are fairly easy to trace back to a specific data center, broader regional system upgrades raise more complex questions about who benefits and how costs are allocated across jurisdictions.

“Maybe they’re upgrading a part of the grid that they were going to have to upgrade anyway because it’s aging infrastructure,” Wayner said. “If that’s the case, they should have to demonstrate that, and then maybe cross socialization makes sense.”

But, she continued, “If that upgrade was not going to be built without the data center, without benefits modeling or just a demonstration of the benefits to the rest of the zone, it’s difficult to make the claim that all ratepayers in that zone should pay for it.”

AES Indiana will serve Google’s data center from its portfolio of shared generation and battery assets. The new generation and storage assets built to meet the additional demand will be owned through a subsidiary by the utility and go into its rate base.

Keep up with the story. Subscribe to the Utility Dive free daily newsletter

In testimony to the commission, a utility representative said the transmission infrastructure included in the Monrovia Project falls into three basic categories: interconnection infrastructure for the generation and storage; “direct connection” infrastructure for connecting the data center to the system; and network upgrades necessary “primarily” to serve Google “but also to meet other customer demand or energy needs.”

Google will pay about $32 million upfront for the direct connection, but $73.8 million in network upgrades will be included in AES Indiana’s transmission rate base and recovered through future rates from all customers, including residential ones.

Commissioners approved the proposal 5-0, saying in their order that “although the Customer may be the impetus for the network upgrades being made, this does not preclude the upgrades from providing system-wide benefits.”

“Network upgrades, as the name implies, are upgrades or additions to the transmission network intended to provide reliability, resiliency, and stability to the system at large,” it said. “Just as the Customer will be allocated a portion of the existing network transmission infrastructure, it is reasonable for existing customers to also be allocated a portion of the network upgrades.”

The Midcontinent Independent System Operator approved some of the network upgrades, which include a new substation, citing reliability and load growth.

Although the order says the portfolio proposed in AES’ filing is for 390 MW of new load with 460 MW of new 4-hour storage and 130 MW of solar generation, the substation planned for the project is designed for 1,200 MW of load, creating opportunity for future expansion at the site.

Read More in Generation

The generation and storage resources consist of one 200-MW and one 130-MW battery energy storage system, called Foundry Works and Hardy Hills, respectively, as well as a 130-MW solar facility paired with a 130-MW BESS called Crosstrack. Their cost is redacted in the case filings.

‘Cost allocation and cost recovery are two different concepts’

Ben Inskeep, program director at the Citizens Action Coalition, a consumer advocacy group that intervened in the case, sees the deal as running counter to President Donald Trump’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge signed earlier this year by tech companies and utilities, including Google and AES Indiana.

“These network upgrades are specifically driven by the Google data center,” Inskeep told Utility Dive in an interview. “Instead of making the cost causer pay, AES Indiana has decided to spread the costs out to other ratepayers, and our commission has unfortunately approved that.”

Ben Gavelek, a spokesperson for the commission, declined to comment on the deal. Google did not respond to requests for comment.

Claire Rice, a spokesperson for AES Indiana, said in an email that although the transmission assets are being allocated through the normal cost-of-service process, Google’s rate includes a “separate incremental-cost test designed to recover the incremental costs required to serve Google, including the network upgrades.”

“Cost allocation and cost recovery are two different concepts,” she added.

Many of the exact terms of the service agreement, including monthly energy and demand charges and riders, are redacted in the public record. Parts of other contracts underpinning the deal are also confidential.

Read More in Generation

The assets will be included in future base rate case filings. Until those new rates are established, the utility plans to recover those costs through its Environmental Cost Recovery and netted with contract revenues.

The commission’s order says AES Indiana’s accounting and ratemaking proposals enable it to “match” the project costs with revenue collected through Google’s electric service agreement and “flow” those contributions “back to existing and future customers” through riders.

AES says using this arrangement, Google will pay $300 million toward fixed costs through the end of the contract period at the minimum demand level, including 100% of the annual revenue requirement associated with the network upgrades. The utility expects Google to pay approximately $770 million at the expected level of demand.

Company representatives told regulators that its cost allocation framework is not based on “direct cost method” but instead uses a modified “slice of system” approach.

Another point of contention is that the tech giant’s rates will be based on a 90% load factor, which AES says is high compared to all other customers, but critics said amounts to a 10% discount.

The commission’s order said using the 90% estimated load factor “recognizes the Customer’s substantial and continuous utilization of the system capacity without assuming that the Customer’s maximum demand occurs exactly when the system peaks each month.”

Advocates call for legislative reform

Even though the network upgrade costs are not allocated to Google alone, AES Indiana Vice President of Commercial Patrick Maguire said in an interview that revenue from the company will “more than offset” residential customers’ portion.

“Customers’ rates are not impacted by those transmission investments at all,” Maguire said.

State regulators approved a $71 million rate hike for AES customers in June, attracting the ire of Gov. Mike Braun and setting off a chain reaction of turnover at the commission, which voted in September to rehear the case, the Indiana Capital Chronicle reported. The first of two increases has already taken effect, with another scheduled for January, despite the rehearing.

The utility’s next rate case is scheduled for 2029. That is also when AES plans to share a full cost-of-service study, cost allocation and rate design principles associated with the Monrovia Project.

Inskeep said it’s not clear if there will be a net savings for Indiana utility customers from Google’s contract with AES when factoring in other costs, such as congestion pricing, rising labor and equipment costs, new generation and potentially more network upgrades.

“We really do need some legislative reforms to increase transparency and establish better protections for ratepayers,” Inskeep said.

In the meantime, the grid operator is undergoing reforms to address the rapid scale-up of large load data center additions and associated transmission upgrades.

Jonathan Neal, a spokesperson for MISO, said in an email that the grid operator has undertaken an Expedited Project Review and Expedited Resource Addition Study to try and bring generation and transmission online more quickly.

MISO is also “working with our stakeholders” to make improvements around cost transparency, speed to partial power, a non-firm service option and market operations and processes.

Many of these reforms respond directly to concerns noted by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission when it issued Show Cause Orders to six grid operators, including MISO, directing them to overhaul their processes for interconnecting large loads.

Wawa appears to have multiple sites it’s working on in South Carolina. Franklin Daniels, an attorney with the law firm with Maynard Nexsen, speaking for the project, said that the site would be the first or second Wawa in South Carolina.

However, the Council highlighted language in the bill that could benefit fossil fuel, mining, data centers and other industrial projects more than clean energy.

text:
Laura Lundquist

(Missoula Current) Conservationists called for the U.S. senators to postpone a permitting bill that has more negatives than positives when it comes to the environment. But their calls fell on deaf ears.

On Monday afternoon, the U.S. Senate voted 73-25 to begin debate on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA. Debate on the bill - S. 5653 - has yet to be scheduled and some anticipate it won’t happen until after Veterans Day.

It was a disappointment for tribes, environmental groups and other activists who don’t want to exchange more rollbacks of environmental laws and community protections for streamlined infrastructure permitting, even if some of the permits are for clean energy projects.

Minnesota tribal spokesman Dallas Goldtooth said the bill’s title has all the right words - bipartisan, affordability, jobs - but it’s wrong because it removes protections that tribal nations use to protect sacred sites and ancestral lands. The bill minimizes public input before a project is built, and then, it eliminates the ability of communities to challenge harmful projects in court.

“The supporters call it a permitting reform - they say it’s going to help build infrastructure faster. Look, we need infrastructure - clean energy, good paying jobs. But why does development always seem to involve making it harder for communities to protect ourselves?” Goldtooth said in a Nov. 8 social media post. “Republicans and Democrats are pushing this bill, talking about eliminating ‘red tape.’ But what exactly is red tape? I’ve got news for you: Our communities are not red tape. Our rights are not red tape.”

BAAJA proponents say more energy generation and transmission lines are needed to bring down high energy costs. To do that, permitting processes need to be streamlined because it takes too long to build large projects. However, that streamlining would weaken protections of the Clean Water Act and the Endangered Species Act, and eliminate the public participation requirements of the National Environmental Policy Act and tribal consultation under the National Historic Preservation Act.

The fossil-fuel industry backs BAAJA because it could also fast-track permits for more fossil-fuel, mining and data center projects. In a Nov. 8 social media post, President Donald Trump said the legislation could “ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines, and Power Plants faster than ever before.” In a statement Monday, Trump said he wouldn't approve wind turbine projects.

Supporters say the bill has gone through years of negotiation, but after introducing it on Sept. 30, sponsors are trying to push it through Congress before the end of the year. Seeing that Utah Senator Mike Lee is one of the sponsors caused public land supporters to be wary, because Lee has sponsored a number of bills that would eliminate public land. But Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., is also a sponsor, and Heinrich has been a staunch supporter of public land issues.

The Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes asked Montana’s Congressional delegation to vote “No,” partly because the bill hasn’t gone through the normal Congressional process. It wasn’t heard by the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources before being brought to the Senate floor and it was drafted without input from the Senate Committee on Indian Affairs. The CSKT are particularly concerned with potential changes to the Endangered Species Act, Federal Power Act and Clean Water Act, in addition to the National Historic Preservation Act. Neither Daines nor Sheehy have mentioned BAAJA, but both voted Monday to debate the bill.

“This process lacks transparency and is not the way to legislate policy of such magnitude, particularly with respect to the special relationship between Indian Tribes and the United States. A change to any one of these statutes requires careful and thoughtful consideration regarding how the change will impact the environment and cultural resources, as well as the complex framework of federal, state and tribal jurisdiction,” the CSKT said in their Oct. 7 letter.

Several groups have lobbied Heinrich and co-sponsor Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., saying the streamlining goes too far and sponsors should withdraw the bill and start over.

The Natural Resources Defense Council praised the intent of the bill, saying new clean energy projects and better power transmission would aid decarbonization of the power industry and help reduce greenhouse gases. However, the Council highlighted language in the bill that could benefit fossil fuel, mining, data centers and other industrial projects more than clean energy.

“The backdrop, of course, is the Trump administration’s nonstop attacks on clean energy projects, tax incentives for clean energy, and climate standards,” the Council said in a Oct. 26 statement. “The Lawmakers should push for tangible evidence that this has changed before voting on the legislation.”

But not all green groups oppose the bill. The Citizens’ Climate Lobby is focused on reducing greenhouse emissions, so unlike the Natural Resources Defense Council, the Climate Lobby said it has no reservations about the bill because most of the new infrastructure that’s proposed are clean-energy projects so permitting needs to move quickly.

On Monday, Heinrich and Whitehouse announced that they’d listened to the public and had written an amended bill that addressed some of the concerns. But that just added calls for the sponsors to go back to the drawing board, with one social media commenter saying “You can’t fix a bad bill with 494 pages of revisions.”

The National Congress of American Indians issued a statement Monday saying the amendments did little to address tribal concerns about reductions to the National Historic Preservation Act.

“Tinkering with these harmful BAAJA provisions does not resolve their fundamental flaws or the cumulative impact on Tribal cultural heritage from BAAJA and the ACHP rulemaking. Tribal sovereignty, meaningful consultation, and the protection of sacred places are not negotiable,” said the tribes’ letter.

The Montana Wildlife Federation also issued a statement Monday saying it appreciated some aspects of the bill but couldn’t support it in its current form.

“Faster permitting and strong conservation safeguards can go together, yet this package gives up the second to get the first. Its changes … put Montana’s rivers, elk and grizzly bear habitat, and public lands at risk of certain and often irreversible harm. The benefits it promises are not guaranteed, and projects built on rushed review are more likely to be poorly sited and short-lived,” said Frank Szollosi, Executive Director of the Montana Wildlife Federation.

The National Park Conservation Association said that even with the amendments, the bill would “seriously jeopardize” national parks, particularly those established to preserve historic sites or those containing critical wildlife habitat.

The first? Look for the Jaecoo ET (yeah, that’s a boring name, for sure), which is essentially a rebadged Exeed ET—a five-seat, all-electric midsize SUV built on the EOX platform, which underpins all the larger electrified vehicles from Chery Automobiles.

The thing you have to understand is that Exeed is one of Chery’s most popular brands in China. It offers fairly luxurious vehicles, though not quite as luxurious as those under the separate Luxeed brand, whose products are truly breathtaking. Exeed serves the domestic market exclusively, while Exelantix sells basically the same vehicles outside of China.

Confused? Well, Omoda-Jaecoo Canada doesn’t want customers to be, so the Exeed (or Exelantix) ET will be sold as the Jaecoo ET over here, with the vehicle getting minor tweaks and unique design cues such as a front grille featuring vertical openings.

A Midsize SUV

Let’s be honest, the ET isn’t exactly a looker. Styling is generic, and it’s unclear what market segment it belongs to. While bigger than a Ford Mustang Mach-E or a Tesla Model Y, the ET is aimed at the same drivers, only offering more space, luxury and comfort. It shows what the company is capable of in terms of build quality and refinement, so it won’t be perceived as just another cheap Chinese vehicle.

Naturally, the ET will have to prove itself. Standing 5 metres long with a 3-metre wheelbase, it comes standard with all-wheel drive and dual electric motors that deliver a combined output of 473 horsepower. There’s an 800-volt architecture built around a 100kWh battery, which is expected to provide a WLTP-estimated range of approximately 525 km—or about 410 km according to EPA standards. That’s disappointing, just like the ET’s average energy consumption approaching 25 kWh/100 km. Hopefully these preliminary figures will be revised by the time sales begin.

The ET will support DC fast charging up to 290 kW, which is excellent. On the other hand, it misses an NACS connector, settling for a CCS1 port instead. This is something that will be addressed in the coming years, the company assures, but there wasn’t enough time before the Canadian launch scheduled for late winter or early spring.

The good news is that thermal management and battery preconditioning come standard, as well as several Canadian-exclusive features designed to tackle winter and the cold. These include a heated steering wheel, heated side mirrors, heated front and rear seats, a rear camera washer and a radiant-heated windshield. The pop-out door handles have been replaced with more conventional handles that can better withstand ice buildup. The same applies to the charge port door: the original design would have been too flimsy to endure our tough climate conditions.

The interior of the Jaecoo ET further stands out with Nappa leather, a microsuede headliner, attention to detail that eclipses Tesla’s, plus front and rear seats with a massage function. On top of that, it boasts an electrochromic glass roof, a 2,140-watt, 23-speaker audio system and dual displays that incorporate all the technologies and apps Canadians look for, starting with Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.

How Much?

That’s probably the number one question on people’s minds. We believe the Jaecoo ET could start anywhere between $65,000 and $70,000, effectively blurring the line that separates mainstream EVs from their premium counterparts. The combination of luxury and comfort will prove quite attractive for many potential customers, provided that leasing options are competitive. Again, this is something the company is currently working on, in collaboration with J.D. Power and various financial institutions.

title: Indiana Democrats End 14-Year GOP House Supermajority - Capital B Gary
description:
For Democrats, who spent more than a decade powerless and unable to stop anything in the Indiana House, the change is largely a matter of math.
Republicans have held a two-thirds supermajority in the chamber since the 2012 election.
State Rep. Earl Harris Jr., D-East Chicago, whose district includes parts of Gary, said the gains matter beyond the walkout option.
“It’s important that we don’t fail on that.” State Rep. Phil GiaQuinta, who will serve in his fifth term as Indiana House Democratic Leader, echoed Harris’ sentiments.
House Democrats picked up 16 seats, and for the first time in 14 years, House Republicans will not hold a supermajority,” GiaQuinta said in a statement.
text:
Gary’s Democratic lawmakers have spent 14 years in a Statehouse where Republicans could hold sessions, pass bills, and set the agenda without them. Starting in January, that changes.

For Democrats, who spent more than a decade powerless and unable to stop anything in the Indiana House, the change is largely a matter of math.

Last Tuesday’s Election Day results saw Democrats pick up 16 seats, leaving Republicans with a projected 54-46 majority. Republicans have held a two-thirds supermajority in the chamber since the 2012 election. That was enough to reach a quorum and do business with no Democrats in the room. Last session, they enjoyed a 71-29 advantage in the House.

State Rep. Earl Harris Jr., D-East Chicago, whose district includes parts of Gary, said the gains matter beyond the walkout option. Under the old numbers, he said, the occasional Republican who crossed over to vote with a Democrat couldn’t change the outcome.

“If four or five of them broke with their caucus and voted with Democrats, it didn’t mean anything because they still had the votes,” Harris told Capital B Gary. “Well, now that we’re closer, that means something.

“We as Democrats have more negotiation power and ability to work on things because our votes now have more meaning,” he added.

Harris points to projects the Northwest Indiana delegation secured even with Democrats in the super-minority — state money for the Gary/Chicago International Airport, the casino relocation that became Hard Rock Casino Northern Indiana, and the Lake County convention center planned for Gary.

“Hopefully, this will continue to grow things in Gary as well as all Northwest Indiana,” he said.

The Indiana Black Legislative Caucus also has a new chair. Harris said his four years in the role have ended and that state Rep. Carolyn Jackson, D-Hammond, will lead the caucus. Harris said the caucus settled on utilities as its focus for the 2027 session and spoke with constituents about that during its town halls across the state this summer.

Harris said the Aug. 11 derecho and widespread outages that followed have since shaped the type of legislation they will file related to utilities for 2027.

He was less certain about whether Republicans will make a second attempt at mid-decade congressional redistricting after the Indiana Senate rejected a new map last year. Speaker-elect Ben Smaltz, R-Auburn, carried the redistricting bill in the House.

“Before Election Day, with the numbers what they were, I would’ve said definitely yes. Now that the numbers are different, I don’t know,” Harris said. He’s confident, however, that voters’ rejection of the effort was part of the message they sent at the polls. “If they do, then we will fight it again as we did previously.”

The majority that Republicans still hold makes the prospect of redistricting a reality, warns Laura Merrifield Wilson, professor of political science at the University of Indianapolis.

“I would expect the state legislature revisits the redistricting conversation, but with the sober reality for some that the stakes are high and the consequences are serious,” Merrifield Wilson told Capital B Gary.

“Otherwise strong incumbents fell to challengers, well-funded and endorsed with the presidential seal of approval, for seemingly nothing other than their opposition to redistricting off-cycle. They were threatened for that position, and the threat was realized when they lost in the primaries to those challengers,” Merrifield Wilson said. “The stakes are high, and the threats are very real — the reminder of what happened to colleagues is in the not-so-distant past and a warning to those who consider following the same path.”

Harris added that the bigger Democratic caucus now faces a new pressure of its own.

“More of us were elected as a message to say, ‘OK, we’re trusting in you. Do something,’” he said. “It’s important that we don’t fail on that.”

State Rep. Phil GiaQuinta, who will serve in his fifth term as Indiana House Democratic Leader, echoed Harris’ sentiments.

“Hoosiers voted for balance. House Democrats picked up 16 seats, and for the first time in 14 years, House Republicans will not hold a supermajority,” GiaQuinta said in a statement. “I’m proud to welcome our new members to a caucus that now has a real voice at the Statehouse, and I’m grateful to Reps. [Cherrish] Pryor and [Carey] Hamilton for continuing to serve in leadership alongside me.

“We don’t take this moment lightly. Voters didn’t send us here to keep score. They sent us with a clear message: They’re tired of what years of one-party rule have given them. They want groceries, rent, and utility bills they can afford. They want public schools that are fully funded. And they want data centers and Big Tech to pay their fair share of taxes.”

Organization Day, the ceremonial start to the new session, will be Nov. 17.

text:
More than 2,000 new jobs are expected from a new Ohio factory that Honda Motor Co. will build with an investment of about US$3 billion to meet growing US demand for hybrids.

The project, announced by the Japanese carmaker on Monday (9 November), will add capacity for 240,000 vehicles a year.

Honda’s annual North American capacity will consequently reach 1.91 million vehicles, compared with 1.67 million now.

The end of US tax credits for electric vehicles under President Donald Trump’s administration in autumn 2025 was followed by a sharp decline in demand for them.

High fuel prices, meanwhile, have helped increase demand for hybrids, prompting Honda to concentrate more on that market.

Addressing a press conference in Marysville, Ohio, Bob Nelson, executive vice president at American Honda Motor Co., Honda’s US unit, said the factory “will be one of Honda’s most advanced in the world” and “will be built for flexibility”.

The plant, he added, “will have the capability to produce hybrids, gasoline-powered, and battery electric vehicles, giving Honda the ability to adjust our production as customer demand and market conditions change”.

Expected to enter production in 2029, the factory will be located near Honda’s existing East Liberty plant and become its sixth vehicle assembly facility in the United States.

Most of its output is likely to consist of hybrid sport utility vehicles (SUVs).

Honda also intends to introduce 15 new hybrid models worldwide by fiscal 2029.

text:
The costs of keeping Louisiana homes and businesses comfortable can add up quickly. Air conditioners often run for most of the year, while older buildings, insufficient insulation and inefficient equipment can drive electricity consumption even higher.

Entergy is helping residential and business customers address those challenges through programs that identify sources of wasted electricity, recommend practical improvements and provide financial incentives to make upgrades more affordable.

Energy Smart is a longstanding program for Entergy New Orleans customers, while Entergy Solutions is available for Entergy Louisiana customers. Both programs offer customers a free energy assessment, recommendations for efficiencies and connections with certified contractors who can make improvements.

“People often know their energy usage is increasing, but don’t know what to address first. They might know their air conditioner needs cleaning, or an appliance is getting older. They may not necessarily think about insulation and ductwork. Those are all things we can help with,” said Heather LeBlanc, a manager of energy efficiency with Entergy Louisiana. “Our certified energy assessors identify the areas that can benefit most from upgrades and guide the customer toward improvements that will yield the most savings.”

Since launching in New Orleans in 2010, Energy Smart has helped more than 176,600 residential and business customers, awarded more than $86.7 million in incentives and helped the community save more than 569 million kilowatt-hours of electricity. Those are tangible impacts, especially in a city that faces unique energy challenges.

Nate Wolf, Entergy New Orleans energy efficiency project manager, said the city’s infrastructure frequently creates a heat island effect. That means certain areas – particularly ones with dense buildings, little greenspace and minimal tree cover – can be 8 to 10 degrees hotter at times. Meanwhile, building codes have evolved significantly, leaving many older homes without the modern standards required to drive energy savings.

Energy Smart addresses these challenges with solutions tailored to the local climate and housing stock.

“Once the assessment is complete, we send recommendations to area contractors who meet our program criteria. They have gone through our vetting process and are our on-the-ground experts,” Wolf said. “Beyond making efficiency improvements, they are trained to look for potential health and safety issues. For example, they won’t do anything that exacerbates other problems, such as moisture or mold.”

Energy Smart, created by the New Orleans City Council and administered by Entergy New Orleans, is inclusive by design, and all Entergy New Orleans residential, commercial and industrial electric customers are eligible to participate, regardless of income. All customers can receive cash incentives and rebates to cover significant portions of upgrade costs. Customers with household incomes at or below 80 percent of the Area Median Income can access additional benefits.

Common Energy Smart upgrades include smart thermostats, power strips, energy-efficient air conditioners, ENERGY STAR-certified appliances, attic insulation and air sealing.

“I think there’s still sometimes a misperception that not everyone can participate in Energy Smart, but it is open to everybody,” Wolf said. “Energy affordability is at the heart of what we do. We know rising costs are a real burden. That’s why we want to help all customers reduce their energy consumption and thus lower their monthly energy bills.”

On the commercial side, Wolf said Energy Smart has helped entities from small businesses to large industrial facilities. Businesses receive a free comprehensive assessment, and can receive cash incentives for upgrading HVAC systems, lighting, refrigeration and other equipment.

“We can do prescriptive improvements, or custom improvements based on the specifications of each building or system,” Wolf said. “There can be huge savings to business owners, depending on the size and scope of their facility.”

Entergy Solutions offers energy-saving opportunities for Entergy Louisiana customers, including homeowners, renters and businesses. Following a detailed assessment, customers can receive financial discounts and incentives for upgrades such as air conditioner tuneups, air sealing, duct sealing, improved insulation and smart thermostats.

“A lot of residential customers get the most savings from AC tuneups and duct sealings,” LeBlanc said. “In a lot of homes, we find little to no attic insulation, or holes or leaks in the ductwork. We also do a lot of high efficiency AC tune-ups that cleans the outside and inside units. South Louisiana temperatures mean that ACs can run daily for more than half of the year. That makes it important to keep those units clean and in top condition.”

LeBlanc said Entergy Solutions contractors are fully vetted and trained to prioritize improvements that will make the most impact. They also offer recommendations on everyday habits that can improve efficiency, such as setting the thermostat higher when a building or home is empty, closing blinds, turning off lights and fans when possible, unplugging items that aren’t in use and cleaning appliance vents and filters regularly.

“Once the Entergy Solutions upgrades are made, the savings are almost immediate if a customer is paying a monthly bill. If they are on Level Billing, it may take a little more time because a customer’s bill is based on their rolling twelve-month billing average,” LeBlanc said.

Over the last 11 years, Entergy Louisiana has given back over $65.5 million in customer incentives for energy efficiency upgrades in customers’ homes and businesses. These upgrades have an estimated 1,338,742 GWh of lifetime savings. The Entergy Solutions program has an additional $100 million in customer incentives available for customers to apply for over the next four years.

Through myEntergy and the Entergy mobile app, customers can access billing information, review energy usage and explore payment options. LeBlanc said monitoring that data can help customers see the impact of energy efficiency measures. Customers with advanced meters can access usage information through their online accounts or the Entergy mobile app.

“It’s important to watch that kilowatt-hour usage each month to see how it fluctuates, especially in conjunction with your billing,” she said.

In New Orleans, Wolf said a new program helps customers compare their energy usage to homes that are similar in size, age and location.

“That gives people some context and insights,” he said. “We’re always looking for opportunities to help customers gain more information and take more steps toward efficiency.”

Entergy New Orleans customers can learn more about Energy Smart at EnergySmartNOLA.info or call 504-229-6868.

Entergy Louisiana customers can visit EntergyLouisiana.com/EnergyEfficiency, call Entergy Solutions at 844-829-1300 or email entergysolutionsla@entergy.com for information about available assessments, incentives and energy-saving services.

text:
Industrial equipment manufacturer Alfa Laval is expanding the use of low-carbon steel in its heat exchangers, moving beyond early prototypes toward commercial applications. The effort is part of its Concept Zero initiative, which aims to develop a heat exchanger with no embedded fossil carbon emissions by 2030.

The initiative focuses on emissions generated before equipment reaches customers, including those associated with raw materials and manufacturing. Steel is a particular concern, with production responsible for approximately 7% of global carbon emissions.

For industrial buyers, the development raises questions about how equipment manufacturers can reduce embodied carbon while maintaining performance, managing material costs, and providing reliable emissions data across their supply chains.

Low-Carbon Steel Moves Into Commercial Applications

Alfa Laval's work with Swedish steel producer SSAB began in 2022, when the companies developed a heat exchanger incorporating fossil-free steel. A subsequent prototype used SSAB Fossil-free steel in the frame and pressure plate of a gasketed plate heat exchanger, providing an early demonstration of how alternative materials could be integrated into industrial equipment.

The partnership has since expanded into customer installations. At the European Spallation Source (ESS) in Lund, Sweden, Alfa Laval is supplying heat exchangers incorporating low-emission steel from SSAB. The equipment will help recover surplus heat from the research facility for use in Lund's district heating network.

The ESS installation addresses two different sources of environmental impact. Lower-emission materials can reduce the carbon footprint associated with equipment production, while heat recovery allows energy that would otherwise be lost to serve local heating demand.

Alfa Laval is also introducing low-CO2-emission steel into its T21 plate heat exchanger, an established commercial product. Integrating alternative materials into existing equipment lines represents a different challenge from building prototypes, particularly when manufacturers must maintain established technical specifications and production volumes.

Another application involves EcoDataCenter, which is deploying Alfa Laval heat exchangers manufactured with SSAB Zero steel. The material is produced from recycled steel using a process that, according to SSAB, does not generate new fossil CO2 emissions during steelmaking.

For data center operators, the collaboration highlights the role of equipment procurement in reducing emissions associated with infrastructure development. Heat exchangers are used throughout cooling and thermal management systems, making their material composition relevant to assessments of embodied carbon.

Concept Zero Targets Manufacturing Emissions by 2030

Alfa Laval's Concept Zero program extends beyond substituting conventional steel with lower-emission alternatives. Its longer-term objective is to eliminate embedded fossil carbon emissions from heat exchanger production by 2030, requiring changes across materials sourcing, component manufacturing, and supplier operations.

Achieving that target will depend on developments outside Alfa Laval's direct control. The availability of fossil-free steel, expansion of low-emission manufacturing capacity, and improvements in other industrial materials will influence how quickly the company can scale its approach.

The distinction between lower-carbon steel and a finished product with no embedded fossil carbon emissions is important. Even when steelmaking processes eliminate new fossil CO2 emissions, upstream material processing, transportation, other components, and assembly operations may still contribute to the equipment's overall carbon footprint.

That distinction also matters for customers evaluating supplier emissions claims. Verified product carbon footprints and consistent lifecycle assessment methods can help procurement teams compare equipment options and determine whether material substitutions deliver meaningful reductions in Scope 3 emissions.

For Alfa Laval, the next challenge will be demonstrating how improvements in individual components translate into measurable reductions across complete heat exchangers. Scaling those changes across commercial product lines will require reliable material supplies, manufacturing adjustments, and documentation of emissions performance.

The broader implications extend to industrial equipment procurement. As manufacturers work to address emissions embedded in machinery and infrastructure, buyers may increasingly evaluate equipment based on both operational efficiency and the emissions associated with its production.

description:
As its first major activation, Yes/Detroit is launching a global innovation challenge to identify and deploy technologies that can make the infrastructure people rely on in Detroit every day more affordable, reliable, safe, and sustainable.
Yes/Detroit, led by Michigan Central in collaboration with Amazon Web Services (AWS), Cisco, Deloitte, and Oracle, is a local initiative of Yes/Cities, a global programme of the World Economic Forum.
About Michigan Central Michigan Central is a 30-acre technology and cultural hub in Detroit, where leaders, thinkers, communities and creators come together to accelerate bold ideas and technologies that shape our collective future.
By providing access to world-class infrastructure, tools, and resources, Michigan Central inspires innovators and community members to collaborate on real, ground-breaking solutions to global problems.
Since opening in April 2023, Michigan Central has grown into a diverse ecosystem of nearly 250 companies and startups working at the intersection of mobility, technology and society.
text:
Share this article:

Amazon Web Services, Cisco, Deloitte, Michigan Central, Oracle, World Economic Forum, and more than two dozen local organizations collaborate to launch Yes/Detroit

DETROIT, Nov. 10, 2026 – Today, Yes/Detroit officially launched as part of the World Economic Forum’s global Yes/Cities initiative, becoming the fourth city after Boston, USA, San Francisco, USA, and Bengaluru, India. As its first major activation, Yes/Detroit is launching a global innovation challenge to identify and deploy technologies that can make the infrastructure people rely on in Detroit every day more affordable, reliable, safe, and sustainable.

Yes/Detroit, led by Michigan Central in collaboration with Amazon Web Services (AWS), Cisco, Deloitte, and Oracle, is a local initiative of Yes/Cities, a global programme of the World Economic Forum. The initiative also works in close collaboration with the City of Detroit and the State of Michigan and more than two dozen local organizations. The initiative’s inaugural innovation challenge will attract startups from around the country and world to Detroit to address four areas of resilient urban infrastructure: housing and the built environment, transportation and mobility, energy and the grid, and water and waste systems. Selected innovators will have the opportunity to deploy their solutions in Detroit, drawing on the region’s longstanding manufacturing strengths and real-world testing capabilities.

“Detroit has always been a city of builders and problem-solvers, and today we’re inviting innovators from around the world to build with us. Like many older cities, Detroit faces real infrastructure challenges, and we look forward to seeing which solutions can be tested here and make a difference for our residents and neighborhoods,” said Mayor Mary Sheffield. “To the innovative thinkers, we are making Detroit a great place in the country to start, grow, and scale a business or idea.”

“At Michigan Central, we’ve built an ecosystem that brings together entrepreneurs, industry, and community around Detroit’s long history of making and problem-solving,” said Awenate Cobbina, CEO of Michigan Central. “Yes/Detroit gives us an opportunity to bring those strengths to some of the challenges cities face every day. By helping develop solutions that work here in Detroit, we can make an impact locally while creating models that can be applied in communities far beyond our city.”

“Lasting impact happens when industries and cities connect policy, investment and innovation to local priorities,” said Ramya Krishnaswamy, Senior Director, Centre for Experience Economy and Cities at the World Economic Forum. “Detroit helped build the last century on manufacturing and Yes/Detroit is how it builds the next one — through innovation and resilient infrastructure.”

“At AWS, we believe technology should be a powerful equalizer, and through our work with Yes/Detroit, we’re putting the power of cloud innovation directly into the hands of social enterprises, community leaders and individuals who are driving Detroit’s future forward,” said Kat Esser, Head of Global Impact Accelerators at Amazon Web Services.

Detroit built machines and methods that helped shape the modern world, and it remains a center of industrial innovation. The metropolitan region is number one in the United States for deployed industrial robots, home to 96 of the top 100 global automotive suppliers, and ranks in the top ten nationally for AI and machine learning patents. Michigan Central partnered with Newlab, a global commercialization platform for critical technology startups, to provide the physical foundation needed to take Yes/Detroit’s urban infrastructure challenge from idea to real-world application. Selected cohort innovators gain direct access to a state-of-the-art prototyping facility and specialized fabrication shops.

Detroit also faces a challenge shared by many older cities: it was built to serve two million people, with a current population of 700,000. As the city’s population has decreased, the deficit in tax revenue isn’t able to cover the maintenance and modernization of the city’s infrastructure. In February 2025, a water main installed in the 1930s burst in Southwest Detroit, flooding hundreds of homes. Together, Detroit’s industrial strengths and its infrastructure needs make it a proving ground for solutions with relevance for cities facing similar challenges around the world.

“Detroit has an amazing ecosystem of organizations, assets, and talent,” said David Parent, Deloitte’s Michigan Managing Principal. “Deloitte is pleased to be part of this collaborative effort to mobilize these resources to promote innovation and advance growth for our region.”

2026 Innovation Challenge: Building Resilient Urban Infrastructure

The Yes/Detroit Innovation Challenge is seeking early-stage innovators applying novel technologies including robotics, autonomy, sensing, simulation, and connected systems. Innovators should have the potential to deploy in Detroit within 18 months. They will also be evaluated on how their solutions can support Detroit workers, including through new or retained jobs, transferable skills and training pathways, safer work, or increased productivity.

Selected startups will participate in an 18-month program led by Michigan Central designed to support deployment and commercialization in Detroit, including opportunities for funding, introductions to corporate collaborators and mentors, community organizations, and policymakers, as well as access to physical AI infrastructure, Newlab’s member ecosystem, and other benefits. Select participants will also have access to the World Economic Forum’s Yes/Cities Innovator Programme, providing additional visibility, connections, and resources to support growth beyond Detroit.

“The path from a successful pilot to broader adoption can be challenging for an emerging company to navigate,” said Dounia Senawi, US Chief Commercial Officer, Deloitte. “Yes/Detroit connects innovators with collaborators, testing opportunities, and local expertise to help them solve real infrastructure challenges here—and help build a platform to grow their businesses and scale those solutions to communities across the country and around the world.”

Yes/Detroit builds on Michigan’s broader push to help new companies start, scale, and stay in the state, including investments in emerging sectors such as advanced mobility and autonomous systems, as well as the statewide Innovation Alliance of more than 100 partners launched earlier this year.

Yes/Detroit is supported by a growing coalition of more than two dozen organizations spanning the public, private, nonprofit, and philanthropic sectors. The full list can be found on the challenge website here.

Applications are now open and due by December 22, 2026, with a cohort announcement planned for March 2027.

Akinlana Abdalla worked for years inside a sprawling Milwaukee factory repairing generators for onshore wind turbines. Ingeteam, a Spanish manufacturer, opened the plant in 2011 to serve America’s clean energy industries, fixing and producing equipment from its industrial site between the Milwaukee Brewers baseball stadium and the shores of Lake Michigan.

As Ingeteam was settling into Wisconsin’s largest city, a new industry was emerging off the country’s eastern coast. Big energy firms, utilities, and state and federal officials were preparing to build the first U.S. offshore wind farms to provide power for the region’s densely populated and land-constrained communities. Since American companies didn’t yet make key turbine parts, most of those pieces would come from Europe.

This seemed like a promising new opportunity for workers like Abdalla, who is now a business representative for the factory’s union shop, the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers Local 2150.

Offshore wind developers needed domestically made generators, turbine towers, steel foundations, and other equipment to help drive down their high construction costs and reduce project timelines. Building up a substantial U.S. supply chain was expected to require nearly $23 billion in investment by 2030 to meet rising demand for components, port infrastructure, and specialized vessels.

By late 2022, Ingeteam’s Wisconsin plant was gearing up to produce more onshore turbine generators — the machines that convert the energy harnessed by propeller-like blades into electricity — partly thanks to federal incentives under the Inflation Reduction Act passed that August. ​“There’s this hunger right now to make Milwaukee the capital of the renewable energy revolution,” Garan Chivinski, a former Ingeteam human resources manager, told BizTimes Milwaukee that fall.

The company and union representatives began having early-stage discussions in spring 2024 about making offshore generators as well, Abdalla said. This was before Donald Trump was elected that November, when the U.S. was projected to build 39 gigawatts of offshore wind by 2035, according to BloombergNEF. (Around 0.3 GW of capacity was online nationwide at the end of 2024.)

“We were going into this whole new boom, like this could really take off,” recalled James Meyer, the business manager of IBEW Local 2150, which has some 6,300 members in Wisconsin and in Upper Michigan.

But the anticipated boom never arrived.

Instead, offshore wind has floundered in recent years. Economic headwinds and Trump’s political attacks have vaporized the project pipeline and scrambled plans for a supply chain renaissance, setting the industry back by perhaps a decade, experts say. Today, manufacturers that aimed to serve offshore wind have pivoted to other markets or tabled their ambitions. This means that future installations, should the industry make a comeback, will take longer and cost more to complete.

And talks of moving into offshore wind manufacturing fizzled out in Milwaukee, according to Abdalla and Meyer, who spoke in a joint interview from the union’s office in Menomonee Falls. (Ingeteam, for its part, says it never planned to manufacture offshore wind generators at the site.) In January 2025, the company also began cutting jobs from its onshore wind team owing to ​“market-related factors,” an Ingeteam spokesperson said.

“We had a double-edged sword there of losing onshore and offshore [wind],” Meyer said. ​“To get it taken away was really disheartening for the community.”

When hope met headwinds

America built its first commercial offshore wind farm, the 30-megawatt Block Island, in 2016 off the coast of Rhode Island.

But momentum truly picked up after President Joe Biden took office in 2021 and called for a massive offshore wind buildout to meet the nation’s decarbonization goals and to accelerate clean energy manufacturing. His administration started leasing huge tracts of federal waters for development in the Atlantic and Pacific oceans and in the Gulf of Mexico. The Inflation Reduction Act also created tax credits that offset up to 30% of project costs.

In recent years, developers have completed — or are nearly finished building — six utility-scale installations in swaths of ocean from Massachusetts down to Virginia. Together, they represent nearly 6 GW of clean energy capacity, enough to power millions of homes.

Those projects enlisted hundreds of companies spanning 40 states that have fulfilled or are fulfilling supply contracts, according to the trade group Oceantic Network.

It was during this initial wave of optimism that Gulf Wind Technology (GWT) opened for business in Avondale, Louisiana. In early 2022, the company built a facility as long as a football field near the banks of the Mississippi River, where it performed advanced testing on giant wind-turbine blades. The goal was to help energy firms develop turbine rotors that were capable of generating enough power to make wind projects in the Gulf commercially viable.

“If you can only sell the electron produced from the turbine at a certain price, then everything has to be designed and built around that price,” explained James Martin, the firm’s co-founder and CEO.

GWT found partners in oil and gas giant Shell and the Germany energy firm RWE, both of which were considering developing projects in the hurricane-prone region. In 2023, RWE won a federal auction for a swath of water off the coast of Lake Charles, Louisiana, with the potential to host 1.24 GW of capacity.

Other Louisiana firms also went to work for offshore wind. Edison Chouest built two $100 million specialized vessels along with tugs and barges at Gulf Coast shipyards to serve East Coast projects. Keystone Engineering designed and built lattice-like steel foundations for Block Island.

State officials and policymakers ​“were outwardly bullish about the offshore wind industry and ready for that to play a role in diversifying, especially, the offshore oil and gas sector,” said Katharine Kollins, president of the nonprofit Southeastern Wind Coalition.

Yet it wasn’t long before Martin saw trouble brewing in the fledgling market.

Rising inflation, high interest rates, and supply chain disruptions — spurred by the Covid pandemic and Russia’s war in Ukraine — were undercutting his customers’ business cases for developing in the Gulf. In 2023, developers canceled a quarter of East Coast projects under contract. Siemens Gamesa ​“discontinued” a $200 million initiative to build the nation’s first offshore wind turbine blade facility at the Port of Virginia. In New Jersey, EEW American Offshore Structures lost a key customer for its steel-turbine foundations that year, leading to the manufacturer’s bankruptcy filing last April.

Still, industry experts described these setbacks as temporary pain, not an existential threat. Then Trump began his second term in January 2025 with a laser-focused mission of gutting offshore wind development.

Last year, the administration issued multiple stop-work orders to projects under construction. Federal judges allowed work to continue, but not before developers had lost huge sums of money and nearly missed key deadlines. The Interior Department is now seeking to reevaluate federal approvals for planned offshore wind farms and even Revolution Wind, which fully came online in October.

The department has also taken the unprecedented step of paying private energy companies to abandon their offshore wind leases, including RWE, which received $1.22 billion to give up its leases off the coasts of Louisiana, California, and New York. Eight eastern states and California are suing to block the Trump administration’s agreements with RWE and other developers.

In Avondale, GWT’s offshore wind opportunities have vanished. But the company has managed to pivot, Martin said. It is using the same wind-testing and engineering equipment to analyze large satellite dishes, drones, and other defense and aerospace applications. GWT’s onshore wind business is growing, and it also operates in Brazil, Canada, the Dominican Republic, and England — places where some of the firm’s engineers have moved in order to keep working in offshore wind.

“Our market has been taken away, but the incentive to manufacture domestically and supply the [other] emerging industries is high,” Martin said. ​“We’re willing to be agile and diversify, and that’s keeping our profitability.”

Offshore wind’s murky, costly future

Other manufacturing firms and hubs have also found opportunities beyond the domestic offshore wind market.

At the Sparrows Point shipyard in Maryland, the developer US Wind planned to open a steel manufacturing plant to make parts for offshore wind turbines. But in October, the company turned over its lease to Anduril Industries, which is slated to make steel components for nuclear submarines.

Down the Atlantic coast, in South Carolina, Nexans invested heavily to transform its power-cable facility near Charleston into a factory for high-voltage subsea cables, which opened in 2021. The subsea wires carry the electricity produced by wind turbines to an offshore substation, then run for miles along the seafloor to reach onshore substations.

Nexans, a global industrial firm based in Paris, has supplied and installed cables for most of the major U.S. offshore wind farms, including the completed South Fork Wind and Revolution Wind and the in-progress Sunrise Wind and Empire Wind. The Charleston plant employs over 200 people, who are still making subsea cables — only now for offshore wind projects in Europe, said Pascal Radue, executive vice president for Nexans’ power transmission division.

“We built up quite a skilled workforce there,” Radue said, ​“and we have every intention to maintain the maximum possible load at that plant, even without having any [new] U.S. offshore wind projects.” He added that the company remains committed to serving the American market, should it rematerialize.

India-based JSW Steel invested hundreds of millions of dollars in recent years to expand its steel mills in Mingo Junction, Ohio, and Baytown, Texas, in order to produce high-grade plates for offshore wind infrastructure. When recently asked about the buildout, a spokesperson said the company’s investments ​“are built to serve many markets, including infrastructure, energy, pipe, and wind. That agility lets us grow with our customers wherever demand is strongest.”

While the firms’ ability to pivot is good news for their workers and local economies, the Trump administration’s maneuvers have ultimately redirected resources and expertise away from the emerging offshore wind supply chain. That will make it far harder for the industry to gear back up, even long after Trump’s presidency ends in January 2029.

“There has been long-term damage done to the U.S. reputation,” said Harrison Sholler, a wind analyst at the consultancy BloombergNEF. ​“No investor or banker worth their salt is going to be moving forward with an offshore wind project right now, even if a more favorable executive administration were to come into power.”

Given that offshore wind farms can take nearly a decade to build, he doesn’t expect any additional offshore wind projects to come online by 2035 without major policy changes. ​“Now that developers see the U.S. as a market with potential political risk, it’s going to take a lot to change their minds,” Sholler said.

The U.S. is staring down an electricity supply crunch as the demand from data centers, electric vehicles, and home electrification continues to climb — and as extreme weather events increase the need for ample and reliable power supplies. California and eastern states have no clear path to hit their ambitious decarbonization goals unless they add gigawatts of wind power off their coasts. Only now, building all that clean power will take even longer to do, potentially translating into higher costs for consumers.

Back in Milwaukee, Abdalla, the union leader and former Ingeteam worker, said that Trump’s hostility to wind and the broader misinformation about renewables doesn’t change those market realities.

“We have to diversify our power generation portfolio,” he said, a fact that ​“is not going to change.” As for the union’s workforce, he added, ​“We’ll be here. We’re trained to do it.”

text:
Honda plans to invest $3 billion to build a new vehicle assembly plant in Ohio, according to an announcement. The automaker said the new plant, which will be located near its other facilities in Marysville, Ohio, is expected to begin production in 2029. It will have an annual production capacity of 240,000 vehicles and create more than 2,000 jobs.

The facility is expected to produce vehicles powered by traditional internal combustion engines, as well as all-electric and hybrid models, which have been growing in popularity in the U.S.

The plant is expected to increase Honda’s U.S. light-duty vehicle production capacity to 1.3 million units annually. The company currently operates 12 manufacturing plants in the United States, eight of which produce engines or light-duty vehicles.

“This is not simply an investment in another plant. It is an investment in the future of Honda manufacturing in America,” Bob Nelson, executive vice president of American Honda Motor, said during the announcement at the company’s U.S. heritage center in Ohio.

READ: Meta enters nuclear power deals with three companies (January 9, 2026)

The auto industry has been looking to localize production as President Donald Trump’s tariffs and rising logistics costs put pressure on profit margins.

Nelson told CNBC after the event that tariffs were affecting the company’s business, but said the new plant was primarily driven by Honda’s ambitions to expand its U.S. operations.

“Tariffs are an impact to us, even with the high localization rate that we have,” he said. “But the real impact is that we have customers out there wanting Honda product and we can’t give it to them. That’s the real area.”

Nelson said Honda did not work with the Trump administration ahead of Monday’s announcement.

The announcement follows German automaker Audi’s plans to invest $4.2 billion in its first U.S. vehicle assembly plant in Georgia. The facility is expected to produce 200,000 SUVs annually and create approximately 4,500 jobs. Trump announced the investment at a campaign rally in Perry, Georgia, on Oct. 24. The proposed factory will be located near Macon and is expected to manufacture some of Audi’s largest and most premium sport utility vehicles for the North American market.

Honda’s new facility will be the company’s first new mass-production vehicle assembly plant in the U.S. since it opened a facility in Indiana in 2008. The automaker also opened a $70 million performance vehicle facility in 2016 and a multibillion-dollar joint-venture battery plant earlier this year, both in Ohio.

The latest investment comes after Honda indefinitely suspended an $11 billion plan in May to produce all-electric vehicles and batteries in Canada. It also canceled three planned EV models for the U.S. market.

READ: Apple pledges another $100 billion investment in US manufacturing (August 7, 2025)

Jennifer Thomas, senior vice president of corporate affairs at American Honda Motor Co., said the company needs to expand domestic production to remain competitive.

“In order to be competitive in this market, you’re going to need to build products here. We are focused on trying to maximize the existing capacity that we have, but we are at capacity, and so we’re exploring all options,” she said.

Thomas also warned that the automotive industry faces a “catastrophic” scenario if the U.S. and Canada fail to reach a new trade agreement by the end of this year. Trump has threatened to double tariffs on Canadian vehicles and parts from 25% to 50% on Jan. 1 if the two countries do not reach a deal.

Honda said it has built more than 33 million vehicles and more than 39 million engines in the U.S. since beginning automobile production in the country in 1982. The company employs more than 30,000 people in the U.S.

authors: Mark Trahant, Levi Rickert, Native News Online Staff, Aaron Payment
