text:
Guest Opinion

There’s a story about Napoleon Bonaparte I have always liked. Something along the lines of “I know he’s a good general, but is he lucky.” Lucky. So often in my career I have been in the exact right place at the right time, being at places where I didn’t plan. Lucky.

Last week I was honored with a Rural Power award by Groundswell and its Rural Renaissance Roadshow. Kenrick J. Escalanti, Quechan, nominated me for this honor to “recognize individuals whose leadership, ideas, storytelling, and service are helping shape a stronger and more equitable future for rural communities.” Instead of a mail-order plaque, the group gifted me a unique embroidered jean jacket to wear proclaiming “Rural Power.” Way cool.

To read more articles by Mark Trahant, go to: Marktrahant.substack.com

Here’s the lucky part. I have been thinking a lot about the debate going on in tribal and rural communities about data centers. It’s absolutely fine for tribes to pause or just say no. But could there also be a deeper conversation, what do we need when it comes to data storage, AI, and a digital future? Where is the richer conversation?

Turns out that was the theme of the conference: “At the Data Center Crossroads.”

The awards’ panel was first evening of the conference; a start of the conversation. And one of the first questions from the audience asked where I stood on data centers. I jumped right into the deep end.

Two things. First, we need a better conversation about data centers and where they should be located. And, second, no elected official should ever sign a Non Disclosure Agreement. I think that runs counter to the public good. Transparency is an important value and the lack of it is exactly why we are having a terrible conversation about what’s needed and why.

Data Centers at scale

“What is a data center and what do people know?” asks Sherry Stout, program manager for the National Laboratory of the Rockies. She works with state and tribal governments.

“So first and foremost, 38% of people statistically in this room, you live within five miles of a data center and you just might not know it,” she says.

“If you ask what national polls say 35% of people would say that they have heard —quote — a lot about data centers in this past year. And why is that? … there’s 632 local governments have taken up the issue of data centers this year alone.

It’s these very conversations that are so twisted. Data centers are pitched as inevitable on private and public land and many of the people involved won’t answer questions because they’ve signed those NDAs.

Sherry Stout:

“People are encountering news stories. They’re encountering political processes. They’re encountering social media that’s all about data centers. We’re seeing states that have paused large scale data centers and we’re seeing moratorium that are placed to say we need to pause and figure out what are these things? How are they affecting us and how do we need to go forward? There’s also, let’s just talk about the reality. There are a few very visible, very poorly done examples of data centers and those are going to drive conversations like it or not. NDAs are becoming a greater and greater issue. I spent a lot of last week with some of the hyperscalers talking about the issue of NDAs and it used to be in business that NDAs would actually speed things along because you would have some of that non-compete. But now the second a community finds out that their council has an NDA with a hyperscaler, that has changed the conversation and transparency is really changing. How we think about data transparency and what’s going on is really changing. Then there’s also just some of the reality of there’s a huge worldwide debate right now on the future of artificial intelligence or super intelligence if you work in the federal world. Data centers often can be the face, the physical manifestation of that conversation.”

Billions, not millions

Pearl Eva Walker is a member of the Memphis City Council where a huge generative A-I data center, Colossus, was built by Space X — Elon Musk —for Grok and is now leases computer capacity to Anthropic. Walker said the bill for that lease is $1.5 billion per month. (Soon to be Colossus 2 and Colossus 3.)

More than 7,500 construction workers are building the facilities. That number of workers has caused significant impact to the communities in Memphis, including those across the line in Mississippi that don’t get the same benefits.

“… God didn’t create data centers and they are not all good,” Walker said. “How do they become better? Hopefully all good. That’s up to us.”

When all this started there were not many community rules in place. So the community had to develop legislation as the data centers were under construction while learning about the impacts as (or after) they happened. That leaves few paths forward for to protect the public.

“What do municipalities need to know? If you’re thinking that a data center could come to your city or town, you need to check on the legislation that you have first concerning data centers,” she said.

That means a comprehensive legislative plan that outlines what companies have to do and how to hold them accountable.

Council Member Walker:

“We’ve been accused of signing NDAs. I have not signed an NDA. I have not been asked to sign an NDA. Why? Because they didn’t need us for anything. Why not? Because we didn’t have any guardrails and moratoriums or anything that kept them from coming in. And then on the other side, there were entities such as the chamber that helped them come into the city and maneuver certain spaces and circumstances. But you want to start with the zoning because they can’t do anything without a parcel. So keep that in mind. The Paul Laurie location, it’s been zoned for commercial industrial since the 1950s. And we are in the process of doing some rezoning for the entire city already. And it will include zoning specific to data centers. That is very important because that’s going to guide your municipality, your leadership, the business community, how they maneuver this space.”

A couple of lessons from Memphis: Be clear about the rules. And have in place a funding mechanism for community benefits, money that can be directed to improve the quality of life for people in the region. Tennessee law, for example, doesn’t allow a city to take money directly from a company for such activities.

Remember that the infrastructure problems will be greater than most people think. Imagine the impact of a “temporary” work force of 7,500 people.

“So when you use the word infrastructure as it relates to these data centers, you’re thinking about infrastructure build out,” she says. “They say 7,500 employees, people who are just in town for the project. Most of them at one time, not necessarily all of them at one time. So with that, we have their vehicles. We have the charter buses. So what they have set up around the area where there’s a mall, a shopping center, a grocery store, a movie theater, they are leasing parking lots around residential neighborhoods.”

That includes traffic, accidents, and rows of motor coaches lined up to take people to specific sites.

In that area of the city there’s a school that attracts students from across the city and region — and now student schedules are impacted because the traffic makes their commutes so much worse.

Council Member Walker:

“In between Colossus two and the middle school is a graveyard. You can hear, ladies talk about the noise. You can hear the humming from the football field at the school. It’s just that close. And the traffic, a lot of this is residential. We have churches, businesses, things like that. And so people have had to adjust their lives. They have had to adjust their lives. The time they leave to go to work, the time that they leave to take the children to school. And this particular school is something that we call an optional school. And optional schools, they have special curriculums and there’s a process to get your child in. Well, optional schools bring in people from all over the city, which means this is not an area where children can just get up and walk to school.

“So we have the extra traffic because people are coming from all over the city because of the type of school that it is. And then you have churches over there. And so what is my point? It’s a whole lot of traffic y’all that’s not being reported on and we’re just, it’s I guess assumed that we should make adjustments for that. But these are the kind of questions that you want to ask ahead of time.”

None of this makes me want to have a data center built near where I live. But at the same time, Council Member Walker said not all companies are doing this the same way.

This is whythe rules are so important, and include any community priorities that should be enforced.

For example the power requirements of data centers are enormous. But what if a regional power plan could include upgrading and paying for a smarter energy plan for the region, a shopping list that might include cheaper power for all, plus the weatherization of homes in the area to make them more efficient? Again, think of the scale, if a computer-time lease pays $1.5 billion per month, what would it be worth make the project’s neighbors whole by paying for all homes to be more energy efficient? (Saving power and money.) The cost of doing business as part of the answer.

Community sound ordinance also need to be re-drafted. Instead of just focusing on loudness — decibels — there must be attention paid to the impact of low frequency rumbling. Perhaps more strict set-back regulations.

We also know that data center operators take advantage of the jurisdictional maze; tribal, city, county and states all have different regulatory frameworks and companies should not profit from that.

And the federal government pretty much builds data centers without asking any community for permission. Last year, for example, the Idaho National Laboratory announced it plan to “develop cutting-edge AI data center and energy generation projects. This selection is a next step in the Trump administration’s goals of utilizing Federal lands to lower energy costs and help power the global AI race.” Cutting-edge, in this context, is building mini-nuclear plants to power data centers. (I live about 40 miles from that one.)

Private data centers have their own way around state or tribal rules.

At Colossus 2, the gas burns in Mississippi and generates electricity for Tennessee. Those gas turbines were installed under a Mississippi law that allows portable equipment to operate for up to a year without air permits. (The basis of at least one lawsuit.) By July the plant had a capacity of about 1,775 megawatts, rivaling the state’s largest power plants—and enough to electrify more than 1.4 million homes.

Beyond playing one state against another, there is the issue of how to transmit electricity across an aging grid. That’s a problem that tribes can help solve (even without data centers). Most of the power lines that cross reservations will need major upgrades because more electricity is being used everywhere. So instead of just rewriting the lease, why not rebuild the lines as a tribally-owned transmission line?

That was the story in Southern California with the Morongo Band of Mission Indians.

From my 2021 piece in ICT:

“The tribe had the corridor and created Morongo Transmission, LLC., to invest some $400 million or up to 50 percent of the project. That’s all been approved by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission.

“The deal will be “hugely profitable” for the tribe but will not cost the utility’s ratepayers any more than it would have cost without the tribe’s involvement. Because of the way utilities are structured, the very right to invest in a project is valuable.

“Thus Morongo Transmission gets the same revenue that Edison would have received and will earn a profit based on a formula. And Edison saved money in the deal because it did not have to pay as much as $500 million for the right of way (since it does not own the lines, the tribe does).”

We think of data centers as only Artificial Intelligence — and that’s been a big part of the rush to build. But data (and energy) are growing faster than our ability to plan.

There’s also the we. We want our phones (creating and storying more data than what was in a data center just a few years ago). Our social media. Our online bill paying. And so now our world is full of ones and zeroes.

Take health care. A few weeks ago I went into a dental surgeon for some work on my teeth. I could see the imaging process in action and how that had changed. It was all AI; a wand in my mouth and then within seconds a 3D rotating image showing a path to fixing my teeth. Stunning really.

The scale of data generation is stunning too. HealthTech estimates that an average hospital produces roughly 50 petabytes of data every year, more than twice the size of the contents housed in the Library of Congress.

And the amount of data being generated (and then needed to be stored somewhere) is increasing at a rate of roughly 47% per year. And the total health care data reflects about a third of the world’s total data volume.

So how do tribes and communities get ahead of this? What is the direction pointing to a better conversation?

Sherry Stout said in Colorado recently a city council passed a resolution supporting data center construction in rural communities. Away from people. The logic: We want the value of data, what it means to our lives, but we don’t want the negative impacts.

“We want our ChatGPT, we want our cloud, we want our cloud storage, we want all of those things, but we would rather you put it somewhere else, somewhere where it’s away from what we consider away from people and away from people is going to inherently mean increasingly rural,” Stout says. “How we think about rural impacts is going to change as this conversation continues to see these type of ordinances saying, ‘Go out there.’”

But we who live out there might have something to say about that.

text:
Nov 10 (Reuters) - Tesla’s move to discontinue ⁠its Cybertruck next year is perhaps the highest-profile flameout in a category that automakers had once hyped: huge electric ⁠pickups.

Tesla CEO Elon Musk said in a social media post on Saturday that the automaker would ramp up ‌Cybertruck production at its Austin, Texas, factory to meet an "order backlog” before dismantling the assembly line around June or July. He said the wind-down would allow Tesla to produce more Cybercab robotaxis, which have yet to be sold commercially.

But sales of Tesla’s stainless-steel, angular truck — once described by MotorTrend magazine as having a “stealth-bomber-refrigerator ​design theme” — sagged 28% this year through September, to about 11,600 trucks, according ⁠to an estimate from research firm Motor Intelligence.

That sales ⁠pace is far off the 250,000-truck annual level Musk once predicted. Musk's other big company, SpaceX, also bought Cybertrucks worth $131 million ⁠from ‌Tesla at list price last year, according to a federal regulatory filing.

MORE MONEY FOR LESS TRUCK

The market for large electric pickups has been a rough road for Tesla’s competitors, too. Even the Cybertruck’s relatively meager deliveries have outpaced sales of ⁠electric trucks from rivals General Motors and Ford Motor, where executives once had ​high hopes that battery-powered versions of their ‌full-size pickups — their biggest moneymakers — would be major hits.

Detroit’s automakers pivoted to EV pickup trucks early this decade in ⁠part to fend off ​entries from Tesla and Rivian. GM, Ford and Ram maker Stellantis for decades have cultivated legions of loyal truck customers by offering pickups with ever-increasing levels of horsepower and towing capability.

But the companies have not been able to translate that formula to EV trucks, said Karl Brauer, executive analyst ⁠at vehicle research site iSeeCars.com. For one, the trucks are pricey, in ​part because their massive batteries are extremely costly. GM’s Chevrolet Silverado EV, for example, starts at around $62,000.

Second, the trucks often struggle to perform tasks that owners of internal-combustion pickups have come to expect, like towing a horse trailer or hauling heavy equipment.

“So in the end, ⁠you have to pay more money for a vehicle that is less functional,” Brauer said.

AUTOMAKERS GO SMALLER, ADD GAS TO EXTEND RANGE

Ford CEO Jim Farley acknowledged those tough economics during an earnings call last year, explaining why the company would discontinue the Ford Lightning, the electric version of its popular F-150 pickup that had been a relative hit for a few years before demand cooled.

“The larger ​the vehicle, the bigger the battery, the more pressure on margin because customers will not ⁠pay a premium,” Farley said.

Ford’s focus is now on a smaller electric pickup, the Fathom, which it plans to roll out late next ​year at a starting price of about $28,000.

Automakers also are looking toward hybrid technology to ‌deliver truck customers the functionality they need in an electric form. ​Stellantis next year plans to launch an extended-range electric pickup truck, which will use a gas-powered generator to recharge the battery on the go.

(Reporting by Mike Colias in Detroit and Nathan Gomes in Bengaluru; Editing by Matthew Lewis)

text:
By Christopher Boan

A new rule approved by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency could help get high-polluting vehicles off the road and replaced with cleaner alternatives in Arizona’s Maricopa County.

That’s because the EPA greenlit the municipality’s Rule 205, a first-in-the-nation program allowing fleet owners and operators in the state’s most populous county to generate Emission Reduction Credits by upgrading their vehicles with cleaner technologies.

Those credits can, in turn, be purchased by factory owners or others that are considered “stationary emissions sources” to offset any potential emission increases that come from expanded operations.

The newest rule is the brainchild of the Phoenix-based Maricopa County Air Quality Department, which reports to the county’s Board of Supervisors.

Board Chair Kate Brophy McGee told The Center Square on Thursday that the county’s newest emissions rule will allow business to expand in the region, without harming air quality.

She also noted no taxpayer dollars would be spent as part of the implementation of Rule 205, as was the case with Rule 204, a similar policy that concerned non-road vehicles such as locomotives and construction equipment.

“Maricopa County has an incredible air quality division, and they are they’re basically Department of Super Nerds,” Brophy McGee told The Center Square. “And we have been working on this as a county because we’ve been hovering on the edge of non-attainment for a long time, and a large part of it, I will tell you, is due to factors outside our control.”

Sandy Bahr, who is the director of the Sierra Club’s Grand Canyon Chapter, told The Center Square that the new EPA rule does little to address the county’s ongoing pollution problem.

“Our concerns about these two pollution trading rules the county has just adopted is that they will result in the status quo or worse for our air quality and our health,” Bahr told The Center Square. “Ozone shortens our lifespan and is especially harmful to the most vulnerable, children, the elderly, and those with respiratory issues.

“Maricopa County should be designated as “serious” for ozone, but through machinations at the Trump EPA where they put polluters first, we are considered moderate. What does that mean? We have bad air, but are not doing nearly enough to improve it,” she added.

What Rule 205 entails

When Brophy McGee talks of the county’s nonattainment status, she’s referencing stipulations put in place on municipalities by the Clean Air and Water Act.

Those regulations state areas that fail to meet certain air quality metrics must go through extra steps to approve permits for higher-emission projects, such as factories and data centers.

Maricopa County is ranked as a moderate nonattainment zone for ground-level ozone, which Brophy McGee attributes to Phoenix’s place at the bottom of the greater Salt River Valley.

“We’re in a bowl,” Brophy McGee said. “The particulates and things settle in the bowl, and then the sun comes along and heats it up. And that creates the ozone.

“But what (Rule 205) does is say, ‘Hey, the stuff that we’re actually doing, the pollution that we’re actually generating, let’s cut back on that. And here’s an incentive to do that’,” she added.

Bahr believes that the county’s air pollution rules do little to solve the county’s ongoing ozone pollution problem, allowing large-scale emitters to continue doing so and further degrading the region’s air quality as a result.

“We should be reducing pollution from non-road construction equipment and the like and further reducing pollution from stationary sources like power plants and other industrial sources,” Bahr said. “The American Lung Association gives Maricopa County a failing grade for ozone and particulates. These rules will do nothing to change that.”

What it means for Arizona

Mike Martucci, the EPA Pacific Southwest regional administrator, told The Center Square that the county’s newest air pollution rule has the potential to pay huge dividends for the quality of life for residents.

Martucci said anyone looking for a permit for a certain number of emissions per year would have to purchase that amount plus 15% more from those fleet operators. He said that would provide the operators with the money needed to overhaul their fleets and introduce more efficient vehicles that cut down on emissions in the long run.

He said credits are paid out to fleet operators depending on how much of an emissions upgrade they make. Those who exchange older diesel-powered trucks with newer versions are considered to be on one level for credits. But bus operators that go from diesel to compressed natural gas or electric-powered vehicles can reap greater benefits.

“At its core is a science-backed approach to make sure that we’re maintaining that 115%,” Martucci told The Center Square.

Opening new opportunities

Brophy McGee said Rule 205 has the potential to open new doors for manufacturers that are butting up against environmental emissions regulations, fueling the county’s economic aspirations, both in the short and long term.

“We have businesses who want to come here and build,” Brophy McGee said. “A high-profile example would be the Taiwan Semiconductor Co,, and in order to do that, they need air quality credits.”

The Arizona native cited the example of a beat-up tractor trailer that you’d see chugging along the interstate as a reason why Rule 205 is important. The rule is designed to incentivize fleet operators to get those trucks off the road and replaced by ones that operate more efficiently.

“They need [air quality credits], and we need to continue to meet the federal standards for clean air,” she said. “And so, businesses are incentivized to clean [their fleets] up and to get newer technologies to replace those old, on-road motor vehicles.”

Danny Seiden, president and CEO of the Arizona Chamber of Commerce and Industry, seconded Brophy McGee’s comments.

Seiden commended the EPA for finding a solution to the region’s environmental problems that doesn’t kneecap business development along the way, providing positive results for all involved.

“This is a big win for Arizona’s economy and another important step toward addressing the air quality challenges that have made it increasingly difficult for businesses to build and expand in Maricopa County,” Seiden told The Center Square. “For too long, the shortage of available emission reduction credits has been a major obstacle to new investment, even for companies committed to meeting stringent environmental standards.

“Rule 205 offers a practical, market-driven solution that helps remove that barrier while encouraging cleaner air,” he said.

text:
The governors of Louisiana and Alabama are petitioning the Environmental Protection Agency for a waiver from the Renewable Fuel Standard.

In a letter to EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin yesterday, Governors Jeff Landry and Kay Ivey requested a partial waiver for 2027, calling it “targeted, prospective and temporary” and saying it “would not prevent ethanol from continuing to be blended wherever the economics support it.”

In a post on X, Gov. Landry called on fellow governors of Texas, Mississippi and Arkansas to join them in petitioning for a waiver of the RFS claiming “Americans are paying more for gas and diesel because of the Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS).”

The Iowa Renewable Fuels Association (IRFA) reacted to the petition saying that “blaming the RFS for high fuel prices is misguided and ignores the important role renewable fuels play in expanding U.S. fuel supplies, strengthening energy security and providing consumers with more affordable choices at the pump.”

“With all due respect to the governors, during this time of high fuel prices, the last thing you want to do is reduce supply,” said IRFA Executive Director Monte Shaw. “The real solution is to unleash additional U.S. supply, which Congress can do by removing barriers to year-round E15 sales. Ethanol lowers fuels prices because it is less expensive than gasoline and adds gallons to the market. Expanding the use of low-cost ethanol, made right here in America, would lower prices at the pump. Consumers need real solutions, not ineffective political potshots.”

text:
The Illinois Environmental Protection Agency (Illinois EPA) issued a competitive Call for Partners (CFP) for the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (U.S. EPA) 2026 Diesel Emissions Reduction Act (DERA) National Program. Illinois EPA seeks partners that currently operate fleets of diesel-powered on road or nonroad equipment within the State of Illinois and are willing to collaborate on eligible projects that will reduce harmful diesel emissions while strengthening the long-term operational resilience of Illinois fleets amid rising diesel fuel costs.

“Illinois is pursuing every available funding opportunity to help address the rising cost of diesel and accelerate the transition to cleaner transportation,” said Illinois EPA Director James Jennings. “With this Call for Partners we are trying to leverage every available resource and bring together public and private partners to tackle two interconnected challenges—the fuel cost crisis facing our businesses and communities and the climate crisis.”

U.S. EPA announced the availability of up to $12 million for individual awards (with $180 million in total program funding) under the 2026 DERA National Program (Funding Opportunity Number: EPA OAR OTAQ 26 01). This competitive program provides financial assistance to incentivize and accelerate the upgrade or retirement of legacy diesel engines, vehicles, and equipment. Eligible activities under this funding will focus on the replacement of existing medium and heavy-duty diesel vehicles and equipment with newer technologies – certified or verified by U.S. EPA or California Air Resources Board (CARB)– that achieve the greatest possible reductions in diesel emissions.

Interested parties should review the 2026 DERA National Program NOFO in its entirety before responding to this CFP. This solicitation does not obligate Illinois EPA to select any partners identified through this process. Illinois EPA may elect to pursue any proposed projects, alternative projects, or none at all. Proposals must be submitted to EPA.DERAgrants@Illinois.gov by 11:59PM on December 4, 2026, Central Standard Time.

PROGRAM BACKGROUND

Illinois EPA’s efforts under this CFP are supported by the Illinois Clean Trucks Program, which supports the reduction of emissions from medium and heavy-duty vehicles by enabling the adoption of cleaner, lower emission, or zero emission technologies in sectors with significant diesel pollution impacts under the broader Driving a Cleaner Illinois (DACI), the State of Illinois’ primary initiative for reducing emissions from mobile sources. DACI operates under the foundational agency powers of the Illinois Environmental Protection Act (415 ILCS 5/4), which empowers Illinois EPA to design and administer grant and incentive programs to reduce air pollution from vehicles and equipment using state and federal funding. DACI incorporates funding from the Volkswagen Environmental Mitigation Trust (established under the federal court-approved Environmental Mitigation Trust Agreement) and allocations provided under Public Act 102 0662 (the Climate and Equitable Jobs Act), among other sources.

These efforts are further informed by Illinois Executive Order 2021 08, which directs state agencies to integrate lower and zero emission vehicle technologies into state fleet procurement, “to the maximum extent practicable,” and to support statewide transportation emission reduction efforts. This Executive Order reinforces the goals of DACI and aligns with efforts to assist Illinois fleets in reducing diesel dependence and managing operational challenges associated with rising and increasingly volatile diesel fuel costs.

Proposals submitted under this CFP must be no more than two pages in length (excluding optional attachments) and should provide a brief statement of interest that addresses the following elements:

ELIGIBLE PROJECTS

Eligible projects under this CFP will focus on high impact diesel emissions reduction activities permitted under the 2026 DERA National Program. Illinois EPA is specifically seeking proposals that replace high use diesel equipment and vehicles with those EPA or CARB certified options that deliver the greatest achievable reductions in diesel emissions. Prioritized project categories include, but are not necessarily limited to, the following:

Airport ground support equipment (GSE): replacement of eligible diesel powered GSE, such as baggage tractors, belt loaders, and tugs

Ground power and auxiliary equipment: replacement of diesel ground power units and similar auxiliary equipment that contribute to airport area noise and emissions

Nonroad heavy equipment: Replacement of eligible diesel construction, industrial, or material handling equipment used in freight, logistics, construction, and other high impact sectors

Medium and heavy duty on road vehicles: replacement of eligible diesel vehicles, including long-haul tractors, vocational trucks, refuse trucks, delivery vehicles, and other Class 5–8 fleet assets, with comparable vehicles capable of achieving measurable and sustained reductions in diesel emissions

PROPOSAL REQUIREMENTS

Proposals submitted under this CFP should be no more than two pages in length (excluding optional attachments) and should provide a brief statement of interest that addresses the following program elements:

1. Project Introduction: a short description of the applicant organization, its operations, and the diesel-powered vehicles or equipment currently in use

2. Equipment or Vehicles Proposed for Replacement: identification of the specific diesel vehicles, engines, or equipment proposed for replacement, including quantities and general operational roles. Applicants should describe the replacement units proposed for their project(s) by make and model, and may describe the expected reductions in diesel emissions consistent with DERA eligibility requirements – USE DIESEL EMISSIONS QUANTIFIER (optional; attach)

3. Project Cost and Funding Request: a summary of anticipated project costs and the amount of DERA funding requested through Illinois EPA

4. Cost Share Commitment: a statement affirming the applicant’s ability to meet the required cost share, including the source of cost share funds and confirmation that the funds are available, eligible, and not derived from other federal assistance

5. Additional Benefits to Illinois: a brief description of any benefits beyond diesel emission reductions – examples may include noise reductions, operational improvements, or benefits to local communities or economic activity

EVALUATION

Illinois EPA will review submissions based on the following factors:

Eligibility: confirmation that the applicant and proposed project elements meet federal DERA eligibility requirements

Emission Reduction Potential: the extent to which the proposed vehicle or equipment replacements are expected to deliver significant, quantifiable reductions in diesel emissions consistent with DERA program priorities

Project Feasibility: the likelihood that the applicant can successfully implement the proposed replacement project, considering fleet operations, organizational capacity, and product availability given extended industry lead times

Cost Share Availability: the applicant’s demonstrated ability to provide the required non federal cost share from eligible sources

Additional Benefits to Illinois Residents: identification of any benefits beyond diesel emission reductions, including potential operational improvements, reduced noise, or other benefits to local communities or the Illinois workforce

Illinois EPA may also consider geographic diversity, project type diversity, and overall alignment with statewide transportation and air quality priorities when determining which partners to include in a future application to U.S. EPA.

text:
Warren County Economic Development has highlighted an opportunity for small- and medium-sized automotive supply chain businesses in the area.

Indiana Economic Development Corporation has introduced ADAPT —  Accelerated Development of Automotive Propulsion Technology. The application window is through Jan. 7. Grants can range from $100,000 to $1 million. A 1:1 company match is required.

“The program is funded by a $70.79 million award from the U.S. Department of Energy,” reads the information from IEDC. “Indiana was one of five states with a significant automotive workforce selected to receive a share of $50 million designed to support the transition to new vehicle and engine models while creating and preserving hundreds of jobs at small and mid-size suppliers.”

Indiana has more than 500 automotive parts suppliers, according to the information, and produces 1.3 million cars and trucks annually. Indiana is second in the nation in overall production. About 320 of the businesses are small and medium sized and provide more than 34,000 jobs in 63 Indiana counties.

A business is eligible for ADAPT application if it is headquartered in Indiana and conducts “a significant portion of its operations from Indiana”. It must be able to provide at least a 1:1 investment match in each expense category. This can include capital equipment, capital-expense software or workforce training. The awards are reimbursement based, so the company must make the investment first and then is reimbursed for eligible expenses. \

“Proposed projects should be a new initiative or expansion focused on commercial-ready capabilities related to and required for hybrid, plug-in hybrid, battery­electric and hydrogen fuel cell vehicles that would not otherwise happen without the grant award. Businesses in manufacturing subsectors that are expected to face greater headwinds as hybrid and electrified propulsion grows will be given preference in funding,” according to information from IEDC.

“Applicants may have no more than 1,500 total employees (including any parent or affiliated companies), and the Indiana facility where the project will be implemented must have 500 or fewer employees. All funding must be spent exclusively in Indiana, and grant-funded equipment must remain in the county where it is installed.”

All projects must be completed by Dec. 31, 2029.

Businesses can apply for ADAPT on the Indiana Economic Development Corporation website, iedc.in.gov . The materials will be reviewed by IEDC and its industry partner Conexus Indiana to make sure the applicants meet the eligibly requirements.

After pre-screening, companies advancing will complete a core application which must be done by Feb. 12. This must include “comprehensive budget with individual lines items that can be verified for reimbursement; a budget narrative (an explanation of the line items and designation of award and matching funds); and equipment quotes. Technical assistance is available to support this process as needed.”

IEDC representatives and a peer review committee will evaluate the applications. “This industry panel will include senior industry leaders from across Indiana that have relevant subject matter expertise related to automotive manufacturing environments,” it reads.

Once that process is fizzled and award recommendations are made by IEDC, the company and project information will be submitted to the U.S. Department of Energy for final review and due diligence. The awards are executive to be finalized next spring.

Those selected must meet federal requirements including submission of all project information and reimbursement documentation, quarterly reporting, compliance with National Environmental Policy Act, and federal statement of project objectives.

Those who wish more information can reach out to Heather Deno at Warren County Economic Development at 765-762-6055 or ledo@warrenadvantage.com .

text:
WASHINGTON — The Senate on Monday advanced bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews to power data centers and other infrastructure projects, in the first major action since last week's election that soundly repudiated President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans.

The Senate voted 73-25 to formally take up the bill, which senators and the president have pushed as a way to meet growing demand for electricity and other forms of energy that now face yearslong delays in getting to the grid.

The legislation's sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to get big energy projects started — both for clean energy and fossil fuel projects — and make sure data centers pay for the energy they use. Anger over artificial intelligence data centers and rising electricity prices helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the massive, energy-hungry structures.

Trump urged senators to vote for it, calling it a "BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE." in a social media post on Sunday. The bill will "ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines, and Power Plants faster than ever before, lowering Energy Costs for American Families," Trump wrote.

Major industry groups representing developers in clean energy and in the oil and gas sector also support the bill.

However, many environmental organizations have panned the deal because they say it would lock in fossil fuel development, weaken environmental safeguards and make it harder for communities to challenge energy project approvals.

While the bill has received bipartisan support, the Democrats' sweeping midterm win could complicate its passage.

Some Democrats say the party should use its stronger position in the next Congress to pass legislation that produces needed clean energy but limits expansion of oil, natural gas and mining. Some critics have said the permitting bill as proposed could lead to a vast increase in exports of liquefied natural gas and facilitate a "reckless" build-out of data centers powered by natural gas.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, a New York Democrat who is expected to become speaker in January, criticized the bill last week, with his office saying it "falls short" in a number of areas.

Major environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and National Wildlife Federation, have strongly opposed the measure in recent days, citing concerns about its limits on judicial review and changes to the National Environmental Policy Act and Endangered Species Act. The environmental policy law, known as NEPA, requires agencies to consider a project's possible impacts and allows the public to be heard before a project is approved, but supporters of an overhaul say that causes yearslong delays in federal permitting.

The bill's four main champions — two Democrats and two Republicans — released a detailed set of amendments Saturday designed to bolster support for the legislation.

The four senators, who lead the chamber's energy and environment panels, negotiated the deal weeks before the election. Republican Sens. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah and Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island say Americans are tired of paying more in utility bills while projects that could lower costs sit stuck in the planning phase for years.

"Americans can't afford to wait for lower electricity prices. We need to pass this bill now," said Heinrich.

Trump promotes expanding production of oil, natural gas and coal and he particularly dislikes offshore wind. His administration has been paying energy companies to walk away from offshore wind projects under development. It has spent nearly $4 billion on such settlements.

Whitehouse said a provision in the permitting bill would end the buyouts, so the administration will no longer be able to use public money to pay clean energy developers to relinquish wind energy leases and oblige them to invest in fossil fuels instead.

Trump told reporters Monday that he still opposes wind energy. When told that wind is part of the bill, Trump replied: "Well, the bill hasn't been fully negotiated. I will not approve wind turbines because wind turbines are a major loser."

Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland voted against moving the legislation forward, in part due to Trump's opposition to offshore wind. Van Hollen said the bill does not fully address the administration's efforts to block Maryland's pending offshore wind project, which he said would lower energy costs for households across the state and create thousands of jobs.

At a press conference with Heinrich on Monday, Whitehouse said the bill is "the floor, not the ceiling, of our climate and environmental aspirations. And we look forward to working to accomplish big things with our big Democratic majorities" over the next two years.

Whitehouse said Trump's support should help the bill move toward a vote in the House.

Heinrich said he worked hard to incorporate feedback from tribal leaders on the initial proposal, adding that the amended version requires federal agencies to consult with tribes on projects that affect important cultural sites.

Sponsors also extended the window for objections to agency reports and strengthened opportunities for states to weigh in, Heinrich said.

If passed, the bill will save households billions on electricity costs, create jobs, cut emissions and force big corporations to pay their full share for data centers instead of pushing energy costs on consumers, he said.

Capito called the bill "a win for America,'' adding: "We cannot let this moment pass by. The reality is this, over the next several years, we will have no choice but to increase our national energy production. This is an unprecedented opportunity ... to come together to show the American people we are listening to you."

Industry leaders are advocating for the bill's passage, including leaders of the American Clean Power Association, which represents clean energy developers, and the American Petroleum Institute, the oil and gas industry's top lobbying group.

But Bradley Campbell, president of the Conservation Law Foundation, said it would be a "terrible mistake" to proceed with the bill in the waning days of the current Congress.

text:
WASHINGTON — The Senate on Monday advanced bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews to power data centers and other infrastructure projects, in the first major action since last week's election that soundly repudiated President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans.

The Senate voted 73-25 to formally take up the bill, which senators and the president have pushed as a way to meet growing demand for electricity and other forms of energy that now face yearslong delays in getting to the grid.

The legislation's sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to get big energy projects started — both for clean energy and fossil fuel projects — and make sure data centers pay for the energy they use. Anger over artificial intelligence data centers and rising electricity prices helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the massive, energy-hungry structures.

Trump urged senators to vote for it, calling it a "BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE." in a social media post on Sunday. The bill will "ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines, and Power Plants faster than ever before, lowering Energy Costs for American Families," Trump wrote.

Major industry groups representing developers in clean energy and in the oil and gas sector also support the bill.

However, many environmental organizations have panned the deal because they say it would lock in fossil fuel development, weaken environmental safeguards and make it harder for communities to challenge energy project approvals.

While the bill has received bipartisan support, the Democrats' sweeping midterm win could complicate its passage.

Some Democrats say the party should use its stronger position in the next Congress to pass legislation that produces needed clean energy but limits expansion of oil, natural gas and mining. Some critics have said the permitting bill as proposed could lead to a vast increase in exports of liquefied natural gas and facilitate a "reckless" build-out of data centers powered by natural gas.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, a New York Democrat who is expected to become speaker in January, criticized the bill last week, with his office saying it "falls short" in a number of areas.

Major environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and National Wildlife Federation, have strongly opposed the measure in recent days, citing concerns about its limits on judicial review and changes to the National Environmental Policy Act and Endangered Species Act. The environmental policy law, known as NEPA, requires agencies to consider a project's possible impacts and allows the public to be heard before a project is approved, but supporters of an overhaul say that causes yearslong delays in federal permitting.

The bill's four main champions — two Democrats and two Republicans — released a detailed set of amendments Saturday designed to bolster support for the legislation.

The four senators, who lead the chamber's energy and environment panels, negotiated the deal weeks before the election. Republican Sens. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah and Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island say Americans are tired of paying more in utility bills while projects that could lower costs sit stuck in the planning phase for years.

"Americans can't afford to wait for lower electricity prices. We need to pass this bill now," said Heinrich.

Trump promotes expanding production of oil, natural gas and coal and he particularly dislikes offshore wind. His administration has been paying energy companies to walk away from offshore wind projects under development. It has spent nearly $4 billion on such settlements.

Whitehouse said a provision in the permitting bill would end the buyouts, so the administration will no longer be able to use public money to pay clean energy developers to relinquish wind energy leases and oblige them to invest in fossil fuels instead.

Trump told reporters Monday that he still opposes wind energy. When told that wind is part of the bill, Trump replied: "Well, the bill hasn't been fully negotiated. I will not approve wind turbines because wind turbines are a major loser."

Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland voted against moving the legislation forward, in part due to Trump's opposition to offshore wind. Van Hollen said the bill does not fully address the administration's efforts to block Maryland's pending offshore wind project, which he said would lower energy costs for households across the state and create thousands of jobs.

At a press conference with Heinrich on Monday, Whitehouse said the bill is "the floor, not the ceiling, of our climate and environmental aspirations. And we look forward to working to accomplish big things with our big Democratic majorities" over the next two years.

Whitehouse said Trump's support should help the bill move toward a vote in the House.

Heinrich said he worked hard to incorporate feedback from tribal leaders on the initial proposal, adding that the amended version requires federal agencies to consult with tribes on projects that affect important cultural sites.

Sponsors also extended the window for objections to agency reports and strengthened opportunities for states to weigh in, Heinrich said.

If passed, the bill will save households billions on electricity costs, create jobs, cut emissions and force big corporations to pay their full share for data centers instead of pushing energy costs on consumers, he said.

Capito called the bill "a win for America,'' adding: "We cannot let this moment pass by. The reality is this, over the next several years, we will have no choice but to increase our national energy production. This is an unprecedented opportunity ... to come together to show the American people we are listening to you."

Industry leaders are advocating for the bill's passage, including leaders of the American Clean Power Association, which represents clean energy developers, and the American Petroleum Institute, the oil and gas industry's top lobbying group.

But Bradley Campbell, president of the Conservation Law Foundation, said it would be a "terrible mistake" to proceed with the bill in the waning days of the current Congress.

While changes announced Saturday address a few concerns, the bill also comes with a gauntlet of new — and at times conflicting — rules, Campbell said. He said the bill maintains a veneer of federal safeguards while in fact stripping the power of federal agencies, states, tribes and communities to identify and prevent serious harm to health and the environment.

Sara Amundson, president of the Humane World Action Fund, said the bill weakens the scientific foundation of the Endangered Species Act and could create new opportunities to exclude needed wildlife protections.

"This proposed rewrite of the 'best available science' standard could give agencies new grounds to unfairly dismiss credible research, including science showing that stronger protections are needed for species at risk," she said, urging lawmakers to drop the provision or oppose the bill.

name: American Energy
title: The Grid Gap: Barriers to Building the Missing Link in Global Electrification
description:
With rapidly increasing global energy demand and accelerating electrification, grid development must keep pace.
Regions can learn from each other’s experiences in overcoming these challenges, and building the necessary transmission infrastructure will require international collaboration.
Global Supply Chain Bottlenecks Slow Development Adding to challenges with transmission financing are global supply chain bottlenecks, which further obstruct international transmission deployment.
Furthermore, high investment risk and financing costs constrain clean energy investment across the continent.
Grid infrastructure is the critical backbone to increasing energy access, bolstering energy security, supporting economic growth, and facilitating the clean energy transition.
text:
As countries gather this month in Türkiye for COP31, energy security, electrification, and the expansion of clean power systems anchor the conversation. The COP31 Presidency’s electrification pledge, which aims to increase electricity’s share of final energy consumption to 35% by 2035, casts a spotlight on the electric transmission infrastructure necessary to meet these goals.

With rapidly increasing global energy demand and accelerating electrification, grid development must keep pace. To achieve global decarbonization goals, improve reliability, and increase access to clean generation, nations around the world must rapidly expand and update their electric transmission infrastructure to connect clean generation sources to demand centers. Effective and resilient electric transmission systems are also essential for expanding energy access, strengthening energy security, and enabling economic development.

However, significant roadblocks stand in the way of needed transmission deployment, from shared global barriers such as financing gaps and supply chain constraints to region-specific obstacles, including ineffective or insufficient policy frameworks, planning, and coordination, permitting and siting challenges, and local opposition.

Regions can learn from each other’s experiences in overcoming these challenges, and building the necessary transmission infrastructure will require international collaboration. Global stages such as COP are prime locations for this collaboration, providing a platform for strengthening global partnerships and discussing innovative strategies for grid expansion.

Barriers to Grid Expansion

Grid Investment Lags Behind Ambition

Although transmission is a critical component of global power systems, investment in grid infrastructure is lagging behind investment in new generation: annual investment in generation has risen nearly 70% since 2015 to around $1 trillion, compared with $400 billion for grids, contributing to congestion and delays connecting new generation.

This financing gap for transmission is shared across many regions, but is especially prevalent in Africa: despite representing 20% of the world’s population, the region attracts only 3% of global energy investment. However, many countries in Africa lack the public capital to deploy the necessary infrastructure for the clean energy transition, including transmission, and investment capital costs in the region are more than triple costs in U.S. and Western Europe. New and sustained sources of grid investment and lower costs of capital will be critical to enabling access to clean, affordable, and reliable energy in Africa, and Gulf countries such as the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia are working to close the gap. These nations have announced more than $175 billion in clean energy investments and commitments in Africa since 2010, with most of this financing announced after 2022. This includes some investment in transmission, but a higher proportion of financing into grid expansion projects across a more diverse set of countries would have a significant impact. In general, additional investment in grids across the world, alongside innovative approaches to financing, would dramatically speed transmission deployment.

In other regions like the U.S., incentive structures and lack of coordination between regional markets can often direct capital toward shorter, smaller lines, creating a financing gap for the most urgently needed and highest value high-voltage, long-distance interregional lines. Significant capital investment will be required to deliver on these high-value additions, but the costs of these investments largely fall to electricity ratepayers. Innovative financing structures, including public-private partnerships and a greater leveraging of public financing tools, including replacing more expensive private capital with lower-cost, tax exempt public debt, can reduce project and system-wide costs. In New England states, for example, public financing options could reduce costs for new transmission projects by as much as 43%, delivering more than $8.3 billion in customer savings. In California, public-private partnerships for transmission development could reduce costs by up to $3 billion annually, or around $123 billion over 40 years. Federal and state governments are already facilitating innovative financing options.

Other regions are also already making progress toward innovative public roles in transmission development to build infrastructure more quickly and affordably. In the United Kingdom, the recently announced Great British Grid initiative will create a publicly owned body to bring together public and private investment to speed infrastructure development and upgrades and will accelerate project delivery.

Global Supply Chain Bottlenecks Slow Development

Adding to challenges with transmission financing are global supply chain bottlenecks, which further obstruct international transmission deployment. A 2025 report from the International Energy Agency found that delays for procurement for transmission components have increased significantly in recent years, with procurement for cables and transformers often taking almost twice as long as in 2021. In addition, prices for cables have nearly doubled since 2019, while costs of transformers have increased by approximately 75%. These changes are occurring alongside increasing demand: for example, in the US, power transformer demand increased by 116% between 2019 and 2025. When combined with supply chain bottlenecks, this led to a 39% market deficit for power transformers in 2025. Commitments to expand manufacturing of transmission components and spur workforce development, while strengthening global trade partnerships, would help alleviate some of these supply chain constraints.

Compounded Challenges in Africa

Africa’s long-term economic development and energy system transformation will depend on strong, financially sustainable power systems. Energy access and reliability varies widely across countries on the continent, but challenges are especially prevalent in Sub-Saharan Africa. Despite major efforts to increase electricity connection, the region accounts for 85% of the global energy access deficit (over 550 million people), up from 50% in 2010. Where grid connections exist, users face significant reliability and affordability issues. 72% of businesses report experiencing outages, resulting in significant losses and necessitating expensive investment in defensive measures. Power utilities continue to face significant operational and financial challenges. Distribution inefficiencies result in substantial electricity losses, undermining utilities’ ability to expand service, invest in modern grid infrastructure, and support large-scale deployment of clean energy technologies. Furthermore, high investment risk and financing costs constrain clean energy investment across the continent.

Insufficient Planning and Permitting Create Added Barriers

In regions with more developed grids, countries are still facing challenges in deploying transmission infrastructure at the pace and scale needed to meet demand growth and decarbonization driven electrification. A lack of long-term, national transmission planning and clear cost allocation frameworks in the U.S., for example, prevent the highest impact lines from being identified and built in a timely manner. In both the EU and U.S., misaligned siting and permitting requirements make the coordination needed to build long-distance, high-voltage lines across multiple jurisdictions difficult. Lack of clarity in approval processes and insufficient government capacity to process permits are also common barriers to deploying new projects at scale.

Despite the need for process improvements, safeguards for communities and environmental protections must be secured. Transmission infrastructure can also face substantial local opposition, which can slow, reroute, or even cancel projects. Robust and inclusive community engagement and public participation throughout the transmission planning process can ensure projects deliver meaningful benefits to communities while simultaneously improving project outcomes.

Even with these barriers, regions like the EU are demonstrating promising policy pathways to bolstering the grid, including through the European Grid Package. Presented in December 2025, the Grid Package aims to increase build out of the EU’s transmission systems, improve EU-level coordination to map and plan the required grid infrastructure and upgrade the EU´s permitting regime. The package consists of a proposal to revise the Trans-European Networks for Energy Regulation and a proposal to accelerate permit granting procedures.

Together, these files will help determine how Europe plans, selects and delivers the cross-border infrastructure needed for a more resilient, integrated, and decarbonized energy system. Both of which are currently in the final stages of the legislative process, with trilogue negotiations underway between the European Parliament, the Council, and the European Commission. Once adopted, they will provide an important blueprint for addressing persistent bottlenecks (e.g. by strengthening data input quality and transparency in transmission planning) and provide a positive example for other regions as an ambitious effort to improve grid planning.

Coordination as a pathway forward

Overcoming the barriers above will require efficient and effective policy and regulatory frameworks, long-term planning, coordinated investment, permitting process improvements, and thoughtful community engagement. In addition, joint commitments to cross-border collaboration and coordination across regions will be essential to expand power systems and strengthen grid resilience.

The stakes are high. Grid infrastructure is the critical backbone to increasing energy access, bolstering energy security, supporting economic growth, and facilitating the clean energy transition. Without strong commitments and dedicated action to expand and modernize the grid, efforts to build new clean generation and meet global electrification goals will fall short. COP31 is a timely opportunity for international stakeholders to recognize these challenges, share lessons learned on overcoming barriers, and identify effective strategies to expand the grid and strengthen global partnerships.

text:
Tender awarded to BADGE Constructions (WA) Pty Ltd to deliver Munster TAFE clean energy facility

Work underway to deliver Midland Clean Energy Skills Hub with interconnected regional campuses

Cook Labor Government preparing for future workforce demands with 22,000 workers needed in clean energy sector by 2035

The Cook Labor Government is powering ahead to deliver the workforce needed for Western Australia's energy transition, today awarding a tender for a specialist facility to be delivered at South Metropolitan TAFE's Munster campus.

BADGE Constructions (WA) Pty Ltd has been engaged to deliver the expansion, which will train the skilled workers needed to support Western Australia's growing clean energy sector and major project pipeline.

A key election commitment, the facility will provide state-of-the-art facilities to deliver training for the renewables industry, including wind energy, battery technology, green hydrogen, electrification, automation, and robotics.

The two-storey building will include classrooms, computer laboratories, automation laboratories, instrumentation laboratories, battery laboratories, and a control room. Once opened, it is expected to support an additional 840 course enrolments annually.

About 22,000 extra workers will be needed in the clean energy sector by 2035, and the Cook Labor Government is focused on training Western Australians to take up these roles.

Work is now also underway to deliver the $32 million Clean Energy Skills Hub at North Metropolitan TAFE's Midland campus, which will facilitate training across clean energy sectors including solar and wind and battery energy storage systems.

The Midland campus will serve as a hub and will connect with up to four interconnected specialist spokes in regional WA, including Central Regional TAFE's Kalgoorlie campus.

The Cook Labor Government has made a number of TAFE courses in the clean energy sector fee free or low fee including the Electrotechnology pre-apprenticeship, Certificate III in Electrotechnology Electrician, and Certificate III in Laboratory Skills.

Comments attributed to Energy and Decarbonisation and Skills and TAFE Minister Amber-Jade Sanderson:

"The Cook Labor Government is preparing WA workers for the jobs of the future.

"We will need about 22,000 workers in our clean energy sector by 2035 and we want Western Australians to seize these opportunities.

"That's why we are constructing a new state-of-the-art training facility at Munster, while continuing to deliver fee free and low fee TAFE courses."

Comments attributed to Cockburn MLA David Scaife:

"With thousands of jobs coming to the Western Trade Coast in renewable energy and green manufacturing, my focus is making sure locals are front of the queue to benefit.

"This investment in Munster TAFE will make Cockburn one of the best places in WA to start a career in clean energy."

title: Nations promise to install more rooftop solar at UN climate talks - ClickOnDetroit
authors: Anton L. Delgado, Sibi Arasu And Suzan Fraser, Associated Press, Anton L. Delgado
description:
The new Global Rooftop Solar Declaration launched Tuesday on the second day of this year’s climate talks, known as COP31.
The U.N. climate talks have been criticized in the past for making promises that later fall flat.
“We now need to see national policies and frameworks in place.” More rooftop solar may help regular people Bangladesh, Kenya, Nigeria and Vanuatu joined Australia by endorsing the rooftop solar declaration in the Turkish resort town of Antalya, where COP31 is being co-hosted by Turkey and Australia.
Nations lean on fossil fuels, despite solar gains Turkey's electrification pledge and Australia's rooftop solar declaration put a spotlight on the energy mix of both nations, which still rely heavily on fossil fuels.
Thailand and Vietnam are offering subsidies for rooftop solar installations, and the Philippines became the second-largest destination for Chinese solar exports in the first quarter of 2026.
text:
ANTALYA – Five countries have backed a plan to double the number of homes with rooftop solar panels worldwide by 2030, as U.N. climate talks in Turkey focus on expanding access to electricity and transitioning away from fossil fuels.

The new Global Rooftop Solar Declaration launched Tuesday on the second day of this year’s climate talks, known as COP31. The aim is to double the number of homes with rooftop solar panels from about 150 million today to at least 300 million by 2030.

“This is the future of affordable energy," said Sonia Dunlop, CEO of the Global Solar Council. "This is the way we can help average working people insure themselves from future price rises to come.”

COP31 comes after a year of deadly climate-related disasters and as concern grows that governments are not doing enough to curb global warming. Recent energy shocks from the Russia-Ukraine war and Iran war have also increased interest in renewables.

The U.N. climate talks have been criticized in the past for making promises that later fall flat. For rooftop solar goals to actually make a dent in the emissions contributing to climate change, experts said policies to upgrade power grids and subsidize solar panels and batteries must quickly follow.

“The pledge is a pledge," said Bruce Douglas, CEO of the Global Renewables Alliance. “We now need to see national policies and frameworks in place.”

More rooftop solar may help regular people

Bangladesh, Kenya, Nigeria and Vanuatu joined Australia by endorsing the rooftop solar declaration in the Turkish resort town of Antalya, where COP31 is being co-hosted by Turkey and Australia.

Lawmakers from 21 other countries — including the United Kingdom, South Africa and Sri Lanka — have also endorsed it. So has Indonesia’s state-owned electric power company Perusahaan Listrik Negara.

The declaration is voluntary and non-binding, like many of the agreements made at U.N. climate talks.

“We know the world is currently facing the greatest energy cost of living crisis the world has ever seen," Dunlop said. “We know that families all over the world are struggling to pay their bills and what we are saying with the Global Rooftop Solar Declaration is that we have a solution that will bring down your bills."

Electrification is a cornerstone of this year's talks, with Turkey pushing for electricity — preferably from renewables like solar and wind — to make up 35% of global energy consumption by 2035.

“Electrification by itself is incredibly beneficial because of the efficiency gains. Renewables by themselves, again, very beneficial. Put the two together and it is really a killer combination,” Douglas said.

Nations lean on fossil fuels, despite solar gains

Turkey's electrification pledge and Australia's rooftop solar declaration put a spotlight on the energy mix of both nations, which still rely heavily on fossil fuels.

In Turkey, home to one of Europe's largest solar farms, solar and wind make up nearly 23% of energy generation. But coal was still the country’s largest source of electricity last year, accounting for 33% of generation, according to Turkey’s Ministry of Energy and Natural Resources.

In Australia, one in three homes has rooftop solar and more than 700,000 homes have batteries to store excess energy. But coal still makes up more than 40% of electricity generation in Australia, which is also one of the world's largest coal exporters.

“Setting ambitious renewable targets without addressing grid capacity, storage and the continued role of coal risks undermining energy security, reliability and affordability," said Michelle Manook of FutureCoal, an industry-backed group formerly known as the World Coal Association.

The tension between renewable rollouts and continued coal use is mirrored in the world's most populous countries, China and India. They have both installed record-breaking amounts of renewables, but sometimes lose the energy because of insufficient transmission and storage capacity.

“Energy storage deployment must catch up with the speed of renewables deployment," said Nikit Abhyankar, with the India Energy and Climate Center at the University of California, Berkeley.

"Otherwise, it creates massive operational challenges for the grid, resulting in significant curtailment," he said, referring to the practice of limiting electricity output because the grid cannot handle it.

Solar spreads, but barriers remain

Rooftop solar panels are often decentralized from power grids, meaning that electricity is generated, stored and managed near where it is consumed, rather than coming from distant power plants.

This makes solar ideal for remote communities and hard-hit areas, like refugee camps and disaster zones.

Renewables, largely driven by solar from China and India, generated more than a third of the world's electricity last year, overtaking coal for the first time.

The Iran war's energy shock has also spurred solar interest in energy-hungry regions, like Southeast Asia, which was hit hard by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and sent into a state of energy triage.

Indonesia pledged to install 100 gigawatts of solar power by 2029. Thailand and Vietnam are offering subsidies for rooftop solar installations, and the Philippines became the second-largest destination for Chinese solar exports in the first quarter of 2026.

National policies must swiftly follow the COP31 promises to address issues like the funding of subsidies for consumers, clearer policies for solar companies and the availability of qualified installers, according to Sheryl Estella, with the nonprofit New Energy Nexus in the Philippines.

“This is an opportunity that we should not waste,” she said. “This is the biggest wave of interest in rooftop solar that we have seen so far.”

___

Delgado reported from Bangkok and Arasu from Bengaluru, India.

text:
Heinrich: “We don’t have to wait for the new Congress to start lowering costs. We can do that today. Let’s pass permitting reform.”

WASHINGTON – Today, U.S. Senators Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, held a press conference urging their Senate colleagues to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), bipartisan legislation to lower energy costs, hold data centers accountable for the costs they impose on American families, and create good-paying jobs.

With the Senate slated to vote on the legislation this evening, Heinrich and Whitehouse highlighted how BAAJA would help address rising electricity costs, accelerate the development of new energy infrastructure, and hold data centers accountable by forcing them to fully pay for their operational costs.

“Just one week ago Americans sent a clear message: They want Congress focused on making their lives more affordable. That’s precisely what this permitting reform bill will do,” said Heinrich. “BAAJA will save households billions of dollars in electricity costs, directly hold data centers accountable, create over 100,000 trades and manufacturing jobs, and cut emissions up to 20% from the power sector over the next decade.”

“The American people spoke loud and clear that they wanted results on affordability. BAAJA will mean billions in lower energy costs, and tens of billions of dollars more in ratepayer savings because of the provisions cracking down on data centers. And it can actually begin to happen now. People want to see Congress do big, good things. This is a big, good thing,” said Whitehouse.

Independent analyses find that BAAJA would lower Americans’ electricity bills by 3–5 percent, save families billions of dollars, nearly double the amount of solar and wind that can connect to the grid, and create up to 105,600 trades and manufacturing jobs. The legislation would also require data centers to cover the increased grid and energy costs they create, estimated at $55 billion over the next decade.

U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee Ranking Member Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) and U.S. Senate Environment and Public Works Committee Ranking Member U.S. Senator Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) host press conference to urge Senate passage of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, November 9, 2026.

Watch the full video of Heinrich’s remarks here.

A transcript of Heinrich’s remarks as delivered is below:

Every once in a while, I don’t wear my Senate pin, even if it means I’m going to get stopped on the way in.

I wear this pin.

It’s my dad’s 60-year IBEW pin, and he spent those 60 years keeping people’s lights on and working to keep their electricity bills affordable.

A little over a month ago, Senator Whitehouse and myself announced, along with our Republican colleagues, our bipartisan permitting bill.

And today, just one week after Americans sent a pretty resounding message about their priorities, we are taking our first vote on that legislation.

And that message that the people sent was pretty clear: they want Congress focused on making their lives more affordable, and that’s precisely what this permitting reform bill will do.

BAAJA will save households billions of dollars in electricity costs, so that families can have money in their pockets for more than just keeping the lights on and their homes warm.

This bill directly holds data centers accountable, forcing big corporations to pay their full share instead of pushing costs on the consumers.

That one provision is worth $35 billion dollars to American households.

That’s pretty remarkable.

BAAJA will create over 100,000 trades and manufacturing jobs, good-paying jobs that workers can be certain will be around to support their families through a project’s completion.

And BAAJA will cut emissions up to 20% from the power sector over the next decade, meaning cleaner air, healthier communities, and fewer healthcare costs.

This bill’s not perfect.

We’ve never pretended it was.

It is, after all, bipartisan, and that means that neither side got everything they want.

We had to find common ground.

We had to make compromises, and we had to work through some very real disagreements.

But bipartisanship doesn’t mean we stop listening, and it doesn’t mean we stop working to make the legislation better.

I have worked hard to incorporate the feedback that we’ve heard from Tribes and New Mexicans into our Manager’s Amendment, and I want to walk you through a few of those changes because they’re pretty important.

First, on Tribal consultation, I’ve heard directly from Tribal leaders about the importance of having a meaningful voice in decisions that affect their communities and affect their ancestral lands.

We work to strengthen that dramatically in this Manager’s Amendment.

Tribes will now have an equal seat with states in transmission planning, and federal agencies will be required, and let me say that again: required “shall” consult, not “may” consult, “shall” consult early with Tribes on projects that will affect important cultural sites, including on what properties are affected, the impacts of the project, and ways to avoid, minimize, or mitigate potential harms, and basically that means that mandatory Tribal consultation is now built into every single step of the Section 106 process by law.

We’ve also extended the window for objections to agency reports.

We’ve strengthened opportunities for states to weigh in, and we’ve given states a way to ask FERC to investigate local utility projects that gouge consumers.

That, in my view, is particularly important as private equity and other outside investors seek to take a larger role in electric utilities.

States need the tools to protect their ratepayers.

Third, we’ve made sure that workers’ rights are protected.

The Manager’s Amendment preserves collective bargaining agreements for union employees of the power of bargaining administrations, so that those workers can continue to bargain collectively and stand up for workers’ rights.

And finally, we’ve added a new Department of Energy Data Center Community Assistance Program because when a community is considering whether or not to grant a permit to a major data center, it needs to understand what that project will mean for its electricity supply, costs, water resources, infrastructure, and local economy, in order for them to make a good decision.

This program will give state, local, and Tribal governments the technical assistance they need to make their own informed decisions.

These are meaningful improvements.

They reflect the feedback that we’ve heard and they make an important piece of legislation, in my view, even stronger.

And importantly, they don’t change what this bill was always about: lowering energy costs, building the infrastructure our country so desperately needs, creating good-paying jobs, protecting our communities, and making sure that data centers pay their fair share.

That’s what we set out to accomplish when we started this project, and that’s what we’re still working to deliver.

So I would urge all my colleagues: Let’s get this done.

Let’s make it possible for America to build big things in this country again.

The people sent us a very clear message on Tuesday that they expect us to lower the costs in their daily lives.

We don’t have to wait for the new Congress to start lowering costs.

We can do that today.

So let’s pass permitting reform.
