title: US issues landmark construction permit for Texas SMR plant - World Nuclear News
description:
Later that month, the construction licence application for the plant was submitted to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC).
The construction permit authorises the facility to be built, but does not authorise operation: a separate operating licence will be needed before the reactors can be fuelled or operated.
The NRC completed its safety review for the plant when it released its Final Safety Evaluation Report for the construction permit application on 30 October.
"Today, the new NRC is issuing America's first construction permit for a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor in more than half a century," NRC Chairman Ho K. Nieh said.
"We delivered on the 18-month schedule, proving we can do rigorous safety reviews on predictable timelines that move advanced nuclear technology from design to construction."
text:
The plant, known as the Long Mott Generating Station, is being developed through Dow's wholly owned subsidiary, Long Mott Energy, in collaboration with X-energy under the US Department of Energy's Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program (ARDP).

Industrial giant Dow signed a joint development agreement with reactor developer X-energy in 2023. In March 2025, the company, alongside other major energy users, signed a pledge supporting the goal of at least tripling global nuclear capacity by 2050. Later that month, the construction licence application for the plant was submitted to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC).

Dow has not yet made a final decision to proceed with construction of the proposed facility: before potential construction activities could begin, further milestones including continued engineering and design finalisation and review by Dow's Board of Directors must be completed. But if approved, construction could begin later this decade, with startup early next decade, the company said. The company is expected to consider a preliminary investment decision in 2027.

The construction permit authorises the facility to be built, but does not authorise operation: a separate operating licence will be needed before the reactors can be fuelled or operated. However, the companies said, this means they can also work on maturing the supply chain for long-lead components and materials, as well as on their operating licence application. Ensuring the design, equipment, and materials are in place before allocating major capital for full-scale construction is consistent with Dow's global project management practices, and, for a first-of-a-kind project, reduces schedule and cost risk once work begins on site.

The NRC completed its safety review for the plant when it released its Final Safety Evaluation Report for the construction permit application on 30 October. X-energy CEO Clay Sell said the construction permit had been received earlier than expected, thanks, in part, to "thorough and efficient" work by the NRC plus Congressionally-mandated reforms put in place over the past six years. "This milestone is further validation of the XE regulatory approach that can be replicated across our growing commercial pipeline, giving our customers greater confidence in the regulatory process and a clearer path to deployment," he said.

Edward Stones, business vice president, Energy & Climate at Dow, described the issuance of the construction permit as a "testament to the thoughtful, thorough and efficient review conducted by the NRC", appreciating the regulator's commitment to maintaining the highest safety standards while advancing a clear and predictable regulatory process for advanced nuclear technologies. "As we move forward, we will continue to evaluate the project through the lens of competitiveness, execution readiness, and capital affordability before any decision regarding construction is made," he said.

A rendering of the plant (Image: X-energy)

Regulatory firsts

X-energy's Xe-100 is an 80 MWe/200 MWt high-temperature gas-cooled reactor which uses advanced TRISO-X coated particle fuel. The passive physics of the fuel - with the coating in effect providing each fuel particle its own containment for fission products which is stable up to very high temperatures - gives it a safety profile expected to support a 400-metre emergency planning zone, compared with 10 miles (16 kilometres) for conventional light-water reactors, enabling new generation to be safely sited closer to the point of need.

The proposed Long Mott plant is intended to provide both electricity and high-temperature steam to Dow's Seadrift site, replacing existing energy and steam assets near their end-of-life and providing clean industrial power to the site for 60 years and is expected to be the first advanced nuclear project deployed at an industrial site in North America.

The construction permit also marks several regulatory firsts for the NRC: its first approval of a multimodule advanced reactor facility; its first approval of a reactor with a pebble-bed core; its first approval of a design featuring online nuclear refuelling; and its first review of a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor under the agency's risk-informed, technology-inclusive Licensing Modernisation Project framework.

"Today, the new NRC is issuing America's first construction permit for a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor in more than half a century," NRC Chairman Ho K. Nieh said. "We delivered on the 18-month schedule, proving we can do rigorous safety reviews on predictable timelines that move advanced nuclear technology from design to construction."

title: This invisible, super-polluting gas is a climate villain the world is failing to tackle | CNN
description:
In the US, Carbon Mapper satellites have identified oil and gas sites with strong evidence of persistent methane pollution.
Global methane levels have been rising over recent years, reaching unprecedented highs in 2025.
Even as methane pollution increases, there are some positive signs.
Some companies are doing good job of accurately measuring, monitoring, reporting and reducing methane pollution, Brownstein said.
Companies have a responsibility to manage their methane pollution, “because a lot of this has an economic payback,” he said.
text:
Every day, two satellites crisscross the planet from north to south around 16 times, taking hundreds of photos. They’re hunting something invisible and odorless, but which has an outsized impact on our lives: methane.

The satellites are run by Carbon Mapper, a non-profit environmental organization that patrols the globe remotely looking for methane “super-emitters,” the small number of sources — from oil and gas operations to landfills — that make up a big percentage of total methane pollution.

In the US, Carbon Mapper satellites have identified oil and gas sites with strong evidence of persistent methane pollution. So far this year, Orla, Texas, tops its list with eight large plumes recorded, followed by Stanton, Texas, and Ringold, Louisiana.

🌬️ Get your local forecast from the CNN Weather app.

Mega-leaks are not just happening in the US, they are a global problem, from Turkmenistan to Venezuela. They used to be invisible — under-monitored and underestimated — but these plumes are now increasingly spotted from space as high-resolution satellites pinpoint them with precision.

Carbon dioxide is the number one driver of climate change, but methane is a much more powerful planet-heating gas in the short term — trapping roughly 80 times more heat over a 20-year time frame. The super-pollutant is responsible for about 30% of today’s warming.

If humanity is to have any chance of keeping a livable planet, tackling methane offers one of the fastest ways to reduce global temperatures. “Any reductions that we make today on methane, we could see (the benefits of) within our lifetime,” said Dan Cusworth, vice president of science at Carbon Mapper. “It makes a lot of sense to go after it.”

Yet global methane levels continue to rise, and experts say efforts to tackle the crisis are fragmented and insufficient to meet the urgency of the situation. Worse still, some countries are backtracking.

About 40% of methane comes from natural sources like wetlands. The rest is produced by human activities, including oil, gas and coal production, farming and landfills.

Global methane levels have been rising over recent years, reaching unprecedented highs in 2025. China was the biggest methane polluter last year, mostly due to its coal mining operations, followed by the US and Russia, according to a recent IEA report.

Around 35% of human-produced methane comes from the fossil fuel industry, and there is “still no sign” of it falling, the report found.

The good news is that it’s not that hard to tackle. Technology exists to cut around 70% of emissions from fossil fuel production, according to the IEA. What’s more, methane can be harnessed for value — it’s a potential fuel.

“This is one of the ironies,” said Edward Parson, an environmental law professor at UCLA. “If you’re in the oil and gas production business, methane is a potential product.” It’s a particularly attractive prospect as the Iran war pushes up oil and gas prices.

Yet, governments have recently moved to undo or postpone action on the super-pollutant.

Last month, the Trump administration announced plans to significantly weaken Biden-era rules targeting the amount of methane the oil and gas industry can produce — these were projected to have cut the sector’s pollution by 80% through 2038.

The Environmental Protection Agency has proposed to significantly weaken these rules, including eliminating the “Super Emitter Program” — an initiative to detect, investigate and fix large methane releases or leaks — and relaxing rules for “marginal” wells which don’t produce much oil and gas but do produce a lot of methane pollution.

The EPA is selling the rollback as an economic boon, saying it will save $45 billion in consumer and business costs and casting it as the latest salvo in President Trump’s pledge to “end the war on oil and natural gas.”

Critics pushed back strongly. “The American people pick up the tab three times over,” said Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, a Democrat representing Rhode Island. “Higher energy bills from wasted natural gas; higher health care costs, as the fumes pollute our air; and higher climate change costs through higher insurance premiums and more burned and flooded homes.”

The US is not alone in reducing ambition. The European Union voted last month to approve a three-year delay for rules requiring foreign oil, gas and coal importers to monitor and report their methane pollution. It’s not a trivial move, said Mark Brownstein, senior vice president of energy at the Environmental Defense Fund. “Every year of delay comes with real cost.”

UCLA’s Parson puts the blame for backtracking seen this year on intensifying pressure from fossil fuel interests. “It’s an indication of the determination and muscle of the industry to fight on every front to resist any regulatory restrictions,” he said.

Holly Hopkins, a vice president at the American Petroleum Institute, which represents the US oil and gas sector, said the industry “is working every day to reduce methane emissions while meeting growing demand for affordable energy.” The API “supports the direct regulation of methane emissions” and is working with the administration on a “balanced, workable approach,” she added.

Even as methane pollution increases, there are some positive signs.

Oil and gas production has been rising globally, yet the industry’s methane pollution has remained fairly flat. Some companies are doing good job of accurately measuring, monitoring, reporting and reducing methane pollution, Brownstein said. Although, he added, “you’re not seeing that level of progress uniformly across the entire industry.”

There have also been fewer super-emitting events from countries such as Argentina and Algeria, as well as signs that growth in China’s coal mine methane pollution might be slowing, according to the IEA.

And in the US, while the federal government may be undoing methane regulations, several states, including California and New Mexico, have their own regulations.

Still, many want far more ambition. “Having really strong government leadership is so critical to this,” Carbon Mapper’s Cusworth said.

Changing industry norms is also key, according to Brownstein. Companies have a responsibility to manage their methane pollution, “because a lot of this has an economic payback,” he said.

As the planet heats up and enters a new era of climate extremes, from deadly flooding to brutal heat waves, the spotlight should be on methane, according to Brownstein. “Virtually the only thing that we can do to lessen the frequency and severity of events like that is reduce methane emissions,” he said.

While the world decides how fast it wishes to tackle this super-pollutant, satellites will continue to orbit the Earth making clear the scale of the problem.

It can be frustrating, Cusworth said. “You see a lot of things that could be fixed relatively easily,” he said, “sometimes it’s like I want to get on a plane with a wrench, go out and fix it.”

For drivers tired of watching fuel prices swing, the VF 8 offers a compelling alternative: significantly lower energy costs, a 10-year warranty, and the peace of mind of knowing what ownership will look like years from now. For Canadians looking beyond the sticker price, VinFast gives them plenty to think about.

text:
WeaveGrid, a grid orchestration software provider for electric utilities, has launched a managed charging program in partnership with North Carolina’s Electric Cooperatives, an organization that supports the state’s 26 community-based electric cooperatives.

The new program, EVConnectNC, allows members of participating cooperatives to earn incentives by charging their EVs during off-peak hours.

EVConnectNC uses connected vehicle and charger data to help cooperatives monitor charging patterns and encourage members to shift electricity use to lower-cost periods. The program is already operating at two North Carolina cooperatives, Roanoke Electric Cooperative and South River EMC.

North Carolina’s Electric Cooperatives and its member utilities operate the program, and WeaveGrid provides the software platform.

Utility customers enrolled in the program can earn up to $120 annually by charging at least 90% of the time during off-peak hours and using a minimum of 200 kilowatt-hours per month.

At the moment, the program appears to work only with certain EVs, including models from Dodge, Jeep, Lexus, Tesla and Toyota; and certain home chargers, including models from ChargePoint, Emporia and Wallbox.

EVConnectNC also provides participating cooperatives with information about the effects of EV charging on their electrical systems. WeaveGrid’s grid orchestration software is designed to help utilities manage increasing electricity demand by aligning consumption with available grid capacity. Through its Distribution-Integrated System Capacity Orchestration (DISCO) platform, the company provides asset-level visibility and device-level control to manage EVs, batteries and other flexible electrical loads.

“As member-owned, not-for-profit utilities, electric cooperatives have a long history of embracing innovative solutions that deliver value to our members,” said Nikki Lynberg, Manager of Innovation and Business Development for North Carolina’s Electric Cooperatives. “This program gives EV-driving members a way to save on charging costs while helping cooperatives manage energy use more efficiently.”

“Managed charging isn’t just a tool for large investor-owned utilities,” said Apoorv Bhargava, CEO and co-founder of WeaveGrid. “It’s a practical, member-focused way for cooperatives to meet growing demand without passing new costs on to the people they serve.”

title: The suburbs are getting a makeover. That's a climate win.
description:
For generations, suburban development in the U.S. has largely followed the same simple formula, leading to virtually identical big box stores, drive-through restaurants, and McMansions across the country.
That’s all good news for the climate, because business-as-usual sprawl increases climate pollution and complicates efforts to adapt to extreme weather.

text:
For generations, suburban development in the U.S. has largely followed the same simple formula, leading to virtually identical big box stores, drive-through restaurants, and McMansions across the country.

But that’s changing.

Outside Austin, Texas, a defunct shopping mall and its parking lots were turned into a dense neighborhood where people can navigate between offices, apartments, restaurants, parks, and educational spaces without a car.

Austin, Texas’s former Highland Mall was transformed into a walkable neighborhood anchored by a community college campus. (Image credits: BGK Architects (left), © Dror Baldinger, FAIA)

In Babylon, New York, a site containing a strip mall and parking lot was redeveloped to provide high-quality high-rise housing and amenities for residents of a poor community.

In an affluent suburb of Charlotte, North Carolina, a golf course was turned into a dense, walkable district complete with a park designed to reduce flood risk.

That’s all good news for the climate, because business-as-usual sprawl increases climate pollution and complicates efforts to adapt to extreme weather.

June Williamson, an architecture professor at the City College of New York, said projects like these are becoming so common that within a few decades, suburbia at large could look and function very differently.

“Over time, site by site, you’ll begin to see a pretty substantial transformation,” she said.

Business-as-usual suburban development is a climate problem

In the Charlotte suburb of Ballantyne, a golf course was replaced by a dense neighborhood and a park designed to reduce flood risk. (Image credits: Sarah Wesseler (left); courtesy of LandDesign)

The sheer scale of the American suburbs makes them an important focus for climate action. Car-centric suburbs account for the vast majority of the developed land in major American cities and, according to Williamson, house about 60% of the country’s residents.

“The United States is a suburban nation – has been for some time,” she said.

People living in these areas have higher carbon footprints than their city-center counterparts. Car dependency is partly to blame, as common suburban design features like cul-de-sacs, winding roads, and large parking lots lock in high rates of car use, helping make transportation the U.S.’s largest source of climate pollution.

And detached single-family houses – the only form of housing that’s legally permissible to build in many U.S. communities – require more energy to heat and cool than homes with shared walls, such as row houses and apartments.

These community designs also complicate efforts to adapt to climate change. On hot days, large paved surfaces like parking lots reflect heat instead of absorbing it, unlike natural surfaces like grass and soil. Paving also raises the risk of flooding by preventing rainwater from soaking into the ground.

What’s more, Williamson said, suburban developers have often built housing in floodplains, as well as on the fringes of wild areas, where fire risk can be higher. Both flooding and wildfires are getting more frequent and extreme because of climate change, increasing the danger to residents.

The rise of suburban retrofits

Williamson and Ellen Dunham-Jones, an architecture professor at Georgia Tech, have written several books about the growing wave of suburban development focused on existing sites, which they refer to as suburban retrofitting.

Created through a public-private partnership between the city of Austin and a real estate developer, Austin’s Mueller neighborhood replaced a defunct airport with a walkable community. (Image credit: Philip Jones)

Compared to developments that follow a standard template, these projects take a much more nuanced, customized approach, focusing on bringing specific benefits to their communities. Typically led by some combination of local governments and private-sector groups like property owners and developers, many of these projects are also supported, or even initiated, by local residents, as well as designers, nonprofits, and universities.

Collectively, these projects have adopted a more environmentally friendly approach than the suburban development template established in the wake of World War II, which relies heavily on cookie-cutter subdivisions and shopping centers fronted by large parking lots.

“When these suburbs were designed, almost nobody was using the word ‘sustainability’,” Dunham-Jones said.

But protecting the environment is often not the main driver for suburban retrofits. One common motive is raising public revenue. When developments like malls and office parks fail, they can leave a huge gap in their communities’ finances, prompting local governments to seek other uses for the sites.

“They desperately need the tax revenue,” Dunham-Jones explained.

Housing demand is also a factor.

“We’re in the biggest housing shortage in generations,” said Katharine Burgess, the vice president of programs and operations at Smart Growth America, a nonprofit focused on sustainable communities. “To accomplish some of the very ambitious housing goals that cities and regions have right now, we really need to look more broadly at opportunities for infill beyond just downtown-type sites.”

Infill refers to development that occurs within existing neighborhoods.

Reducing car dependency

High demand for communities where people can meet their daily needs without having to drive also plays a role. These projects can help offer the walkable lifestyles that Americans are hungry for, but that are available in only a tiny fraction of the country.

“People want alternatives,” said Williamson.

Another factor is the growing awareness that car dependency harms public health and reduces affordability.

The Pike District in Montgomery County, Maryland, a suburb of Washington, D.C., offers one example of an ambitious project aiming to reduce car dependency. Since 2010, the county government and local partners have been working to transform a four-mile-long suburban corridor into a walkable district combining residential buildings, offices, and commercial facilities. The project also provides residents, workers, and visitors access to trains, bus rapid transit service, and bike trails.

Increasingly ambitious projects

In the two decades that Dunham-Jones and Williamson have been studying suburban retrofits, ambitions for these projects have expanded in scope.

“Increasingly, communities are saying, ‘OK, while you’re reducing automobile dependency, what are you doing to improve public health, to support an aging population, especially in suburbia?’” Dunham-Jones said. “‘What are you doing to leverage social capital for equity? What are you doing to compete for jobs?’ And then the big one of climate change: ‘What are you doing to add water and energy resilience?’”

These challenges have complementary solutions. Creating denser developments with multifamily housing options close to common destinations like workplaces, schools, stores, and parks can help reduce car dependency, generate tax revenue, and support public health by enabling people to get more exercise walking and biking.

Thoughtful, community-centered project planning can support social equity and help people of all ages thrive, in part by reducing the need to own, maintain, and buy gas for expensive private cars that children and some older people can’t rely on to get around independently.

In Babylon, New York, a suburban site was redeveloped to provide high-quality housing and amenities for an economically disadvantaged population. The project team included local governments and a nonprofit sustainability group. (Image credit: Phillip Jones)

And the nation’s vast supply of existing suburban sites is a critical resource for helping communities meet their needs in the coming decades.

“We don’t have to tear down another tree, ever. We can accommodate our growth now,” Dunham-Jones said. “We have so much of this stuff.”

text:
(MARYSVILLE, Ohio)— Ohio Governor Mike DeWine joined leaders from Honda, JobsOhio, One Columbus, and Union County today to announce that Honda will build a new auto plant in Central Ohio, investing approximately $3 billion and creating more than 2,000 new jobs.

Gov. DeWine-

“Honda’s leadership could have chosen to build this plant anywhere in the world, but they chose Ohio because there are so many advantages to being here. For almost half a century, Honda and Ohio have grown together, and generations of families have built their careers on Honda’s manufacturing lines. Today’s announcement isn’t just an investment in a new facility – it’s an investment in Ohio’s people and Ohio’s future.”

The new plant will be Honda’s fourth auto plant in Ohio, building on nearly 50 years of manufacturing in the state. With a planned capacity of 240,000 vehicles a year, it will have the flexibility to produce multiple vehicle types and powertrains, including hybrid, gasoline-powered, and battery-electric vehicles.

MORE: Interview with Gov. DeWine, Event B-Roll, and Full Recording of Event

In addition to the new plant, Honda is also investing in Honda’s Anna Engine Plant and Honda Transmission Plant-Ohio to expand production of engines and hybrid systems. In total, Honda’s new commitment in Ohio is 2,390 new jobs and a new investment of $3.38 billion.

Bob Nelson, executive vice president, American Honda Motor Co., Inc.

“Ohio and its workforce have laid the groundwork that has written some of the most impactful chapters in Honda’s story of growth and innovation. This investment reflects our commitment to building products close to our customers, and our confidence in the people, partners and communities of Ohio.”

The plant will be located between Honda’s Marysville and East Liberty auto plants, and production is expected to begin in 2029, pending final government approvals. When it comes online, the plant will be one of the most advanced in the world, with leading-edge automation, data-driven technologies and flexible production systems.

Honda selected Ohio based on a number of factors, including its highly skilled workforce; close proximity to a large concentration of Honda’s U.S. supply base; nearby vehicle development operations, including Honda Development & Manufacturing of America, the North American Automotive Development Center and the Transportation Research Center; existing Honda manufacturing operations for vehicles, engines and hybrid systems; and the L-H Battery Company joint venture, which will have the flexibility to produce battery cells for both hybrid and all-electric vehicles.

Honda also announced the retooling of its Honda Transmission Plant-Ohio in Russells Point, Ohio, to support production of two next-generation Honda Hybrid systems, which will increase Ohio’s hybrid system production capacity by 250 percent in the coming years. Honda Transmission Plant-Ohio will also serve as the lead plant for a new Honda hybrid system for larger models. Honda will also retool a production line at the Anna Engine Plant to build a next-generation four-cylinder engine and expand an on-site parts consolidation center.

JobsOhio President and CEO J.P. Nauseef

“This latest investment reinforces the state’s position at the forefront of the automotive industry’s future. With the nation’s second-largest auto manufacturing workforce and a robust supplier network at the heart of the North American auto market, Ohio is the ideal destination for Honda’s first greenfield auto assembly facility of this scale in Ohio in more than 35 years. Honda isn’t just investing in a new facility. It’s doubling down on our people, our manufacturing strength, and the next generation of workers who will build the future of the automotive industry.”

Jonas Peterson, chief economic development officer and president of One Columbus

“Honda’s long history in Union County got us to the starting line. The Region won this investment by demonstrating the skilled workforce, manufacturing know-how, and regional collaboration Honda needs to build its future. The message is unmistakable: the next generation of Honda has a home in the Columbus Region.”

The project was approved for a tax credit this morning by the Ohio Tax Credit Authority. Honda also plans to pursue assistance from JobsOhio, which will be made public after a final agreement is executed. Start of construction is pending government approvals.

Honda announced its first Ohio plant in 1977 and began building motorcycles in Marysville with 64 associates in 1979. In 1982, it built the first Japanese-brand car made in the United States at the Marysville Auto Plant. Since then, Honda’s Ohio operations have grown to more than 15,000 associates and more than $15 billion in investment. Today, Ohio is home to the Marysville and East Liberty auto plants and the Performance Manufacturing Center; the Anna Engine Plant, Honda’s largest engine plant in the world; Honda Transmission Plant-Ohio, which builds two-motor hybrid systems for U.S.-made Honda vehicles, including the CR-V, Accord and Civic; Honda’s largest research and development center outside of Japan; and the L-H Battery joint venture with LG Energy Solution in Fayette County.

Honda’s growth has helped make Ohio a leader in American auto manufacturing. Ohio ranks No. 1 in the nation in engine production and No. 2 in transmissions, and about 100,000 Ohioans work in the auto industry. Honda works with more than 750 original equipment suppliers in North America, and many of the suppliers that support Honda’s Ohio operations are based in communities across the state.

Ohio was named America’s No. 1 Top State for Business in 2026 by CNBC. Since 2013, JobsOhio has helped win more than 130 economic development projects with Japanese-owned companies, and more than 65,000 Ohioans work at Japanese-owned facilities across the state.

text:

Electric vehicles have plenty going for them. They're quiet, deliver instant acceleration, and let owners skip the gas station altogether. That's an appealing combination, especially for anyone who's tired of watching fuel prices fluctuate. But spending money on a new car takes more than a little enthusiasm for new technology. Based on recent research, Canadians are increasingly intrigued by EVs.

J.D. Power's 2026 Canada Electric Vehicle Consideration Study found that 34% of new-vehicle shoppers are considering an EV, compared with 28% in 2025 1. This marks the first increase since the study began in 2022.

What's holding others back?

One headwind is ownership costs, particularly when keeping a conventional vehicle on the road is becoming more expensive. In September 2026, J.D. Power reported that the average dealership service bill in Canada had reached C$566 for vehicles aged four to 12 years, a 51% increase from 2020 2.

Electric vehicles have an advantage here. Without an internal combustion engine, there's no need for oil changes, and regenerative braking can reduce wear on conventional brakes.

For automakers hoping to win over Canadian buyers, an impressive specification sheet may no longer be enough as a Leger survey commissions by Rates.ca found that 45% of Canadians interested in or undecided about EVs were concerned about maintenance and repair expenses 3. The vehicle also needs to make financial sense several years after leaving the showroom.

VinFast, the Vietnamese EV manufacturer behind the VF 8 electric SUVs, is tackling that concern with extensive warranty coverage, potentially lower running costs, and a growing range of ownership services.

Warranty terms become considerably more important once the odometer starts climbing.

In Canada, VinFast offers a 10-year or 200,000-km new vehicle limited warranty on the five-seat VF 8, whichever comes first. Their high-voltage batteries receive separate coverage for 10 years with unlimited kilometres under standard personal use, subject to warranty conditions.

To put those numbers into perspective, a driver covering 20,000 km annually could spend an entire decade behind the wheel before reaching the vehicle warranty's mileage limit. Someone travelling substantially farther would also benefit from the absence of a kilometre restriction on the battery warranty.

Beyond warranty protection, VinFast has another argument that may appeal to Canadians who spend plenty of time on the road: electricity generally costs considerably less than gasoline.

The prospect of spending thousand of dollars less on energy over three years is worth examining if you regularly cover long distances.

Then comes charging, which remains a practical consideration for Canadian EV owners, particularly on longer journeys. VinFast's mobile app provides access to more than 250,000 Level 2 and DC fast-charging stations across North America. Besides helping drivers locate participating stations, it can plan routes with charging stops and manage charging sessions, making unfamiliar journeys easier to organize.

For drivers tired of watching fuel prices swing, the VF 8 offers a compelling alternative: significantly lower energy costs, a 10-year warranty, and the peace of mind of knowing what ownership will look like years from now. For Canadians looking beyond the sticker price, VinFast gives them plenty to think about.

WASHINGTON (AP) — Senate Republicans were meeting Tuesday for a “robust conversation” on their future and to decide whether to keep South Dakota Sen. John Thune as their leader, just a week after steep losses in the midterm elections that cost them their majority.

Thune is expected to be reelected, given that he remains popular with his GOP colleagues and is running unopposed. But some Republicans who returned to Washington on Monday for the first time since the election wipeout that cost them at least seven seats said it's too soon to endorse the status quo.

“We need to have some real soul-searching,” said Wisconsin Sen. Ron Johnson, who circulated a letter to the conference asking for a delay in the closed-door, secret-ballot leadership elections. “We can't just continue on business as usual — that kind of defeat demands change.”

Still, Johnson conceded that there's no one else on the ballot.

“That's part of our problem, who would want the job?” he said, turning to a reporter and joking, “Do you want it?”

The angst comes as the party is just beginning to reckon with what the election results mean for GOP lawmakers and how soon they can try to rebuild their ranks. Two additional races remain uncalled in Alaska and Mississippi that could further deplete their numbers.

Thune made clear Monday that the leadership is moving ahead with Senate elections, which will include contests for other party leaders as well. But senators could still seek a vote to delay as they gather Tuesday morning.

Thune said they will have a “very fulsome, robust conversation about where we go from here and then we’ll see what the consensus of the conference is.”

“Ultimately that’s a decision made by Republican senators,” Thune said.

Thune, who replaced Sen. Mitch McConnell of Kentucky as leader in early 2025, has spent much of the last two years navigating President Donald Trump, who has often been at odds with the Senate.

While backing up Trump on most policy, Thune has refused to change Senate rules and scrap the filibuster to pass voting legislation that would require proof of citizenship for all voters — a position that frustrated Trump and enraged some in the president's political base.

But Trump hosted Thune and his family at the White House in October. He said Monday that the GOP leader is “a very fine man.” The election is “up to the Senate,” Trump said.

Thune has made it a point to hear out different viewpoints before he makes major decisions and has maintained close relationships with the rank and file — a different approach from his predecessor, McConnell.

Thune “has widespread support” among Republican senators, said Oklahoma Sen. Jim Lankford, who said he supports having the elections on Tuesday when many of the new GOP senators are already in town for freshman orientation.

It is “a pretty complicated role to be able to manage,” Lankford said. “No one wants that job.”

Still, Johnson and others in his conference say Tuesday’s election is too soon.

Pennsylvania Sen. Dave McCormick in a statement over the weekend said Republicans shouldn’t choose a leader until the lessons of the election have been “digested and debated.” Indiana Sen. Jim Banks said Republicans need to “sit down and have a frank conversation about where we fell short.”

Republican Sen. Mike Lee of Utah, one of a few senators who signed Johnson's letter asking for a delay, said any leadership contest should come after the two outstanding Senate elections in Alaska and Mississippi are decided.

Neither of those races has yet been called, so it’s unclear if Republican Sens. Dan Sullivan of Alaska and Cindy Hyde-Smith of Mississippi will be returning to the Senate next year.

The soul-searching comes as lawmakers are trying to wrap up the year’s work — funding the government and seeing if there are some issues where they can work together, including an energy permitting bill that moved forward on a bipartisan vote Monday evening.

Republicans will try to confirm as many of Trump’s nominees as they can before the new Congress begins Jan. 3, and Democrats will strategize on how to best keep up their momentum into next year.

In his first remarks on the Senate floor since the election, which he called a “tough night," Thune previewed his pitch to his colleagues who are looking for answers on how they will navigate the minority.

Republicans will be willing to work with Democrats, Thune said, but “the American people are not looking for socialist government and leftist fantasies.”

Across the aisle, Democrats who could hold as many as 56 seats next year are having private discussions about whether New York Sen. Chuck Schumer is still the right person to lead them.

Schumer has found critics on the left and the right of his caucus as candidates from both sides declined to say in the campaign whether they would support him as leader. Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen and Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin have both considered challenging Schumer, but neither has announced a run.

Many in the party have said it’s time for generational change after Schumer’s 12 years as leader. Still, Schumer appears to have widespread support from his members after carrying his party to massive wins in Tuesday’s elections.

Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, Schumer’s New York colleague and the head of the Democratic Senate campaign arm, predicted that he will win enough support. Schumer not only won the Senate back but he “cares deeply, and he understands politics well," she said.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., center, poses for a photograph in his office with Sen.-elects Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich., Josh Turek, D-Iowa, Roy Cooper, D-N.C., Juliana Stratton, D-Ill., and Chris Pappas, D-N.H., Monday, Nov. 9, 2026, at the U.S. Capitol in Washington. (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson)

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., heads to an intelligence briefing in a secure room in the basement of the Capitol with the director of national intelligence and other congressional leaders, as Congress returns to work following the midterm elections, at the Capitol in Washington, Monday, Nov. 9, 2026. title: Slight fall in carbon emissions from fossil fuels as Iran war drives renewables push
description:
Soaring oil and gas prices following the war in Iran have encouraged people to look beyond fossil fuels, leading to an easing of climate-damaging carbon emissions this year.
Emissions from burning oil alone will drop by 2% as drivers economise on fuel use and flock to electric vehicles instead.
The reduction in emissions from fossil fuels for 2026 will be about 0.4% compared with last year.
Many factors could disrupt the fragile trend of slowing emissions from fossil fuels, including an intensified expansion of coal in India, an easing of oil prices and US president Donald Trump’s enthusiasm for fossil fuels.
Global emissions must peak imminently and fall rapidly in subsequent years if the world is to have a chance of limiting the “overshoot” of temperatures above 1.5C.
text:
Soaring oil and gas prices following the war in Iran have encouraged people to look beyond fossil fuels, leading to an easing of climate-damaging carbon emissions this year.

Carbon dioxide from oil, gas and coal is forecast to flatline for 2026, based on data from the year so far, according to a comprehensive assessment by scientists. Emissions from burning oil alone will drop by 2% as drivers economise on fuel use and flock to electric vehicles instead.

The findings, presented on Tuesday morning at the Cop31 climate talks hosted by Turkey in Antalya, show both the impact of the Iran war and the global expansion of cheap renewable energy, chiefly solar and wind power.

Talk of a global turnaround would be premature, however, the report’s authors and other analysts said. The report was published in Nature Climate Change. The reduction in emissions from fossil fuels for 2026 will be about 0.4% compared with last year.

Yet this year’s slight fall could be temporary, and was more than offset by increased emissions from deforestation and land use change, following major fires in south-east Asia and further conversions of wild land to agriculture.

Many factors could disrupt the fragile trend of slowing emissions from fossil fuels, including an intensified expansion of coal in India, an easing of oil prices and US president Donald Trump’s enthusiasm for fossil fuels. Much greater investment in renewable energy, and low-carbon technology such as electric vehicles, would still be required to make permanent reductions in annual emissions, the report’s authors said.

Glen Peters, research professor at the Cicero Centre for International Climate Research, said: “A drop in emissions in one year is not a peak, unless it is driven by structural change. Accelerated deployment of solar, wind, batteries and electric vehicles are pushing emissions down in dozens of countries, and slowing emissions growth in many more, but the changes are not sufficient to lock in a peak in global emissions.”

About 38.2bn tonnes of CO2 will be emitted this year, according to the Global Carbon Budget, an annual assessment by scientists from scores of universities and science institutions around the world, published in the journal Earth System Science Data.

Energy demand continues to increase around the world, as more people gain access to electricity and are pulled out of poverty, but two-thirds of the increase is being met from rising generation from the sun and wind and the uptake of electric vehicles.

On the downside, emissions from deforestation and the conversion of land to agriculture have also ticked upward this year, leading to total carbon emissions rising slightly for the year, from 42.8bn tonnes last year to 43.3bn forecast for 2026.

The scientists warned that the world’s remaining “carbon budget” – the amount of carbon that can be poured into the atmosphere before global heating is likely to permanently exceed 1.5C above pre-industrial levels – was about 150bn tonnes, or less than four years at current rates.

Already, temperatures have exceeded the 1.5C threshold for more than two years, and El Niño conditions are heating the sea and air further. Global emissions must peak imminently and fall rapidly in subsequent years if the world is to have a chance of limiting the “overshoot” of temperatures above 1.5C.

China, the world’s biggest emitter of greenhouse gases, is likely to reduce its carbon output by close to 1% this year, mostly because of a 5% reduction in oil use, following the Iran war. Peters said: “China has had flat emissions for the last few years after a fairly steep increase in the last decade. There’s been a lot of discussion about whether China has peaked or not. Whether this is just a one-off and China rebounds next year, we’ll have to wait and see, it’s too early to say.”

India’s emissions have grown strongly, mostly from an increase in coal use, while the country’s oil use has declined slightly. Emissions from the US are likely to fall by about 1.3% this year, as less coal is used, despite Trump’s attempts to boost it.

Bill Hare, chief executive of Climate Analytics, who was not involved in the research, cautioned against taking too much from the report. “The picture from the Global Carbon Budget is a flatline, not a decline – a projected fall of just 0.4% in 2026, a figure that is unfortunately statistically indistinguishable from zero,” he said. “We are heading towards a sustained breach of 1.5C by around 2030. With imminent overshoot, we are entitled to expect governments everywhere to move decisively to cut fossil fuel CO2 emissions.”

There seemed little sign of such a decisive move at Cop31, where more than 90 heads of state and government, and high-level representatives from more than 190 countries are gathering for a fortnight of talks on the climate crisis.

title: Senators Advance Bipartisan Permitting Reform. Democrats Were Divided.
description:

Monday’s vote was a major test of how willing Democrats, fresh off a midterms sweep, are to work with Republicans — especially on a bill Trump supports.
The bill will need to pass a final vote in the Senate and be taken up by the House.
As the procedural vote neared, though, it became clear that fewer Democratic senators were interested in tying themselves to the bill.
“This becomes our biggest implemented climate bill,” he said.
text:
The Senate will move forward with its bipartisan permitting reform package, with the legislation overcoming a key procedural vote Monday. The vote to proceed on the bill passed 73 to 25.

Fifty-one Republicans, 21 Democrats and one Independent voted to advance the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which would make changes to long-standing environmental laws that proponents say could speed up energy and infrastructure development.

That’s a selling point for President Donald Trump, who urged senators to vote in favor of the legislation, plugging it on TruthSocial as a “BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE” that could ensure new pipelines, mines and power plants get built.

But the bill has also attracted support from climate solutions advocates, who say the reforms are key to unlocking a transition to clean energy and reducing climate-warming emissions.

Trending

The package also includes provisions that would force data center developers to pay more for connecting to the power grid, and includes a community assistance program that would offer analysis and help for local governments where data centers are proposed.

The deal was negotiated between Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-Rhode Island), Martin Heinrich (D-New Mexico), Mike Lee (R-Utah) and Shelley Moore Capito (R-West Virginia). Monday’s vote was a major test of how willing Democrats, fresh off a midterms sweep, are to work with Republicans — especially on a bill Trump supports.

The bill will need to pass a final vote in the Senate and be taken up by the House. Trump’s support may buoy the deal’s chances in the House, where Republicans hold a narrow majority, though it remains to be seen where House Democrats will fall. Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries indicated opposition to the bill before the amendment was released and said Monday he was still reviewing the package.

After a weekend amendment that responded to critiques from environmental groups, tribal leaders and the utility industry, the bill received fresh support from outside groups. As the procedural vote neared, though, it became clear that fewer Democratic senators were interested in tying themselves to the bill.

Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Oregon) voted against taking up the bill, saying he’d rather punt the issue to the next Congress with a Democratic majority. Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Illinois) voted no, saying she was concerned the package could hand Trump more power. Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-New Mexico) also voted against the bill, citing concerns from tribal leaders.

Over the weekend, Evergreen Action, a climate advocacy group, put its weight behind the package. The Edison Electric Institute, which represents investor-owned utility companies that historically have not backed permitting reform attempts, said it would “help put more steel in the ground, cut unnecessary government red tape, and deliver more affordable, reliable energy.”

The Heritage Foundation was impressed that the amendment strengthened reliability requirements and tied transmission costs to demonstrable economic benefits.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune also called for Republicans to support the bill in a speech on the Senate floor Monday afternoon, framing it as a “bipartisan win” that Congress could notch before both chambers turn blue.

But opposition, particularly from the left, has also grown. A group of tribal leaders and other advocates dedicated to protecting the National Historic Preservation Act rallied in front of the Capitol on Monday afternoon, calling for legislators to kill the bill.

Several House Democrats spoke in opposition to the bill, including Reps. Jared Huffman of California, Melanie Stansbury of New Mexico, Rashida Tlaib of Michigan and Adelita Grijalva of Arizona.

Leonard Forsman, the chairman of the Suquamish Tribe who has worked in cultural resources management as an archaeologist, called on the Senate to reject the bill.

“Efficiency must never come at the expense of tribal sovereignty, treaty rights, or the destruction of sacred places,” he said. “We should not have to choose between responsible development and protecting our ancestors. We can do both.”

Concerns from tribal leaders prompted Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto (D-Nevada), who has called for permitting reform legislation in the past, to say she would not support the bill unless provisions that affect tribal rights are removed, Punchbowl News reported. Cortez Matso voted in favor of the Senate considering the bill.

“I cannot ignore the concerns that Tribes in Nevada have with this bill text,” Cortez Masto said.

The bill split some of the Senate’s most climate-focused Democrats.

Sen. Brian Schatz (Hawai’i), an outspoken climate advocate, voted yes, saying the bill presents a “rare opportunity” to pass bipartisan legislation that could lower costs and build clean energy. Schatz said he would introduce amendments and continue working to “ensure Native Hawaiian organizations and Tribes have a meaningful voice in decisions affecting their communities.”

Sen. Adam Schiff (D-California), also a climate advocate, voted against it.

Green groups are also divided on the bill. The Environmental Defense Fund said it supported allowing the process to move forward and for improvements to be made.

The League of Conservation Voters, which also said it still had concerns about the legislation after the amendment, said it would not “score” lawmakers on Monday’s vote, allowing Democrats to support the bill in moving forward without being docked on their climate record. But a spokesperson said the organization reserves the right to score future votes, depending on further changes.

Jenn Tyler, head of government affairs for Citizens Climate Lobby, a nonpartisan group advocating for federal climate solutions, told The Sun the bill could be a key to tackling carbon emissions.

“It’s pretty clear to us that the only real ways to address climate change are either to have an economic collapse, or to build stuff faster — to build clean energy faster,” she said. “We’d rather not have an economic collapse, so we are fully behind, how do we build clean energy faster?”

After weekend amendments, new modeling from Greenline Insights and the Center for Climate and Energy Solutions said that by 2035, the bill’s provisions could reduce climate-warming emissions from the power sector by about 10% and lower residential electric bills by $1.8 billion.

Delaying reform would forego roughly $50 billion in electricity system savings and 600 million metric tons of emissions reductions through 2040, according to the modeling.

Whitehouse called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act an “affordability bill,” a “data center bill” and a “climate and clean energy bill” that would have more of an impact on clean energy than former President Joe Biden’s legacy climate legislation, the Inflation Reduction Act.

“This becomes our biggest implemented climate bill,” he said.

If the package doesn’t make it to Trump’s desk before the end of this Congress, the outlook for passing a new permitting reform bill could be “bleak,” Tyler, of Citizens Climate Lobby, said.

“The opportunity is now,” she said.

text:
ANTALYA – Clean Air Task Force (CATF) welcomes Türkiye’s announcement of the Global Geothermal Ambition 2050 at COP31, an important step toward strengthening international cooperation and accelerating the development and deployment of next-generational geothermal energy.

“Next-generation geothermal has the potential to fundamentally expand the world’s clean energy options, providing reliable, around-the-clock power from domestic resources. But realizing that potential will take more than technological innovation alone,” said Terra Rogers, Senior Director for Clean Power at CATF. “Governments must work together to create the conditions for deployment, from supporting early-stage exploration and demonstration to establishing clear regulatory frameworks and building the supply chains we need to scale. Türkiye’s announcement at COP31 is an opportunity to build that international momentum.”

CATF’s recent report, Next-Generation Geothermal at Scale: A Global Action Framework, identifies the policy and institutional measures governments and multilateral institutions can take to accelerate geothermal deployment. CATF has also called for deeper international partnerships to connect countries across the geothermal value chain, from research and development to manufacturing, project construction, and deployment.

“COP31 can help lay the foundation for a more coordinated international approach to geothermal development,” said David Yellen, Director, Cross-Regional Impact at CATF. “The priority now is to establish a lasting framework for cooperation that brings more countries into the effort, mobilizes investment, and helps translate technological progress into projects around the world.”

CATF, Iceland, and New Zealand will co-host a press conference at COP31 on November 17, from 11:30 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. TRT, bringing together ministers from Iceland and New Zealand to discuss opportunities for global geothermal collaboration and priorities for 2027. The discussion will explore lessons learned from both countries and how international partnerships can accelerate technology development, mobilize investment, and overcome shared barriers to deployment. text:
Uncertainty surrounding the Environmental Protection Agency's 2027 emissions regulations is putting a damper on new Class 8 truck orders, despite improving freight rates and ongoing equipment replacement needs.

That's the message from FTR Transportation Intelligence and ACT Research, which both reported disappointing preliminary North American Class 8 truck orders for October.

Ad Loading...

October is typically a strong month for truck orders as fleets plan equipment purchases for the following year. But this year, orders came in at roughly half the historical average, according to FTR.

“While spot rates remain supportive of equipment demand, the lack of clarity around EPA 2027 rules and associated costs has left OEMs and fleets unable to plan for next year,” said Carter Vieth, research analyst at ACT Research.

“It’s not a lack of desire for new equipment holding fleets back, but rather the inability to make informed investment decisions in the face of regulatory and economic uncertainty.”

Ad Loading...

What Will 2027 Trucks Cost?

The EPA earlier this year proposed changes to its 2027 nitrogen oxide (NOx) emissions regulations, but the final requirements remain uncertain.

That uncertainty affects both truck manufacturers and their fleet customers.

According to FTR, truck makers have begun opening their 2027 model-year order boards, but some may not yet be releasing all their production slots or finalizing prices until they know exactly what the regulations will require.

Detroit Opens Orders for EPA 2027 Engines

Fleets, meanwhile, may be holding off on purchases in hopes of getting more favorable pricing once the rules are finalized.

And the potential cost differences are significant.

Ad Loading...

Under the proposed regulatory framework, nonconformance penalties could add an estimated $6,000 to $7,000 per engine if manufacturers pass those costs along to buyers, according to FTR. That's compared with an estimated $8,000 to $12,000 premium for engines that fully comply with the stricter emissions standards.

Actual costs will depend on the final regulations and manufacturers' pricing decisions.

Rising Costs Add to the Pressure

Emissions regulations aren't the only thing holding back truck purchases.

Fleets are dealing with rising operating costs, even as freight rates improve. Higher diesel prices, insurance premiums, and labor costs are squeezing margins and limiting how much money carriers have available to invest in equipment.

“Fleet capital spending priorities may be shifting toward trailers rather than tractors in the near term,” said Dan Moyer, FTR's senior analyst for commercial vehicles.

Ad Loading...

Cummins Adjusts 2027 Engine Rollout After EPA Proposal

That shift may already be showing up in trailer orders. According to ACT Research, preliminary U.S. trailer orders jumped 311% year over year in September to 42,700 units, up 75% from August. Although the year-over-year comparison was exaggerated by unusually weak orders in September 2025, the seasonally adjusted total was the third highest in 55 months. ACT said the strength reflects both seasonal buying patterns and an unusual order cycle that saw purchases delayed last year.

Another factor is that the earlier rush to buy trucks ahead of anticipated 2027 emissions requirements has largely run its course.

That means future orders will depend more on fleet profitability, replacement needs, and confidence in equipment costs.

How Far Did Class 8 Orders Fall?

The two research firms reported somewhat different preliminary figures, but both point to a sharp slowdown.

FTR estimated 15,600 Class 8 net orders in October, down 36% from a year earlier and 24% from September.

ACT Research estimated 13,500 orders, down 45% year over year.

Ad Loading...

FTR's October estimate was nearly 50% below the 10-year average of 31,089 orders for the month.

The weak October figures followed a relatively soft September. Combined orders for the two months were down 20% from the same period last year, according to FTR, suggesting a slow start to the 2027 truck-order season.

That contrasts with the stronger ordering activity earlier this year. FTR reported year-to-date Class 8 orders of 278,201 units, up 74% from the same period in 2025.

Medium-duty trucks, however, are showing a different trend. ACT Research reported preliminary October orders for Classes 5-7 of 18,000 units, up 14% from a year earlier.

Delayed Orders or Lost Sales?

Despite the weak October numbers, FTR sees reasons for optimism.

text:
By Mike Colias

Nov 10 (Reuters) - Tesla's move to discontinue its Cybertruck next year is perhaps the highest-profile flameout in a category that automakers had once hyped: huge electric pickups.

Tesla CEO Elon Musk said in a social ‌media post on Saturday that the automaker would ramp up Cybertruck production at its Austin, Texas, factory to ‌meet an "order backlog" before dismantling the assembly line around June or July. He said the wind-down would allow Tesla to produce more Cybercab robotaxis, which have ​yet to be sold commercially.

But sales of Tesla's stainless-steel, angular truck — once described by MotorTrend magazine as having a "stealth-bomber-refrigerator design theme" — sagged 28% this year through September, to about 11,600 trucks, according to an estimate from research firm Motor Intelligence.

That sales pace is far off the 250,000-truck annual level Musk once predicted. Musk's other big company, SpaceX, also bought Cybertrucks worth $131 million from Tesla at list price ‌last year, according to a federal regulatory filing.

MORE ⁠MONEY FOR LESS TRUCK

The market for large electric pickups has been a rough road for Tesla's competitors, too. Even the Cybertruck's relatively meager deliveries have outpaced sales of electric trucks from rivals General ⁠Motors and Ford Motor, where executives once had high hopes that battery-powered versions of their full-size pickups — their biggest moneymakers — would be major hits.

Detroit's automakers pivoted to EV pickup trucks early this decade in part to fend off entries from Tesla and Rivian. GM, Ford and ​Ram maker ​Stellantis for decades have cultivated legions of loyal truck customers by ​offering pickups with ever-increasing levels of horsepower and towing ‌capability.

But the companies have not been able to translate that formula to EV trucks, said Karl Brauer, executive analyst at vehicle research site iSeeCars.com. For one, the trucks are pricey, in part because their massive batteries are extremely costly. GM's Chevrolet Silverado EV, for example, starts at around $62,000.

Second, the trucks often struggle to perform tasks that owners of internal-combustion pickups have come to expect, like towing a horse trailer or hauling heavy equipment.

"So in the end, you have to pay more money for a vehicle ‌that is less functional," Brauer said.

AUTOMAKERS GO SMALLER, ADD GAS TO EXTEND ​RANGE

Ford CEO Jim Farley acknowledged those tough economics during an earnings call last ​year, explaining why the company would discontinue the Ford ​Lightning, the electric version of its popular F-150 pickup that had been a relative hit for a ‌few years before demand cooled.

"The larger the vehicle, the ​bigger the battery, the more ​pressure on margin because customers will not pay a premium," Farley said.

Ford's focus is now on a smaller electric pickup, the Fathom, which it plans to roll out late next year at a starting price of about $28,000.

Automakers also are ​looking toward hybrid technology to deliver truck ‌customers the functionality they need in an electric form. Stellantis next year plans to launch an extended-range electric pickup ​truck, which will use a gas-powered generator to recharge the battery on the go.

(Reporting by Mike Colias ​in Detroit and Nathan Gomes in Bengaluru; Editing by Matthew Lewis)

text:
TOKYO – Honda’s net profit rose 66% in the first half of its fiscal year, the Japanese automaker reported Tuesday, driven by strong motorcycle sales.

Tokyo-based Honda Motor Co. reported a profit of 516.76 billion yen ($3.3 billion) for the six months through September, up from 311.83 billion yen a year earlier. First half sales rose 13% to 12 trillion yen from 10.6 trillion yen.

The robust results came despite costs in its electric vehicle program, where it dropped some models. Honda said EV-related losses erased 484.8 billion yen from its operating profits.

But officials stressed that Honda expects battery EVs might eventually become more popular and it will remain flexible enough to switch to EV production in the future.

Honda raised its full-year operating profit forecast to 780 billion yen from 650 billion yen.

Honda attributed the more optimistic forecast to favorable exchange rates and efforts to reduce the impact of U.S. tariffs, including shifting production to the United States.

The maker of the Super Cub motorcycle and Accord sedan also announced major production investments in North America and Brazil.

Honda plans to build a new auto production plant in Ohio, increasing production capacity in North America to 1.91 million vehicles by 2029 from 1.67 million. The company expects U.S. demand to grow, especially for its hybrid models.

Honda also plans to expand production of its motorcycle business at its Manaus factory in Brazil, increasing capacity to 2.3 million motorcycles by 2029 from the current 1.6 million.

Honda marked a record for fiscal first half sales in its motorcycle division, as its models proved popular in Brazil and India. It sold 11.9 million motorcycles during the six months, up from nearly 10.8 million the previous year.

However, Honda sold 1.57 million automobiles globally in the first half of the year, down from 1.68 million.

Honda shares, which have risen over the past year, had slipped 1.6% in Tokyo trading on Tuesday before the financial results were released.

title: As Texas embraces carbon storage, a Black community questions the risks
