text:
CHEEK — On a rural road outside Beaumont, a Texas energy giant is preparing to pump carbon dioxide underground to permanently store it and keep the gas from contributing to global warming. The project could be the first of its kind to start operating in the state.

It’s a long-awaited milestone for the oil and gas industry, which has touted carbon capture and storage as an important tool for cleaning up industry emissions. Texas lawmakers threw their support behind the technology, while state regulators spent years seeking permitting authority from the federal government to try to clear projects faster.

The Texas Railroad Commission, which oversees the oil and gas industry, won that authority late last year and approved this ExxonMobil project in September. But the nearby community of Cheek has asked commissioners to reconsider the permit decision.

The area close to the project is predominantly Black, and many residents are working class or elderly. People there don’t trust the company’s assurances that it will keep residents and their groundwater safe.

Only a small number of carbon storage wells have been permitted so far across the United States, and some CO2-related accidents have already happened. Experts and community advocates have warned of the risk for pipeline accidents and potential underground leaks. Leaders in Cheek are concerned the injected carbon dioxide could contaminate groundwater or get into the air and suffocate them. They worry emergency responders won’t be equipped to rescue them.

“We’re just shocked that they would want to do this so close to homes,” said Douglas Cormier, the 67-year-old president of the Cheek Texas Community Association, who grew up in the rural town and lives there with his wife near his daughters and grandkids.

Residents explained they don’t want to be the test subjects for the technology, and some experts argue it’s more distracting than effective in fighting climate change. Harvard University History of Science Professor Naomi Oreskes, who studies disinformation and climate change, has called carbon capture and storage “mostly a dangerous distraction.”

A recent investigation by Drilled and ProPublica showed it would take more resources than feasible for carbon capture and storage to reduce emissions enough to avoid extreme warming. Companies have canceled or paused nearly a third of 19 proposed carbon storage projects in Texas so far.

But carbon capture supporters argue that storing emissions is an important part of an “all of the above” approach to fighting climate change. Federal tax credits support carbon capture projects. Locally, East Texas remains attractive because of its existing carbon dioxide pipeline network (owned by ExxonMobil), its geology and nearby industrial facilities that might pay for their carbon to be stored.

ExxonMobil has seven agreements with companies to store the greenhouse gas. The volume of carbon dioxide injected underground through those agreements will equal emissions from 2 million cars.

“The community’s concerns around safety of any sort of an injection project are valid and real and need to be taken seriously,” said Nichole Saunders, senior director and lead counsel for energy transition with the Environmental Defense Fund. “At the same time, the need for more carbon management infrastructure to get to where we want to go on climate is also real.”

So far, the case has raised questions about whether companies and the Railroad Commission are doing enough to address community concerns as a backlog of projects awaits approval.

Agency watchdogs say the commission has a history of failing to keep communities safe from industry risks. It’s also facing pressure from state Rep. Drew Darby, leader of the House’s energy resources committee, who told the agency at a September hearing that carbon-capture projects needed to be moving at “utmost pace while protecting the public.”

In a statement to the Tribune, Railroad Commission spokesperson Bryce Dubee said the organization has a record of protecting drinking water while regulating injection wells. Winning the authority to regulate carbon storage “speaks volumes to this expertise,” Dubee said.

ExxonMobil held early meetings with community members in Cheek. The company’s permit requires it to install automatic shut-off systems for the injection wells, monitor the underground carbon dioxide plume and post a phone number where the operators can be reached around the clock.

The permitting program requires coordination with local emergency officials, according to the commission. ExxonMobil sponsors emergency training programs through the Texas A&M Engineering Extension Service in College Station.

“We want community members to know they can count on us to operate responsibly, communicate openly, and put safety first every day,” Senior Vice President Dominic Genetti wrote in a blog post.

But the day following Darby’s comments, after hearing ExxonMobil hadn’t talked with the community since the residents hired lawyers, Railroad Commission Chair Christi Craddick scolded ExxonMobil for not supporting residents enough. Some people from Cheek had taken a bus to be there to voice their concern.

“Give them information,” she said. “Be there for their safety. Give ‘em a fire truck if that’s what they want.”

Then Craddick voted for the permit.

Community distrust

Photos and posters about the area’s decades-long history hosting local rodeos hang in 81-year-old Preston Frank’s self-made museum in Cheek. Like many who live here, Frank, an upholsterer, inherited the land from his family. He considers it an important way to build generational wealth.

“That’s the reason why we’ve been fighting ExxonMobil,” he said. “We don’t want them coming in here and diminishing the value of the land.”

Just west of Beaumont off Interstate 10, the unincorporated community of Cheek is split by the highway and railroad, with many homes sitting on large tracts of land dotted with cattle and horses. People wave to each other. On the north side, there’s a Catholic and a Baptist church. Once a year, residents gather for a community picnic at the park.

ExxonMobil plans to compress carbon dioxide into an “almost liquid state,” pump it thousands of feet deep into the Earth and let it flow into little spaces in the rock, where scientists expect some to dissolve into salty water in those spaces or get stuck like a drink spilled in sand. Residents from the start had concerns.

How does ExxonMobil know where the molecules will go? What if they don’t behave as expected? What if the project gets abandoned?

Carbon dioxide leaking into water could increase its acidity and cause metals to contaminate it, according to advocacy groups and experts. If it leaks back into the air or a pipeline ruptures and people are caught in a big enough plume, they won’t be able to breathe or run gas-powered cars to escape.

“Contamination of drinking water with CO2, or with metals or chemicals leaching out of rock due to CO2 acidification of the water, could be very costly if the affected aquifer is used by a lot of people,” Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory researchers wrote in a 2007 paper. “[O]nce any aquifer is contaminated, it will remain so.”

The Cheek Texas Community Association signed on in July 2025 with attorneys at the nonprofit Earthjustice, which charges no cost. They fought the permit approval all the way to a state administrative hearing in March this year where they argued ExxonMobil hadn’t done enough to adequately ensure water and public safety would be protected and wasn’t monitoring a large enough area underground.

“It’s the first one in an area so close to a community, and that’s why the water issues and the safety issues are so paramount here,” said Jen Powis, who leads Earthjustice’s Gulf regional office.

The project also raised familiar concerns over environmental justice, a term used by researchers who have shown communities of color suffer a greater proportion of environmental harm than whiter, wealthier areas. Residents feared ExxonMobil saw in their homes a place where the company could more easily and cheaply push a project through.

The company already built three unassuming injection wells at the edge of the community. Only some residents in Cheek signed so-called pore space agreements with ExxonMobil for use of the small pockets in underground rock where the carbon dioxide will be stored and that property owners control under current case law.

“I’m just thinking they found an area where they can do it and not expect a lot of resistance,” said James Strambler, 70, a former IBM technician who moved there around 2017.

After the March hearing, a technical examiner and administrative law judge recommended moving the permit forward to the commission for a vote.

State gains power

Texas’ work to win the authority to permit carbon storage wells dates back more than a decade.

In 2009, Texas lawmakers passed a law authorizing the railroad commission to design a framework for how the state would regulate these projects in a way that upheld federal law. In 2022, the state formally applied to the Environmental Protection Agency for that authority.

At a virtual July 2025 hearing held by the EPA, the Texas Oil and Gas Association, a trade group representing 90% of the state’s fossil fuel production, said approving carbon capture and injection would be an economic boom for the state.

Gaining permitting power for carbon storage wells was “essential for our state’s economic future and energy leadership,” said Todd Staples, the group’s president, following the hearing.

Supporters of the technology are quick to point out that carbon dioxide makes sodas fizzy and creates the tunnels of fog that Texas football teams run through. They cite a study done by Texas A&M researchers that found the danger of leaks presents “a low probability of occurrence” — a risk that can be monitored and managed.

Advocates also point to the state’s decades-long history of injecting carbon dioxide into wells under a different type of permit as a way to draw more oil out of the ground and also store some of the greenhouse gas, a process known as enhanced oil recovery, which ExxonMobil has pursued for decades.

“This has been put in place now for over 50 years,” said Scott Castleman, spokesman for the Gulf Coast Carbon Capture and Storage Alliance, which represents Calpine, Chevron and ExxonMobil. “Certainly, there is more discussion and opportunity for this industry to scale, and so that’s where you’re starting to see projects and interest in areas that may not have seen this before.”

Establishing community trust will “make or break” projects as the industry grows, said Sophia Cunningham, executive director of the Houston Energy Transition Initiative at the Greater Houston Partnership. Best practices include engaging the community early and providing different, meaningful ways for people to give input and discuss possible benefits.

“It’s a technology that can reduce emissions associated with our industrial activities, and so that is a good pursuit and it’s important to support that,” Cunningham said. “But it’s also reasonable to expect that not everybody in a community is going to want that.”

Residents near projects should be asking whether there would be a helpline to call for any issues, or whether truck drivers would observe weight limits for roads and bridges, said Susan Hovorka, a research professor at the University of Texas at Austin’s Bureau of Economic Geology. In Hovorka’s mind, research and experience have already proven the technology to be safe.

“It’s not utterly without peril, and so people are not foolish to ask,” Hovorka said, “But … their anxiety is sometimes maybe higher than is practical and realistic.”

But there have been serious incidents in other parts of the U.S.

In Mississippi, a carbon dioxide pipeline ruptured in 2020 after heavy rain caused a landslide, releasing a vapor cloud of CO2. A government investigation found that first responders had not been notified about the safety risks and “had to guess” what they were. Dozens of people went to the hospital.

Injected fluid at another facility in Illinois leaked into “unauthorized zones” underground, which most residents learned about in a news article.

Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry paused the state’s review of new applications to ensure any permit issued would be in compliance with state regulations, citing a need for a review process that considers “the safety of our citizens and environment and that streamlines the process for greater efficiency.” Louisiana has permitted three carbon dioxide wells to be constructed so far but not to begin operating.

In other states with permitting authority as of mid-October, Arizona hasn’t permitted any carbon injection wells. North Dakota has approved eight active injection wells across three projects, and Wyoming has approved five wells in one project.

“The benefit isn’t there,” said Naomi Yoder, an environmental researcher who opposed Texas’ bid to regulate the technology and raised concerns about potential harm to the environment and communities. “So it doesn’t make any risk worth it, and there is risk involved. You can’t possibly sequester enough carbon dioxide to make it worth it.”

Can Texas improve?

In the Texas state hearing in September, the day before ExxonMobil’s Cheek permit won initial approval, Darby reiterated the importance of supporting the industry. Virginia Palacios, executive director of the agency watchdog group Commission Shift, told him they should also ensure companies pay for equipment and training for emergency responders.

Meanwhile, Railroad Commissioner Wayne Christian has vehemently opposed these projects. Christian has argued carbon dioxide is good for plants, rather than acknowledge the robust science that shows people burning fossil fuels has caused carbon dioxide concentrations in the atmosphere to rise, driving up global temperatures.

He voted against ExxonMobil’s permit, saying he didn’t think it was safe.

Newly elected Railroad Commissioner Jon Rosenthal, who will join Craddick and Christian on the three-person commission, told Inside Climate News he supported the state taking over regulation of the wells.

Some projects have meanwhile stalled. Oxy said in its latest earnings call in August that its carbon storage project — the first and only other one approved in the state so far — was coming online “as we look forward.”

Other projects are moving forward, including ExxonMobil’s second project near a community not far from Cheek, called Nome. The commission is collecting public comment on that project this week at hearings on Monday and Tuesday. ExxonMobil named this one “Sunflower,” fitting with the Cheek project called “Rose.”

In late October, environmental and community advocates knocked on residents’ doors to invite them to a meeting about how to advocate for themselves. Only one person from the project’s area attended. Several arrived from Cheek, lending advice on what they’d learned while attendees ate pasta and salad.

The meeting hosts characterized the technology as a financial boon to industry and the Railroad Commission while putting drinking water at risk. The colorless, odorless gas can also cause suffocation, presenter Alexis Iwasiw warned the group.

“At high concentrations … it can lead to serious injury or death,” she said.

The next night, ExxonMobil held an open house in the small Nome City Hall. They served boudin balls and shrimp and offered colorful pamphlets about the company’s safety record, how to respond in an emergency and how drinking water would be protected. They displayed a poster of other pipelines in the area.

As the sun went down, the group of several dozen made its way outside, where the ExxonMobil presenters enthusiastically launched into explaining how CO2 is safe at certain levels. With a call of “let it rip, tater chip,” they released the gas from a demonstration pipeline, where it puffed out visibly like white smoke.

Mike Doguet, a 72-year-old rice and turf farmer turned real estate developer, looked on. He believed the company did a much better job communicating with residents in advance here than in Cheek. The company is paying for new firefighting equipment, he said, among other community support. (Cheek community leaders have a list of wants too, including improved roads, a community center and an emergency warning system.)

One of the Sunflower project’s injection wells sits across the street from Doguet’s home in Nome, making neighbors wonder if there was oil. Doguet’s daughter lives next door and his son isn’t far. He wasn’t worried about safety.

“In my mind, it’s going to encourage new industry. It’s going to be good for the environment. It’s all positive to me,” Doguet said. “I don’t see the negatives.”

As the presentation went on, a resident from Cheek peppered the ExxonMobil employees with questions. One of the ExxonMobil presenters snapped back, telling her they were in the business of keeping substances in pipelines and would always err on the side of safety.

A former ExxonMobil employee and Nome resident in the crowd, 77-year-old Lawrence Riley, piped up to say that in his decades of experience, he’d never had a pipeline emergency: “They are very, very safe, I am telling you,” he said.

Wearing an ExxonMobil hat, 71-year-old Mayor Kerry Abney at one point walked through the CO2 cloud. He thought the project was great: Workers were shopping at Big D’s in town, contributing to sales tax, he said. People had a chance to make money in a place where agriculture is tough.

As Abney put it in an interview: “Santa Claus came.”

The Cheek resident watching the plume crossed her arms, looking skeptical.

Carlos Nogueras Ramos and Zach Leggio contributed reporting.

text:
While North Carolina Democrats digest their stunning success on Election Day that gave the party control of the N.C. House and touching distance of taking over the N.C. Senate, supporters are wondering what the changes in the state legislature will mean in practice.

One of the issues top of mind for residents, and one that became a campaign issue in the bruising race between Sen. Michael Lee, R-New Hanover, and victorious Democratic challenger Jessica Bichler, was what the changes could mean for environmental enforcement − specifically when it comes to “forever chemicals.”

“We’re at the end of the river, that’s just geography, and we have some real nasty stuff in it,” NC Rep. Deb Butler said.

The Wilmington StarNews first broke the story in 2017 of the chemical discharges into the Cape Fear, which serves as the primary drinking water supply for nearly 500,000 people in Southeastern North Carolina, that couldn’t be filtered out by local utilities before the water reached homes and businesses. Since then, testing also has found extensive PFAS contamination in groundwater and the environment across the Cape Fear region.

Formally known as per-and poly-fluoroalkyl substances, PFAS are manmade substances used in a range of products from medical devices to nonstick cookware that don’t break down quickly − hence their name forever chemicals − and have been tied to a host of health problems, including several types of cancer, immune suppression issues and organ disruptions.

The GOP-dominated General Assembly has been seen by many as dragging its feet on going after Chemours and other PFAS polluters, in effect placing business interests ahead of the health of residents and the environment.

‘So far not done what’s necessary’

Republicans have disputed those claims, stating that there needs to be a balanced approach to fixing the problem. They also note that the 2026 budget, authored by the GOP, includes several provisions to help local utilities and funding to continue programs to help private well owners deal with polluted water and to research and remediate PFAS contamination at fire stations.

But environmental groups and grassroots organizations, especially those downstream of Chemours’ Fayetteville Works plant roughly 75 miles upstream of Wilmington, say federal and state officials have largely failed to hold the PFAS polluters’ feet to the fire and force them to take responsibility for the mess they’ve created. They’ve also failed to adopt strong rules that would reduce the contamination and potential future health risks associated with the continued release of forever chemicals into the environment.

“The status quo is not and has not been acceptable,” said Jean Zhuang, senior attorney with the Southern Environmental Law Center. “It’s clear our state legislature has so far not done what’s necessary to protect our communities.”

State Rep. Deb Butler said she expects there to be renewed focus on a host of issues, including the state’s environmental woes, once Democrats gain some of the levers of power in January 2027.

“People aren’t satisfied, and they showed that with their votes,” said the Wilmington Democrat who has served in the House for nearly a decade and is likely to have a leadership role in the new-look chamber.

‘Real nasty stuff in it’

Steps Democrats in the N.C. House could take to strengthen PFAS enforcement include appointing new members to the state Environmental Management Commission, which has hobbled attempts by state regulators to adopt tougher water quality standards. Legislators also could pressure state officials to tighten discharge permits and requirements under existing rules for PFAS releases.

“Let’s keep this stuff out of the environment in the first place,” Butler said. “That just makes good common sense.”

In a press conference Wednesday, Nov. 4, Gov. Josh Stein, a Democrat, said he was excited about moving North Carolina forward after record voter turnout and was looking forward to working with leaders from both sides of the political aisle.

“Voters across North Carolina have made their voices heard, and together, we restored common sense to the General Assembly,” he said. “North Carolinians have sent a clear message: They want real action from their elected officials − leaders who are committed to serving them.

“I look forward to working on the issues that matter the most, from lowering the cost of living to keeping people safe and continuing to invest in the people who make North Carolina the best place to live, work, and raise a family.”

The Stein administration in early September 2026 announced a $600 million settlement with Chemours and DuPont over contamination tied to the decades-long production of forever chemicals at Fayetteville Works.

The legal fight to get the companies to pay for clean-up and mitigation efforts has dragged on for years, frustrating residents and local officials. State regulators have been more successful in stopping new discharges from Fayetteville Works by threatening to pull the facility’s permits if Chemours didn’t clean up its act, but even those actions haven’t moved quickly enough for many.

While the settlement represents a step in the right direction, environmental and clean water advocates have said there remains much work to be done to clean up the mess left behind by decades of unregulated dumping of manmade chemicals into North Carolina’s environment.

Advocates also say other lingering water quality woes, such as 1.4-dioxane getting discharged in the Piedmont and eventually reaching the Cape Fear River basin, remain to be tackled.

“We’re at the end of the river, that’s just geography, and we have some real nasty stuff in it,” Butler said.

text:
Moments before Sandra Edwards was set to address the media on Monday about the years-long neglect of a contaminated cancer cluster site near her Fifth Ward home, a friend approached her and told her another neighbor died.

Edwards collapsed and cried out, saying she was having trouble breathing. A small group of people, including U.S. Congressman Christian Menefee, gathered around her and said a short prayer.

The information may have influenced the remarks of the speakers at Monday’s news conference; Edwards and Menefee refused to say, “good morning,” noting that there was nothing good about what is happening to the residents of Fifth Ward, Kashmere Gardens and Denver Harbor. They claim the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency is gatekeeping a draft health risk assessment that could help families determine whether it’s safe to go outside.

“You have played with our lives for way too long,” Edwards said, directing her remarks to the EPA. “You have hurt this community. Stop dragging your ass. I just found out a friend died from cancer. We’re tired of this mess. I’m not asking. I’m telling you.”

Representatives from the EPA did not attend Monday’s gathering, and spokespeople from the Texas district office and the Washington, D.C., office did not respond to requests for comment.

The Texas Department of State Health Services confirmed contamination on the Union Pacific Rail Yard, formerly a Houston Wood Preserving Works site, in 2019. Since then, several people have died, including 13-year-old Corinthian Giles, who contracted leukemia in 2016 and was gone five years later.

“The site has legacy contamination from the plant; this is not disputed,” Menefee said. “The people living in this area have been pushing to understand what that means for their health. Person after person after person has either passed away from cancer, is dealing with it right now, or has a close family member who is dealing with it.”

“People in these communities are suffering, and the Environmental Protection Agency needs to do its job and give this report to communities so they can know what’s what, provide public comment and finally get the justice they deserve,” he added.

The affected neighborhoods are historically Black communities, and the residents say they’ve been treated like their lives don’t matter, even though there’s substantial evidence that they’ve been exposed to creosote, a likely carcinogen or cancer-causing substance.

The federal government launched a contamination investigation in 2023, and a draft report has allegedly existed for more than a year, but Menefee said Monday the EPA hasn’t publicized its findings or explained what it plans to do to remediate the site.

“We’re here today because Trump’s Environmental Protection Agency has sat on a draft health risk assessment for 396 days,” Menefee said. “The families who live beside the rail yard have never seen [the report]. I’m here today as the congressman for this neighborhood to demand that the EPA release the draft and start the public comment period.”

Joetta Stevenson, chair of the EPA’s Community Advisory Group, said samples were collected in December 2024, and it should have only taken a few months to analyze the results.

“It doesn’t make any sense,” Stevenson said of the delays. “This is intentional, this slow walking. We have been diligent. We have been focused. We have been doing everything we can to make sure this moves forward. EPA, we want you to move on this. The people who are dying deserve it. We ain’t playing with you. Give us that report.”

Community members have been told that the draft report was submitted to the Trump administration and would be released in 2025. When that didn’t happen, they were told it would come out in early 2026.

Menefee sent a letter to the EPA in July of this year, asking for the status of the investigation, a timeline for the report’s release and whether Union Pacific has requested extensions. He said he received a response in September that provided a link to the agency’s website and a statement that they wished to “continue working with local government officials.” The letter did not offer a timeline for when the report would be released.

“The document that matters is the health risk evaluation,” Menefee said. “It tells people what the testing means for their health and what remediation should be taken. The EPA has posted soil results but numbers on a page don’t tell a mother whether her backyard is safe.”

The congressman said he’s hopeful that since his Democratic Party took the majority in the United States Congress last week, federal agencies will be more responsive to his pleas.

“My message to the EPA is do your job. Fulfill your promises,” Menefee said. “The community is standing right here. Inform them. Enough is enough.”

text:
What to know:

Moratorium on new data centers: Michigan governor-elect Jocelyn Benson is proposing a pause on new data center construction until the state establishes regulations to protect communities and natural resources.

Community input required: Developers would have to hold public hearings before projects move forward, giving residents an opportunity to ask questions and voice concerns.

More transparency: Companies would be required to disclose information about proposed projects to prevent behind-the-scenes agreements that exclude residents.

Protecting water and land: Developers would have to demonstrate before construction that their projects would not harm Michigan’s natural resources.

Michigan governor-elect Jocelyn Benson is proposing a moratorium on new data center construction in the state until regulations require developers to meet specific standards for community transparency, environmental protections, and energy costs.

Under the proposal, Michigan would not allow new data centers until rules require companies to negotiate openly with communities, protect natural resources, and cover the costs of their energy use.

Benson’s plan calls for public hearings before projects move forward, allowing residents to ask questions and share concerns about proposed developments.

It would also require transparency and disclosure reporting to prevent agreements between developers and government officials from excluding community members from the process.

Another part of the proposal would require data center developers to demonstrate before construction that their projects would not negatively affect natural resources, including water and land.

Benson also wants data centers to pay for the additional electricity they use rather than passing those costs on to residential and other consumers.

Her proposal would prohibit data centers from receiving tax breaks.

The plan also calls for union contracts to ensure data center projects create well-paying jobs for Michigan workers.

Benson said companies that violate the proposed requirements would not be allowed to operate in Michigan.

The proposal comes as data center development has become a growing concern for communities worried about energy demand, water consumption, environmental impacts, and the potential costs of large-scale facilities.

Benson’s plan would establish requirements for how future data center projects are reviewed and approved, with an emphasis on community involvement and corporate accountability.

During her one-on-one sit-down with Local 4 anchor Ty Steele, Benson said she supported a moratorium on new data centers until the state establishes safeguards to protect water and energy resources.

Benson also said that companies should be required to pay for the energy they use and address noise pollution concerns.

She proposed requiring community benefits agreements and creating an online portal where residents could track proposed and existing data center projects and provide input.

Benson said the goal was to ensure communities benefit from development rather than simply absorbing its costs.

title: The Cybertruck era is over, but America's electric truck experiment isn't - Grist.org
description:

Ford’s upcoming electric pickup truck coming next year, the Fathom, will be priced starting at $28,400 — well below the price of the average gas-powered pickup.
As the Cybertruck’s production comes to a close, Alexander Edwards, president of the research consultancy Strategic Vision, was cautious about declaring the electric pickup experiment a failure.
In other words, America’s experiment with electrified pickup trucks isn’t over yet.
“I’d say round one went to the gas truck,” Krassner said.
text:
After barely three years on the road, Tesla is planning to kick the Cybertruck to the curb after flagging sales. Elon Musk announced on Friday that the company would wind down production next year to make room for the production of Cybercabs, the robot taxis Tesla hopes will reshape transportation.

In its short lifespan, the Cybertruck managed to become a top candidate for the most polarizing vehicle on the road — ever. Critics called it a “MAGA hat on wheels” and compared it to a dumpster — a resemblance that may have fooled some hungry raccoons that once chewed on the vehicle’s rear vault. It’s already being declared “one of the greatest flops in automotive history,” on par with Ford’s 1957 Edsel. But the polygonal, supposedly bulletproof truck did appeal to a certain demographic.

“It’s the kind of vehicle, as a kid, you imagine for the future,” said Dan Krassner, executive director of the American EV Jobs Alliance, an advocacy organization working to end the partisan divide over electric vehicles. He’s a Republican and a wrestling fan, and noted that some of his favorite pro wrestlers drove Cybertrucks, including the married WWE superstars Seth Rollins and Becky Lynch, along with The Miz and Liv Morgan (though the latter has said it was the “worst investment” she ever made).

Weeks before the Cybertruck rolled out in late 2023, Musk told investors that Tesla would sell 250,000 vehicles a year. But it never came close: Last year, it sold just over 20,000. It’s the latest sign that the attempt to make EVs macho is falling flat, after Ford announced last December that its F-150 Lightning pickup truck, the all-electric version of the country’s most popular vehicle, would be discontinued since it was a money-loser. Sales of Rivian’s electric pickup have been sliding downward each year since 2023; they have also dropped sharply for GMC’s Hummer EV, which was dubbed “the worst-selling pickup truck of 2026.”

Automakers have long tried to shed the saintly, environmentally friendly image of the Toyota Prius, and this shift to big, aggressive electric trucks was an effort to appeal to traditional American pickup buyers. But they not only had to contend with conservatives’ hesitations about EVs, they also had to persuade a public increasingly worried about the cost of living to overcome sticker shock, to fork over thousands, if not tens of thousands, more to buy an electric pickup instead of a gas-powered one. A comparable gas-powered Ford pickup starts at $52,000, about $11,000 less than the Lightning did before Ford discontinued it.

“The first electric trucks weren’t priced for the people who buy trucks, and buyers still have fair questions about charging and towing,” Krassner said. “You know, macho advertising can’t fix the monthly payment.”

The starting price for the 2026 Tesla Cybertruck was just raised to $92,500, and the cheapest Hummer EV is $97,200. Full-size electric pickup trucks need very large batteries to deliver the range and towing capabilities that truck buyers want, leading to higher prices, Krassner said.

But cheaper models are on the way. Ford’s upcoming electric pickup truck coming next year, the Fathom, will be priced starting at $28,400 — well below the price of the average gas-powered pickup. Meanwhile, now that the F-150 Lightning is out of production, with used models going for 50 percent off the sticker price, it’s “selling like hotcakes,” according to the transportation news site Electrek.

“As the electric trucks are more comparable in price to gas trucks, we expect them to be a superior product and be popular with Americans,” Krassner said.

There’s still a large partisan divide on electric vehicles: Roughly half of all new EV registrations in the U.S. from 2012 to 2023 went to the 10 percent most Democratic counties, according to a study from the MIT Center for Energy and Environmental Policy Research. Because electric trucks performed better in Republican-leaning areas — though not as well as Tesla and Ford had hoped — the researchers suggested they could still be a way to broaden EV adoption. And some of Republicans’ resistance to electric vehicles has begun to ease, Krassner said. The share of Republicans who agree that EVs are “for people who see the world differently than I do” fell from 59 percent in November 2023 to 49 percent in November 2025, according to polling from EVs for All America.

As the Cybertruck’s production comes to a close, Alexander Edwards, president of the research consultancy Strategic Vision, was cautious about declaring the electric pickup experiment a failure. He sees the F-150 Lightning as a lesson in making sure that trucks can perform the jobs their owners bought them to do — including towing a camper across several states without worrying about range and charging access. The Cybertruck, on the other hand, appealed to a sense of individuality, innovation, excitement, but only a relatively small group of people were willing to pay for that experience at a high price point, especially as Tesla became a political target thanks to Musk’s involvement with DOGE.

“I think price, product frustrations, Musk’s politics, and the changing meaning of owning one all need to be part of the discussion,” Edwards said.

High gas prices sparked by the war in Iran, which have stuck around for months, are prompting people to purchase hybrids, though sales of electric vehicles have declined after the Trump administration’s elimination of federal tax credits last year. Krassner is also bullish on a new generation of range-extended electric trucks — EVs with a gas-powered generator — which could ease drivers’ range anxiety.

In other words, America’s experiment with electrified pickup trucks isn’t over yet. “I’d say round one went to the gas truck,” Krassner said. “Round two hasn’t started yet.”

text:
The clean-energy transition is creating a paradox. To expand renewable-energy technologies, electrify transport and build infrastructure for artificial intelligence, society must extract unprecedented quantities of minerals. Demand for many of these ‘critical minerals’ is projected to increase several-fold over the coming decades1. Yet, the technologies used to obtain them remain rooted in an old model through which single metals are extracted from virgin ore2.

The consequences are increasingly apparent (see ‘Critical-mineral supply under pressure’). As deposits of high-grade ores decline, larger quantities of rock must be mined and processed to produce the same amount of metal3. That requires more energy and water. Mining accounts for around 1.7% of global energy consumption and this number is projected to rise by up to eight-fold by 20604. Many critical-mineral projects operate in regions facing high water stress, such as arid parts of Africa and Latin America1.

Mining waste is growing, too. Already, hundreds of billions of tonnes of mine tailings are stored globally. Projections suggest that by 2050, up to two trillion tonnes of extra waste rock and tailings will have accumulated3,5.

Meanwhile, society is producing vast quantities of metal-rich waste that remain a mostly untapped secondary source of metals. In 2022, 62 million tonnes of electronic waste (e-waste) was produced globally — almost 8 kilograms for every person on the planet — and only around 22% of that was formally collected and recycled6.

How to widen access to the critical minerals that the world needs

Many discarded electronics contain valuable metals, including gold, palladium and rare-earth elements — in concentrations that can exceed those found in primary ores. However, recovering these metals remains technically challenging and is often economically unattractive using conventional approaches.

Retrieval of metals and increasing metal circularity should be seen as a strategic capability to offset the growth of metal extraction from virgin ores. Nations that can efficiently recover critical minerals from waste streams, mine residues and low-grade resources will be less exposed to geopolitical disruptions and supply-chain shocks7.

Biology offers a powerful route forwards. Although biomining — which uses microorganisms to extract metals — was once considered a niche approach, it has evolved. Driven by advances in microbial ecology, synthetic biology, structural biology, protein engineering and machine learning, the scientific foundations for a new generation of mineral biotechnologies are emerging at speed8,9. These methods offer potential levels of selectivity for extracting and recovering certain metals that are often difficult to achieve through conventional hydrometallurgical processes.

But, scientific progress alone will not transform mineral supply chains. The main obstacle is no longer a shortage of ideas. It is a lack of pathways from scientific discovery to industrial deployment. Here we outline how to develop those pathways, drawing on discussions at the International Workshop on Biomining of Critical Minerals and Elements, which was sponsored by the Novo Nordisk Foundation and held in Sitges, Spain, in September last year.

Promising technologies

Biotechnologies have demonstrated their industrial potential for decades. Bioleaching and biooxidation processes are already established for recovering copper, nickel, gold and cobalt from ores10. They involve irrigating heaps of crushed ore or treating ground mineral powders with specialist microbes that generate chemicals, such as acids or modifiers of reduction–oxidation reactions, that selectively dissolve either target metals or other minerals found with them.

Advances in synthetic biology have expanded the range of potential applications. For example, engineered microbial systems can be designed to dissolve metals more effectively. Biomolecules (such as the protein lanmodulin) can separate rare-earth elements with yields of 99.9% in one step under conditions that are simpler than conventional techniques, using aqueous solutions rather than organic solvents8,11. AI-assisted protein design is further accelerating the discovery of macromolecules designed to selectively recognize, bind to and separate target metals from complex solutions of several elements9.

How the rush for critical minerals is neglecting human needs

Collectively, these developments suggest that biotechnology could become an important component of future critical-mineral supply chains. However, many promising approaches never progress beyond being validated in the laboratory. They often stall between proof-of-concept studies and commercial demonstration, a challenge familiar throughout industrial biotechnology. Even promising technologies often struggle to attract the capital, infrastructure and industrial partnerships needed to scale them up12,13.

Barriers must be overcome. Although a few bioprocessing pilot projects exist, their capacity is insufficient to evaluate technologies across the diverse types of ore, feedstock and process conditions encountered in practice. Investors are reluctant to finance first-of-a-kind projects when it is uncertain how well they will perform in the real world.

Regulatory frameworks for emerging biomining technologies are also inadequate. They often vary across biotechnology, environmental and mining sectors and between jurisdictions. Developers might need to navigate several regulatory authorities and approval pathways, creating uncertainty and delays as technologies advance.

In the European Union, for example, the use of genetically modified microorganisms and their environmental applications are subject to distinct regulatory frameworks. Genetically modified microorganisms are allowed to be used in contained systems, whereas those used for field applications generally rely on naturally occurring or adapted microbial strains. The United States uses a coordinated multi-agency approach, involving the Environmental Protection Agency, the Food and Drug Administration and the US Department of Agriculture.

Valuable technical knowledge (on protein engineering, mineral characterization, hydrometallurgy and economic modelling, for instance) remains dispersed across disciplines, institutions and jurisdictions. This makes it difficult to generate the necessary evidence base — including long-term continuous operating data, metrics for tracking chemical cycles and validated economic assessments — to support large-scale adoption of such technologies.

The result is a growing mismatch. Scientific advances in mineral biotechnology are accelerating, yet the mechanisms needed to deploy them are not keeping pace. Although billions of dollars are being invested to secure future supply chains for critical minerals, comparatively little attention has been devoted to building the innovation systems required to commercialize biological solutions.

If biotechnology is to contribute meaningfully to critical-mineral security, environmental sustainability and circularity of resource use, then governments, industry, development banks and philanthropic funders must move beyond supporting research alone. They must invest in the institutions that enable translation of these new technologies as well.

Three priorities deserve attention.

Establish test facilities

Countries should establish shared pilot and demonstration facilities dedicated to mineral biotechnology. Individual companies often cannot justify the risks associated with developing specialized infrastructure for technologies that remain commercially unproven. Shared facilities can help to overcome this barrier by allowing several organizations to evaluate biological processes using realistic feedstocks under industrially relevant conditions. These facilities can support both pre-commercial and competitive studies. Similar approaches have been implemented successfully in synthetic biology and bio-refining, advanced manufacturing and in the clean-energy and semiconductor sectors.

The dark side of green technology: what do electric vehicles really cost?

For the mineral sector, such facilities should be located near relevant resource and waste streams, including mining districts, e-waste recycling hubs and sites affected by acid mine drainage or metal-laden urban waste waters. They should have connections to universities, research labs and a skilled workforce.

Access to research and engineering expertise would enable rapid iteration, troubleshooting and integration of mineral biotechnologies with established processes. Such sites would extend beyond technology testing to generate the operational, environmental and economic data needed to inform investment decisions, regulatory approvals and commercial deployment.

text:
Honda will invest $3 billion in a new auto plant in Central Ohio, adding capacity for 240,000 vehicles a year and more than 2,000 jobs. Production is expected to begin in 2029, pending final government approvals. The carmaker is pairing the plant with retooling at engine and transmission operations in Ohio, Alabama and Georgia, with the aim of building more hybrid-electric vehicles and the engines and hybrid systems that power them.

The package lifts Honda’s US auto production capacity to approximately 1.3 million vehicles a year and its North American capacity to approximately 1.9 million. It follows Audi’s announcement of a roughly $4 billion plant in Georgia, and it adds to a run of US investment decisions made while trade policy remains unsettled. AMS has reported that a Democratic Congress can probe auto tariffs but cannot easily scrap them, which helps explain why building close to the customer keeps winning arguments.

A plant designed to 'change its mind'

The new facility will sit on land between the existing East Liberty and Marysville Auto Plants. It will be Honda’s fourth auto plant in Ohio and its ninth auto-related production facility in the US. The capacity figure is modest by the standards of a greenfield site, and the design brief matters more. Honda says the plant will have the flexibility to produce multiple vehicle types and powertrains, including hybrid and gasoline-powered vehicles as well as battery-electric vehicles.

It promises one of the most advanced plants in the world when it comes online, with leading-edge automation, data-driven technologies and flexible production systems.

Honda points to hybrid demand as the driver, yet it is building a plant that can adapt as customer demand, market conditions and electrification trends evolve. Rather than guess where the market lands, the carmaker is paying to avoid having to guess at all. The release names no models for the plant, though it says multiple new models are under development at Honda R&D in the US.

How North America is building resilience through speed, flexibility and disciplined digitalisation

Day 1 of Automotive Manufacturing North America’26 brought together a clear message for North American automotive manufacturing: the industry must adapt faster, but it cannot afford to confuse activity with progress

Why Ohio keeps winning

But why Ohio? The site is home to an established and highly skilled workforce, and critically, is close to a large concentration of its US supply base. Vehicle development sits next door, including Honda Development & Manufacturing of America, the North American Automotive Development Center (ADC) and the Transportation Research Center (TRC). Existing operations already make vehicles, engines and hybrid systems nearby, and the L-H Battery Company joint venture facility has the flexibility to produce battery cells for both hybrid and all-electric vehicles.

“Honda’s leadership could have chosen to build this plant anywhere in the world, but they chose Ohio because there are so many advantages to being here,” said Ohio Governor Mike DeWine. “For almost half a century, Honda and Ohio have grown together, and generations of families have built their careers on Honda’s manufacturing lines. Today’s announcement isn’t just an investment in a new facility - it’s an investment in Ohio’s people and Ohio’s future.”

Honda has also spent four decades building the talent pipeline, including $132 million in research facilities and endowed chairs at The Ohio State University and work-study partnerships with two-year institutions such as Columbus State.

The powertrain story underneath

The assembly plant draws the attention, but the retooling in existing plants shows where the real constraint lies. A hybrid is only as plentiful as its engine and its hybrid system.

At the Alabama Auto Plant, which marks 25 years of vehicle production this fall, Honda is adding equipment and capacity for a new V6 hybrid engine. Line 1 will undergo one of its most significant renovations since the plant opened in 2001, so that it can build the Passport, which is currently made only on Line 2. The change gives the plant two lines that can each build multiple models.

In Ohio, the Anna Engine Plant, the largest Honda engine plant in the world, is retooling an existing line for a next-generation four-cylinder Atkinson-cycle engine for future compact and midsize vehicles built in North America. It is also expanding an on-site parts consolidation centre, expected to begin operating next year.

The most ambitious change takes place at Honda Transmission Plant-Ohio (TMP-O). Honda has begun converting an existing transmission line into a second hybrid system line, even as the plant keeps supporting current vehicle production. The plant has been making a two-motor hybrid system for the CR-V, Accord and Civic built in the US, and it is preparing a next-generation system that goes into production next year. It is also planning a hybrid system for larger models and will serve as lead plant for that system. Together these changes raise hybrid system capacity by 250 percent in the coming years.

Honda Transmission Plant-Georgia (TMP-G), which makes the 10-speed automatic transmission for Honda and Acura models built in Alabama and Ohio, will install a new assembly line for the larger hybrid systems. Its teams will work closely with their Ohio counterparts once production begins.

Development and the Canadian link

Designers and engineers at the ADC operations in California and Ohio are developing multiple new models for the Honda and Acura brands. Their proximity to manufacturing lets production engineers join projects early to improve manufacturability, quality and efficiency at launch.

That matters because Honda announced plans in May 2026 to introduce 15 new Honda and Acura hybrid models globally by 2030, with North America expected to be the primary market for many of them.

Canada is part of the same plan. After 40 years of vehicle production, Honda of Canada Mfg. in Alliston, Ontario, will be updated and retooled for next-generation hybrid-electric and gasoline-powered models, including the reintroduction of engine manufacturing. The project will include future planned investments and related expenses.

Half a century in, still adding

Honda has built cars in North America since 1982, when the Marysville Auto Plant opened in Ohio. In 2025, nearly 99% of the Honda and Acura automobiles sold in the US were made in North America. The carmaker now employs about 33,000 associates across 18 North American plants with annual capacity for 1.6 million automobiles and nearly 2 million engines. Cumulative investment in North American manufacturing exceeds $28 billion, including more than $3.1 billion over the past five years alone.

Bob Nelson, executive vice president of American Honda Motor Co., Inc., framed the move as a long-term commitment. “As Honda approaches 50 years of building products close to our customers in America, we are making one of the most significant commitments in our history to position Honda for the next 50 years,” said Nelson. “These investments strengthen America’s role as a cornerstone of Honda’s global future and reflect our confidence in our more than 30,000 Honda associates and the strength of American manufacturing. By expanding our comprehensive R&D and manufacturing capabilities, we will be better positioned to serve our customers and contribute to the economic vitality of the communities where we operate.”

The $3 billion covers the new plant. Honda has not put a figure on the engine, transmission and Canadian projects around it, so the full cost of the programme is larger than the headline suggests.

The sequencing tells the story. The first next-generation hybrid system is due next year, two years before the new plant builds a single car. Honda is not waiting for a building to make more hybrids. It is rebuilding the hard parts first.

text:
(The Center Square) – The U.S. Senate has voted to advance the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a permitting reform bill that would expedite the buildout of energy-related infrastructure.

The primary purpose of the over 400-page bill is to expedite the permitting approval process for energy-related projects – such as natural gas pipelines, drilling and mining, and data center infrastructure – by scaling back environmental and judicial reviews.

Sponsors of BAAJA say it will increase energy supply, lower electricity costs and create more jobs as the country enters a new era of energy demand. It also requires owners of data centers that draw more than 20 MW of power plugging into the electric grid to pay for the associated grid upgrade costs.

“This is an affordability bill. The American people spoke loud and clear that they wanted results on affordability,” Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-Rhode Island, who helped craft the bill, told reporters prior to the Monday evening vote. “People want to see Congress do good, big things. This is a good, big thing.”

Critics of BAAJA have voiced concerns that it would trample state and local rights, mainly by limiting litigation and local input, overriding environmental rules, and restricting states’ and communities’ ability to deny large projects, including data centers.

The four architects of the bill — U.S. Sens. Martin Heinrich, D-New Mexico; Shelley Moore Capito, R-West Virginia; Mike Lee, R-Utah; and Whitehouse — attempted to mitigate concerns from environmental and tribal rights groups with a package of amendments.

Among other measures, the amended bill strengthens impacted tribal governments’ say in transmission permitting planning, allows harms to “human health” and “the environment” to justify agency action against a permit or project, and establishes in the Department of Energy the Data Center Community Assistance Program, which would provide technical assistance on request to communities impacted by data centers.

Those and other changes, Heinrich assured reporters, “don't change what this bill was always about: lowering energy costs, building the infrastructure our country so desperately needs, creating good-paying jobs, protecting our communities, and making sure data centers pay their fair share.”

But several “troubling” provisions in BAAJA remain unaddressed, dozens of critics say, particularly the bill’s amendments to the Clean Water Act regarding pollution control and environmental impact assessments of large-scale projects.

“This permitting legislation is a giveaway to America’s most polluting industries. By loosening bedrock environmental laws, this bill will fast-track toxic industrial agriculture pollution nationwide,” Food and Water Watch’s policy director Rebecca Wolf, joined by dozens of other organizations, stated Monday. “Congress must stop this cynical industry ploy.”

text:
The US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has proposed requiring larger refiners to absorb all biofuel blending obligations waived for small refineries, in a move aimed at preserving demand for ethanol and biodiesel despite record exemption volumes granted earlier this year.

The proposal follows the EPA's August decision to grant renewable fuel standard (RFS) exemptions to 29 small refineries for the 2025 compliance year, including full exemptions for 18 facilities and partial waivers for 11 others. The agency said the exemptions represented approximately 1.76 billion Renewable Identification Numbers (RINs), the largest volume of small refinery relief issued under the programme.

Under the new proposal, the EPA would reallocate 100% of the waived blending obligations to larger refiners. The agency is considering two options: spreading the additional volume evenly across the 2026 and 2027 compliance years or allocating the entire volume to 2027. Public comments are being accepted until 4 December.

EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said the measure is intended to maintain strong markets for US farmers and biofuel producers while supporting energy security and economic competitiveness. Brooke Rollins, US Secretary of Agriculture, welcomed the proposal, saying it would help sustain market opportunities for agricultural producers and the biofuels sector.

The plan has been broadly welcomed by the biofuels industry after concerns that the exemptions would reduce demand for ethanol and biodiesel feedstocks. Geoff Cooper, chief executive of the Renewable Fuels Association, said the reallocation proposal would help offset lost demand resulting from the exemptions, although he maintained that many of the waivers were unwarranted.

Renewable credit prices for biodiesel and ethanol edged lower following the announcement, according to market participants attending the OPIS biofuels conference in Chicago. The EPA also indicated that implementation of the revised obligations could require an extension to the current 2026 compliance deadline of 31 March 2027.

text:
Contact: Samah Shaiq

Today, the U.S. Senate voted to advance the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), moving this landmark clean energy legislation one step closer to becoming law. In response, Evergreen Action Vice President of Policy Pete Wyckoff released the following statement:

“Today’s Senate vote to advance BAAJA is a big step forward for America’s clean energy economy. In passing this bill, lawmakers can show immediate action on their affordability promises to voters: by delivering legislation that will lower energy costs, strengthen our economy, and build a cleaner energy future. Permitting reform is vital to delivering on that promise.

“We’re grateful to Ranking Members Martin Heinrich and Sheldon Whitehouse for their leadership in getting us here. This is a consequential and complex bill with significant implications for our communities and environment—one that we see leading to meaningful progress. In the weeks ahead, we look forward to continuing thoughtful conversations with Members of both chambers across all perspectives on this legislation.”
