text:
The Senate overcame its first obstacle to advance a sweeping permitting reform package aimed toward speeding up energy projects and strengthening data center regulations, pushing ahead with the bipartisan bill after months of negotiations.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, known colloquially as BAAJA, succeeded in its first procedural hurdle on Monday evening, opening the door for debate and a possibly lengthy amendment process before it reaches a final vote. The fate of the bill remains unclear as its provisions have divided Democrats on Capitol Hill, including those who have suggested waiting until they control both chambers of Congress next year to push through the massive reforms package.

Bipartisan negotiators behind the bill are urging swift consideration as they push to sign the bill into law in the final two months of session, known as the lame-duck session.

“This bill, when it becomes law, becomes the floor for the work that we begin to do to make things better still in the next Congress with working majorities,” Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, one of the authors of the bill, told reporters on Monday. “So people should just cool their jets and have a little faith that this is not the end of the story.”

The comprehensive reform deal was first published last month, tackling issues ranging from data center costs, transmission power lines, environmental review deadlines, clearer guidelines for consultations, and more. The deal was finalized by the top four energy policy legislators on Capitol Hill, including Whitehouse and Utah Sen. Mike Lee, West Virginia Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, and New Mexico Sen. Martin Heinrich.

Environmental groups opposed

The package is backed by several business groups, energy developers and labor unions — and President Donald Trump came out in support of the bill over the weekend. Still, it faces opposition from some tribal leaders and environmental groups who have raised concerns it would benefit oil and gas developers and make it harder to pursue legal challenges.

“If it becomes law, this bill will lock in fossil fuel drilling, hardrock mining projects and AI data centers,” Abby Tinsley, senior vice president of Conservation Programs at The Wilderness Society, told the Deseret News in a statement. “It will completely undermine Tribal and other public participation and make it nearly impossible to undo unlawful development projects. As written, the bill will permanently greenlight endless development and harm for iconic landscapes.”

The negotiators, which includes the top four energy policy legislators on Capitol Hill, have incorporated much of the feedback in their latest version of the bill that was released over the weekend.

Some of those changes include requirements for federal agencies to consult with tribes on permitting projects “that will affect important cultural sites including on what properties are affected, the impacts of the project, and ways to avoid, minimize, or mitigate potential harm,” according to Sen. Martin Heinrich, another co-author of the bill.

The latest version also includes language preserving collective bargaining agreements for union employees as well as a new data center community assistance program within the Department of Energy.

“When a community is considering whether or not to grant a permit to a major data center, it needs to understand what that project will mean for its electricity supply, cost, water resources, infrastructure, and local economy, in order for them to make a good decision,” Heinrich said on Monday. “This program will give state, local, and tribal governments the technical assistance they need to make their own informed decisions. These are meaningful improvements.”

Still, challenges remain. Democratic Sen. Catherine Cortez-Masto of Nevada is demanding changes to the bill’s language related to tribal consultation and project reviews on historically or culturally important sites before she can support the bill.

“I cannot ignore the concerns that Tribes in Nevada have with this bill text,” she wrote in a statement. “The changes to the National Historic Preservation Act were made without their input, and these changes violate the federal government’s responsibility to engage in government-to-government Tribal consultation. That’s why I’m demanding to strike this section from the bill.”

Cortez-Masto said she would introduce an amendment striking that language from the bill — vowing to oppose final passage if it’s still included.

The top negotiators of the bill said they are open to changes through proposed amendments, although it’s not yet clear how long that process could last. The package would then need to be approved by the House before it could be sent to Trump’s desk for his approval.

“This bill is not perfect. We’ve never pretended it was. It is, after all, bipartisan. That means that neither side got everything they want,” Heinrich said. “We had to find common ground. We had to make compromises, and we had to work through some very real disagreements.”

text:
Honda Motor ($HMC) announced a $3 billion auto plant in central Ohio to expand hybrid production, creating more than 2,000 jobs and capacity for 240,000 vehicles annually. Production is expected to begin in 2029, pending final government approvals.

The plant will sit between Honda’s existing East Liberty and Marysville facilities, with flexibility to manufacture hybrid, gasoline-powered and battery-electric vehicles.

The new plant and other manufacturing projects will raise annual production capacity to approximately 1.3 million vehicles in the U.S. and 1.9 million across North America.

Honda plans to increase hybrid-system production capacity in Ohio by 250% and add a hybrid-system assembly line in Georgia.

Alabama investments will expand production capacity and prepare the engine facility to manufacture a new V6 hybrid engine.

Honda will also retool its Alliston, Ontario, operations for next-generation hybrid and gasoline models, including restarting engine manufacturing.

The investments support Honda’s previously announced plan to introduce 15 new Honda and Acura hybrid models globally by 2030.

Honda’s recent lobbying disclosures list auto and steel tariffs, USMCA trade rules, advanced-manufacturing tax credits, and greenhouse-gas and fuel-economy standards among its federal policy issues.

text:
By David Shepardson

WASHINGTON, Nov 9 (Reuters) – Japanese automaker Honda Motor will build a new $3 billion auto plant in central Ohio to make hybrid vehicles, creating 2,000 jobs, it said on Monday.

The company ​said the plant will be able to produce 240,000 vehicles annually ‌and begin production in 2029. It will increase its US auto production capacity to 1.3 million vehicles annually, and North American capacity to 1.9 million.

Honda is also making a C$867 million ($613.6 million) commitment to its Canadian operations, including a C$166 million investment in ‌its Alliston, ​Ontario, operations, maintaining its 4,000-strong Canadian workforce.

The Canadian ⁠government said it is ⁠investing C$313 million in the Alliston project.

Honda plans another $338 million investment in Ohio, and unspecified new investments in Georgia and Alabama.

The company announced plans in May to add 15 new Honda and Acura hybrid models worldwide ​by 2030. It also announced it would scrap electric vehicle sales goals, and indefinitely suspended an $11 billion Canada EV project as part of ⁠a $9 billion EV writedown.

Honda said it will invest ⁠in Alabama to build a new V6 hybrid engine, ​and retool its Ohio engine plant to build a new four-cylinder engine. It ​will also retool transmission plants in Ohio and Georgia, and plans ‌to reintroduce engine production in Ontario.

AUTOMAKERS FACING US TARIFFS

A number of foreign automakers have announced major new investments as they face tariffs imposed by President Donald Trump’s administration.

Last month, Volkswagen luxury unit Audi said it would build a $4 ⁠billion assembly plant near Macon, Georgia to open in the early 2030s that would produce 200,000 SUVs annually and employ 4,500 workers.

Reuters reported last month that ⁠Trump’s administration had promised ‌tariff relief to Audi to help secure the plant’s ⁠future. US officials told Audi executives the government plans to ​offer broad ‌relief from tariffs for automakers making significant investments ​in US production.

In ⁠July, Toyota Motor said it would spend $3.6 billion to build a 2.5-million-square-foot (232,000-square-metre) truck assembly line on its San Antonio, Texas manufacturing campus and shift some truck production to the US from Mexico.

The Japanese automaker said the expansion would be completed by 2030, creating 2,000 jobs.

($1 = 1.4129 Canadian dollars)

(Reporting by David Shepardson; Editing ​by Jan Harvey)

description:
Michigan's Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy said the state's effort to decrease ozone pollution has led to better air quality this year.
This year's report on the season from the state environmental department found that, in general, air quality is improving, continuing a longer-term trend.
"The air quality is continuing to improve, and we are attaining the federal standards throughout much of the state," said Tom Shanley, an air quality evaluation manager with EGLE.

In July, Michigan experienced dangerous air quality levels as wildfire smoke from Canada traveled south.
text:
Michigan's Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy said the state's effort to decrease ozone pollution has led to better air quality this year.

Ozone is a gas in earth's atmosphere that is both human-made and naturally occurring. In the upper atmosphere it protects the earth from ultraviolet radiation. But at ground level, ozone causes smog and can aggravate lung conditions and lead to breathing problems.

From March to October, ozone levels are likely to be elevated.

This year's report on the season from the state environmental department found that, in general, air quality is improving, continuing a longer-term trend.

Holland was the only city that didn't meet federal ozone standards this year. EGLE said that's likely because of pollution that transferred across Lake Michigan from other states.

"The air quality is continuing to improve, and we are attaining the federal standards throughout much of the state," said Tom Shanley, an air quality evaluation manager with EGLE.

Still, Shanley said pollutants from wildfire smoke have been increasingly hurting air quality in the state in recent years.

In July, Michigan experienced dangerous air quality levels as wildfire smoke from Canada traveled south.

"We have, in the last five to 10 years, noticed an increase in impacts from wildfire smoke, whether it's from places [in the] northwest U.S. or in Canada," he said.

text:
As Jim Chalmers, the treasurer, comes under increasing pressure to fight inflation by slashing spending in the midyear budget update, the drumbeat is loudest for cuts in one specific area: green energy subsidies for households.

Receiving the most focus is the cheaper home batteries program, which from July last year has offered a taxpayer-backed 30% rebate to households and businesses.

The scheme has become a victim of its own success. Treasury officials originally estimated it would lead to a million new batteries by 2030 at a cost of $2.3bn. The latest estimate is more than triple that figure, and only after a tweak to the policy.

Also in the crosshairs is the 2022 electric vehicle subsidy, which exempts workers from fringe benefits tax when they lease an EV through their employer and has proved more popular – and expensive – than predicted.

Despite reports that Treasury is pushing for cuts to the home battery scheme, the argument has hardly been made.

There is more than a whiff of politics to the sudden and urgent need to do away with clean energy programs, against, say, scaling back billions of dollars in diesel fuel rebates for miners.

When budget experts are asked broader questions about the big pressures on the federal government’s finances, rarely do they cite handouts for home batteries or tax breaks for electric vehicles.

In a speech on Monday, Angus Taylor, the opposition leader, again promised to “abolish Labor’s ideological climate bureaucracy” as part of his promised $31bn of budget savings over four years.

Meanwhile, the Albanese government’s recent efforts to apply an income test to private healthcare rebates for over-65s was met with howls of protest from the Coalition.

As Stephen Bartos, an economics professor at the University of Canberra, says, in all this talk about cutting spending “nobody is mentioning nuclear-powered submarines”.

Bartos, a former deputy secretary at the Department of Finance and New South Wales parliamentary budget officer, says if the challenge is to close the budget deficit then green subsidies “shouldn’t be their first port of call”.

“Partly because it’s small beer compared to the big-ticket items like health, NDIS and defence. But also because there is a rationale for green subsidies, if a declining one.”

The national disability insurance scheme, for example, was expected to cost nearly $54bn in 2025–26, which has made reining in the cost of the scheme an existential question for the government’s fiscal plans. In 2023, the Parliamentary Budget Office estimated the total cost of acquiring nuclear-powered submarines under the Aukus agreement to be as much $368bn over the life of the program.

The federal fuel tax credit scheme, which mainly helps major global mining companies, costs about $11bn a year and is rising fast.

Bartos is critical of government tax breaks for electric vehicles but says the case for public support for batteries is stronger.

“I would probably be looking at where the price signals encouraging adoption [of clean energy] are weakest, and that’s probably batteries. For EVs, people are shifting no matter what.”

The case for the cheaper batteries scheme has also been undermined by Treasury officials’ abject failure to predict how popular it would be. A month into the program and it was already obvious they had got it wrong, as the expected cost blew out towards $14bn.

Not only was our appetite for subsidised batteries way higher than official forecasts, the original design of the scheme made it more desirable to buy bigger, more expensive batteries.

There has since been a tweak to the design to account for that second issue, which is how Treasury now predicts – for what it’s worth – that the program will cost $7.2bn.

These cost blowouts have amplified derision of the home batteries as “middle-class welfare” of the worst sort.

Alison Reeve, the director of the energy and climate change program at the Grattan Institute, understands the concerns but says the evidence to back that claim “is pretty thin when you look at where the batteries are being installed”.

Notably, this is in homes across outer suburbia, such as western Sydney, and in regional areas. In other words, not in enclaves of the comfortably well-off.

Then there is the bigger-picture issue: that we risk sacrificing long-term clean energy goals in the name of short-term fiscal objectives.

“Batteries are going to be a big part of our energy future,” Reeve says. “We do need to do some stimulating of that industry until it can stand on its own two feet.”

Slashing support for batteries would damage the burgeoning web of small businesses, suppliers and tradies who have invested in servicing the infant batteries industry.

That is not to say there are ways to improve the cost and benefits trade-off in the home batteries program. This could be by ensuring subsidised batteries deliver a community benefit by contributing to the power grid in times of need.

“We need to make sure we are maximising the public benefit, rather than just the private benefit,” Reeve says.

There are lessons in how Western Australia has designed its home batteries support scheme.

“If you look at the west coast, you couldn’t get the state subsidy unless you linked yourself up to a virtual power plan run by the network operator. That was in order to benefit the whole network,” she says.

“We also need a clear path out of the subsidy so it doesn’t grow uncontrollably.”

text:
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act will lower costs, advance clean energy projects

WASHINGTON – Today, U.S. Senator John Hickenlooper released the following statement after he voted to advance the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. The Senate will vote on final passage early next week.

“Democrats across the country ran on lowering costs, holding Big Tech accountable, and stopping the Trump administration’s attacks on clean energy. Now we have an opportunity to deliver on all three.

“This bipartisan permitting deal would help lower electricity bills, make data centers pay their fair share, and accelerate the clean energy projects we need to reduce carbon emissions and combat climate change.

“This bill isn’t perfect. No bill is. We should continue working with Tribal Nations and environmental groups to strengthen it as it moves through the legislative process. But we have a golden opportunity to make good on our promise to voters to make energy more affordable. We cannot afford to let it slip away.”

Hickenlooper has long supported reforms to modernize what is all too often a decades-long timeline to build new transmission lines and energy production projects. He has hosted a series of bipartisan permitting dinners throughout the last three years, bringing key Senate negotiators together to build consensus and help move permitting conversations forward.

text:
Washington, D.C. – Today, Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) released the following statement after the Senate voted to invoke cloture on the motion to proceed to the legislative vehicle for the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), a permitting reform bill:

“Americans are paying too much for energy, and we need to do something about it. For too long, our broken permitting system has held back cleaner, cheaper energy; driven up costs; and delayed good-paying jobs. We should be making it easier to bring affordable energy onto the grid and to ensure data centers pay their fair share, so Americans don’t get stuck with the bill. At the same time, we must uphold the environmental protections that keep New York’s water clean and ensure communities have a voice in what projects are built in their backyards.

“Senators Whitehouse and Heinrich deserve tremendous credit for their hard work bringing this legislation together and moving forward a long-overdue conversation about permitting reform. While I have outstanding concerns with parts of the bill that I’ll fight to address through the amendment process, I’m voting today to move this debate forward. Americans can’t afford more years of delay, higher energy bills, and missed opportunities, but addressing those concerns does not need to come at the expense of protecting our land, water, and communities’ voices. It's time to get this legislation right and deliver for American families.”

text:
Washington, D.C. – U.S. Senator Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) issued the following statement after voting against advancing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA):

“Making it easier to build clean energy and critical infrastructure projects is important for New Mexico and our nation, and Congress has failed to find a path forward for far too long.

“However, I share the serious concerns raised by New Mexicans across the state, particularly our Pueblo and environmental leaders, and believe they must be addressed. After spending the last month listening to these concerns, I cannot support advancing the bill in its current form.

“I remain committed to working with my colleagues to address these concerns, make meaningful improvements, and get this right.”

name: EPA
title: The 2026 Midterm Elections: What a Changed Congress Could Mean for EPA and the ...
description:
The results of the 2026 midterm elections may mark an important turning point in federal environmental policy.
Environmental Enforcement: Changes in Priorities, Not Necessarily an End to Enforcement The election may also affect the direction and intensity of federal environmental enforcement.
A Democratic-controlled Congress may seek to restore or protect funding for environmental enforcement, scientific research, climate programs, environmental remediation, and federal-state environmental partnerships.
Conclusion The 2026 midterm elections introduce a new dimension to federal environmental regulation.
For questions about how the midterm elections may affect environmental regulation, enforcement, or compliance for your business, contact Michael Blumenthal or any member of Frantz Ward’s Environmental Practice Group.
text:
The results of the 2026 midterm elections may mark an important turning point in federal environmental policy. With Democrats projected to take control of both the U.S. House of Representatives and the Senate, the balance of power in Washington is changing as President Trump’s administration enters the final two years of its term.

For the regulated community, the election raises important questions about the future direction of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), the durability of its deregulatory agenda, federal environmental enforcement, and the potential for renewed congressional scrutiny of environmental policy.

Although the election does not change the President’s authority to direct executive branch agencies, the change in congressional control introduces a new institutional dynamic. Congressional oversight, appropriations, legislative initiatives, and confirmation authority could all become important mechanisms through which the incoming Congress seeks to influence EPA’s priorities.

For manufacturers, industrial operators, developers, utilities, and other entities subject to federal environmental requirements, the practical consequences could extend well beyond Washington’s political landscape.

1. Congressional Oversight of EPA’s Deregulatory Agenda

One of the most immediate consequences of the election will likely be increased congressional scrutiny of EPA’s regulatory and deregulatory activities.

The Trump administration has pursued an extensive effort to reconsider, rescind, or modify environmental regulations adopted under prior administrations. These initiatives have addressed significant portions of the environmental regulatory framework, including greenhouse gas regulation, air quality standards, water regulation, chemical safety, and federal environmental enforcement.

A Democratic-controlled Congress will have greater capacity to investigate the legal, scientific, economic, and procedural foundations of these initiatives. Congressional committees with jurisdiction over environmental matters may conduct hearings, request agency documents, issue subpoenas, and examine the extent to which EPA’s actions comply with statutory requirements.

Particular attention may be directed toward:

EPA’s reconsideration of greenhouse gas regulations and the Clean Air Act’s regulatory framework.

Efforts to revise the definition of Waters of the United States (WOTUS) under the Clean Water Act.

Reconsideration of existing air quality and emissions standards.

EPA’s approach to chemical regulation under the Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA).

Changes to federal environmental enforcement priorities and staffing.

The treatment of environmental justice considerations in federal regulatory decisions.

For regulated entities, increased congressional oversight does not automatically invalidate or suspend EPA rulemaking. It may, however, increase uncertainty surrounding the implementation and long-term durability of regulatory changes.

2. The Future of EPA’s Deregulatory Agenda

The election does not, by itself, reverse the administration’s existing regulatory policies. EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin and the administration retain executive authority to pursue their regulatory agenda.

However, congressional control can influence the resources, statutory authority, and political environment in which EPA operates.

The administration’s deregulatory initiatives will likely face more intensive scrutiny, particularly where EPA has relied upon changes in statutory interpretation, reconsideration of prior scientific determinations, or revised approaches to regulatory cost-benefit analysis.

The regulated community should recognize an important distinction: a proposed repeal or reconsideration of a regulation is not the same as a final repeal. Unless and until a regulation is lawfully amended, rescinded, stayed, or vacated, existing legal obligations generally remain in effect.

Moreover, EPA’s regulatory actions remain subject to judicial review. Challenges to the administrative record, statutory authority, scientific analysis, and procedural compliance may determine whether particular deregulatory initiatives survive, regardless of congressional control.

3. PFAS Regulation: An Area of Particular Uncertainty

PFAS regulation is likely to remain one of the most consequential and closely watched areas of environmental policy.

The administration has pursued a more targeted approach to certain PFAS drinking water requirements, while maintaining federal regulation of PFOA and PFOS. EPA has proposed providing public water systems additional time, potentially until 2031, to comply with the PFOA and PFOS drinking water standards. It has also proposed rescinding drinking water regulatory determinations for PFHxS, PFNA, GenX, and the associated mixture.

A Democratic-controlled Congress may seek to challenge these changes, increase oversight of EPA’s scientific and regulatory decisions, and consider additional legislation addressing PFAS contamination, reporting, and liability.

The potential for congressional action is particularly significant because PFAS issues extend beyond drinking water regulation. They affect industrial wastewater discharges, manufacturing processes, chemical reporting, contaminated property, remediation obligations, and CERCLA liability.

For manufacturers and property owners, the distinction between regulatory changes and existing statutory liability is especially important. The election does not eliminate CERCLA liability associated with designated PFAS hazardous substances, nor does it resolve the numerous questions concerning the scope of liability, allocation, contribution, and available defenses.

Businesses should not assume that changes in EPA’s regulatory priorities will eliminate existing environmental obligations or potential exposure.

4. Environmental Enforcement: Changes in Priorities, Not Necessarily an End to Enforcement

The election may also affect the direction and intensity of federal environmental enforcement.

The administration has emphasized a more targeted enforcement approach, focusing on substantial violations, statutory requirements, and matters presenting significant environmental or public health concerns.

EPA’s FY 2027 budget proposal reflects this approach, including proposed reductions in civil and criminal enforcement resources. The proposed civil enforcement budget would decrease from approximately $231 million in FY 2026 to $137 million in FY 2027.

A Democratic-controlled Congress may seek to challenge these proposed reductions through the appropriations process and increased oversight of EPA’s enforcement activities.

The practical implications could include renewed attention to:

Industrial air emissions and Clean Air Act compliance.

Industrial wastewater discharges and NPDES permits.

Hazardous waste management under RCRA.

CERCLA investigations and remediation.

TSCA reporting and chemical management obligations.

Environmental violations involving PFAS and other emerging contaminants.

It is important to distinguish federal enforcement from state enforcement. Even if federal enforcement resources are constrained, authorized state environmental agencies retain substantial independent enforcement authority. In Ohio, for example, Ohio EPA’s regulatory and enforcement responsibilities will continue regardless of changes in federal congressional control.

Consequently, businesses should not interpret a potentially reduced federal enforcement emphasis as a reduction in their underlying compliance obligations.

5. Congressional Appropriations Could Become a Major Battleground

Perhaps the most consequential mechanism available to the incoming Congress will be its control over federal appropriations.

Congress determines the funding available to EPA and can influence how appropriated funds are allocated and used. A Democratic-controlled Congress may seek to restore or protect funding for environmental enforcement, scientific research, climate programs, environmental remediation, and federal-state environmental partnerships.

EPA’s FY 2027 budget request proposed significant reductions in agency funding. Congressional appropriators will have an opportunity to reconsider those proposals and determine whether the administration receives the resources it requested.

Appropriations decisions may have practical consequences for:

EPA inspection and enforcement staffing.

Superfund investigations and remediation.

Brownfield assessment and redevelopment grants.

State environmental program funding.

Environmental research and scientific assessments.

Federal oversight of industrial facilities and contaminated sites.

For the regulated community, these funding decisions may be as consequential as individual rulemakings. EPA’s ability to implement regulations, conduct inspections, process permits, and oversee remediation programs depends in significant part on available personnel and financial resources.

6. The Potential for New Environmental Legislation

Although a change in congressional control creates opportunities for new legislative initiatives, significant environmental legislation will not necessarily follow.

The Senate’s legislative procedures, the potential filibuster, presidential veto authority, and the need for bipartisan support will constrain the ability of a Democratic majority to enact sweeping statutory changes.

Nevertheless, several areas may receive renewed legislative attention:

PFAS regulation and liability allocation.

CERCLA amendments addressing emerging contaminants and responsible-party liability.

Federal environmental permitting reform.

Clean Air Act emissions requirements.

Clean Water Act protections and jurisdiction.

TSCA chemical evaluation and reporting.

Environmental funding and remediation programs.

Of particular interest to manufacturers and commercial property owners will be whether Congress revisits the allocation of PFAS-related cleanup costs and potential CERCLA liability. Bipartisan concerns about the impact of PFAS liability on municipal water systems, airports, manufacturers, and other potentially responsible parties could provide an opportunity for legislative discussions.

However, regulated entities should distinguish between proposed legislation and enacted statutory amendments. Until Congress passes legislation and it becomes law, existing statutory obligations remain controlling.

7. What Should the Regulated Community Do Now?

The change in congressional control creates a period of potential regulatory transition. Businesses should prepare for the possibility that federal environmental policy will become increasingly contested, with competing regulatory initiatives, congressional oversight, and litigation proceeding simultaneously.

We recommend that regulated entities consider the following steps:

Continue complying with existing requirements. Do not assume that proposed regulatory rollbacks, anticipated legislative changes, or shifts in enforcement priorities excuse compliance with existing permits, regulations, and statutory obligations.

Reevaluate environmental compliance programs. Review air, water, waste, chemical management, and reporting obligations to identify potential vulnerabilities before regulatory or enforcement priorities change.

Monitor PFAS developments. Manufacturers, industrial facilities, water utilities, and owners of potentially contaminated properties should continue evaluating PFAS-related regulatory requirements, contractual obligations, and potential CERCLA exposure.

Reassess environmental due diligence. Developers, purchasers, lenders, and property owners should continue incorporating environmental regulatory developments into Phase I Environmental Site Assessments, transaction documents, indemnification provisions, and remediation strategies.

Preserve opportunities for regulatory participation. Companies and industry associations should monitor proposed EPA rules, congressional hearings, and opportunities to submit technical and economic comments. Participation in the administrative record may be important if subsequent regulatory actions are challenged.

Prepare for continued regulatory uncertainty. Businesses should evaluate environmental compliance and capital investment decisions against multiple regulatory scenarios rather than relying exclusively on the continuation of any particular administration’s policies.

Conclusion

The 2026 midterm elections introduce a new dimension to federal environmental regulation. A Democratic-controlled Congress will have additional tools to scrutinize EPA’s actions, influence agency funding, challenge regulatory rollbacks, and pursue legislative initiatives. At the same time, the Trump administration retains executive authority over EPA, and the agency’s existing regulatory agenda will not automatically disappear.

The likely result is not an immediate reversal of federal environmental policy, but an increasingly contested regulatory environment in which agency rulemaking, congressional oversight, appropriations, and litigation will play interconnected roles.

For the regulated community, the principal takeaway is straightforward: regulatory change does not necessarily mean regulatory relief, and a change in congressional control does not eliminate existing environmental obligations.

Manufacturers, developers, and other regulated entities should continue to monitor federal and state developments, maintain robust compliance programs, and assess how evolving environmental requirements may affect their operations, transactions, and long-term business planning.

For questions about how the midterm elections may affect environmental regulation, enforcement, or compliance for your business, contact Michael Blumenthal or any member of Frantz Ward’s Environmental Practice Group.

text:
The following blog is part of a series examining specific provisions in the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA). Clean Air Task Force is taking a close look at the bill to identify opportunities to strengthen its provisions, address potential gaps, and improve its effectiveness in meeting the country’s energy needs reliably and affordably.

CATF has constructively engaged in the permitting reform policy discussion throughout the 119th Congress because we believe that the country needs more effective permitting processes to build clean energy infrastructure and electricity generation required to meet broadly shared economic and emissions reduction goals. Delivering project certainty has been a key bipartisan goal of these permitting reform conversations. Negotiators of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) have on many occasions expressed concerns with the myriad ways the administration has canceled, delayed, or otherwise stymied offshore wind and other clean energy projects. The drafters have included Title IV of BAAJA, which covers permitting certainty, as a way to prevent further meddling.

This post focuses not on whether BAAJA would provide an effective deterrent against future cancellations, but instead on the risk that it could inadvertently make it more difficult for future administrations to issue pollution control standards, including for greenhouse gas emissions. Even after the release of the manager’s amendment, which included changes intended to allay that concern, the problem has been lessened but not eliminated. This post explains how section 1401 of BAAJA creates that risk, why the manager’s amendment fails to resolve it, and provides suggestions for how to ensure future pollution limits do not wind up facing new headwinds.

BAAJA’s permitting certainty title creates risks for future pollution control standards

The goal of section 1401 is to maintain validly-issued federal authorizations and permits by preventing the executive branch from taking actions to cancel or modify them. A particularly egregious example of improper cancellations occurred last December when the administration issued stop-work orders for five offshore wind projects that were under construction. After the wind project developers sued, courts blocked each of those orders. Section 1401 would create legal avenues for the holders of similarly canceled or thwarted projects to seek judicial relief, not only in the form of injunctions and reinstated permits but also including damages awarded from the Judgment Fund, a permanent, indefinite appropriation that is not impacted by the annual appropriations process. The section’s logic is that the threat of costly litigation filed by project developers facing cancelations or delays would deter future actions with those effects.

The terms of section 1401 are remarkably broad. It covers a sweeping range of federal authorizations or permits that are “necessary for the construction or operation at normal capacity of a project,” and, unlike section 1402, is not limited to energy projects or infrastructure. The section would restrict a federal department or agency from taking “any new action that would revoke, rescind, withdraw, terminate, suspend, vacate, remand, reopen, materially amend, or materially alter” such a federal authorization or project. If an agency were to do so, it provides for judicial review in federal district court under a favorable standard for the project applicant—where the government has the burden of proof—and where a court can order reinstatement of the authorization or permit, injunctive relief to prevent further meddling, attorneys’ fees, costs associated with delay, and damages where the agency acted in bad faith.

One concern with this section is that it would make it more difficult for future administrations to adopt pollution control standards that result in changes to permits that affect how projects operate. For instance, if EPA were to issue a future greenhouse-gas pollution limit for power plants, that standard may require changes to existing permits. If that standard is based on a pollution control technology that requires auxiliary energy to operate and thereby drops the net output of the power plant, a plant operator could argue that the revised permit to comply with that standard prevents it from operating at “normal capacity.” Under the Clean Air Act’s judicial review provision, challenges to nationally applicable regulations issued by EPA such as this possible rule can only be filed in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit. However, section 1401 does not have this jurisdictional restriction. It therefore creates a new risk that multiple, project-specific challenges could instead be filed in numerous district courts that, if successful, could not only enjoin the rule’s application but also provide payouts to the polluters.

The section also does not differentiate between unlawfully issued permits or applications—for instance, an authorization for polluting infrastructure rushed through without proper reviews or oil and gas leases that conflict with land use plan requirements or fail to comply with procedural safeguards—and those issued with proper observance of legal requirements. The section therefore creates a risk that it would be difficult for future administrations to unwind hastily issued or unlawful permits and authorizations without facing significant penalties or subsidizing the recipients of those leases.

A major problem with this section is just how uncertain its application would be. As a Congressional Research Service analysis published before the manager’s amendment put it, “Section 1401’s impact on other statutes is uncertain but could be significant if courts were to construe that provision to bar agencies from taking actions authorized by other laws. Under such a reading, Section 1401 could prevent agencies from fulfilling statutory duties to revisit and revise prior permitting and regulatory decisions upon certain triggering conditions.” That risk should give members of Congress significant pause, and it needs thoughtful solutions to eliminate it.

The Manager’s Amendment reduces, but does not eliminate, this risk

The manager’s amendment to BAAJA released on Saturday, November 7, makes several changes to section 1401, many of which improve the section by reducing future risks. However, these changes—revising “full capacity” to normal capacity, revising the list of prohibited agency actions, adding a materiality component to the prohibition on amending or altering a permit, allowing permit changes when they are necessary to prevent harm to human health or the environment, a new section 1401(b)(1)(F) allowing actions “taken pursuant to any applicable law or regulation”, and the addition of a “bad faith” requirement—are insufficient and introduce further uncertainties.

First, although the original version of the text would have barred actions that would have prevented a project’s “operation at full capacity,” the revised text now bars actions that prevent “operation at normal capacity.” This change is a marginal improvement, but the term “normal capacity” is still undefined and leaves open the potential risk that any reduction in production or operation following promulgation of a new pollution control regulation could still be argued by permit holders as interfering with what had previously been the “normal” operation of the facility.

Second, the revised list of prohibited agency actions has now been lengthened to include “vacate, remand, [or] reopen” a permit. This addition may have been motivated by recent motions filed by the Department of the Interior requesting that courts voluntarily remand and, in at least one instance, vacate an offshore wind authorization so that the department can reexamine it. However, because the text refers only to an agency vacating, remanding, or reopening a permit, it is unclear if it would prevent an agency from asking a court to take one of those actions, and then taking the action (for instance, vacating, remanding, or reopening a permit) in response to the court’s order, as acting in response to a court’s order is allowed under the revised text of section 1401.

Third, the manager’s amendment adds a materiality component to the prohibition against amending or altering a permit or authorization. Without this change, there was a risk that this administration could make truly minor changes to a permit or authorization for its favored projects so that the permit holder could challenge the altered permit and obtain injunctive relief that would lock in a future administration from ever modifying that permit. But it also introduces new uncertainties about what makes an amendment or alteration “material.” Other areas of law, such as securities law, have a corpus of caselaw on what materiality means in that context. No such precedent exists for how much a permit must be modified to cross this newly created but undefined threshold. Therefore, even after the manager’s amendment, judicial interpretation of the materiality qualifier is uncertain for agency actions such as tightening an emission standard or adding a new emission limit on a permit. Future cases would have to argue those points, with the possibility of different lines drawn in different courts.

Fourth, the manager’s amendment adds text allowing otherwise prohibited changes to permits or authorizations when “necessary to prevent … harm or damage” to “human health” or “the environment.” That change is unlikely to stop this section from being used to thwart pollution control regulations because the threat must be “immediate, specific, urgent, substantial, and proximate.” Furthermore, the section flips the normal standard for arbitrary and capricious review of agency action on its head by placing the burden on the government, rather than the challenger, to prove that criterion is satisfied. This section invites operators of power plants or other sources to challenge the application to them of any pollution control standard that includes a degree of agency discretion or judgment in setting the acceptable level, or where there is a lag between the discharge or emission and the harm to human health or the environment, or where the harm is general or not sufficiently substantial.

Fifth, and most confoundingly, the new section 1401(b)(1)(F) in the manager’s amendment would allow agencies to change permits so long as the actions are “taken pursuant to any applicable law or regulation.” On its face, this provision would seem to nullify the rest of section 1401. Agencies always point to some law or regulation as justification for their actions. For instance, last year’s stop-work orders for offshore wind projects cited the Outer Continental Lands Shelf Act (OCSLA) or agency regulations as providing purported legal authority. If this is enough, then it is hard to see how any challenger would ever succeed in a section 1401 challenge. But this cannot be what the drafters of this section intended, and a court would likely refuse to interpret this provision as making the entire section irrelevant. The question then becomes, what—if anything—does this provision do?

The answer is almost impossible to pin down, and different federal courts may interpret this unclear provision in different ways. One possibility is that the provision would apply only to some set of non-discretionary actions; in other words, where an agency had no choice. Under this reading, which would interpret “pursuant to” narrowly to mean “required by,” a new agency rulemaking to set a pollution standard, which would involve agency discretion about what level to set the standard at, could still be vulnerable to attack. This reading leaves the problem of section 1401 being used against future Clean Air Act rules very much live. Another possibility would be that only ultra vires claims could succeed—those are claims that an agency acted entirely outside its authority—which are difficult to prove and “essentially a Hail Mary pass.”1 Under that interpretation, canceled clean energy projects like the stop-work orders from last year may not actually be able to access this section’s supposed benefits without clearing a particularly difficult legal bar.

Because this section remains ambiguous, and because these claims would be brought in different courts, it is quite possible that courts would diverge in how they read this provision. Some projects may face an impossible climb to access the section’s benefits, while collateral attacks on otherwise lawful and well-reasoned pollution control standards might still go forward.

At the very least, this section would create new red tape for pollution control rules by requiring agencies to undertake onerous new procedural steps to provide notice to covered projects or actions with a detailed explanation of the action and evidence supporting it under 1401(b)(3). The bar for satisfying these tasks is unclear, and this process would be at best time and resource intensive for an agency issuing a new standard and at worst would leave open risk that implementation of the standard could be frustrated just for failure to jump through those hoops.

Sixth, the manager’s amendment adds a “bad faith” requirement to receive punitive damages. This change is an improvement that decreases the risk of permit holders obtaining particularly lucrative payouts even from well-supported federal rules. Unfortunately, the bad faith requirement only applies to the damages, and does not affect the availability of other relief, including reinstatement of permits, injunctive relief, or attorneys’ fees.

Four straightforward changes are needed to reduce 1401’s risks

Clearer text in section 1401 could eliminate the risk of BAAJA undermining important future pollution control standards. While maintaining the structure of this section, four ways to improve the text would be to (1) limit the scope of permits and authorizations covered by the section; (2) clarify what lawful actions would still be allowed to revise permits or authorizations due to future pollution control standards or to revisit unlawfully issued permits or authorizations; (3) eliminate the reference to “operation at normal capacity”; and (4) make the showing of “bad faith” an element for all potential remedies under section 1401, not just for damages.

Congress should limit the scope of permits and authorizations covered by section 1401

To limit the scope of permits and authorizations covered by section 1401, one approach would be to add an “exclusions” provision to section 1401(a) to narrow the capacious definition of “federal authorization or permit.” This language could state that “In this section, the term ‘federal authorization or permit’ does not include” a defined list of actions taken under specific federal pollution control laws. One item in that list could be “any authorization or permit issued to comply with standards, regulations, or guidelines issued under the Clean Air Act (42 U.S.C. 7201 et seq.).” Other pollution control laws could also be listed. CATF advocated for this fix prior to the release of the manager’s amendment, and we still believe that this text would be preferable to the approach in the manager’s amendment.

This proposed change would require careful drafting to ensure the list of covered statutes is sufficiently comprehensive. Under the statutory interpretation principle of expressio unius est exclusio alterius, which stands for the concept that when some items in a class are specifically listed, others in the class are excluded, a court may assume that any statute not listed would be excluded.

Congress should clarify what lawful actions would still be allowed to revise permits or authorizations due to future pollution control standards or to revisit unlawfully issued permits or authorizations

To clarify what lawful actions would still be allowed to revise permits or authorizations, one option would be to allow actions that amend or alter authorizations or permits if they are carried out as part of the implementation or enforcement of lawfully promulgated regulations of general applicability. This language would make clear that section 1401 only covers actions targeting individual permits and does not restrict implementation or enforcement of lawfully issued rules, whether pollution related or not. This approach would provide greater certainty for judicial statutory interpretation than the language in section 1401(b)(1)(F) while still preserving the animating goal of this section to prevent adverse actions of particular applicability against specific projects.

Congress should eliminate the reference to “operation at normal capacity”

To cut off potential arguments that pollution control standards could interfere with the “operation at normal capacity” of a source pursuant to a permit or authorization, including in situations where an agency had previously determined that no authorization or permit was necessary, the references to “operation at normal capacity” should be eliminated. This term is unnecessarily vague and would lead to arguments that emissions restrictions that have the effect of reducing net output of power plants would be prohibited. Courts may diverge in how they respond to that argument and counterarguments, and the resulting patchwork of interpretations could frustrate effective implementation and enforcement of pollution-control standards.

Congress should make the showing of “bad faith” an element for all potential remedies under section 1401, not just for damages.

To avoid courts reinstating permits or authorizations and enjoining any future changes, including those that may be necessary to reexamine unlawfully issued permits or to comply with future regulations, one option would be to make a “bad faith” showing a requirement for any form of judicial relief, not just damages. The reinstatement of a permit, injunctive relief, and attorneys’ fees are all powerful remedies. From a pollution-reduction perspective, the reinstatement of a permit or authorization and injunction against future actions to modify or cancel a project would cause all of the potential harm. Just because punitive damages are not available under the managers’ amendment does not mean that developers will not bring cases.

Conclusion

Preventing this administration from further meddling in clean energy permits is a difficult task. It is admirable that BAAJA’s drafters attempted to address permit certainty, but the ambiguities and uncertainties in section 1401 create the possibility that vital future pollution control standards will face new legal risks. Clearer language that protects the ability of the federal government to issue valid pollution control rules would eliminate the uncertainty this section would otherwise create.

text:
X-Energy, a developer of advanced nuclear reactors and fuel technology, and Dow, through its wholly-owned subsidiary Long Mott Energy, on Nov. 9 announced that the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission has approved the Construction Permit Application for the proposed construction of four Xe-100 advanced small modular reactors at Dow’s UCC Seadrift Operations site in Texas.

The CPA approval makes Long Mott Generating Station the first advanced nuclear facility approved for an industrial site in the United States, "a historic milestone achieved under the U.S. Department of Energy’s Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program," x-Energy said.

Approval of the construction permit enables X-energy and Dow to continue advancing the proposed project toward construction readiness, finalizing and standardizing the Xe-100 design, maturing the supply chain for long-lead components and materials, and developing an Operating License application for submission to the NRC, x-Energy said.

"This supports Dow’s consideration of the proposed project’s next phases, ensuring the design, equipment, and materials are in place before allocating major capital for full-scale construction, consistent with Dow’s proven global project management practices. For a first-of-a-kind project, this reduces schedule and cost risk once work begins on site, and is aligned to the Company’s established timeline of first delivery in the early 2030s," x-Energy added.

The issuance marks the first NRC CPA approval of a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor in nearly 60 years, the first-ever pebble-bed HTGR approval and the first-ever for a nuclear industrial deployment.

The NRC’s review found that the Xe-100 design can be safely sited and constructed within an operating industrial site.

The proposed plant is intended to provide both electricity and high-temperature steam to Dow’s site, replacing existing energy and steam assets near their end-of-life. The four first-of-a-kind Xe-100s deployed at Seadrift are expected to provide power to the site for 60 years.

The NRC completed its review in alignment with its established schedule, evaluating the safety and environmental impacts of the proposed Xe-100 facility against the global benchmark for safe, responsible operation of nuclear technology.

"Across both parts of the review, the intrinsic safety characteristics of the design and extensive pre-application engagement supported an efficient, thorough, independent review that met or exceeded the NRC’s high standard, supported by decades of U.S. Department of Energy research on HTGRs and TRISO fuel, and strengthened by the passage of the bipartisan ADVANCE Act in 2024," x-Energy said. "CPA approval by the NRC builds on this body of work, and positions future Xe-100 applications for enhanced efficiency in commercial nuclear licensing by incorporating learnings from Long Mott’s review."

Since 2018 and 2023, X-energy and Dow, respectively, have worked with the NRC through extensive pre-application engagement to demonstrate the safety profile of the Xe-100 and its TRISO-X fuel, directly cited by the NRC as a contributor to the application’s efficient review, x-Energy said.

The companies "intend to carry this same discipline and rigor into the next phase of the project, ensuring construction and commercial readiness before major site work begins to reduce cost and schedule risk. Dow is expected to consider a preliminary investment decision in 2027."

Full-scale nuclear construction would begin following Dow’s final investment decision.

title: Congress's Formal and Functional Power After the Midterms - Yale Journal on Regulation
description:
After Democrats’ blowout win in the midterms, Congress will have a lot of formal power to check the administration, particularly through appropriations and oversight.
The effectiveness of those checks, however, may depend importantly on something less tangible: Congress’s functional power to shape public opinion and delegitimate actions it considers unlawful or ill-advised.
In other words, by blocking some actions, courts gain the credibility to settle legal and constitutional doubts about others.
In the second Trump administration, executive officials have defied limits and mandates regarding spending and other matters in ways that even quite popular presidents in the past did not dare.
First, courts (and Congress itself) should buttress Congress’s ability to support or stymie executive initiatives through the “reactive” powers I mentioned earlier—Congress’s powers of oversight and funding.
text:
After Democrats’ blowout win in the midterms, Congress will have a lot of formal power to check the administration, particularly through appropriations and oversight. The effectiveness of those checks, however, may depend importantly on something less tangible: Congress’s functional power to shape public opinion and delegitimate actions it considers unlawful or ill-advised. And that power, unfortunately, seems to have undergone a long-term decline.

At any rate, I speculate about this possibility in a forthcoming essay in the Notre Dame Law Review. (The essay is part of an excellent Gray Center symposium on “What Happened to Congress?”.)

My essay posits that a key feature of separation of powers in the United States has been a process of interbranch legitimation of government action. These days, people often imagine that effective government requires letting majorities get things done. That is true enough but if taken too far it misses that checks and balances may empower government even as they also restrain it. They do so in part by helping ensure the popularity of actions that run the gauntlet of interbranch checks. But checks and balances may also help generate that popularity in the first place by enhancing the legitimacy of actions that the branches jointly approve.

If that idea sounds fanciful, consider the historical role of the Supreme Court. Political scientists have long puzzled over why the political branches tolerate judicial review, given its potential to obstruct their goals. The answer, according to Keith Whittington and others, is that judicial review actually serves the political branches’ long-run interests. In some instances, the Court saves politicians from themselves by taking divisive options off the table. But more generally the Court has helped legitimate contested policies by validating them.

In other words, by blocking some actions, courts gain the credibility to settle legal and constitutional doubts about others. Politicians take the bitter with the sweet. Gaining validation from judicial approval requires accepting judicial defeats—a dynamic very much in evidence in the second Trump administration (and for that matter in the Biden administration, too).

My essay speculates that similar dynamics might be generalized across the three branches. In particular, Congress these days often finds itself in a position analogous to courts exercising judicial review.

Due to broad statutory delegations and accumulated executive practice, presidents can often pursue significant initiatives unilaterally. Congress is then in a reactive posture: it must decide whether to support or stymie executive initiatives. And while that process is partly a matter of exercising its formal power over continued funding, it is also, perhaps more fundamentally, a matter of functionally shaping public perceptions of such actions.

In any event, there is substantial evidence that Congress has historically played the leading role in sustaining broad public acceptance of federal governance. With its distributed representation and capacity for logrolling and compromise, Congress is best positioned among the branches to channel public opinion and promote acceptance of disputed policies. And on matters ranging from war mobilization and industrial policy to welfare and civil rights, Congress has done just that. It has been the central engine of legitimacy for federal governance.

Lately, however, this engine has seemed to splutter. Mired in partisan division, Congress has struggled to legislate on key questions like immigration and the environment; it has instead let the executive branch set policy on its own. Even worse, Congress has largely failed to defend its institutional prerogatives against repeated presidential usurpations. In the second Trump administration, executive officials have defied limits and mandates regarding spending and other matters in ways that even quite popular presidents in the past did not dare.

Now, with the return of divided government, congressional capacity faces an important test. It is possible that Congress will recover some of its ability to negotiate broadly supported compromises and enforce its institutional interests in bipartisan fashion; having larger and more ideologically mixed Democratic majorities in the House and Senate may help.

But Congress is likely to remain highly polarized and President Trump will surely seek to write off congressional checks as partisan posturing; he is reportedly planning to use executive power aggressively. A key question will then be whether congressional opposition stiffens resistance inside the executive branch to unlawful or unwise actions. Can Congress still strip force from actions of which it disapproves, or can presidents ride roughshod over congressional opposition unless and until courts step in to stop them?

Though Congress will hopefully succeed in restoring some of its former strength, I fear that, whatever happens over the next two years, Congress’s decline reflects deep-seated changes in media and society rather than more contingent factors. As Rick Pildes has pointed out, other western democracies with very different systems are facing similar governance challenges and problems of legislative incapacity. Just look at France.

While I don’t have great answers to this problem, the essay suggests two institutional adaptations. First, courts (and Congress itself) should buttress Congress’s ability to support or stymie executive initiatives through the “reactive” powers I mentioned earlier—Congress’s powers of oversight and funding. And second, courts themselves should take care to avoid the sort of excessive politicization that could undermine their own authority, much as fragmentation has done for Congress.

More generally, all sides of current debates should remember that American government has historically been effective because of checks and balances and not despite them. To that extent, removing restraints on majority will could prove self-defeating.

text:
CoTec Holdings Corp. (TSXV:CTH)(OTCQX:CTHCF) ("CoTec" or the "Company") notes the press release issued today by its joint venture, HyProMag USA LLC ("HyProMag USA"), announcing the delivery of the first major process equipment to its rare earth magnet recycling and manufacturing facility in Northlake, Texas (the "Northlake Texas Facility" or the "Project"), marking an important milestone as the Project advances toward financing, commissioning and operations.

Key Highlights

First major process equipment delivered: The first major process equipment has arrived at the Northlake Texas Facility, reflecting continued progress in detailed engineering and procurement.

Site secured in Dallas-Fort Worth: In December 2025, HyProMag USA secured a long-term lease for the Northlake Texas Facility at Ironhead Commerce Center, Building 1, Denton County, Texas, near critical infrastructure, including the BNSF intermodal rail link and Alliance Airport.i

Development advancing: Electrical power capacity secured through Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC, permitting progressing with Weston Solutions, Inc., and contractor selection underway.ii

Phased timeline: Initial magnet cutting and finishing operations targeted for the first half of 2027, followed by commissioning of Phase 1 integrated recycling and manufacturing operations in mid-2028.

Production and jobs: The Northlake Texas Facility targets approximately 1,526 metric tons per year of total payable production upon completion of Phase 2iii and is expected to create approximately 100 direct jobs.

Expansion potential: The Expansion Pre-Feasibility Study ("Expansion PFS") announced on October 27, 2026iv targets approximately 4,192 metric tons per year of neodymium iron boron ("NdFeB") magnet production and approximately 6,000 metric tons per year of total salable materials by 2034 across four plants.

Julian Treger, Chief Executive Officer of CoTec, commented: "The delivery of the first process equipment to the Northlake Texas Facility marks an important milestone for HyProMag USA as we advance toward commercial operations. The Project is expected to create around 100 direct jobs and support workforce training and skills development, helping build the skilled workforce required for advanced manufacturing in the United States. By establishing a domestic source of recycled rare earth magnets, HyProMag USA will strengthen U.S. manufacturing capacity and contribute to a more secure and resilient rare earth magnet supply chain."

Equipment Delivery and Site

The arrival of the equipment reflects continued progress in detailed engineering and procurement as HyProMag USA develops a secure, sustainable and domestic source of recycled rare earth permanent magnets in the United States. In December 2025, HyProMag USA secured a long-term lease agreement for the Northlake Texas Facility, located at Ironhead Commerce Center, Building 1, Dallas-Fort Worth, Denton County, Texas. The Project site is strategically located near critical infrastructure, including the BNSF intermodal rail link and Alliance Airport.

Project Development and Timeline

The Northlake Texas Facility is expected to become one of the first commercial-scale integrated rare earth magnet recycling and magnet manufacturing operations in the United States. Project development continues to advance, with electrical power capacity secured through Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC, permitting progressing with Weston Solutions, Inc., and contractor selection underway. HyProMag USA is targeting initial magnet cutting and finishing operations in the first half of 2027, followed by commissioning of Phase 1 integrated recycling and manufacturing operations in mid-2028.

The milestone follows the successful completion of the Expansion PFS as announced on October 27, 2026, which confirmed the potential to significantly increase HyProMag USA's production capacity while maintaining robust project economics. The Expansion PFS highlighted the opportunity to establish one of the largest rare earth magnet recycling and manufacturing platforms in the United States, targeting approximately 4,192 metric tons per year of NdFeB magnet production and approximately 6,000 metric tons per year of total salable materials by 2034 across four plants.

The Northlake Texas Facility is expected to create approximately 100 direct jobs and play an important role in supporting the development of a secure, resilient and sustainable domestic rare earth magnet supply chain. By recovering valuable magnetic materials from end-of-life products and manufacturing scrap, HyProMag USA aims to transform waste streams into a domestic resource for new magnet production, reducing reliance on imported rare earth materials and supporting U.S. manufacturing.

About HyProMag USA

HyProMag USA is developing advanced rare earth magnet recycling and manufacturing operations to establish a secure domestic U.S. supply chain for NdFeB magnets, essential components for AI infrastructure, medical systems, robotics, electric vehicles, and advanced electronics. Leveraging the revolutionary Hydrogen Processing of Magnet Scrap ("HPMS") technology, developed over 15 years with over US$100 million in R&D investment, HyProMag USA is designed to deliver faster magnet-to-magnet short-loop recycling that uses 88% less energy and reduces carbon emissions by 85% compared to conventional methods. HPMS accepts a wide range of magnet-bearing feedstocks - including end-of-life EV motors, data-center and industrial equipment, consumer electronics, and manufacturing scrap - enabling recovery of magnet-grade material without chemical processing.

Ownership

HyProMag USA LLC is owned 50:50 by CoTec and HyProMag Limited. HyProMag Limited is 100% owned by Maginito Limited, which is owned 79.4% by Mkango Magnetic Materials Limited (AIM/TSX-V: MKA) and 20.6% by CoTec.

For more information on HyProMag USA, please visit www.hypromagusa.com

About CoTec

CoTec Holdings Corp. (TSXV:CTH)(OTCQX:CTHCF) is redefining the future of resource extraction and recycling. Focused on rare earth magnets and strategic materials, CoTec integrates breakthrough technologies with strategic assets to unlock secure, sustainable, and low-cost supply chains.

CoTec's mission is clear: accelerate the energy transition while strengthening strategic mineral supply chains for the countries we operate in. By investing in and deploying disruptive technologies, the Company delivers capital-efficient, scalable solutions that transform marginal assets, tailings, waste streams, and recycled products into high-value critical minerals.

From its HyProMag USA magnet recycling joint venture in Texas, to iron tailings reprocessing and reclamation in Québec, to next-generation copper and iron solutions backed by global majors, CoTec is building a diversified portfolio with long-term growth, rapid cash flow potential, and high barriers to entry. The result is a differentiated platform at the intersection of technology, sustainability, and strategic materials.
