text:
(The Center Square) – A coalition of energy and policy organizations sent a letter to President Donald Trump expressing concern over the harm to national security that is posed by publicly traded U.S. companies – such as Amazon, Apple, and Google – being involved in the climate convention, COP31.

Senior Fellow at the Energy & Environment Legal Institute as well as former Trump administration EPA Transition Team Advisor Steve Milloy told The Center Square: “All US companies, public traded or not, that are involved in COP31 represent a threat to the nation.”

COP31 is an annual climate change conference put on by the United Nations.

Milloy told The Center Square that the letter to Trump “targets publicly traded tech companies like Amazon, Apple and Google for two reasons.”

“First, as publicly traded companies that have an affirmative legal duty to be honest when discussing issues related to their business, supporting COP31 is fundamentally dishonest because there is nothing these companies can do to affect climate,” Milloy said.

“So talking about it like they can is inherently dishonest,” Milloy said. “Next, these tech companies have various national security activities and responsibilities.”

Milloy said China pushes climate-related actions at these conferences in effort to hurt U.S. national security.

“Companies involved in our national security should not be teaming up with Communist China against our national security," he said. “The President should bar federal contractors with national security obligations from participating in a process that only works to the benefit of Communist China.”

Signatories of the letter include Milloy’s organization Energy & Environment Legal Institute along with the American Energy Institute, CFACT, Heartland Impact, The Heartland Institute, and Truth in Energy and Climate.

In their letter, the groups expressed support for Trump’s decision to withdraw from the United Nations Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, while also requesting that the president “take action to ensure that U.S. companies attending the conference do not violate the law and undercut U.S. Policy.”

The letter notes that “both federal law and SEC regulations prohibit [Amazon, Apple and Google] from making false and misleading statements.

“Not only are these companies misleading the public and potentially violating the law by giving the public and investors the impression that they are doing something about supposed ‘climate change,’ but they are also undercutting U.S. foreign policy and national security by participating in COP31,” the letter said.

The Center Square reached out to Amazon, Google, Apple, UN Climate Change, and the White House Press Office for comment. None responded by publishing.

President of The Heartland Institute James Taylor told The Center Square that "publicly traded companies getting in bed with UN global climate governance is a repeat of the societal-wide elimination of our freedoms that took place when government teamed up with big corporations under the guise of fighting COVID and fighting online 'misinformation.'”

“Large corporations should never be allowed to do governments' dirty work that either cannot find the votes to pass through normal legislative processes or is expressly prohibited by our Constitution,” Taylor said

COP31 began on Monday in Turkey.

The climate summit intends to focus on the “implementation of climate solutions and progressing a global energy transition that drives economic growth, more jobs, food security, better health and safety and affordable clean energy.”

title: Major bill to cut red tape for energy projects clears Senate hurdle - Washington Examiner
description:
If passed, the bill would be a major overhaul of permitting for federal projects, including but not limited to highways, pipelines, and power lines.
It would arguably be the most significant bill, in terms of its economic impact, signed by President Donald Trump during his second term.
The bill would also prevent data centers from passing along their electricity and energy costs to consumers.
Key negotiators in the Senate released an updated version of the bill over the weekend, using a process called a manager’s amendment.
However, just minutes before Monday’s vote on BAAJA, Trump said he would not approve any wind farms, calling the projects “losers.”
text:
Ahead of the vote, advocates of the bill said at least 15 to 20 Democrats are needed to back the bill in order to whip votes in the House.

Better known as BAAJA, the legislation has the support of dozens of clean energy and manufacturing associations, more than 300 solar and storage companies, oil companies, utility firms, some climate change groups, and lawmakers across the aisle.

If passed, the bill would be a major overhaul of permitting for federal projects, including but not limited to highways, pipelines, and power lines. It would arguably be the most significant bill, in terms of its economic impact, signed by President Donald Trump during his second term.

While the test vote indicates the bill is on its way to Trump’s desk, it faces an uphill battle in the House, as many Democrats wish to push permitting discussions to the next Congress, when they hold the majority in both chambers.

However, advocates of the bill say that Democrats won’t be able to strike a better deal that Trump would still be willing to sign.

The current bipartisan deal would streamline the federal permitting process through a number of avenues, including reforming the National Environmental Policy Act, a 55-year-old law that requires federal agencies to evaluate the environmental effects of major actions and decisions relevant to their departments, such as issuing permits and licenses for large projects.

The bill would also reform other bedrock environmental laws, such as the Clean Water Act, the National Historic Preservation Act, and the Endangered Species Act.

Broadly, the legislation would shorten the window for lawsuits challenging environmental reviews for new projects. It also includes measures to accelerate the build-out of transmission infrastructure.

One provision sought by Democrats would make it more difficult for the president to revoke project permits, which is a priority because Trump has halted the construction of renewable energy sources.

The bill would also prevent data centers from passing along their electricity and energy costs to consumers.

Key negotiators in the Senate released an updated version of the bill over the weekend, using a process called a manager’s amendment. The amended legislation includes “clarifying, conforming, and technical edits” meant to address several concerns brought forward by environmental groups, tribal communities, and utilities over the last few weeks.

These changes include extending the window for objections to certain environmental reviews, giving states a pathway to ask the federal regulators to investigate local utility projects, preserving collective bargaining agreements for employees at power marketing administrations, and creating a new data center community assistance program within the Department of Energy.

The manager’s amendment also addresses concerns regarding the permit certainty provisions, as critics claimed the legislation would make it difficult to walk back permits of projects that might have a worse environmental impact than previously thought.

Some of the most prominent changes were made to provisions regarding the National Historic Preservation Act, which were widely criticized by tribal groups. Specifically, the amendment version cuts a measure that would let the secretary of the Interior assume responsibilities of a tribal historic preservation officer in some cases, and strikes a controversial definition of “property of traditional religious or cultural importance.”

It would also require more consultation with tribes and native organizations, and require the Interior Department to provide Tribal Historic Preservation Offices with technical assistance, training, and support.

Heinrich told reporters ahead of the vote on Monday that changes to the legislation would also give tribes an equal seat with states regarding transmission planning and would require federal agencies to consult with tribes early on projects that affect important cultural sites.

The changes to the bill, broadly, did not cause any of the more prominent environmental and climate organizations to drop their opposition. Many, including the Sierra Club, the League of Conservation Voters and The Wilderness Society, redoubled their criticisms and pressed lawmakers not to rush to pass the bill.

National Tribal and Preservation Associations also remain largely opposed to BAAJA. The filmmaker and activist Julian Brave Noisecat, though, described the amendment as a “real effort at compromise.”

He specifically pointed to a change that would exclude records that tribes share with states and the federal government from the Freedom of Information Act “to keep sensitive sacred sites from exposure.”

“That sort of in-the-weeds detail—a nod to tribal data sovereignty—tells me that there’s real effort here to try to honor tribal consultation,” he said.

The amendment also prompted an endorsement from the Edison Electric Institute, which represents utility companies across the U.S. This is a significant show of support as major utilities lobbied against a similar permitting reform proposal led by then-Sen. Joe Manchin (I-W.V.) and Sen. John Barrasso (R-WY).

The legislation has the backing of Trump, whose endorsement has been considered crucial in Washington to secure enough Republican votes.

On the eve of the procedural vote, Trump released a statement of support for BAAJA, calling the bill a “BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE AND DOMINANCE.”

The president said the bill would codify his administration’s “America First” energy agenda and speed up the construction of pipelines, mines, and power plants. He also said it would ensure data centers would build and pay for their own electricity and invest in local communities.

Trump’s comments are the first sign directly from the Oval Office that he would be willing to support legislation that would allow for accelerated deployment of renewable energy resources.

HERE’S WHAT’S IN THE BIPARTISAN MEGABILL MEANT TO ALLOW THE US TO BUILD AGAIN

Democrats have been wary of backing the bipartisan bill for fear that the president would not fairly implement the reforms for wind and solar power.

The Trump administration has attempted to assuage these concerns by advancing wind project reviews under the Department of War. While this could be viewed as a sign of good faith, many wind proponents have been quick to point out that the Pentagon was court-ordered to move forward on the reviews earlier this year, after stalling for months.

However, just minutes before Monday’s vote on BAAJA, Trump said he would not approve any wind farms, calling the projects “losers.”

text:
Washington (November 9, 2026) - Senator Edward J. Markey (D-Mass.), a member of the Environment and Public Works Committee, released the following statement on the Senate’s vote to invoke cloture on the motion to proceed to the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) of 2026.

“We need to stop the Trump administration’s weaponization of our government against clean, affordable, and ready-to-go energy sources, and we need to build an energy grid that works for Americans now and into the future—that means cutting emissions and cutting costs. But as currently drafted, this bill attempts to address these goals by asking communities to trade the benefits of interstate transmission and the ability to make data centers pay more for grid power for the sacrifices of weakened clean water protections, intrusion on sovereign Tribal rights, and limits on the ability to be heard and considered during federal approval of projects ranging from hyperscale data centers to petrochemical plants. Legal experts have also raised serious concerns about the potential unintended effects of provisions that are meant to prevent Trump’s misuse of the permitting process but could impair environmental protections into the future at taxpayers’ expense. And without a committee process and sufficient time to work through and resolve these tradeoffs and questions, we do not have the answers we need.

“Voters sent a clear message last week that they want better deals than the ones they’ve gotten under unified Republican leadership. I believe we owe it to them to fight to win a better deal that delivers clean energy megawatts and jobs, near- and long-term savings on energy bills, and real climate benefits without leaving so many important members of our community on the losing side of the ledger.

“Because of these issues on timing, transparency, and threats to our clean air, water, and Tribes, I will vote against the motion to invoke cloture on this legislation. I will continue to discuss all these issues with my colleagues, both in the coming days and into the next Congress, and hope to work toward a better deal in the future.”

text:
Construction Permit issuance completes NRC Safety and Environmental reviews

Proposed four-unit Xe-100 plant at Dow’s Seadrift site would be the first advanced nuclear facility to power an industrial site in the United States

Historic milestone achieved under U.S. Department of Energy’s Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program

ROCKVILLE, Md. – November 9, 2026 – X-Energy, Inc. (Nasdaq: XE) (“X-energy” or “the Company”), a leading developer of advanced nuclear reactors and fuel technology, and Dow (NYSE: DOW) through its wholly-owned subsidiary Long Mott Energy, LLC (“Dow”) today announced that the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (“NRC”) has approved the Construction Permit Application (“CPA”) for the proposed construction of four Xe-100 advanced small modular reactors at Dow’s UCC Seadrift Operations site in Texas. The CPA approval makes Long Mott Generating Station the first advanced nuclear facility approved for an industrial site in the United States, a historic milestone achieved under the U.S. Department of Energy’s Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program (“ARDP”).

Approval of the construction permit enables X-energy and Dow (the “Companies”) to continue advancing the proposed project toward construction readiness, finalizing and standardizing the Xe-100 design, maturing the supply chain for long-lead components and materials, and developing an Operating License application for submission to the NRC. This supports Dow’s consideration of the proposed project’s next phases, ensuring the design, equipment, and materials are in place before allocating major capital for full-scale construction, consistent with Dow’s proven global project management practices. For a first-of-a-kind project, this reduces schedule and cost risk once work begins on site, and is aligned to the Company’s established timeline of first delivery in the early 2030s.

Issuance marks the first NRC CPA approval of a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor in nearly 60 years, the first-ever pebble-bed HTGR approval and the first-ever for a nuclear industrial deployment. The NRC’s review found that the Xe-100 design can be safely sited and constructed within an operating industrial site. The proposed plant is intended to provide both electricity and high-temperature steam to Dow’s site, replacing existing energy and steam assets near their end-of-life. The four first-of-a-kind Xe-100s deployed at Seadrift are expected to provide clean industrial power to the site for 60 years.

The NRC completed its review in alignment with its established schedule, evaluating the safety and environmental impacts of the proposed Xe-100 facility against the global benchmark for safe, responsible operation of nuclear technology. Across both parts of the review, the intrinsic safety characteristics of the design and extensive pre-application engagement supported an efficient, thorough, independent review that met or exceeded the NRC’s high standard, supported by decades of U.S. Department of Energy research on HTGRs and TRISO fuel, and strengthened by the passage of the bipartisan ADVANCE Act in 2024. CPA approval by the NRC builds on this body of work, and positions future Xe-100 applications for enhanced efficiency in commercial nuclear licensing by incorporating learnings from Long Mott’s review.

X-energy’s Xe-100 is an 80 MWe/200 MWt high-temperature gas-cooled reactor designed to ensure safety through the passive physics of its advanced TRISO-X coated particle fuel, as well as traditional defense-in-depth systems. TRISO fuel encompasses, in one component, many barriers to the release of radionuclides, and has been described by the DOE as, “the most robust nuclear fuel on earth.” This safety profile is expected to support a 400-meter emergency planning zone, compared to 10 miles for conventional light-water reactors, enabling new generation to be safely sited closer to the point of need.

Since 2018 and 2023, X-energy and Dow, respectively, have worked with the NRC through extensive pre-application engagement to demonstrate the safety profile of the Xe-100 and its TRISO-X fuel, directly cited by the NRC as a contributor to the application’s efficient review. The Companies intend to carry this same discipline and rigor into the next phase of the project, ensuring construction and commercial readiness before major site work begins to reduce cost and schedule risk. Dow is expected to consider a preliminary investment decision in 2027. Full-scale nuclear construction would begin following Dow’s final investment decision, advancing a shared, generational vision for next-generation nuclear technology to commercial scale under ARDP.

Quotes

J. Clay Sell, CEO of X-energy said, “This is an important day. Getting the construction permit earlier than expected is reflective of the thorough and efficient work of the NRC, the reforms that have been put in place by the Congress over the last six years, and the phenomenal work of the X-energy and Dow teams. This milestone is further validation of the XE regulatory approach that can be replicated across our growing commercial pipeline, giving our customers greater confidence in the regulatory process and a clearer path to deployment.”

“This is another important milestone for the proposed Long Mott Generating Station project and a testament to the thoughtful, thorough and efficient review conducted by the NRC,” said Edward Stones, Business Vice President, Energy & Climate at Dow. “We appreciate the NRC’s commitment to maintaining the highest standards of safety while advancing a clear and predictable regulatory process for advanced nuclear technologies. As we move forward, we will continue to evaluate the project through the lens of competitiveness, execution readiness, and capital affordability before any decision regarding construction is made.”

“Today, the new NRC is issuing America’s first construction permit for a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor in more than half a century,” NRC Chairman Ho K. Nieh said. “We delivered on the 18-month schedule, proving we can do rigorous safety reviews on predictable timelines that move advanced nuclear technology from design to construction.”

“This milestone marks a significant step forward for the Department of Energy’s Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program and our efforts to bring next-generation nuclear technologies to market,” said Principal Deputy Assistant Secretary for Nuclear Energy Mike Goff. “The NRC’s approval demonstrates meaningful progress toward deploying advanced reactors that can deliver reliable power and industrial heat, strengthen American energy leadership and expand the role of nuclear energy in meeting our nation’s growing energy demands.”

###

About X-energy X-energy, Inc. is a leading developer of advanced small modular nuclear reactors and fuel technology designed to establish a new standard in clean, safe, reliable energy. X-energy’s intrinsically safer Xe-100 high-temperature gas reactor and TRISO-X particle fuel expand applications for nuclear technology, with commercial projects underway with Dow, Amazon, and Centrica across grid, industrial, and AI applications. Together, X-energy’s technology drives enhanced safety, lower cost, faster construction timelines, and scalable deployment when compared with other SMRs and conventional nuclear.

text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Senate on Monday is set to take up bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews for data centers and other infrastructure projects, in the first major action since last week’s election that soundly repudiated President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans.

The Senate is expected to hold a procedural vote on the bill, which senators and the president have pushed as officials seek to meet growing demand for electricity and other forms of energy that now faces yearslong delays in getting to the grid.

The legislation’s sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to get big energy projects started — both for clean energy and fossil fuel projects — and make sure data centers pay for the energy they use. Anger over artificial intelligence data centers and rising electricity helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the massive energy-hungry sites.

Trump urged senators to vote for it, calling it a “BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE.” in a social media post on Sunday. The bill will “ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines, and Power Plants faster than ever before, lowering Energy Costs for American Families,” Trump wrote.

Major industry groups representing developers in clean energy and in the oil and gas sector also support the bill.

However, many environmental organizations have panned the deal because they say it would lock in fossil fuel development, weaken environmental safeguards and make it harder for communities to challenge energy project approvals.

While the bill has received bipartisan support, the Democrats’ sweeping midterm win could complicate its passage. Some Democrats say the party should use their stronger position in the next Congress to pass legislation that builds out needed clean energy. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, a New York Democrat who is expected to become speaker in January, criticized the bill last week, with a spokesperson saying it “falls short” in a number of areas.

Major environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and National Wildlife Federation, have strongly opposed the measure in recent days, citing concerns about its limits on judicial review and changes to the landmark National Environmental Policy Act.

The bill’s four main champions — two Democrats and two Republicans — released a detailed set of amendments Saturday designed to bolster support for the legislation.

The four senators, who lead the chamber’s energy and environment panels, negotiated the deal weeks before the election. Republican Sens. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah and Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island say Americans are tired of paying more in utility bills while projects that could lower costs sit stuck in the planning phase for years.

“Americans can’t afford to wait for lower electricity prices. We need to pass this bill now,” said Heinrich.

Seeing this work take shape really gives me confidence that we can turn a corner in the climate crisis.
Do you think AI will help or worsen the climate crisis?
text:
Fervo, which completed its initial public offering in May, is a poster child for how the combination of AI-driven electricity demand and energy crisis security concerns have led to a clean-energy tipping point. Around the world, countries and companies are turning to technologies that were developed as climate solutions and now also offer energy security, speed, reliability, and increasingly attractive economics.

In March, in the wake of the attack by the U.S. and Israel on Iran, Chinese exports of solar panels soared to record levels, up 49% from the previous record, according to Ember, an energy think tank, and battery electric-vehicle sales rose 45% when you exclude the U.S. and China. In all, the International Energy Agency expects $2.2 trillion in clean-energy investment in 2026 compared with $1.2 trillion for fossil fuels. At the same time, the early-stage companies deploying clean-energy tech—from nuclear to battery storage—have seen an uptick in funding as investors increasingly eye opportunities to make a big return by building a new energy system.

“Technology has developed a lot in the last decade, particularly on the electricity side: renewables, storage, EVs, etc.,” says Ernest Moniz, the founder of the Energy Futures Initiative and a former U.S. Secretary of Energy. “The situation is prime for a push on low-carbon energy.”

And yet riding the coattails of the data-center build-out and the economic disruption caused by the war in Iran comes with big risks. The scale of the AI boom is enormous, but it could easily be cramped by slowing interest from Wall Street. And volatile politics have proved to be just that, uncertain and subject to sudden shifts. Even so, there’s no question that this moment is an inflection point. Old assumptions about the nature of the energy system have been broken—and clean technologies are positioned for success.

So it came as a surprise to find myself caught in a mid-morning traffic jam as I headed into town from the Cape Station site. Road improvements, in progress ahead of Fervo’s rapid expansion, along with a slew of trucks carrying equipment, were slowing things down.

Milford, it turns out, is a bit of a boom town. The night before my visit to Fervo, representatives from Google had pitched residents on a new data-center complex co-located with Fervo’s operations: two data-center buildings to start, growing to as many as eight. Hundreds of residents showed up, peppering the companies with questions about power and water. “People asked some really, really good questions,” Milford Mayor Nolan Davis told me from his office.

Talking with Latimer, it can sound almost as though Fervo was purpose-built for this moment. Advanced geothermal lacks the intermittency issues that have contributed to wind and solar opposition. And it relies on technology used in the oil and gas industry, which helped it gain quick acceptance from the legacy energy industry. It’s a rare favorite for politicians on both sides of the aisle.

One of the company’s biggest advantages comes from a decision Latimer made early on to focus specifically on selling to Big Tech companies. In the mid-2010s, myriad clean-energy companies failed. In many cases, these companies had made big technological advances but struggled to connect their product with customers. “A lot of folks had this ‘If you build it they will come’ mentality,” says Latimer. “I think that was dead wrong.”

But Big Tech firms wanted low-carbon power too, and they had the money to pay for it. In 2021, Google became one of Fervo’s first customers, committing to a pilot in Nevada that helped prove Fervo’s approach. That early relationship has expanded with time. In September, the companies announced that Google would buy 400 megawatts of geo-thermal power from Cape Station. Enough to serve 200,000 homes, the electricity will power data centers instead. “We always thought that hyperscalers would be a customer segment for us,” says Latimer, using a common term for the Big Tech companies investing in AI infrastructure.

Hyperscaler demand drummed up interest for Fervo’s initial public offering in May, making it the most closely watched IPO from a clean-energy company this year. In Latimer’s telling, the more than $2 billion the company raised will help unlock a dramatic expansion. As drilling costs fall, advanced geothermal will be economically viable in more and more places in the U.S. and around the world. Markets like Japan—where Fervo has made early inroads—are particularly attractive because of the high energy-price environment caused by the Iran war. “We are getting calls all the time,” Latimer says.

Fervo has become in many ways this moment’s clean-energy golden child, but it’s far from alone. Analysis from Dealroom, a company that tracks private-market deals, identified more than $44 billion in climate venture funding raised in the first three quarters of 2026 and projects $59 billion for the full year, up 42% from last year.

The companies receiving sizable checks run the gamut. Energy-storage companies experimenting with new battery chemistries have become hot commodities. Investors have poured money into new ways of producing nuclear energy, from small modular reactors to new engineering architecture for mega–-nuclear power plants. Even companies developing nuclear fusion, a technology proven technically possible but far from commercially viable, have received big checks.

Publicly traded companies that manufacture technologies to electrify the economy have seen their stocks surge too. Bloom Energy, a maker of fuel cells, has increased more than ninefold since the start of 2025. Stock in GE Vernova, a legacy maker of electrification equipment, has grown -sixfold since it started trading in 2024. These aren’t just numbers on a spreadsheet.

For companies making energy hardware, scaling up requires factories, specialized equipment, and years of engineering before products earn a return. Investor enthusiasm makes years of development possible. Buoyed by investors, GE Vernova, for example, has planned $11 billion in investments that includes both R&D and capital investments focused on everything from on-grid hardware to small modular nuclear reactors. Even as gas turbines remain Vernova’s biggest business, the company has declined to build new turbine factories.

Catching up on the news after my three-hour drive from Milford back to Salt Lake City, it was hard not to fixate on the headlines focused on the battering of AI-infrastructure stocks. Markets have grown wary of the hyperscaler plans to build trillions in new data centers, and AI-related stocks are periodically sent into tailspins as a result. For better or worse, clean-energy stocks are now a part of that basket.

In most conversations today, talk of an AI bubble draws comparison to the dotcom boom in the early 2000s that led to a wave of bankruptcies that thinned out the ranks of early internet companies. But mention a bubble in clean tech and another period comes to mind: the wave of bankruptcies that followed exuberant investment in climate technologies in the late 2000s and early 2010s. From 2006 to 2011, venture-capital firms invested more than $25 billion into clean--energy startups, according to an analysis from MIT. More than half of that money was lost as tech breakthroughs failed to yield commercial products.

There is no question that hitching clean energy to AI today comes with risks. If and when the AI bubble pops, there will be collateral damage. Energy tech focused solely on data centers (think of components that live within the centers’ walls) may be hardest hit, but the most speculative energy technologies without clear commercialization pathways may also be difficult to justify financially.

Despite all that, it’s fair to say that while the AI boom may have given clean tech a lifeline, the fate of the sector doesn’t depend solely on AI. Around the world, electricity demand is spiking for a variety of reasons, from economic growth in developing countries to the need for air-conditioning in areas experiencing more extreme heat. And, even as it has largely fallen off the list of priorities in Washington, the emissions that cause climate change remain a concern in most parts of the world.

Perhaps most importantly, the attack on Iran and the subsequent on-and-off-again closure of the Strait of Hormuz have made clean energy, produced locally, more valued than ever before. Back in Utah, the appeal is easy to understand. Fervo’s power plants don’t depend on shipments of fuel from halfway around the world. “There’s just a lot about what’s going on globally right now,” says Latimer, “that’s driving demand for what geothermal can provide—an energy resource where the fuel is right beneath the power plant.”

Clean energy helps lock in costs, avoiding volatile markets. Another country can’t simply decide to cut off the supply, as with fossil fuels moved around the world by ship and pipeline. Even if the U.S. and Iran declared an end to the conflict tomorrow, leaders across businesses and governments expect volatility to remain. Clean energy will keep the lights on.

One of the most exciting aspects of the AI boom is its potential to help the world mitigate and adapt to the climate crisis. Juliet Rothenberg leads the team at Google that’s producing tools to do just that, like FireSat, a constellation of satellites designed to detect a 5x5 meter (16x16 ft.) wildfire anywhere on Earth within 20 minutes, and Flood Hub, which uses AI-driven forecasting to predict floods days earlier than other models to help communities stay safe. Earlier this year, Flood Hub expanded its AI flash flood predictions to cover urban areas. —Jessica Hullinger

What is the single most important action you think the public, or a specific company or government (other than your own), needs to take in the next year to advance the climate agenda?

We need to keep progressing on mitigating climate change, but it’s very clear that we’re headed past the 1.5° Celsius threshold that scientists believe is critical to reducing the most damaging effects of climate change. And especially with the Super El Niño this year, we also need to recognize that climate change is here today. Aligned with the U.N.’s Early Warnings for All initiative, we need to start moving towards a world where no one is surprised by a natural disaster. This means putting in place comprehensive forecasting, monitoring, alerting, and response systems globally, so that we can protect lives and livelihoods from the climate crisis.

What’s one sustainability effort you personally will try to adopt in the next year, and why?

For many of us, air travel is the single largest contributor to our personal carbon footprint; a single long-haul flight can easily eclipse our household, diet, and driving choices combined. We often look at aviation solely through the lens of fuel burn, but short-lived climate forces like contrails actually account for more than a third of aviation's total warming footprint. While my team works on improving the global AI models that have already helped airlines and air traffic control reduce contrails by over half, I want to personally align my consumer habits—making sure my own travel choices support the carriers paving the way for sustainable skies.

That’s why my personal commitment this year is to make my essential travel as contrail-conscious as possible. This means prioritizing airlines that actively participate in contrail avoidance programs, favoring morning or daytime flights when contrails are less warming, or better yet checking out the Google Flights tooltip on the likelihood of contrail warming for a given flight, and also opting for rail over short-haul flights wherever feasible.

What is a climate solution (other than your own) that isn't getting the attention or funding it deserves?

I’ll share a solution from one of our partners: FireSat, by the Earth Fire Alliance. When fully operational, the FireSat constellation will be able to detect a garage-sized wildfire within 20 minutes, anywhere on Earth. Fire authorities say that this will be a gamechanger for their ability to respond to devastating wildfires, like those in France and Spain this summer, because the greatest gift that we can give firefighters is time.

FireSat has the first 4 satellites in orbit, and a 20-minute revisit will be achieved once the constellation reaches 52 satellites. Google.org, Bezos Earth Fund, and the Moore Foundation have all supported FireSat, and more funding is needed to realize the potential of this vision.

What gives you hope about the future of the planet/climate movement?

I’m tremendously optimistic about the ability of AI to accelerate the rate of scientific progress towards climate-friendly technologies. This is a dramatic change since I started working in the field 22 years ago. As a case in point, our climate teams are now able to build software prototypes for things like satellite detection in less than an hour, which previously would have taken months, and now they can even develop novel hardware solutions in months that would previously have taken years.

Climate change won’t be solved by a single silver bullet. It will take hundreds of practical, durable innovations working in parallel to deliver impact at scale, which is why it’s so exciting that the pace of innovation is accelerating dramatically.

Do you think AI will help or worsen the climate crisis? How?

My job day in and day out is to apply AI to help solve the climate crisis, and I’m a big believer in that potential because we're already seeing it in action. For example, our Contrails project targets an impact equivalent to roughly 4% of the impact that today’s warming will have over the next 20 years (known as global warming potential, or GWP20), or 1-2% of the impact over the next 100 years (GWP100). In live commercial flights across U.S. and international airspace, we’ve proven that AI predictions can help pilots cut contrail formation by more than half, avoiding these warming zones in a way that’s just as simple as avoiding turbulence.

We’re also working with dozens of governments that are using our cutting-edge crisis models for hazards like floods, fires, and cyclones in service of our team’s north star: that no one should ever be surprised by a natural disaster coming their way.

And it’s important to acknowledge that AI will have additional energy demands. My team is hard at work on applying agentic AI for science to accelerate the development of clean, low-cost energy solutions—expect to hear more from us there over time.

Correction, Nov. 9

The original version of this story misstated which projects Rothenberg's team produces. They have worked on FireSat and Flood Hub, but not WeatherNext.

The nonprofit Rainforest Alliance, headed by Santiago Gowland, runs one of the world’s largest sustainability certification programs—partnering with farmers and brands around the world to support climate resilient growing practices under its iconic green frog seal. In 2025, the organization’s efforts resulted in some 5.5 million metric tons of emissions being avoided or sequestered.

The group recently announced a new regenerative agriculture standard aimed at transforming the way tropical commodities are grown, certified, and traded. The standard supports farmers looking to better understand and employ regenerative agriculture practices—focusing on areas such as soil health and fertility, biodiversity, and crop resilience. The first crop the framework is focusing on is coffee, but the organization plans to extend the certification to cocoa, citrus, and tea. —Simmone Shah

What is the single most important action you think the public, or a specific company or government (other than your own), needs to take in the next year to advance the climate agenda?

The single most important action we can take to advance the global climate agenda is to accelerate the transition to regenerative agriculture by making it the smart economic choice for producers, supply chains, governments, impact investors, philanthropies, and consumers.

Agriculture, forestry, and other land use account for about 22% of global greenhouse gas emissions. At the same time, nature-based solutions, which protect, restore, and improve ecosystems, could deliver roughly a third of the climate mitigation needed by 2030. Regenerative agriculture connects these two realities by putting nature-based solutions to work on farms. Through practices such as agroforestry, cover cropping, and water conservation, it shifts food production from a process that depletes soil, water, and biodiversity to one that restores them.

No single actor can deliver this transition at scale; it takes an alliance whose individual actions reinforce one another. Food companies provide dependable purchasing agreements that reward regenerative production and share transition costs, making farm investments easier to finance. Governments align agricultural policy and incentives, while philanthropy helps absorb risks that unlock affordable capital.

This investment, combined with practical support on the farm, enables producers to deliver verified results. Brands and retailers make that progress visible through credible, accessible regenerative products. Consumer purchases generate revenue for companies, giving them a commercial reason to expand regenerative sourcing and investment. That growing market attracts more producers and gives participating farmers the income and confidence to reinvest. Verified results and demonstrated demand strengthen the case for further financing, funding the next round of regeneration.

This is how regenerative economies deliver lasting climate benefits: the cycle gives producers and communities the means and incentive to keep protecting and restoring ecosystems. Starting in tropical forest landscapes, where the risks are acute and the immediate gains greatest, we can sustain emissions reductions, carbon storage, and forest protection while safeguarding biodiversity, livelihoods, and food security.

What is a climate solution (other than your own) that isn't getting the attention or funding it deserves?

We need to put much greater emphasis on local bioeconomies to ensure that forests are worth more standing than cleared. Tropical forests hold vast reserves of living carbon and are estimated to harbor roughly half of the world’s species on just 7% of [all the earth’s] land. Indigenous and community-led forest enterprises connect people’s economic futures to the continued health of their forests.

Take Carmelita, a community in Guatemala’s Maya Biosphere Reserve, as an example. Here, local carpenters turn responsibly harvested timber into furniture. Guides and cooks earn income taking visitors into the forest. The community cooperative invests in fire prevention, forest monitoring, and reforestation. The forest sustains an economy, and that economy helps protect the forest. Across the reserve’s successful community forestry concessions, deforestation has remained near zero for more than 20 years.

This achievement rests on communities having the rights, institutions, and economic opportunities to manage their forests for the long term. Sustaining that success requires investment that strengthens both forest protection and local livelihoods.

I see this as a direct investment in climate mitigation and adaptation. Standing forests retain carbon, protect watersheds, and help regulate local temperatures and water cycles. Those functions help farmers cope with heat and water stress and keep producing food in a changing climate.

Climate investors need to back the institutions and businesses that make forest protection economically durable, helping more communities build on Carmelita’s example. Financing local processing allows communities to retain more value from what they produce, while working capital and dependable buyers give enterprises the stability to grow. Secure community rights, combined with a reliable livelihood from healthy forests, give people both the confidence and the incentive to protect and invest in a forest their children will inherit.

What gives you hope about the future of the planet/climate movement?

That companies are beginning to recognize that their own future depends on investing in people and nature.

Climate action gains staying power when people have a direct stake in its success. Better livelihoods give farmers reasons to continue investing in their land. More resilient production gives businesses reasons to support them. Turning those shared interests into lasting commitments is how we accelerate regeneration. Seeing this work take shape really gives me confidence that we can turn a corner in the climate crisis.

Do you think AI will help or worsen the climate crisis? How?

I believe AI can accelerate climate action, provided we manage its own energy use and emissions.

At the Rainforest Alliance, we already use AI-powered remote sensing and deforestation risk mapping to identify risks in coffee and cocoa supply chains. That work depends on information from farmers and knowledge of conditions on the ground. Human expertise is fundamental to making the technology useful.

Connecting farmers’ knowledge with field, weather, and satellite data can improve advice, identify climate risks, and make verification more accessible. Better evidence must then translate into practical support and financing for farmers restoring soils, integrating trees, and strengthening resilience to climate shocks.

Who controls that information matters. Farmers and Indigenous communities must determine how their knowledge and data are used, and share in the value they create. People must remain responsible for consequential decisions, and farmers must be able to challenge them.

AI’s climate contribution must be judged by measurable results: less forest loss, lower emissions and more farmers equipped to regenerate their land and withstand a changing climate. Those benefits must justify the technology’s environmental cost.

description:
The Energy Institute Statistical Review of World Energy 2026 puts fossils at 86% of total energy supply (TES) in 2025 — not electricity alone.
Stu’s Take Brenda Shaffer’s Nov. 9 question — will the blue wave lower energy prices?
Energy Institute Statistical Review of World Energy 2026: fossil fuels 86% of 2025 total energy supply (TES).
Eurostat Oct. 30, 2026 household electricity note: Germany about €0.36/kWh in H1 2026; Ofgem Oct.–Dec.
Appendix E | Background Responds to Brenda Shaffer, “Will the Blue Wave Lower American Energy Prices?,” RealClearWorld, Nov. 9, 2026.
text:
Her RealClearWorld essay names AOC, El-Sayed and Texas’s Railroad Commissioner-elect. We checked the quotes, the 86% fossil figure, the UK–Germany bill comparison — and the consumer traps already forming in Virginia, New York, Texas and California.

By Energy News Beat | As of November 9, 2026 CST

Sources opened Nov. 9, 2026 CST | Not investment advice

She asked the question voters already asked

In a RealClearWorld commentary dated Nov. 9, 2026, Brenda Shaffer asks: “So let’s ask: Will the blue tsunami really lower energy prices?” (Bio in Appendix E.)

She writes that Democrats “successfully blamed the Iran war” for hardship where “diesel, gasoline, and electricity prices stand front and center,” and that “Voters overwhelming [sic] voted to halt data center buildout, which they blame for high electricity prices.” Their main answers — leaving the Persian Gulf, renewable subsidies, barriers to domestic oil and gas, and stopping data-center growth — will not, she argues, “address the major challenges that have caused the current energy price surge.”

The people she names — and what the record actually shows

Shaffer writes: “Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, co-sponsor of the Green New Deal, aims to end all use and production of fossil fuels and phase out nuclear energy.” Ocasio-Cortez introduced H.Res. 109 (she is its lead sponsor). A 2019 office FAQ said the plan “would not include creating new nuclear plants” and aimed to “transition off of nuclear and all fossil fuels as soon as possible” (FAQ text provided to NPR); her office later called that FAQ an unfinished draft posted by mistake (FactCheck.org). The resolution text itself does not ban nuclear.

Michigan senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, she says, “favors Michigan and the US transferring to 100% renewable energy and vows to ‘take on the Chevrons and the Exxons of the world.’” He won Michigan’s Senate seat on Nov. 3, defeating Mike Rogers. His Planet Detroit questionnaire says he “strongly support[s] transitioning our economy to 100% clean, renewable energy.” The “take on the Chevrons…” wording is Shaffer’s quote of him; a 2021 clip that resurfaced (as reposted by Townhall; original not reviewed) has him saying he does not think ‘the Chevrons and the Exxons of the world … should continue to exist.’ We quote Shaffer’s line as hers.

She cites “Joe Rosenthal … elected Texas Railroad Commissioner” as supporting “greater restrictions on Texas’s natural gas production.” The winner is Jon Rosenthal — first Democrat on the three-member Railroad Commission in more than 30 years; Republicans still hold a 2–1 majority (Texas Tribune, Nov. 9). His platform ends routine flaring and venting — tougher rules on how gas is produced (no routine flaring, leak detection, capture baselines, a wastewater-disposal fee), not a call to cut output (jonrosenthaltx.com). Her supply thesis — “reducing production of US oil and gas will raise US energy prices, not lower them” — is her economics

The 86% fossil share — and the UK–Germany bill warning

“[F]ossil fuels provide 86 percent of global energy consumption,” she writes. The Energy Institute Statistical Review of World Energy 2026 puts fossils at 86% of total energy supply (TES) in 2025 — not electricity alone.

“Ask the British and the Germans, where electricity prices are among the highest in the world.” Eurostat’s Oct. 30, 2026 note shows Germany at about €0.36/kWh in H1 2026 — among the EU’s highest, tied with Belgium and behind Ireland. The UK is no longer in Eurostat; Ofgem’s Oct.–Dec. 2026 cap is 26.32p/kWh (Direct Debit, VAT now removed), still well above the U.S. average. High prices are real; her causal link is incomplete — network charges, taxes, gas spikes and policy also share the bill.

America’s own gap: 52.5% higher in Harris states — correlation only

ENB’s equal-weighted check of EIA Table 5.6.B (Jan–Aug 2026 YTD, released Oct. 23) shows 23.90¢/kWh across 19 Harris states versus 15.67¢ across 31 Trump states — 52.5% higher, DC excluded (about 47% sales-weighted). Correlation, not causation. (State counterexamples in Appendix F.)

Data centers: about 4% of the past rate rise — and a PJM counterexample

Shaffer says halting data-center buildout “will have minimal impact on electricity prices, especially in the short to mid-term,” while helping China in AI. The Cost of Intelligence (Rana, Kaps, Netessine) estimates 2020–25 additions raised regional residential prices about $1.7/MWh (0.17¢/kWh) — about 4% of the observed residential price increase since 2020, not 4% of bills (author abstract). The Washington Post reported the study on Nov. 6 (Shannon Osaka).

Separately, the PJM market monitor found higher 2025/2026 capacity clearing prices were “primarily the result of existing and forecast data center load and market design flaws” (Part H, July 31, 2025).

The consumer problems already forming after the wave

Virginia. Gov. Abigail Spanberger, in office since January, will support Dominion–NextEra only with consumer conditions including a six-year residential base-rate freeze (29News, Oct. 20). Dominion and NextEra accepted some SCC staff and Attorney General recommendations but rejected others, including a three-year rate freeze and a 10-year staffing guarantee; Spanberger’s own asks — a six-year base-rate freeze and a $29 monthly bill credit — were not addressed in their rebuttal (Virginia Mercury, Nov. 4).

New York. The 2026 budget amended the Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act (2040 interim target; GWP100 accounting; regulations deadline moved to 2028 — Greenberg Traurig, May 2026). National Grid Ventures floated new Long Island gas units aimed at firing up by 2035 (NY Focus, Nov. 2).

Texas. Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa pledged a data-center approval pause until the Legislature writes protections — see Hinojosa Can Pause Data Centers. She Can’t Rewrite Texas Power Alone. A pause is not an automatic rate cut.

California. Voters rejected Proposition 45 (KQED). EIA warned in July 2025 that Phillips 66’s Los Angeles-area shutdown and Valero’s Benicia closure would remove about 17% of California’s refining capacity.

Congress. Sherrod Brown defeated appointed Sen. Jon Husted, who led the Senate Ratepayer Protection Act push (AP; Roll Call, Sept. 30). Who pays for large loads is now a majority question.

Diesel, Hormuz and the Northeast winter angle

Shaffer puts diesel at the center of the wartime shock — Russia and Saudi Arabia among top exporters after the U.S. (2025 rankings). Russia banned diesel exports in July 2026 (Reuters, July 8). Her claim China limited diesel exports “most likely to weaken Trump” is speculation; Reuters reported Beijing restricted fuel exports in March after the Iran war began, eased in July and paused October exports to preserve domestic stocks (Reuters, Oct. 1). Northeast heating oil: see Oil Crashed. Your Diesel Didn’t.

Shaffer writes that “Maine Senator-elect Troy Jackson told CNN that if the US pulls out of the Gulf, Iran will allow ships to pass,” then adds: “Good luck with that, Troy.” Jackson defeated Susan Collins. A Mediaite opinion column (Oct. 25) quotes CNN’s Dana Bash exchange, in which Jackson said, “I’m sure that if we move out of Iran, things will stabilize and prices will probably go down” — that excerpt does not contain her ships-to-pass line (Mediaite). Exact Shaffer wording also in Appendix B. CNN video not watched.

What consumers and investors should watch

Consumers. Midterms alone won’t cut the bill. Watch Virginia merger conditions, New York climate-law vs. gas reliability, Texas large-load rules after Hinojosa’s pledged pause, and California supply after the two closures EIA said would cut about 17% of capacity. Separate generation policy, T&D spend, fuel and weather.

Investors. Affordability pledges can freeze rates or slow large loads; diesel and refining still price geopolitics. PJM capacity prints can move before data halls energize. Not a buy/sell call.

Caveats and fair criticism

Shaffer is writing advocacy. Numbers that check out: 86% fossils; high German prices; El-Sayed’s 100% renewable stance; Rosenthal’s election. Soft edges: AOC’s nuclear FAQ history; Rosenthal’s flaring focus vs. her “greater restrictions on Texas’s natural gas production”; El-Sayed’s exact “take on” wording; China’s export motive. In October Bessent urged the World Bank to drop its ban on upstream oil and gas finance; the Bank still excludes gas exploration but funds some gas transport/LNG projects (Climate Home News, Oct. 16). Blue–red gaps are correlations. The 4% figure — covered by the Post on Nov. 6 — is a share of the increase, not of the bill. Forecasts are not facts.

Stu’s Take

Brenda Shaffer’s Nov. 9 question — will the blue wave lower energy prices? — is the right frame. Her 86% fossil share matches the Energy Institute’s 2026 Review (86% of 2025 TES). Germany ~€0.36/kWh in H1 2026 ranks among Europe’s highest (Eurostat). EIA Table 5.6.B still shows Harris-state residential averages at 23.90¢/kWh vs 15.67¢ in Trump states for Jan–Aug 2026 — 52.5% higher (about 47% sales-weighted), correlation only. Data centers explain about 4% of the 2020–25 residential rate increase (Kaps et al.) — not of bills — while PJM’s monitor cites existing and forecast data-center load plus market-design flaws in the 2025/26 auction. Watch Spanberger’s Dominion–NextEra conditions, New York’s climate-vs-gas collision, Hinojosa’s pledged Texas pause, California’s ~17% refining cut (EIA, July 2025), and who pays for large loads. Supply sets the ceiling; politics sets who gets the bill.

Buckle up, as the Republicans could not articulate energy policy impacts your pocketbook. We will see how all of this pans out, in the mean time, I highly recommend getting back up for your homes, water supply, food and energy backups. Rolling blackouts are projected to be on the rise in 2027, and with the political insatiability moving forward, the grid will follow.

title: What the US midterm elections mean for energy - Wood Mackenzie
description:
The language being used to describe the Democratic Party’s successes in the US midterm elections has been dramatic.
Wood Mackenzie analysts have been looking at what are likely to be the most material consequences of the elections for US energy.
State and local restrictions on data centre development Nearly everywhere they were given the option, voters repudiated data centre development.
There has been particular interest in Texas, which has more proposed new data centre capacity than any other state.
For a good overview of the outlook for data centre development, listen to Episode 7 of our podcast, The Load Down, from August 2026.
text:
The language being used to describe the Democratic Party’s successes in the US midterm elections has been dramatic. The results, which will make the Democrats the largest party in both the Senate and the House of Representatives, have been called “an extinction-level event” and “a Chernobyl-level disaster” for the Republicans.

But despite the adrenaline-fuelled commentary, not much will change in US energy policy when the new Congress is seated next year. President Donald Trump has pledged to use his veto power to block legislation he sees as harmful, and the Democrats will not have the two-thirds majorities in the Senate and House needed to override those vetoes. To pass, legislation will need support from Republicans, probably including the president.

Meanwhile, President Trump will retain the ability to implement his agenda through regulations and executive actions. The signature initiatives of his second term, his tariff strategy and the conflict in the Middle East, have been pursued without any formal support from Congress, and he will have broad leeway to take action despite the gains made by Democrats.

The most significant impact on President Trump’s actions is likely to come from increased scrutiny, as a result of Democrats taking control of Congressional committees and setting their own agenda for investigations.

In many areas, the Democrats will not want to force a sharp break with the Trump administration. One of the critical factors behind their election success was American voters’ concern about the cost of living, and the Democrats have pledged to improve the affordability of essentials including energy. They have shown little enthusiasm for taking actions that could restrict oil and gas production and drive up prices.

That said, some aspects of US energy will be affected by the election results, with some impacts growing in significance over time. Wood Mackenzie analysts have been looking at what are likely to be the most material consequences of the elections for US energy.

What could change with a Democratic-controlled Congress

Permitting reform

For the US energy industry, the most important issue in Congress right now is permitting reform: proposed changes in how permits for large infrastructure projects are awarded and reviewed, with the goal of expediting development and controlling costs.

A permitting reform bill with backing from both Republicans and Democrats, the proposed Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), was launched last month, and will be voted on in Congress this week.

Wood Mackenzie analysts believe that permitting reform legislation, if passed in a form close to the BAAJA, could make a material difference to development timelines for projects including oil and gas pipelines, power transmission lines and wind farms.

The bill has won bipartisan backing by striking a compromise between the interests of the oil and gas industry and low-carbon energy sectors, with support from groups representing both. But it has also been attacked from both sides, as a “fossil fuel giveaway” and as a way to “re-open the taxpayer and ratepayer spigot to endless and endlessly expensive wind and solar”.

Supporters of the bill have hoped to get it passed this year. But the Democrats’ success in the midterm elections has led some to suggest that they should refuse to support the current proposed legislation, in the hope of securing a better deal when they control Congress next year. Others have argued that the BAAJA, which has support from President Trump, is likely to be the best deal available.

The outlook for the legislation is uncertain, and the energy industry will be closely watching how events in Congress play out over the next few weeks.

Legislation to compel data centre developers to pay for new generation and grid upgrades

Other potentially significant legislation addresses public concerns about data centre development and its impact on electricity costs. The proposed Ratepayer Protection Act was passed with overwhelming support in the House in September, but has not yet come up for a vote in the Senate. If passed, it would require state regulators to consider adopting standards to compel new data centre projects to cover the full costs of the grid and the generation infrastructure needed to support them.

The bill still leaves ultimate decision-making in the hands of the states, and has been criticised for not doing enough to ensure residential customers are protected. Another proposed bill, the GRID (Guarding Ratepayers from Increased Demand-costs) Savings Act, would go further. It would establish a national mandate for data centres and other large loads to cover their associated electricity costs, and direct the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to establish national rules to enforce that.

Action to protect customers from rising electricity costs has bipartisan support, and will be on the agenda for the next Congress. President Trump launched his own Ratepayer Protection Pledge in March, with backing from the leading tech companies.

However, the president is also a strong supporter of the development of advanced AI capabilities, as both an economic and national security priority for the US. He will be reluctant to impose additional burdens on the industry that could curb its growth. Negotiations over a possible compromise on data centres and electricity bills are likely to take place next year.

State and local restrictions on data centre development

Nearly everywhere they were given the option, voters repudiated data centre development. There were 41 proposals related to data centres on the ballot in 13 states, and on 40 of those a majority of voters backed restrictions on development.

Candidates who spoke out against data centres often did well in state and local races. But opposition to uncontrolled development has been bipartisan, with Republican governors including Ron DeSantis of Florida and Greg Abbott of Texas announcing restrictions.

There has been particular interest in Texas, which has more proposed new data centre capacity than any other state. Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat who will be the state’s next governor, said that under her leadership “we will have laws to protect Texans, and we need to stop what we are doing with data centres until we have those protections”.

She has argued for an extension in the pause in approvals for new data centre projects that was put in place by Governor Abbott. She also wants to ensure that data centres are covering their electricity infrastructure costs. But projects that are already under construction will be allowed to continue, and Governor-elect Hinojosa has said she does not want to stop data centre development altogether.

“We can have economic development and we can have protections for Texans. These things are not mutually exclusive,” she has said.

Wood Mackenzie analysts have modelled a Moderated Demand scenario showing the possible implications for the electricity industry of increased restrictions on data centre development, worsening delays for grid connections and continued equipment shortages. That scenario still envisages significant growth in data centre demand, albeit at a slower pace than in our base case forecast. For a good overview of the outlook for data centre development, listen to Episode 7 of our podcast, The Load Down, from August 2026.

Immigration reform

In an interview over the weekend, President Trump identified immigration law reform as a priority for working with Democrats in Congress. Depending on how the reform is structured, that could help ease the skills shortages that are growing problems for energy and other infrastructure projects.

Ideas for a future Democratic administration

The resounding success for Democrats in the midterms has inevitably raised expectations that they could enjoy further success in the 2028 presidential election. Taking the presidency, and retaining control of Congress, would give the Democrats the ability to reshape the US energy landscape.

Two years is a long time in politics, and any number of events might deliver a different outcome. But that has not stopped speculation about the possible energy policy agenda for a future Democratic president.

One comprehensive set of ideas for the Democrats’ agenda has come from the Thriving Economy Project from the Sustainable Energy & Environment Coalition Institute. The group, working with Democratic House members who are interested in energy and the environment, has produced a “menu of ideas” for the incoming Congress, and the next administration.

Its proposals include tax incentives, regulations and government financing to support the development of low-carbon energy. It addresses issues of environmental protection and emissions reduction to tackle climate change, which were priorities for the Biden administration. But it also has much more of a focus on issues that are of more immediate interest to American voters, including energy prices and the cost of living in general.

Based on that report, and other ideas that have been circulating in Washington, these are some of the possibilities that are being talked about for a future Democratic administration.

An Inflation Reduction Act 2.0

The Inflation Reduction Act of 2022, which expanded and extended tax credits for renewable energy, was passed with support only from Democrats, and many of its key provisions were subsequently repealed by the Republicans. Many in the renewables industry want to avoid a repeat of that policy whiplash.

Ray Long, president and chief executive of Acore, the renewable energy industry group, told me on a recent edition of the Energy Gang podcast that the starting principle for any future tax framework should be durability. Banks and investors will have more confidence in the prospects for renewable energy projects if they can expect that taxes and regulations will remain stable through changes of administration and changes of control in Congress. That will mean bipartisan support for any proposed legislation.

Tax incentives that serve bipartisan goals, such as the 45X credits for advanced manufacturing, are most likely to be strengthened.

A windfall tax on oil and gas

The Thriving Economy Project report suggests creating a “strategic energy affordability reserve”, funded by a windfall tax on the profits of the oil and gas industry. If the president declares an energy emergency, funds from the reserve would be released to the states, to help residents with energy bills and transport costs, and to subsidise purchases of energy-efficient appliances.

This proposal is likely to be one of the most controversial for any future administration, if it is taken up in earnest. Disincentivising investment by imposing additional taxes on the oil and gas industry could hit production, working against the goal of bringing fuel costs down.

New controls on energy exports and scrutiny of LNG project approvals

As fuel prices have surged this year, the Trump administration has evaluated possible export controls, but it has not imposed any restrictions. The consensus view in the industry, shared by Wood Mackenzie analysts, is that such controls would have been counter-productive, actually raising costs for American consumers.

However, the Democrats on the Thriving Economy Project have suggested an “energy price safety valve” mechanism that would temporarily constrain exports of LNG, gasoline, diesel and home heating oil.

Their report also says the government could ensure that any new LNG export projects would not raise costs for American consumers before issuing any approvals.

The Biden administration’s review of US LNG exports in 2024 suggested that the industry’s growth would have only a fairly modest impact on the prices paid by American residential customers. Even in the Department of Energy’s low gas supply scenario, projecting growth in LNG exports to meet global demand resulted in modelled residential prices in 2050 rising just 7%. In the middle scenario, modelled prices rise by 4%.

However, those estimates were drawn up before the most recent projections of strong growth in US gas demand for power generation, which could amplify the impact of LNG exports.

A mandate for data centres to use renewables and storage

Although data centre developers can avoid putting additional strain on grid infrastructure by building their own power plants, they can still put upward pressure on gas prices if they are using gas turbines and engines. And if gas prices rise, that will in turn put upward pressure on power prices. To prevent that, the Thriving Economy Project proposes a mandate for all new data centres to use renewables and energy storage for their power supplies.

Power market reform and a review of utility returns

Another focus for the Thriving Economy Project’s is wholesale electricity markets. The report argues that even before the AI boom, there was already a strong case for power market reform to encourage investment in wind, solar, and battery storage. The surge in electricity demand for data centres has made the case for reform urgent, it adds, because better price signals could reduce total system costs.

The report also suggests a review of utility business models to ensure that they prioritise affordability for ratepayers as well as reliability. Regulation could be reformed to strengthen incentives for utilities to bring down costs.

Other views

Putting the 'renew’ into renewables – Simon Flowers, Gavin Thompson, Søren Lassen and Charles Coppins

Speed to power: solutions to US data centres’ challenges – Simon Flowers

Adapt or die: why oil refineries must evolve to survive – Chris Barry, Alan Gelder, Savankumar Aghara and Kian Akhavan

El Niño's long shadow over fuel demand – Gordon McManus and Edgar Manzano

Need to know: gas in Winter 2026-27 – Randall Collum and others

Three key takeaways from our Houston Energy Trading Conference – Jim Mitchell and others

US wind: what utilities and developers need to know – Diego Espinosa, Kárys Prado and Tyler Gifford

Quote of the week

“I would if necessary, but we hit them really hard… So it’s highly unlikely I’ll have to.”

President Trump’s answer when asked during an interview with CNN whether he expected to escalate US attacks on Iran. Qatar has been working on a plan to resolve the conflict and allow free movement of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

WASHINGTON--Japanese automaker Honda Motor will build a ‌new $3 billion auto plant in central Ohio to make hybrid vehicles, creating 2,000 jobs, it said on Monday.

The company said the plant will be able to produce 240,000 vehicles annually and begin production in 2029. It ​will increase its U.S. auto production capacity to 1.3 million vehicles annually, and North ​American capacity to 1.9 million.

Honda is also making a C$867 million ($613.6 million) commitment ⁠to its Canadian operations, including a C$166 million investment in its Alliston, Ontario, operations, maintaining ​its 4,000-strong Canadian workforce.

The Canadian government said it is investing C$313 million in the Alliston project.

Honda ​plans another $338 million investment in Ohio, and unspecified new investments in Georgia and Alabama.

The company announced plans in May to add 15 new Honda and Acura hybrid models worldwide by 2030. It also announced it would scrap ​electric vehicle sales goals, and indefinitely suspended an $11 billion Canada EV project as part of ​a $9 billion EV writedown.

Honda said it will invest in Alabama to build a new V6 hybrid engine, and ‌retool its ⁠Ohio engine plant to build a new four-cylinder engine. It will also retool transmission plants in Ohio and Georgia, and plans to reintroduce engine production in Ontario.

A number of foreign automakers have announced major new investments as they face tariffs imposed by President Donald Trump’s administration.

Last ​month, Volkswagen luxury unit ​Audi said it ⁠would build a $4 billion assembly plant near Macon, Georgia, to open in the early 2030s that would produce 200,000 SUVs annually and employ 4,500 ​workers.

Reuters reported last month that Trump’s administration had promised tariff relief to Audi ​to help ⁠secure the plant’s future. U.S. officials told Audi executives the government plans to offer broad relief from tariffs for automakers making significant investments in U.S. production.

In July, Toyota Motor said it would spend $3.6 billion ⁠to ​build a 2.5-million-square-foot (232,000-square-meter) truck assembly line on its San Antonio, ​Texas, manufacturing campus and shift some truck production to the U.S. from Mexico.

The Japanese automaker said the expansion would be ​completed by 2030, creating 2,000 jobs.

title: Democratic US senators push for energy permitting bill ahead of key Senate vote | Politics
description: By Nichola Groom Nov 9 (Reuters) - Democratic US Senators Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island rallied on Monday for a bipartisan energy permitting bill
text:
By Dan Rosenzweig-Ziff WASHINGTON, Nov 9 (Reuters) - The US …

By Andrew Chung Nov 9 (Reuters) - The US Supreme Court gave …







US Senator Martin Heinrich (D-NM) walks at the US Capitol in Washington, DC, US, November 9, 2026. REUTERS/Kylie Cooper

US Senator Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI) walks at the US Capitol in Washington, DC, US, November 9, 2026. REUTERS/Kylie Cooper

By Nichola Groom

Nov 9 (Reuters) - Democratic US Senators Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island rallied on Monday for a bipartisan energy permitting bill ahead of a preliminary vote, arguing recent changes to the legislation and assurances from the Trump administration on stalled wind projects should help win over skeptics in their party.

The Senate is expected to vote on Monday evening to open debate on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a sweeping package that would speed approvals for power plants, transmission lines, mines and other infrastructure projects while requiring large data centers to pay more of the costs of grid upgrades needed to serve them.

The vote is an early test of whether the bill's Democratic sponsors can hold their party together behind a measure that some environmental and tribal groups oppose, but which its backers say would lower electricity costs.

The package of changes unveiled on Saturday added requirements for consultation with Native communities, expanded states' role in transmission planning and utility oversight, modified provisions affecting electric cooperatives and public power utilities, and established a new Department of Energy program to provide communities with assistance on data-center impacts.

The senators pushed back on suggestions that Democrats should shelve the legislation until next year, arguing the measure would deliver savings on electricity costs and provide a foundation for additional environmental legislation under a Democratic-controlled Congress.

"This bill is the floor, not the ceiling, of our climate and environmental aspirations," Whitehouse said. "We look forward to working to accomplish big things with our big Democratic majorities."

The legislation still faces opposition from environmental and Native American groups. The National Congress of American Indians, the largest advocacy group for tribes, on Monday urged Congress to halt consideration of the bill, saying it would weaken tribal sovereignty and protections for sacred sites.

Heinrich said the changes strengthened tribal protections by requiring federal agencies to consult with tribes throughout the permitting process, giving tribes an equal role with states in transmission planning and expanding opportunities to object to projects affecting cultural resources.

"We worked to strengthen that dramatically," he said.

Environmental group League of Conservation Voters and the left-leaning think tank Center for American Progress said the changes were improvements but the bill still carries significant risks for public lands and environmental protections.

TRIBAL AND ENVIRONMENTAL CONCERNS PERSIST

Oregon Democratic Senator Jeff Merkley, a leading Senate voice on environmental issues, said he opposed the overall package because it would speed construction of natural gas pipelines and LNG export facilities, weaken environmental protections and limit tools to challenge projects.

"I will vote against the bill before us today, but I look forward to working with my colleagues to get permitting reform right," he said in a statement.

Nevada Democratic Senator Catherine Cortez Masto said she would support opening debate on the bill but would oppose final passage unless provisions affecting the National Historic Preservation Act are removed, citing tribal concerns.

Seeking to reassure Democrats worried about the Trump administration's treatment of renewable energy projects, Whitehouse said the administration had assured him that a backlog of hundreds of wind energy permit applications stalled at the Department of Defense would begin moving through the approval process.

The bill, years in the making, has provisions intended to provide developers greater confidence that approved projects will move forward without delays or permit reversals.

The senators also expressed confidence about the bill's prospects in the House of Representatives, citing support from Democratic members and from President Donald Trump.

House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, asked at a press conference whether he would support the bill following the amendments, said it was "still under review."

(Reporting by Nichola Groom; editing by Timothy Gardner and Aurora Ellis)
