title: Senate weighs sweeping energy legislation in first major action since midterm elections
authors: MATTHEW DALY, JENNIFER McDERMOTT Associated Press, JENNIFER McDERMOTT - Associated Press
description: The Senate is set to consider bipartisan legislation to speed up permitting for data centers and infrastructure projects. This move comes after last week's election, which was a setback for
text:
The Capitol is seen under a gray autumn sky in Washington, Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026.

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., speaks at a news conference in Washington, Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026.

Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., walks through the Capitol basement, Monday, Nov. 9, 2026, in Washington.

FILE - Ranking member Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., speaks during a hearing on Capitol Hill, June 18, 2025, in Washington.

FILE - Meta data centers operate Sept. 5, 2026, near Social Circle, Ga.

WASHINGTON (AP) — The Senate on Monday is set to take up bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews for data centers and other infrastructure projects, in the first major action since last week’s election that soundly repudiated President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans.

The Senate is expected to hold a procedural vote on the bill, which senators and the president have pushed as a way to meet growing demand for electricity and other forms of energy that now faces yearslong delays in getting to the grid.

The legislation’s sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to get big energy projects started — both for clean energy and fossil fuel projects — and make sure data centers pay for the energy they use. Anger over artificial intelligence data centers and rising electricity helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the massive, energy-hungry structures.

Trump urged senators to vote for it, calling it a “BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE.” in a social media post on Sunday. The bill will “ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines, and Power Plants faster than ever before, lowering Energy Costs for American Families,” Trump wrote.

Major industry groups representing developers in clean energy and in the oil and gas sector also support the bill.

However, many environmental organizations have panned the deal because they say it would lock in fossil fuel development, weaken environmental safeguards and make it harder for communities to challenge energy project approvals.

While the bill has received bipartisan support, the Democrats' sweeping midterm win could complicate its passage.

Some Democrats say the party should use its stronger position in the next Congress to pass legislation that produces needed clean energy but limits expansion of oil, natural gas and mining. Some critics have said the permitting bill as proposed could lead to a vast increase in exports of liquefied natural gas and facilitate a “reckless” build-out of data centers powered by natural gas.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, a New York Democrat who is expected to become speaker in January, criticized the bill last week, with his office saying it “falls short” in a number of areas.

Major environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and National Wildlife Federation, have strongly opposed the measure in recent days, citing concerns about its limits on judicial review and changes to the landmark National Environmental Policy Act. The 1970 law requires agencies to consider a project’s possible impacts and allows the public to be heard before a project is approved, but supporters of an overhaul say that causes yearslong delays in federal permitting.

The bill's four main champions — two Democrats and two Republicans — released a detailed set of amendments Saturday designed to bolster support for the legislation.

The four senators, who lead the chamber’s energy and environment panels, negotiated the deal weeks before the election. Republican Sens. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah and Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island say Americans are tired of paying more in utility bills while projects that could lower costs sit stuck in the planning phase for years.

"Americans can’t afford to wait for lower electricity prices. We need to pass this bill now,” said Heinrich.

Thanks! You’re all set.

Watch your inbox for Daily Headlines.

Trump promotes expanding production of oil, natural gas and coal and he particularly dislikes offshore wind. His administration has been paying energy companies to walk away from offshore wind projects under development. It has spent nearly $4 billion on such settlements.

Whitehouse said a provision in the permitting bill would end the buyouts, so the administration will no longer be able to use public money to pay clean energy developers to relinquish wind energy leases and oblige them to invest in fossil fuels instead.

At a press conference with Heinrich on Monday, Whitehouse said the bill is “the floor, not the ceiling, of our climate and environmental aspirations. And we look forward to working to accomplish big things with our big Democratic majorities” next year.

Whitehouse said Trump's support should help the bill move toward a vote in the House.

Heinrich said he worked hard to incorporate feedback from tribal leaders on the initial proposal, adding that the amended version requires federal agencies to consult with tribes on projects that affect important cultural sites.

Sponsors also extended the window for objections to agency reports and strengthened opportunities for states to weigh in, Heinrich said.

If passed, the bill will save households billions on electricity costs, create jobs, cut emissions and force big corporations to pay their full share for data centers instead of pushing energy costs on consumers, he said.

Industry leaders are advocating for the bill's passage, including leaders of the American Clean Power Association, which represents clean energy developers, and the American Petroleum Institute, the oil and gas industry’s top lobbying group.

But Bradley Campbell, president of the Conservation Law Foundation, said it would be a “terrible mistake” to proceed with this in the waning days of the current Congress.

While the transmission and grid provisions are salutary and the changes announced Saturday address a few concerns, Campbell said the bill also comes with a gauntlet of new, and at times conflicting, rules. He said the bill maintains a veneer of federal safeguards while in fact stripping the power of federal agencies, states, tribes and communities to identify and prevent serious harm to health and the environment.

McDermott reported from Providence, R.I.

Honda leadership, Ohio lawmakers, and others gathered Monday at Honda Heritage Center in Marysville to celebrate the announcement of a new central Ohio auto plant.

"Today we are taking another historic step. Honda will invest $3 billion to built a new auto plant right here in Ohio," American Honda Motor Co. executive VP Bob Nelson said.

Applause filled the room.

The new plant in Union County will be built between existing Honda facilities in Marysville and East Liberty. Nelson said it will create more than 2,000 new jobs.

Gov. Mike DeWine, who attended Honda's announcement Monday, said that the impact is greater than that and will stretch beyond central Ohio.

"We knew what was at stake when we were talking to Honda it was not just for 2,000 jobs, it was many, many other jobs that would grow over the years in auto suppliers," DeWine said. "You know, Ohio is an auto production state, but it's also a great auto parts state."

Nelson said the plant will be flexible, with the capability to produce gas-powered cars, hybrids, and battery-electric vehicles. It will be able to produce around 240,000 vehicles a year.

The new plant is meant to meet growing customer demand in North America, including increased demand for hybrids.

Nelson told members of the media that 50% of the company's CRVs and 30% of its overall vehicle lineup are now hybrids.

"The market has changed dramatically, and it changed very quickly. Faster than we could catch up, it seemed at times," Nelson said. "But we're quickly developing new products based on the customers, and the hybrid is very popular now for us."

Nelson lauded the planned Union County plant as the "centerpiece" of Honda's broader manufacturing projects in America.

Honda is also increasing capacity at its Alabama auto plant and will begin producing hybrid systems for larger vehicles at the Honda transmission plant in Georgia in the coming years.

Honda selected Ohio for the new auto plant because of the existing supply chain, established workforce, and the proximity to the company's vehicle development operations.

"Ultimately, this investment is about our customers. It will give Honda greater flexibility to build more of the vehicles they want with durability, quality, reliability that they expect from us," Nelson said.

Nelson confirmed that Honda will receive both state and local "incentives" for building in Union County, but neither he nor DeWine elaborated on the details. The company will likely receive tax breaks.

Nelson and DeWine both looked to the Honda's history in Ohio while they spoke about its future. Honda has been producing automobiles in Marysville since 1982. The new plant will be the company's fourth in Ohio.

DeWine said he is the ninth governor to work with Honda. Governor-elect Amy Acton will be the tenth.

"That relationship is going to be strong no matter who the governor is. It doesn't matter whether it's a Democrat or Republican, doesn't' matter who it is. That relationship has stood the test of time for close now to 50 years," DeWine said.

He noted that discussions with Honda for the new plant happened quickly, coming together over the course of the last several months.

text:
Electric vehicle (EV) makers are joining a broad rebound in growth shares, and Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA | TSLA Price Prediction) is climbing even as its chief executive warns that many Cybertruck buyers won’t get their trucks. Tesla stock is at $376.68, up 5% so far this afternoon. U.S. stocks are mounting a broad rally as investors return to artificial intelligence (AI) and growth names after last week’s post-midterm selloff.

That risk appetite is the best-supported driver of the rebound in Tesla, which follows a rough stretch. Even with the bounce, Tesla stock is down 6% over the past week. On October 21, the company reported its Q3 2026 adjusted earnings per share (EPS) of $0.48, ahead of estimates, on revenue of $28.05 billion.

Musk Warns Many Cybertruck Deposits Will Be Returned

Tesla CEO Elon Musk wrote in a post on November 9, as reported by Yahoo Finance: “Cybertruck order rate far exceeds our production rate. We will try to make as many as possible before shutting down the line in about 8 months, but will have to return deposits for a lot of people.” Musk’s message followed his announcement, reported on November 6, that Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas gigafactory around the middle of next year to make room for more Cybercab robotaxi output. He also argued that “the opportunity cost of the complexity of Cybertruck is vastly outweighed by the value of incremental Cybercab production.”

Each Cybertruck deposit is $1,000, according to Yahoo Finance, and Tesla built annual Cybertruck capacity of 250,000 units at Giga Austin. Cox Automotive’s Kelley Blue Book estimated total Cybertruck sales since the 2023 launch at 71,000, far below that capacity. How many deposits Tesla might return remains unclear. The refund warning repeats Musk’s own words on Tesla’s October 21 call: “Demand is growing rapidly for our vehicles. It’s exceeding our production by a significant margin.”

Lucid Rallies Into Its Q3 Report While Rivian Lags

Third-quarter deliveries at Lucid Group (NASDAQ:LCID) fell to 3,806 from the second quarter, and the company reports its Q3 results after the close on November 9. Lucid stock is trading at $3.54, up 8%. Over the past week, the stock has gained 17%.

Cash burn is central to Lucid’s report. The company’s Q2 free cash flow was negative $1.48 billion, and CEO Silvio Napoli stated on the August 4 call that “bringing it down is an immediate priority.” Uber Technologies (NYSE:UBER) committed to at least 35,000 Lucid vehicles for robotaxis, so launch timing matters.

Rivian Automotive (NASDAQ:RIVN) stock is at $13.82, up 2%. The smaller gain trails both peers mentioned today, even though Rivian stock is up 14% over the past week. On October 29, the company reported third-quarter results with revenue of $2.155 billion, up 38.3% year over year, while its automotive gross loss narrowed to $80 million from $130 million, helped in part by regulatory credits and a tariff refund receivable.

How Tesla’s Business Model Stands Apart From Lucid and Rivian

Tesla’s reach extends well beyond cars, including energy storage, a Supercharger network, Full Self-Driving (FSD) software, Optimus humanoid robots and in-house AI compute. Lucid sells premium-priced Air and Gravity models, draws backing from Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund and is building a factory in that country.

At Rivian, R1 and R2 consumer vehicles sit alongside electric delivery vans and a software joint venture with Volkswagen. That range gives Tesla more ways to handle a Cybertruck exit, while Lucid and Rivian lean more heavily on their vehicle ramps.

Cybertruck Refunds and Lucid’s Earnings Set Up the Next Test

Investors will be watching whether Lucid’s Q3 report shows cash burn shrinking from the second quarter’s pace. Lucid has missed EPS estimates in five straight quarters, so another miss could quickly undo the recent run.

Tesla’s bulls argue that Cybercab, FSD and energy storage can grow fast enough to make lost truck sales a footnote. Skeptics say refunding deposits on a product with strong orders gives up near-term revenue before robotaxi income arrives. For Rivian, the R2 ramp and its December 9 Autonomy and AI Day are the next markers, though the company still reports losses. A conservative investment approach may be warranted until the Lucid cash-burn question resolves.

text:
For the next two weeks, country leaders will be in Antalya, Turkey, for the annual United Nations climate conference, called COP31. This year, the ongoing U.S.-Israeli war with Iran will loom over the negotiations. Now in its ninth month, the war has sparked a global energy crisis. The unprecedented closure of the Strait of Hormuz and spiking oil and natural gas prices have laid bare the fragility of relying on fossil fuels.

But this energy crisis – unlike the energy crisis in the 1970s and the one following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 – is different, says Kingsmill Bond, an analyst at the energy think tank Ember.

"This is the first time you've really had a global energy shock where you've got really cheap solutions to address it," Bond says.

Those solutions include solar panels, batteries and electric vehicles. In recent months, countries around the world have pivoted sharply towards these technologies. Many of them are produced in China and offer economic security, as well as reduced emissions.

The economic case for climate solution technologies will make it easier for countries to support them at the conference, Bond says. "There's much more opportunity, I think, for people to get behind change at COP."

Here are three things you need to know about this year's COP.

It's all about electrification

Climate technologies like solar, batteries and electric vehicles are also called electrification technologies. Bond says that's why some are calling this "the electrification COP."

"The big target that the COP is setting is for the world to increase the electrification rate from around 23% today to around 35% by 2035," Bond says. "So 35 by '35 is the mantra."

These electrification goals assume countries will grow their electricity mix with cleaner renewable energy. Energy experts say that is a reasonable assumption, because that's what has been happening in recent years. Large solar and wind projects provide more cost-competitive energy than natural gas and coal projects, according to financial services firm Lazard.

"Think about solar, wind," says Li Shuo, director of the China Climate Hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute. "More green energy will help you decarbonize better and faster."

Roadmap off fossil fuels

As the COP process enters its 31st year, many countries have argued that the U.N. process has not done enough to tackle the single biggest driver of climate change: burning fossil fuels.

Fossil fuel producers such as Saudi Arabia and Russia have consistently opposed having fossil fuel language in the text of final conference agreements.

In April, more than 50 countries came together to discuss ways to phase out oil, gas, and coal at the First International Conference to Transition Away from Fossil Fuels. Conference organizers told NPR the conference was a way to complement the U.N. process.

More than 25 of those nations are developing a legally binding treaty that would advance a phase-out of fossil fuels. Supporters of the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative hope more countries will join their cause at COP31.

The U.S. is not in the room

The U.S. State Department told NPR in an email that the U.S. will not be sending a delegation to COP31. They also did not send anyone to last year's COP in Brazil.

The Trump administration has reversed action on climate progress, phasing out subsidies for electric vehicles, solar and wind, reducing regulations for greenhouse gases, and halting renewable energy projects.

Last year, some countries told NPR they were happy that the Trump administration was not at the climate talks. "Generally, it's a good thing they're not here because we have less recalcitrants to deal with," Ralph Regenvanu, minister of climate change of Vanuatu, told NPR then.

But some democratic lawmakers will be at COP31, including Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, a Democrat representing Rhode Island. Fresh off Democrats' midterm victory sweep, Whitehouse says he and the other lawmakers plan to keep the focus on fossil fuels and a potential carbon pricing mechanism.

" It cannot remain free for the fossil fuel industry to pollute if we want to have any chance of a pathway to climate safety," Whitehouse says.

title: US midterms deliver a Democratic Congress: What this means for energy markets
description:
Democratic control of Congress will constrain the administration’s domestic legislative agenda and yet leave considerable presidential discretion over foreign policy.
A Democratic Congress could raise the political cost of further escalation against Iran, complicate potential concessions to Russia and increase scrutiny of trade policy.
Gridlock at home, an executive workaround abroad Our outlook described a Democratic sweep producing legislative gridlock with some horse-trading on domestic energy policy.
On Russia, a Democratic Senate adds votes on Ukraine aid and the power to delay envoys and sanctions officials, which makes concessions pressed on Kyiv harder to sell.
For renewables, a Democratic Congress protects the surviving credits from further repeal and gains bargaining power over budget and debt-limit votes.
text:
The 2026 US midterm elections have delivered a significant political setback to President Donald Trump, but their implications for US policy and global energy markets are far from straightforward. Democratic control of Congress will constrain the administration’s domestic legislative agenda and yet leave considerable presidential discretion over foreign policy. The outcome closely matches Scenario C of our 5 October outlook: legislative gridlock at home, greater congressional influence over spending and appointments, and potentially increased reliance on executive powers to define the administration’s policies abroad. Rather than reversing the direction of US policy, the elections may change how it is pursued.

The US remains deeply involved in the Middle East conflict, energy prices remain elevated, and Washington increasingly uses sanctions, trade restrictions and energy resources as instruments of negotiation. A Democratic Congress could raise the political cost of further escalation against Iran, complicate potential concessions to Russia and increase scrutiny of trade policy. Yet, congressional constraints could also encourage greater reliance on executive action, potentially increasing rather than reducing geopolitical uncertainty. For energy markets, the most consequential effects may therefore emerge abroad, while domestic oil and gas production continues to respond primarily to market fundamentals.

Hence, there are important limits to what the election can change. The White House retains considerable authority over the instruments that impact global energy markets most directly: sanctions implementation, diplomacy and certain trade measures. Congress retains authority over trade legislation, appropriations and war powers, while the Supreme Court has already established legal limits on the use of emergency economic powers to levy tariffs. The election result would therefore put more political and institutional constraints on the administration’s actions, rather than fundamentally altering the powers available to it.

Domestically, US oil and gas production will remain driven by market fundamentals, investment economics and infrastructure constraints. Critical-mineral supply chains, nuclear energy and geothermal retain scope for bipartisan cooperation. Data-center electricity demand adds a further dimension, with states, utilities and regulators holding substantial influence over investment and the allocation of infrastructure costs.

Timing now matters. The outgoing Congress retains its authority until the new one convenes on 3 January, and fiscal decisions taken in that window could constrain its successor. Subsequent budget and debt-limit negotiations will provide the first indication of how the new political balance translates into policy. The midterms will not resolve the strains from conflicts in the Middle East and Eastern Europe, or from transatlantic and US-Canada trade tensions. Still, they will change the political environment in which Washington responds to them. The central question for 2027 is whether these new constraints encourage accommodation, produce prolonged paralysis or drive the administration toward a more assertive use of executive power, with potentially significant consequences for global energy markets.

The results

Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate. In the Senate, the party flipped seven seats, in Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, Maine, North Carolina, South Carolina, and Texas, well beyond the net gain of four it needed, and now holds 54 seats to the Republicans’ 44, with Alaska and Mississippi still uncalled. In the House, it is estimated Democrats will hold between 251 and 268 seats once all votes are counted, although dozens of races, 68 by the Associated Press’s count on 4 November, had not yet been called.

Five of the seven flips came in states the Cook Political Report had rated toss-ups before the vote (Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Ohio, and Texas). The other two, in North Carolina and South Carolina, fell outside that list. As of 6 November, two Senate races, in Alaska and Mississippi, remained uncalled. Neither can change control of the chamber.

Gridlock at home, an executive workaround abroad

Our outlook described a Democratic sweep producing legislative gridlock with some horse-trading on domestic energy policy. Each side’s agenda stalls, but must-pass bills could force trades. In foreign policy, the scenario points to an executive workaround. Congress will seek to codify pressure on China and Russia and to add institutional brakes, while the White House could lean more on executive power to pursue its priorities abroad.

The president keeps his veto. Overriding one requires 67 senators and 290 House members, and the projected House majority – while larger than the narrow margin our analysis assumed – remains well short of that threshold. History points in the same direction. Over the last five presidencies, 81 of 84 vetoes came after the president’s party lost a chamber. Congresses seated after such a flip enacted an average of 391 public laws, compared with 514 for all others.

The main new lever is control of money and people. Both chambers now control funding, and the Senate controls confirmations. On Iran, both chambers can pass war-powers resolutions, but the veto still holds, so the practical leverage lies in holding back war funding and confirmations. Our analysis concluded that Democratic gains make post-election escalation costlier and a deal likelier. On Russia, a Democratic Senate adds votes on Ukraine aid and the power to delay envoys and sanctions officials, which makes concessions pressed on Kyiv harder to sell. On China, a Democratic Congress could try to write chip export licenses, rare-earth rules and outbound-investment rules into statute through the defense bill and Senate holds on trade nominees.

Venezuela’s current output is safe under this scenario. Congress cannot revoke executive oil licenses, but both chambers can deny authority and funding for the Pentagon’s 35% stake in the North American Blue Energy Partners concessions. In that case, the expansion proceeds on private capital, more slowly and without a federal backstop. On tariffs, review bills would get a Senate vote but likely not the 60 needed for it to pass. The tariff authority in the Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act remains with the White House.

Domestic energy: Direction holds, scrutiny rises

Our outlook concluded that US oil and gas production stays driven by market fundamentals, investment economics and infrastructure constraints, whichever party controls Congress. That conclusion still holds.

Approvals for building liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminals for the 2026-31 period stand. New approvals beyond 2031 could face more hearings and scrutiny, and slower confirmations at the Department of Energy (DOE) and the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) could add friction. On federal leasing, output follows price and capital discipline, and acreage is not a constraint. Democrats can now attach appropriations riders to Interior’s budget and influence confirmations of the officials who run lease sales. The sales themselves are statutory, however, and permits on existing leases continue.

For renewables, a Democratic Congress protects the surviving credits from further repeal and gains bargaining power over budget and debt-limit votes. Longer battery-storage credits are the most plausible gain. Restoring wind and solar credits remains out of reach. Nuclear, geothermal and critical minerals keep cross-party support and funding. Coal remains as backup capacity where grid operators require it, while storage and transmission support become tradable.

Financing levers and the lame-duck window

The outgoing Congress keeps its authority until the new one convenes on 3 January. It faces an 11 December funding deadline and the 31 December expiry of the Export-Import Bank charter. A lapse remains very unlikely. If the outgoing Congress chooses a short renewal, though, the decision moves to the new Congress, where Democrats can add ethics rules and terms on default-rate exemptions. For the Development Finance Corporation, our analysis expects friction rather than reversal, with conditions on the budget and the new $3 billion equity fund as the primary levers.

Governor races shape data-center policy

Our outlook highlighted that 29 of the 36 governor races determine who appoints the chair of the state public utility commission. These commissions set data-center tariffs, allocate grid costs between large users and households, and approve new plants and power lines. Democrats flipped five governorships in Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio and Texas and held Arizona, Maine, Michigan and Wisconsin.

name: EPA
title: The Voters Have Spoken. Who Speaks for Everyone Else? Human Rights After the Midterms
description:
The views expressed below are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect those of the Carr-Ryan Center for Human Rights or Harvard Kennedy School.
This commentary looks at the midterms from a human rights standpoint.
Most of what concerns human rights does not appear in any post-election analysis I have read.
America should again put its support behind human rights, democracy, and rule of law everywhere.
A human rights perspective cannot dictate a party platform, but it can ask whether any vision includes people who cannot vote.
text:
The views expressed below are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect those of the Carr-Ryan Center for Human Rights or Harvard Kennedy School. These perspectives have been presented to encourage debate on important public policy challenges.

Voters have told this administration that it must answer to them. The task now is to make power answer to everyone else too, and to hold ourselves to the same standard.

On November 3, American voters delivered the sharpest rebukes of a sitting president in half a century. The list of grievances is long: a war most Americans did not want, one that also raised prices at home; tariffs that unsettled farms, factories, and family budgets; immigration enforcement that left many Latinos, immigrant communities, and many others feeling that this country was not for them; a turn toward Moscow at Ukraine's expense; sustained pressure on universities, civil service, and public health agencies; threats and insults toward neighbors and allies, from Canada to EU countries to Greenland; and indifference to climate change and to the governance of AI. One could go on — and it is striking how long the list grows after only a minute's reflection.

On Tuesday, the electorate said that enough was enough.

Part of me wants to think the American electorate just did to Trump what Joseph Welch did to McCarthy in 1954: the electorate asked the president whether he had any sense of decency. From what I can tell, there is no serious doubt that this election was about America repudiating its president. But things are more complicated, and we should read this election in two registers. Voters held their government to account for what it did to them, and several of the issues I just listed mattered deeply for that. Whether the country will hold its government to account for what it does to everyone else is a separate question. Tuesday's returns do not settle it. This commentary looks at the midterms from a human rights standpoint.

Human rights rest on the idea that people have claims on those who hold power over them simply because they are people. Their lives are not bargaining chips, and their protection does not depend on citizenship, usefulness, loyalty, or membership in a favored civilization. The Universal Declaration opens with equal dignity, not with a ranking of peoples. So consider the election from the standpoint of those who cannot vote for or against the powerful: children who will inherit a hotter planet, foreigners at a border, civilians in a country under threat, people on the wrong side of a larger state's ambitions. For them, institutions are the means by which claims get pressed. When institutions are dismantled or captured, obligations become optional.

What happened

A few races remain uncalled at this writing, including Senate contests in Mississippi and Alaska, and House totals are still moving. The outline is not in doubt. Democrats won the House by a wider margin than most forecasts anticipated, and they won the Senate, a prospect widely considered out of reach a few months ago. Trump has often compared his election results to landslides. In this instance, that finally is true. He is now the president who lost the Republican Party Kansas, Texas, and South Carolina. Governor Ron DeSantis called the outcome "close to an extinction-level event" for Republicans.

Reuters found that Republicans lost ground, relative to Trump's 2024 showing, in 99% of the roughly 2,200 counties where most votes had been counted by Wednesday morning. Majority-Hispanic counties moved furthest. The New York Times estimates that Republicans lost the national House vote by about thirteen points, the worst result for a president's party since the aftermath of Watergate.

The clarity of these outcomes matters greatly, for the United States and for the world. It was widely expected that the Trump administration would move heaven and hell to contest election results. These margins make such contestation now immensely implausible. The American electorate has spoken too loudly and too clearly for that. Not even all the redistricting has done any good to the Republican prospects. It seems the Democrats won this particular fight. Without losing sight of all the damage Trump and his cronies have done to democracy, human rights, rule of law and plainly to the future of humanity — and they will take decades to repair — for now we can utter a sigh of relief. American democracy is resilient. The country, it seems, has started to free itself from Trumpism.

Why Republicans lost

The explanations that appeared within hours converge to an unusual degree, and they come from every direction.

Prices. Voters blamed the administration for the cost of living and linked it to tariffs and to the war with Iran, which closed the Strait of Hormuz and pushed fuel prices sharply up. About two-thirds of respondents in the AP Voter Poll said Trump's policies had made the economy worse. The facts created by this war are so stubborn that all of Trump’s gaslighting could not outmaneuver them.

The war. Roughly six in ten voters called the decision to attack Iran wrong, and large majorities said it figured in their vote. It also felt like a broken promise: Trump campaigned on no new wars. There used to be a perception of Trump that violence was repulsive to him. That perception has faded away during this second round in the White House.

Corruption. More than half of voters in the AP poll called government corruption crucial to their vote, and about two-thirds said Trump had the wrong priorities. The reporting about a ballroom financed with corporate donations, a family enriched by cryptocurrency, and a closing campaign speech devoted to a reflecting pool evidently landed. Resistance to corruption has deep roots in American conservatism. While conservatives were willing to give Trump credit for achieving many of their goals, his corruption finally might have proved too much for many of them.

Candidates. Trump pushed aside Senator John Cornyn for Paxton, whom two-thirds of Texas voters said lacked the character for the job, and installed Darline Graham, whom six in ten South Carolinians said lacked the experience. Voters in both states signaled that they expected more of Republican candidates than the president's favor. One gets the eerie feeling that with Paxton and Graham, Trump tried to assess how much he would get away with. The voters showed him his limits.

Congress. About seven in ten voters said Congress was not doing enough to check the president, including roughly four in ten Republicans. Separation of powers is a commitment that runs deeply in the American political psyche. The Republican Party of the current Congress, under Mike Johnson nominal leadership, has done little else but cozy up to the president. It is a fair guess that the 119th United States Congress – seated between January 2025 and January 3, 2027 — marks a true low point in the history of modern parliaments, with most of the blame going to the Republicans.

Two cautions are in order. The Democratic Party won no ringing endorsement: fewer than half of voters in the AP poll viewed it favorably, though more did so than viewed the Republican Party favorably. Many people voted Democratic as a rebuke. And the president's party usually loses seats in midterms, which explains part of the result but not its breadth.

What the vote tells us about answerability

Voters punished the administration chiefly for what it cost them: what they paid at the pump, what they feared about their prospects, who was getting rich. Most of what concerns human rights does not appear in any post-election analysis I have read. A country can reject a war because it is expensive. That is better than not rejecting it, but it is a rather thin foundation. If gasoline prices fall, the pressure to end the war might just fall with them, while the people in its path remain where they are. A rights-protecting politics cannot depend on the price of diesel. Americans can expunge Trumpism, and they can even investigate him and his cronies for their corruption — but Iranians and Ukrainians do not get a voice.

Still, the election did more than register pocketbook anger.

Checks and balances are popular. For two years the debate over executive power has been conducted largely in law reviews and among advocates. But what we see now is that voters hold the underlying view in plain form: the person at the top should have to answer to someone. That includes a large minority of Republicans.

Evidence still matters. The Times reports that after federal agents killed two people in Minneapolis in January, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, both on video, Trump told advisers he did not like how the videos looked, and Democratic internal polling showed the party leading on immigration for the first time. A majority of Americans now hold an unfavorable view of ICE, according to Pew. Officials had characterized both victims as terrorists or assassins before any investigation. That effort to set the narrative met recorded evidence and public witnesses, and it did not hold. Video, a free press, and citizens who watch and compare are genuine rights infrastructure. Here it did indeed work.

Those closest to enforcement voted. Hispanic voters moved sharply away from Republicans. In Hidalgo County, on the Texas border, the Republican share fell by about twenty-five points compared with 2024. Black voters, especially Black men, also moved, according to the AP. Immigration enforcement was one factor among several, but people who live nearest the coercive power of the state — in this case, people who have experienced the new formations of what I have called the intimidating state — tend to know what it looks like, and they become a political force when given the chance.

Corruption is a rights issue voters recognized. When a president's family and associates profit from his office, and access to government appears to depend on tribute, public power is exercised for private ends and equality before the law is compromised. Voters did not need the vocabulary to feel the wrong.

What was not on the ballot

The election decided little about the matters below. Each tests whether power answers to people who cannot answer back at the polls.

Climate. In February the Environmental Protection Agency rescinded the 2009 finding that greenhouse gases endanger public health, which underpinned much federal regulation of them. In July 2025 the International Court of Justice advised that states have binding obligations to protect the climate system. Reasonable people disagree about carbon pricing, nuclear power, and who pays for a transition. A human rights approach does not settle those disputes, but it refuses to treat foreseeable threats to life, health, food, and water as negligible because responding would burden powerful constituencies. Those who bear the consequences, such as a child in a lethal heatwave, a farmer in a flooded delta, or a generation not yet born, are largely absent from American decisions. The irony is that high fuel prices helped sink a government that had just removed the legal basis for regulating the pollutant behind them. A reaction to prices is not a mandate on obligations to people who cannot vote here. Trump’s war on the future affects many who can do nothing about it whatsoever.

Iran. On April 7 the president wrote that "a whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again," and ended the post with a blessing for the Iranian people. Whether it meets the elements of any offense is a question for lawyers. The UN Charter forbids threats of force, and the law of armed conflict forbids threats meant to terrorize civilians. What matters is what was said: a civilization is made of people, most of whom have no say in their government's decisions. Iran's government is repressive, but that does not make its population available for collective punishment. Voters objected to the cost of the war. They were not asked about its menace to those on whom it falls.

Ukraine. Russia's invasion violates the prohibition on aggression, and the International Criminal Court has issued an arrest warrant for Vladimir Putin over the deportation of Ukrainian children. In February 2025 the United States voted with Russia against a General Assembly resolution condemning the invasion. Negotiation by itself is not betrayal, but the test is what diplomacy secures and whom it respects. Does Ukraine decide its own future? It is hard to tell a story about America's current relationship with Ukraine that does not involve treating Ukraine's security as a chip in a larger bargain with Putin, and abandoning values America once championed: human rights, democracy, the rule of law, and loyalty to those who share them. Congressional and Republican criticism of Trump's October agreement to buy Russian diesel, which blindsided Congress, was an institutional check operating belatedly.

Universalism. Human rights are not prizes for civilizational membership, and protection should follow need, not identity. That is why it matters that the refugee system has been sharply narrowed, with places going overwhelmingly to white South Africans. Their claims count as much as anyone's, and that is the point. People have also been removed to a notorious Salvadoran prison without hearings. In Noem v. Abrego Garcia the Supreme Court ordered the government to facilitate the return of a man wrongly sent there, so the state acted first and corrected itself only when forced. Due process matters because it comes before the government is proved right. The same troubling attitude shows toward friends: Canada was told it might become a "51st state," and Greenland's future was treated as open to American pressure. Peoples have a right to determine their own political status, not merely to state preferences before a stronger country decides. The Trump government has done great damage to a kind of universalism that the United States had done a lot to build in the first place.

Artificial intelligence. The administration's AI Action Plan makes American dominance its central aim, and it came some months after Trump rescinded Biden’s modest requirement that developers of the most powerful models share safety-test results with the government. Capability is not leadership. Leadership asks whether people subject to powerful systems can learn how decisions were made about them, challenge errors, and obtain a remedy. The alternative to public-interest regulation is not the absence of political choices; it can be political direction exercised through government contracts. Elon Musk, who spent more than $450 million to aid Republicans, lost in Texas. Great wealth cannot buy every outcome, but unaccountable private power has not gone away. Under Trump the American government has largely withdrawn from regulating AI, and American recalcitrance in this domain is the single biggest obstacle to global regulation around AI. As far as AI is concerned, to my mind the United States under Trump currently poses the biggest existential threat to humanity that might come from this technology because of its unwillingness to engage in serious oversight. In this regard too, the Trump administration wages war on the future.

Rights at home. The Justice Department has moved to dismiss police-reform agreements in Minneapolis and Louisville, and a 2025 order told agencies to abandon disparate-impact liability wherever possible. Particular applications of that doctrine can fairly be criticized, but abandoning it wholesale makes some discrimination hard to challenge at all. Students and scholars have been detained or had visas revoked over speech the government disliked. After Harvard declined demands about its internal governance, roughly $2.2 billion in research funding was frozen, and in September 2025 a federal judge found the terminations violated the First Amendment and federal procedural requirements. Universities have failed in real ways, but the remedy is open argument, lawful investigation, and a chance to answer, not a funding freeze outside any such process. That Harvard won in court shows that safeguards still work, and also what they exist to prevent.

Military restraint. A professional military is defined by restraint as much as by force, and military lawyers are the institutional form of the trust that soldiers will refuse unlawful orders. In February 2025 the Defense Secretary dismissed the top uniformed lawyers of at least some of the services. Since September 2025 the military has destroyed boats it says carry drugs, killing those aboard without trial. Human Rights Watch and many legal experts call this extrajudicial killing and have not accepted the claim that an armed conflict with trafficking organizations makes it lawful. Replacing officials does not by itself prove unlawful intent, and many service members uphold their values in hard conditions. My charge is against leadership that celebrates force while eroding the restraints that make its use legitimate. The attitudes toward military ethics articulated by Pete Hegseth are dramatic outliers in the historical canon of the Christian just war doctrine as well as in the American tradition of military ethics.

I certainly do not write from an imagined innocent America. Slavery, the dispossession of Indigenous nations, imperial wars, and torture are part of this country's record, and the standards I use judge every administration. This administration also deploys the language of freedom and peace. What sets it apart is the sustained effort to weaken the means by which that language could be held against it. A government that violates a principle can still be called to account. A government that dismantles the means of calling it to account has turned obligation into a matter of convenience. That is unfortunately the government that we currently have — and that is the government that got rebuked on November 3.

What power remains

I do not want to overstate the effect of the result. Four limits matter.

First, the president retains his constitutional authority over foreign policy, the military, and much of trade. The tariffs, the war, and the Caribbean strikes did not need Congress to begin, and ending them will require either a veto-proof majority, which Democrats lack, or a presidential change of mind. Trump has said he will become "Mr. Veto." The new Congress also does not take office until January. A weakened president might escalate, especially the conflict with Iran. Nothing in the returns retracts the threats of April.

Second, in June the Supreme Court held in Trump v. Slaughter that the president may remove members of independent regulatory agencies at will, overturning a ninety-one-year-old precedent. That weakens institutions on which enforcement of disclosure, competition, and consumer protection depends. The election does not reverse it. Moreover, Trump v. United States greatly limits possibilities of criminal prosecution against Trump for official acts.

Third, the harms already done are in important respects permanent. An election cures none of the following: those killed in Minneapolis or at sea or abroad, the trust spent with allies, the scientists who have left, the people removed without hearings. The world will not easily forget the ugly face that America shows under Trump.

Fourth, a majority built on dissatisfaction can dissolve if it is not used well. Clearly, America’s politics is a highly volatile affair.

The president said that he accepts the results and is willing to work with Democrats — and that does matter. He also wrote that "I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE," and blamed "lazy" candidates. That is not a refusal to accept the outcome, but it reflects a habit of treating defeat as someone else's failure. It would be naïve to believe the president’s acquiescence in his resounding defeat will remain his prevailing attitude in the next two years. That he appointed MAGA hardliner Stephen Miller as his chief of staff as the first major response to his resound defeat speaks for itself.

And, yes, it is worth saying this one more time: Trump, just now, did indeed finally get his landslide.

Tests for the new majority

Rights standards are not partisan. They bind those who gain power as well as those who lose it. I would propose five tests for the incoming Congress.

Oversight must meet the standards it demands of the executive. Legitimate enforcement differs from its inversion in three ways: it applies the same standards to allies and opponents, it is proportionate, and the person investigated has a real chance to answer. House Democrats have promised aggressive investigations, and one prospective chair has summed up his plans in two words to the administration: "lawyer up." The discipline I ask is that investigations follow evidence, treat Republicans and Democrats alike, and respect targets' rights to counsel and response. If oversight becomes retribution, it will teach what the last two years taught: that accountability is for the other side.

Fair maps matter regardless of who benefits. Reporting indicates that Trump's mid-decade redistricting largely backfired. But Democrats in California and Virginia also redrew maps in response, and the Supreme Court's weakening of the Voting Rights Act allowed several Southern states to redraw districts that had been majority- or near-majority-Black. One party's gerrymander is not justified by the other's. Citizens are entitled to maps drawn by a process they can regard as fair, and Democrats now have both leverage and reason to want rules that bind everyone.

Lethal force and war powers deserve hearings. A Congress that wants to repair answerability should investigate the Minneapolis killings, the boat strikes, and the conduct of the Iran war, including civilian casualties such as the reported killing of children at a school in Minab, with subpoenas and public testimony. It should force the war powers vote the Constitution contemplates, and it should ask what legal advice the Defense Department received and why its senior lawyers were dismissed. These are not partisan questions. They are what any republic asks about the use of force.

Independence needs statutory protection. Statistical agencies, inspectors general, civil rights enforcers, and military legal officers can be insulated through legislation and appropriations, but only if the bills survive a veto, which will require Republican votes. The four in ten Republican voters who said Congress was not checking the president adequately are the constituency for this work.

Transparency about AI should not wait. Requiring developers of the most capable systems to disclose test results, permit independent examination, and preserve records of consequential changes is among the few measures with potential cross-party support. Whether the new majority pursues it will show whether it treats technology policy as more than a fundraising question. In recent times Republican lawmakers too have been increasingly worried about AI. We must hope they are now willing to act on these worries even if this might mean overruling Mr. Veto.

Apart from the operations of Congress, we must hope the Democratic Party will offer a vision for the future now that the country has asked precisely that of them. To my mind, economic justice should be central to this vision, including economic policies that integrate adaptation to and mitigation of climate change and policies that focus on AI in the spirit of augmentation rather than automation. America should again put its support behind human rights, democracy, and rule of law everywhere. America still needs its reckoning with the past, but such reckoning should be done in a way that does not make another culture war the dominant feature of political discourse. A human rights perspective cannot dictate a party platform, but it can ask whether any vision includes people who cannot vote.

Whom does power answer to?

The election shows that a president with low approval, unpopular policies, and flagrant self-dealing remains answerable to voters in the way the constitutional design intends. The same country that gave this administration two years of largely unchecked power has taken a large part of it back, in a single night. That is worth defending and building on. When courts rule, journalists report, videos circulate, and citizens vote, power can be made to answer.

But answerability to voters is not answerability to everyone the exercise of power affects. For those dependent on a government whose next move is anyone's guess, unpredictability is itself a harm. A child in a heatwave, a farmer in a flooded delta, a Ukrainian family sheltering from drones, an Iranian family hearing that their civilization might die tonight, a person at sea in a small boat, a man sent to a foreign prison without a hearing: none of them voted on November 3. No one on the ballot answered to them. Human rights exist for this gap. Some claims do not depend on whether the claimant can punish the powerful at the polls.

Closing that gap requires something no election supplies: a political culture in which Americans recognize that people on the receiving end of their government's decisions have claims whether or not they can reward or punish it, and institutions strong enough to act on that recognition. Voters have told this administration that it must answer to them. The task now is to make power answer to everyone else too, and to hold ourselves to the same standard.

title: Senate's bipartisan permitting bill faces crucial test | Latitude Media
authors: Catherine Boudreau, Maeve Allsup, Seyed H. Madaeni, Shayle Kann

He added that advocacy groups have historically relied on litigation to stop bad projects, but the existing permitting system slows down good projects, too.

text:
Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich (N.M.) and Sheldon Whitehouse (R.I.) on Monday pitched their bipartisan permitting reform bill as a way to deliver results for Americans who want Congress to make their lives more affordable and hold data centers accountable for their costs.

Their comments came ahead of a major test of the bill’s support scheduled for this evening, when the Senate will vote on a procedural measure that determines whether it advances to the floor for chamber-wide debate. Heinrich and Whitehouse, two of the main negotiators of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, said they expect to have the votes to secure its passage after making some changes to the bill. The permitting bill needs 60 votes to proceed.

The changes helped BAJAA win some newfound support among utilities and labor unions who were on the fence, adding to the long list of clean energy, oil and gas, manufacturing, and more moderate climate groups who were already on board. But many environmental advocates and Tribal nations remain opposed.

“Americans sent a resounding message about their priorities,” Heinrich said during a press conference, referencing the midterm elections marked by a blue wave of wins at the state and federal levels. “They want Congress focused on making their lives more affordable, and that’s precisely what this permitting reform bill will do.”

Heinrich cited estimates by the Brattle Group that BAAJA would force data centers to pay $35 billion more for energy infrastructure over a decade compared with current law, due to provisions that effectively double-charge the industry for using the grid. The Rhodium Group also forecasted that average annual household electricity bills would be $50 to $78 lower in 2040 if BAAJA were enacted, while planet-warming pollution from the power sector would drop by between 1% and 18% — mainly depending on clean energy’s price competitiveness with gas.

Whitehouse is optimistic that clean energy will win the market, even as President Donald Trump advances policies that favor fossil fuels, because the vast majority of new generation applying to connect to the grid is solar, wind, and batteries. He also argued that the so-called “permit certainty” provisions of BAAJA — and, separately, assurances from the Trump administration — would lift the current blockade of clean energy projects on federal lands, including by ending federal buyouts of offshore wind leases.

“We’ve been discussing with the administration that there needs to be an end to the deliberate mischief against clean energy, and we have some real assurances,” Whitehouse said, adding that he expects the Department of the Interior to “have something to say” after today’s vote. “We have been clearly told that the existing backup at the Department of Defense of as many as 250 projects are subject to these permit certainty provisions, and must begin to move.”

Neither the Department of the Interior nor the Pentagon responded to questions from Latitude Media by the time of publication.

Trump on Sunday endorsed BAAJA on Truth Social, stating that the bill will ensure the U.S. can quickly build pipelines, mines, and power plants and lower energy costs for Americans. He also said it codifies the White House’s ratepayer protection pledge, ensuring data centers pay for their own electricity and invest in their local communities.

Green groups dig in on fossil concerns

The potential for the Senate permitting bill to expedite new oil and gas infrastructure, including LNG export terminals, combined with provisions that limit the ability of states and courts to block those kinds of projects has led many environmental groups to oppose BAAJA. That includes the Natural Resources Defense Council, which for the first time on Sunday announced its opposition despite the changes senators announced over the weekend.

NRDC, which is suing the Trump administration over a wide range of its climate and environmental rollbacks and restrictions on clean energy development, said recent changes to BAAJA’s project certainty section don’t sufficiently alleviate concerns that the bill will make it harder for groups like NRDC to challenge unlawfully issued permits. That’s despite the fact that the new text explicitly allows federal agencies to revoke or alter permits if ordered by a court. NRDC also cited provisions that limit a courts’ ability to halt construction of projects, regardless of whether an environmental review is deemed deficient.

Manish Bapna, president and CEO of NRDC, said the group will keep working with Congress on changes to the bill. The League of Conservation Voters took a similar stance.

Heinrich on Monday acknowledged that the bill isn’t perfect, but said that senators had to make compromises to secure bipartisan support. He added that advocacy groups have historically relied on litigation to stop bad projects, but the existing permitting system slows down good projects, too.

“Changing that is hard,” Heinrich said. “It means organizations are going to have to reevaluate the best way to move the clean energy transition forward. In my view, if we can create an open, competitive playing field, clean, cheap energy wins the marketplace.”

Utilities sign on

Senators’ revisions to BAAJA’s transmission policy were enough to win the endorsement of EEI, which represents investor-owned utilities. That is significant because the bill still contains provisions that the industry has historically opposed, including granting the federal government greater authority and oversight of utilities’ plans to build transmission lines. EEI has withheld support for previous attempts at permitting reform and some of its members, including Duke Energy and Southern Company, individually lobbied against them.

EEI president and CEO Drew Maloney, in a letter to congressional leaders, said the group worked daily with the White House and Congress on changes to local transmission planning and oversight and “duplicative” planning requirements.

For example, the new BAAJA text clarifies that state energy regulators can refer a utility’s transmission planning to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission for an investigation if it suspects a utility is building inefficient and costly local projects that inflate costs for ratepayers. FERC could also reject a state’s request to investigate.

Maloney added that EEI would work with FERC and state regulators to implement the law.

“Our priority will be to ensure that new transmission requirements strengthen the grid, protect reliability, shield existing customers from costs that should be paid by data centers, build on the considerable expertise of grid planners and state and local leaders, and support regulatory certainty so that we can continue to build for the future,” he said.

EEI’s endorsement may help shore up support among some House Republicans, particularly those representing districts in Alabama, Florida, Georgia, North Carolina, and South Carolina who tend to align with investor-owned utilities in those states.

But it’s unclear whether BAAJA could pass the House during the lame duck period, especially because of Democrats’ resounding victory in the midterm elections. That could give the party more leverage next year — though waiting risks losing the backing of the president, who’d have to sign a permitting reform bill regardless of which party has control in Congress.

text:
Lehigh has received $1.6 million to participate in the “Commonwealth of Pennsylvania EGS Pilot Demonstration,” a U.S. Department of Energy-funded project led by the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection. The total project budget is about $14 million. The “EGS” stands for enhanced geothermal system.

“This project shows what’s possible when faculty work across disciplinary and college boundaries,” said Robert Flowers, Herbert J. and Ann L. Siegel Dean of the College of Arts and Sciences. “Earth scientists from the College of Arts and Sciences and engineers from the P.C. Rossin College of Engineering and Applied Science are bringing complementary expertise to a problem neither could solve alone. Research like this matters because discoveries don't stay in the lab. It’s designed to bring new possibilities to Pennsylvania communities, and it reflects Lehigh’s commitment to scholarship that serves the people and places around us.”

The goal is to generate one megawatt of electricity from a low-enthalpy, underperforming Marcellus Shale gas well in Indiana County, Pennsylvania. The project will draw heat from an underperforming natural gas well by circulating water at depth, and then bring that heated water to the surface. That heated water energy will produce electricity for the local grid and supply direct-use heat to nearby homes and businesses.

“Pennsylvania’s conventional hydrocarbon industry, followed by the shale oil and gas revolution left behind a vast network of wells and related infrastructure ,” said Frank Pazzaglia, professor of Earth and environmental sciences in Lehigh’s College of Arts and Sciences and the principal investigator. “This project asks whether we can give that infrastructure a second life as a clean, renewable energy source.”

The pilot will use a deep existing unconventional gas well in Indiana County, PA where the geology is favorable for tapping geothermal resources. The well is operated by CNX Green Ventures, an Appalachian oil and gas producer.

“Repurposing abandoned hydrocarbon wells for low-enthalpy geothermal mining represents an economic and environmental opportunity, transforming the methane-leaking liability into a predictable source of clean, local energy,” said Carlos Romero, professor of mechanical engineering and mechanics in the Rossin College and director of Lehigh’s Energy Research Center.

Project leaders say the approach could also create opportunities for displaced oil, gas, and coal workers, whose subsurface experience transfers directly to the geothermal industry. By extending the useful life of existing wells, the project aims to stimulate geothermal energy development, particularly in the eastern US where geothermal resources are more restricted than in the western US, and demonstrate that the approach is portable.

“The project is a chance to train the next generation of scientists and engineers while helping to show that geothermal energy can work in places many people wouldn’t expect,” Pazzaglia said.

Lehigh’s funding will support five researchers and students from two units. The Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences (EES) will include three principal investigators, a postdoctoral researcher and a graduate student, while the Energy Research Center will include two principal investigators and a graduate student. Project personnel from Lehigh include Frank Pazzaglia; Steve Peters, associate professor of EES; Anne Meltzer, professor of EES; Carlos Romero and Muhannad Suleiman, professor of civil and environmental engineering.

DEP is the project lead, working in coordination with the Pennsylvania Geological Survey. Partners include Gradient Geothermal Inc., Teverra Inc., Idaho National Laboratory, CNX Green Ventures, and Seequent, in addition to Lehigh University.

text:
I’d like to take some time talking to EV owners and others about why electric vehicle tax credits were created in the first place.

Lately, the conversation around EV incentives focuses almost entirely on tech pushes, market forces, or supply chains. But for many of us, the decision to go electric wasn't just about grabbing the latest tech gadget or government handout, it was driven by a desire to meaningfully cut down on greenhouse gas emissions for our children’s sake. I fall Into that category.

That exact objective is explicitly written into the federal legislation that established and refined these incentives.

When Congress first established the federal plug-in credit in the Energy Improvement and Extension Act of 2008 (Public Law 110-343), the legislative preamble defined its core purpose:

"...to amend the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 to provide incentives for energy production and conservation, to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, and for other purposes."

When the tax credit was updated under Section 30D of the Internal Revenue Code via the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (Public Law 117-169), Congress legally defined eligible vehicles around zero tailpipe pollution:

Section 30D: "...which is propelled to a significant extent by an electric motor which draws electricity from a battery... and produces no greenhouse gas emissions..."

Yes, “Well to Wheel” isn’t zero but it almost is compared to ICE, Cradle to Grave.

The goal wasn't simply to push new technology for technology's sake. It was a deliberate strategy to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from the transportation sector. Cutting greenhouse gas emissions was a major factor in making the switch, and it remains just as relevant today.

Moving forward, I will be starting a series dedicated to the impacts of global warming. This isn't a hoax or political fear-mongering, it is real, grounded in data, and something that needs to be talked about openly and directly… again.

This is a list of things we are experiencing around the world that scientists for 5 decades were trying to prevent.

Follow and like for more on this and other EV topics.

Dutch development bank FMO identifies the capacity to multiply its financial exposure in Peru and potentially reach USD 2 billion , with investment opportunities in renewable generation, transmission infrastructure and projects that incorporate energy storage.

“We have concrete opportunities, but we believe there is room for further development. We have $200 million in exposure, but we can increase it up to ten times more. We have the capacity to do so, as Peru is a macroeconomically stable country with a good credit rating,” revealed Patricia Vargas SC Oliveira, Investment Officer at FMO , in an exclusive interview during the Future Energy Summit (FES) Peru 2026 .

Vargas Oliveira believes that this growth could begin to materialize as early as 2027, provided that initiatives that meet its bankability requirements are implemented.

The bank already has a track record of financing wind, solar, hydroelectric projects and transmission lines , segments in which it seeks to expand its participation through debt schemes adapted to the characteristics of each investment.

Among the completed transactions, the financing of USD 100 million for the 296.4 MW Punta Lomitas wind farm , developed by ENGIE Energía Perú, stands out. FMO also has participation in electricity transmission infrastructure projects, where concession terms allow for structuring longer-term loans.

The entity's interest coincides with a portfolio of 22,701 MW of solar and wind projects with Pre-Operational Studies (EPO) approved by the Economic Operation Committee of the System (COES), according to a survey by Energía Estratégica .

Of that universe, 19 initiatives totaling 3,714.5 MW have definitive concessions , while 14 projects totaling 2,772.4 MW have an estimated entry horizon between 2026 and 2027, according to their respective studies.

Among the developers that make up this portfolio are Continua Energías Positivas, Grupo Enhol, Orygen, Zelestra, ACCIONA and ENGIE, among other players that are advancing with renewable projects of different scales in the country.

In that sense, Vargas Oliveira explains that Peru's macroeconomic stability and the presence of commercial banks influence FMO's strategy, which seeks to complement the existing financial offering through long-term solutions, rather than competing with traditional lenders.

What does FMO require to finance new renewable energy projects in Peru?

The developer's experience and the strength of the contractual structure are the first aspects that FMO evaluates before committing financing for a new renewable energy plant.

“I believe that a good sponsor is the first thing one wants,” said Vargas Oliveira, who explained that the bank prioritizes companies with knowledge of the Peruvian market or, failing that, international developers associated with local partners who have verifiable experience.

Another determining factor is the track record of the EPC contractor , responsible for engineering, equipment procurement, and construction of the facilities. The entity specifically analyzes its capacity to execute solar or wind projects and its history of meeting deadlines.

Once these elements have been evaluated, the analysis focuses on the bankability of the power purchase agreement (PPA) , particularly its duration, termination clauses, and conditions that allow for projecting sufficient income to meet financial obligations.

During her participation in the FES Peru 2026 panel, the executive also identified regulatory stability and dispatch conditions as relevant elements, which affect risk assessment and revenue predictability.

Consequently, the contract term is crucial for structuring financing under the project finance modality, where debt repayment depends primarily on the cash flows generated by the asset itself.

“If the auction results in longer-term bankable contracts, I think there will also be more room for project finance,” the FMO representative noted.

The Peruvian market is awaiting regulatory definitions that could facilitate the financial closing of new renewable energy projects . The Ministry of Energy and Mines (MINEM) expects to approve the pending regulations for electricity and ancillary services tenders before the end of 2026, as recently announced by Minister Guillermo Shinno.

In particular, the bidding regulations, linked to Law No. 32249 , seek to establish new conditions for energy procurement, including long-term agreements and mechanisms that allow for greater participation of solar and wind technologies in the regulated market.

The draft regulations contemplate contracts of ten to fifteen years , while various companies in the sector requested modifications to facilitate the bankability of new investments.

Among these proposals, ACCIONA suggests extending contracts to 20 years and increasing the proportion of contracted demand on a long-term basis. ENGIE, for its part, requests greater clarity in the participation requirements and the possibility of submitting indivisible bids that cover different time blocks.

The observations also extend to the conditions of competition . While EDF Perú and Ignis Energy propose prioritizing new projects in long-term tenders, Kallpa, Statkraft, ENGIE, and Fenix Power , among other companies, argue that existing power plants should also be able to participate in the bidding processes.

However, FMO maintains that new tenders are not essential to secure financing in the Peruvian market , as it has alternatives adapted to current contractual conditions.

“We can do corporate finance, pooling projects into a portfolio to finance the portfolio as well,” explains Vargas Oliveira.

The entity also contemplates operations with free clients and industries that demand shorter supply contracts, even of five years , through corporate financing structures adjusted to the duration of the agreements.

Likewise, during the FES Peru panel , the executive acknowledged the possibility of financing projects with a merchant revenue proportion , directly exposed to the conditions of the electricity market and without long-term contracts.

In these cases, FMO considers more stringent debt coverage criteria to mitigate the business risks associated with revenue volatility.

Another alternative identified by the executive is the mini-perm , a shorter-term loan used primarily during construction, which can later be refinanced with other banking entities or through bond issuances.

However, FMO seeks to differentiate itself from commercial banking by offering longer-term solutions , capable of supporting projects both during their construction phase and during operation, with repayment schemes linked to the income generated.

“We want to offer perhaps a long-term solution, not only during construction because we can take construction risk, but also until the end of the project, with repayment through project cash flows to avoid the risk of not finding financing,” the bank representative stated.

This flexibility allows projects to be evaluated under different contractual structures, without limiting financing opportunities exclusively to developments that have 15 or 20 year power purchase agreements.

Storage: the potential of 2 GW of solar power and the pending conditions

On the other hand, hybrid projects that incorporate battery storage systems are also among the opportunities analyzed by FMO , although their financial viability will depend on the definition of regulatory mechanisms that allow remuneration for the services provided by these technologies.

“Hybrid is always being discussed, and all developers are waiting for the regulation,” the executive stated, referring to the still pending regulations for complementary services.

The ancillary services regulation , whose approval is also planned before the end of 2026, could provide greater clarity on the participation and remuneration of battery systems in the Peruvian electricity market.

During her participation in the FES Peru 2026 panel, the FMO representative also put forward an estimate of the photovoltaic growth that the Peruvian market could register during the next few years, with up to 2 GW of solar accompanied by storage .

“A guess estimate for a couple of years could be 2 GW of solar accompanied by about 20% battery,” says Oliveira, when assessing the potential for incorporating both technologies into the electrical system.

Regarding stand-alone storage projects , Vargas Oliveira acknowledges that FMO has not yet identified sufficiently advanced initiatives to begin concrete discussions about their financing. This estimate does not constitute a committed financing target for FMO, but rather an approximation of the volume of renewable energy development that could materialize under favorable conditions.

In this way, the bank keeps open various alternatives to expand its exposure in Peru, both in conventional renewable projects and in transmission infrastructure and hybrid developments.

“There are quite a few companies developing projects here that are recognized efforts, that know how to work, that know the market, and that we would love to support with financing,” Vargas Oliveira emphasized.

Thus, the possibility of FMO multiplying its exposure tenfold and potentially reaching USD 2 billion will depend on the realization of projects with technical backing, experienced developers and bankable financial structures , regardless of whether the new tenders materialize in the short term.
