November 9, 2026

****************************************************

National Taxpayers Union urges all senators to vote “YES” on the Manager’s Amendment to H.R. 2347, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) sponsored by Sens. Capito (R-WV), Lee (R-UT), Whitehouse (D-RI), and Heinrich (D-NM). This legislation would be a meaningful step toward restoring common sense to the federal permitting process, unleashing private investment, creating jobs, and making it easier and more affordable to build the infrastructure America needs.

The need for permitting reform is serious. An increasingly complex web of government red tape suffocates investment and makes it unnecessarily difficult, costly, and time-consuming to build in America. From oil refineries and wind farms to interstate highways and advanced manufacturing facilities, projects that could strengthen our economy, create good-paying jobs, and improve Americans’ quality of life are routinely subjected to years of regulatory delays.

In some cases, securing an energy permit can take more than four and a half years, while approval for a new transmission line can take as long as eight years. These prolonged delays drive up project costs, discourage investment, and ultimately leave consumers and utility ratepayers footing the bill through higher energy prices.

Thankfully, BAAJA fixes these government-caused problems. It includes important provisions to protect approved energy projects from being arbitrarily canceled by future administrations, providing the regulatory certainty businesses need to make billions of dollars in long-term investments across both clean and fossil fuel energy. It also curbs frivolous litigation that has allowed anti-energy activists to tie up major infrastructure projects for years, creating costly uncertainty for developers. It also rightly modernizes the Endangered Species Act and Clean Water Act to ensure projects proceed safely, responsibly, and efficiently.

Permitting reform won’t lead to lower energy prices today, but it will help us meet future energy needs. It means extracting underground oil faster, building more efficient refineries to turn oil into gasoline, and utilizing abundant solar and wind energy to power our homes and businesses. While this bill is imperfect, particularly some of the language pertaining to transmission lining and new mandates on data centers, enacting this legislation would still rank among the most consequential pro-growth achievements of Congress in a generation and should not be delayed.

Roll call votes on the Manager’s Amendment to H.R. 2347 will be included in NTU’s annual rating of Congress and “YES” votes will be considered the pro-taxpayer position.

If you have any questions, please contact NTU’s Vice President for Federal Affairs Thomas Aiello at Taiello@ntu.org

text:
Congress is back in Washington this week facing a lengthy list of priorities before the end of the year, but toward the top of the agenda should be swiftly passing bipartisan permitting reform. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) represents one of the most consequential pieces of legislation Congress could send to the president’s desk this session. Passing BAAJA would be a meaningful step toward restoring common sense to the federal permitting process, unleashing private investment, creating jobs, and making it easier and more affordable to build the infrastructure America needs.

The need for permitting reform is serious. An increasingly complex web of government red tape suffocates investment and makes it unnecessarily difficult, costly, and time-consuming to build in America. From oil refineries and wind farms to interstate highways and advanced manufacturing facilities, projects that could strengthen our economy, create good-paying jobs, and improve Americans’ quality of life are routinely subjected to years of regulatory delays.

In some cases, securing an energy permit can take more than four and a half years, while approval for a new transmission line can take as long as eight years. These prolonged delays drive up project costs, discourage investment, and ultimately leave consumers and utility ratepayers footing the bill through higher energy prices.

Fortunately, Senate Republicans and Democrats have come together around a bipartisan opportunity to fix this broken system and unleash American economic growth. BAAJA represents a rare, potentially once-in-a-generation opportunity to rein in federal bureaucracy, remove unnecessary barriers to investment, and get the government out of the way of responsible development. The legislation deserves swift consideration and passage so it can reach the president’s desk without delay.

BAAJA includes many important provisions that NTU has advocated for over the years. Specifically, it ensures future administrations cannot simply cancel projects that are approved. That means pipeline companies can build energy infrastructure without fear that a Democratic president will kill their project. Likewise for clean energy projects like wind and solar that could face threats from a Republican president. No one wins from tit-for-tat energy policy. Projects of this scale are capital-intensive, requiring billions of dollars in upfront costs and often take years—or even decades—to recover.

The bill also finally ends “lawfare,” a tactic employed by anti-energy radicals to gum up the permitting process. Currently, lawsuits challenging National Environmental Policy Act reviews can be filed up to six years after a permit approval. This leaves agencies and developers uncertain long after the review has been completed and a permit issued. Consider the Dakota Access Pipeline, which, until recently, was stuck in limbo for almost a decade due to unserious legal challenges. It’s a similar story for SunZia, the largest renewable project in the country.

BAAJA establishes a 150-day statute of limitations for challenging federal agency approvals of energy and mineral projects. That means companies spend less time tied up in courtrooms and more time building the infrastructure America needs.

Additionally, BAAJA includes:

Reforming the Clean Water Act (CWA): Promoting regulatory certainty by refocusing Section 401 certifications on water quality and ending preemptive and retroactive vetoes under the EPA Administrator’s Section 404(c) authority.

Modernizing the Endangered Species Act (ESA): Providing states with greater flexibility to conduct Section 7 consultations and ensuring ESA determinations are grounded in the best available science.

Advancing complementary permitting reforms: Reforming transmission policy to ensure the electric grid can meet growing demand, streamlining the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA), unlocking America’s geothermal energy potential, and providing greater certainty in the mining permitting process.

There is growing Beltway speculation that last week’s election results could derail this hard-fought agreement. Even Hakeem Jeffries, the likely next Speaker of the House, has suggested the deal falls short of what his conference wants and that Democrats will seek a “better” agreement in the next Congress.

Let’s hope that doesn’t happen. This agreement represents the best possible outcome for taxpayers, the clean and fossil fuel energy industries, and the countless businesses forced to navigate an increasingly complex federal regulatory system. Delaying action now would risk squandering a rare bipartisan opportunity and could seriously jeopardize the prospects of reaching another agreement anytime soon.

Permitting reform won’t lead to lower energy prices today, but it will help us meet future energy needs. It means extracting underground oil faster, building more efficient refineries to turn oil into gasoline, and utilizing abundant solar and wind energy to power our homes and businesses. The sooner this bill can get to the president’s desk, the sooner energy developers can build again and Americans can enjoy the abundant, cheap energy they deserve.

text:
A Clean Energy Future Built with Rural Communities

BOLD Energy Builders works with rural communities to ensure that the people who live on the land help shape—and share in the benefits of—America’s clean energy future. Through local organizing, education, legal support, and alliances that cross political and cultural divides, BOLD helps residents protect their land and property rights while pursuing energy investments that strengthen their communities.

More About BOLD Energy Builders

Rural America has much of the land needed to expand wind and solar power. Too often, however, outside developers enter communities without first building trust, listening to local concerns, or ensuring that the economic benefits will be widely shared. BOLD advances a different model: treating communities as essential partners in the clean energy transition.

BOLD brings together farmers, ranchers, tribal nations, union workers, climate advocates, and other local leaders around shared priorities—including protecting land and water, strengthening public services, creating good jobs, and keeping rural communities vibrant. Through door-to-door conversations and locally tailored information, its organizers also help residents separate legitimate concerns about energy development from misinformation designed to divide communities.

A central part of BOLD’s approach is helping residents negotiate a legally binding Community Benefit Agreement or CBA. These agreements allow communities to determine how energy projects should be developed and what benefits developers must provide in return. In the New Rockford area of North Dakota, residents secured an agreement connected to a wind project that included new community investments and $350,000 to renovate a historic theater—a gathering place that residents hope will help revitalize their town.

By putting rural residents at the negotiating table, BOLD is demonstrating that communities do not have to choose between clean energy and local control. Its work offers a path toward energy development that respects rural culture, protects property rights, builds community wealth, and gives more people a stake in the transition.

Democrats are unlikely to be in a compromising mood on legislation, just weeks away from taking control of both chambers. That means continued work on big-ticket items like the Protect College Sports Act, meant to introduce new regulations around college athlete compensation, and a bipartisan energy permitting overhaul will likely wait until the new term.

With slim majorities in both chambers, they could also have to contend with some attendance problems after a demoralizing performance in last week's midterm elections. That further complicates passing legislation through chambers already governed by the thinnest of majorities.

Mike Ricci, a Republican strategist with the group Seven Letter and aide to former Speakers of the House John Boehner and Paul Ryan, told NPR that a number of forces could help draw reluctant lame duck legislators back to Washington, including winding down their offices, finding new work and attending the White House Christmas party.

text:
The 31st convening of the United Nations climate conference, known as COP31, began Monday in Turkey, with representatives from major governments and businesses coming together to address climate change. But for the second year in a row, the United States has not sent a delegation.

A White House official told Spectrum News the “summit rejects reality by failing to acknowledge that extremist climate policies are destroying countries around the world.” The Trump administration is instead focusing on “implementing a commonsense energy dominance agenda,” the official added.

According to the UN, COP31 will include negotiations “on issues such as adapting to climate impacts, reducing greenhouse gas pollution, climate finance for developing countries and a just transition for workers and communities.”

The UN said this year’s meeting will also emphasize what it calls its Climate Action Agenda, which will bring together cities, states, businesses and civil society to propose solutions to climate change issues, including its impact on health and food and how to make cities more resilient.

The Democratic governors of California, New Mexico and Wisconsin, along with 35 mayors and 50 other city officials from 26 states, attended last year’s COP30 conference in Brazil, according to the U.S. Climate Alliance. The group, which describes itself as a bipartisan coalition working toward a net-zero future by advancing state-led, high-impact climate action, said over 120 state and local leaders will attend COP31.

Democratic New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham is leading the coalition, along with Palo Alto, California, Mayor Vicki Veenker, and Raleigh, North Carolina, Mayor Janet Cowell.

“Our delegation is traveling to COP31 in force to make it clear to the world that states and cities across the U.S. are undaunted, undeterred and stand ready to strengthen our global partnerships,” Lujan Grisham said in a statement last week about the UN climate conference. “It’s through this deep and sustained collaboration that we make life better for people — ​and confront this global challenge.”

It’s been 11 years since dozens of countries signed the historic Paris Agreement to reduce global greenhouse gas emissions 50% by 2030. While the U.S. was one of the original signatories, President Donald Trump has pulled out of the agreement twice — most recently in January 2025.

According to the open-access global greenhouse gas tracking portal known as Climate TRACE, climate-changing gas emissions hit a record high last year. While the portal found that emissions from China’s power sector decreased year over year, that decline was offset by an equivalent rise in emissions from U.S. power production.

Trump has spent much of his second term in office rolling back U.S. climate policies set in action by prior presidents. The Climate Action Campaign’s Trump Rollback Tracker lists dozens of significant steps his administration has taken since the beginning of his second term in office, including the end of wind, solar and electric vehicle tax credits and rollbacks of pollution and energy efficiency standards.

COP is seeking to build on the Paris Agreement adopted in 2015 by 195 parties. That agreement set a goal of limiting global temperature rise to well below 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) by reducing greenhouse gas emissions.

The clock is ticking to limit those emissions before what scientists say is the point of no return. The price is also increasing. The UN estimates the cost of fighting climate change and achieving pollution reduction goals is $5.53 trillion per year through 2030, while the cost of inaction costs the world more than $1.5 trillion annually.

The conference is being hosted in Antalya, Turkey, by Turkey’s minister of environment, urbanization and climate change, Murat Kurum. Australia’s minister for climate change and energy, Chris Bowen, will preside over negotiations.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan opened the summit that will be attended by 37 heads of state, 35 heads of government, eight vice presidents, 7 deputy prime ministers, and institutional representatives from 95 countries and seven international organizations, according to the Turkish Ministry of Environment.

Brazil’s recently reelected president, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham are among the small handful of G20 leaders who are scheduled to speak at the summit, which runs through Nov. 20. Chinese Vice President Han Zheng will attend as a special representative of Chinese President Xi Jinping.

title: Democrats plan to push clean energy to lower bills and challenge Trump's fossil fuel agenda
authors: JENNIFER McDERMOTT Associated Press, Times Leader
description:
With new majorities in the House and Senate after last week’s midterms, Democrats can set an agenda boosting clean energy and addressing climate change.
Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, the top Democrat on the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works, said Trump’s clean energy attacks drove up prices for taxpayers.
At the same time, the administration canceled many clean energy projects and grants and slowed clean energy permitting.

At the federal level, Stokes is optimistic about extending clean energy tax credits since some Republicans support that.
text:
Some Democrats are promising to push for more clean energy to help tackle rising energy costs when they take control of Congress in January, though President Donald Trump says he will use his veto power aggressively.

With new majorities in the House and Senate after last week’s midterms, Democrats can set an agenda boosting clean energy and addressing climate change. While those are traditionally core priorities of the party, climate was not a central topic in this election cycle.

Democrats can begin investigations and hold hearings into climate policy rollbacks and elimination of green energy grants by the Republican administration, potentially trying to undo some changes and restore renewable energy incentives.

Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, the top Democrat on the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works, said Trump’s clean energy attacks drove up prices for taxpayers. He said Democrats will “work every angle to lower consumers’ energy costs, and we will demand accountability for the massive corruption wrought by Trump’s fossil-fuel donors.”

American Clean Power Association CEO Jason Grumet said everybody who is trying to build clean energy “feels bolstered.”

Enacting major changes would require Republican support because Democrats will lack the numbers to override presidential vetoes. Even then, lower energy bills are not guaranteed because prices also depend on fuel costs, demand and the expense of maintaining the electric grid.

“The wins give Democrats more leverage over spending and more political power to advance a coherent agenda; the question is whether they’ll use that power effectively,” said Lisa Sachs, director of the Columbia Center on Sustainable Investment. “The vote was for affordability and opportunity. Democrats now need to be clear about which policies deliver them.”

Trump holds veto power

Trump said after Tuesday’s election that Democrats will send over “things that are insane” and he will veto them, speaking generally about legislation. But in the comments to Fox News, he predicted that “after a couple of months of vetoes,” he and Democrats will find ways to work together.

The White House said in a statement Wednesday that Trump is “committed to unleashing reliable, affordable, and secure energy sources to lower prices, strengthen our grid, and protect our national security, and is willing to work with anyone to accomplish this.”

Trump promised to lower energy prices. Instead, his war with Iran and other policies increased the price of gasoline, diesel and electricity. At the same time, the administration canceled many clean energy projects and grants and slowed clean energy permitting.

Trump particularly dislikes offshore wind. Developer Orsted said Thursday that Revolution Wind, a large wind farm in federal waters off Rhode Island, has started operating commercially.

Will the president change his tune on green energy? That’s doubtful, said former Sen. Byron Dorgan, D-N.D., co-chair of the government relations practice at ArentFox Schiff.

“He is likely to keep pushing his energy issues, and I think he will be forced to give some room for a new Congress to recreate a different strategy that will add clean energy,” Dorgan said in an email.

Trump promotes expanding production of oil, natural gas and coal, which cause climate change, because he argues that would give the U.S. the lowest-cost electricity. Mike Sommers, CEO of the American Petroleum Institute, the oil and gas industry’s top lobbying group, said that as voters have changed the balance of political power in Washington, “the affordability message is unmistakable.”

Sommers said in a statement there is a real opportunity for bipartisan cooperation to reduce costs and strengthen the economy, starting with an energy permitting reform proposal announced in September. The legislation is aimed at shortening the timeline to get big energy projects started.

Ife Kilimanjaro, executive director of the U.S. Climate Action Network, said Democrats should reject that proposal and use their stronger position to pass legislation that actually builds out much-needed clean energy.

Reversing Trump’s policies

The administration has reshaped the Environmental Protection Agency, reversing pollution limits as it promotes fossil fuels.

Clear Street energy transition analyst Tim Moore said he expects Democrats to investigate the climate and environmental rollbacks, in an effort to block some from taking effect. Democrats could also try amending the Clean Air Act to cut carbon pollution and push back against EPA budget cuts, he added.

Rep. Sean Casten, D-Ill., said he is cautiously optimistic some Republicans will now seek to differentiate themselves from Trump and back pro-environmental policies. But without Republican support, Democrats’ more ambitious bills will largely lay out their agenda for 2028, he added.

Climate is not necessarily at the top of Democrats’ list of priorities. They are targeting healthcare access, trade tariffs and the Iran war.

Rep. Frank Pallone, the New Jersey Democrat who is expected to become chair of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, said the party should focus on healthcare, affordability, consumer and environmental protections, clean energy and regulating Big Tech.

A potential stalemate

David Victor, a professor of innovation and public policy at the University of California, San Diego, largely expects a stalemate at the federal level on climate and energy policy because of the divided government. He said agreement could come on some bipartisan measures such as a permitting overhaul.

Victor thinks Democratic-led investigations and hearings will center on corruption and other topics that may only touch on energy and climate. Like Casten, Victor said many of the Democratic bills likely will not become law, but will outline what Democrats could accomplish if they win the White House in 2028.

“The Democrats are going to be drafting things that the administration’s not going to like. They don’t have the votes to override a veto, and on top of it, the administration is going to be in turmoil because of its own electoral failures and because of all the investigations,” Victor said. “This seems to me, at the federal level, largely a recipe for kind of intense chaos over the next two years.”

One of the biggest wild cards is the behavior of the administration, which could use executive power to double down on rollbacks of climate and environmental rules, he said.

States could advance clean energy

Democrats scored victories in races for governor in states long controlled by Republicans, including Texas and Georgia.

Leah Stokes, a political scientist at the UC Santa Barbara, said there could be a lot of state action on climate next year because of those wins. That is where climate leadership has traditionally come from, she noted. At the federal level, Stokes is optimistic about extending clean energy tax credits since some Republicans support that.

Jay Inslee, a former Democratic governor and congressman from Washington, also expects growing momentum for clean energy in states that elected Democratic governors, particularly in states where they also won legislative majorities.

“This is a really powerful instrument for the United States to join the rest of the world and get back in a leadership position, even if we still have a climate denier that might exercise a veto on some things that we want to do federally,” Inslee said. “So I hope people will pay attention to the big progress we’re going to make on a state-level basis.”

title: Honda commits $3B to new Ohio plant as hybrid production expands - CBT News
description:
Honda is expanding hybrid powertrain production in Ohio and Georgia, including a planned 250% increase in hybrid system capacity at its Ohio transmission plant.
The facility is set to begin production in 2029, pending final government approval and will have an annual production capacity of 240,000 vehicles.
According to the company’s announcement, the new facility will feature production capacity for hybrid, gas-powered, and battery-electric vehicles.
Investments will be made across Ohio, Alabama, Georgia, and Canada to expand production of hybrid-electric vehicles, engines, and hybrid systems.
At the Honda Transmission Plant in Ohio, Honda is converting an existing transmission production line into a second hybrid system line, increasing hybrid system production capacity by 250% in the coming years.
text:
On the Dash:

Honda plans to invest $3 billion in a new Ohio assembly plant with annual capacity for 240,000 vehicles and more than 2,000 jobs, with production expected to begin in 2029.

The expansion will increase Honda’s annual U.S. vehicle production capacity to approximately 1.3 million units and North American capacity to 1.9 million.

Honda is expanding hybrid powertrain production in Ohio and Georgia, including a planned 250% increase in hybrid system capacity at its Ohio transmission plant.

On Nov. 9, Honda announced it will invest $3 billion to build a new auto plant in Central Ohio, creating over 2,000 new American jobs. The facility is set to begin production in 2029, pending final government approval and will have an annual production capacity of 240,000 vehicles. The plant will sit between Honda’s existing East Liberty and Marysville plants, making it Honda’s fourth auto plant in Ohio and its ninth auto-related plant in the U.S.

According to the company’s announcement, the new facility will feature production capacity for hybrid, gas-powered, and battery-electric vehicles. Currently, the automaker anticipates that the new plant, along with related manufacturing projects, will boost annual vehicle production capacity in the U.S to approximately 1.3 million units and North America’s capacity to around 1.9 million.

Sign up for CBT News’ daily newsletter and get the latest industry stories delivered straight to your inbox.

In May 2026, Honda announced plans to introduce 15 new Honda and Acura hybrid models globally by 2030, with North America expected to be the primary market for many of these models. Investments will be made across Ohio, Alabama, Georgia, and Canada to expand production of hybrid-electric vehicles, engines, and hybrid systems. Additionally, the automaker is positioning its manufacturing network to support both hybrid and gasoline-powered vehicles as customer demand and electrification trends evolve.

Honda describes the planned facility as one of its most advanced manufacturing plants when it opens in 2029. Planned capabilities include:

Leading-edge automation

Data-driven technologies

Flexible production systems designed to enhance efficiency, quality, and competitiveness

Notably, Honda selected Ohio for the new plant due to its skilled workforce, strong supplier network, nearby research and development operations, and existing capabilities in vehicle, engine, and hybrid system manufacturing. The region also houses the L-H Battery Company joint venture facility, which can produce battery cells for hybrid and all-electric vehicles. So far, Honda has invested over $132 million in research facilities and endowed chairs at Ohio State University and has established regional workforce partnerships.

North American projects

According to the automaker, it plans to invest in its Alabama Auto Plant, which will mark 25 years of vehicle production in 2026. This investment aims to expand production of a new V6 hybrid engine and renew key vehicle and engine operations. The plant will undergo significant renovations of Line 1, which hasn’t been updated since production began in 2001.

At the Anna Engine Plant, Honda is retooling an existing production line to manufacture a next-generation four-cylinder Atkinson-cycle engine for future compact and midsize North American vehicles. Additionally, a new on-site parts consolidation center is expected to begin operations next year to enhance logistics efficiency and support production growth.

At the Honda Transmission Plant in Ohio, Honda is converting an existing transmission production line into a second hybrid system line, increasing hybrid system production capacity by 250% in the coming years. The facility currently manufactures two-motor hybrid systems for U.S.-built CR-V, Accord, and Civic models. Production of a next-generation hybrid system is expected to commence next year, with plans for a larger hybrid system for future U.S.-built models.

Manufacturing footprint

Meanwhile, the Honda Transmission Plant in Georgia will begin producing next-generation hybrid systems for larger vehicles in the coming years. This facility currently produces 10-speed automatic transmissions for Honda and Acura models built in Alabama and Ohio. The project will require a new transmission assembly production line, with Georgia associates collaborating with their counterparts at the Honda Transmission Plant in Ohio on the larger hybrid system. Additionally, Honda will also update and retool its manufacturing operations in Alliston, Ontario, to support next-generation hybrid-electric and gasoline-powered models.

As of 2025, nearly 99% of Honda and Acura vehicles sold in the U.S. were manufactured in North America. The company employs approximately 33,000 associates in North America and operates 18 manufacturing plants.

According to the automaker’s press release, Honda’s North American operations have an annual capacity to produce:

1.6 million automobiles

Nearly 2 million engines

52,000 power equipment products

Approximately 250,000 powersports products

In total, Honda has invested more than $28 billion in North America.

title: BLM Moves to Undercut Its Planning Framework and Most Important Conservation Tool
description:
BACKGROUND In 1976, the Federal Land Policy and Management Act became law, establishing a broad framework for the management of U.S. public lands.
Despite this obligation, BLM went more than 50 years without issuing comprehensive ACEC regulations, until the 2024 Public Lands Rule finally remedied that gap.
However, the Trump administration rescinded the Public Lands Rule just one year later once again leaving BLM without comprehensive ACEC regulations.
Despite its lackluster performance around ACECs, the ACECs that BLM has designated play an outsized role for at-risk species.
Current ACECs overlap the ranges of at least 260 threatened and endangered species, as well as numerous BLM sensitive species.
text:
The Bureau of Land Management today announced a proposed rule that would weaken how the agency develops and revises land use plans, as well as how it designates and manages Areas of Critical Environmental Concern. The proposed rule would make it dramatically more difficult for the public to weigh in on land management decisions affecting 245 million acres of public land in the West and would weaken the standards for one of BLM's primary conservation tools, Areas of Critical Environmental Concern, which help protect irreplaceable habitats and imperiled plants and animals.

"Resource management planning is meant to provide the public a real say in how BLM manages our shared public lands, and Areas of Critical Environmental Concern are how the agency turns that input into on-the-ground protections for special places and important wildlife habitat,” said Maddy Munson, senior policy and planning specialist at Defenders of Wildlife. “Cutting back public participation and narrowing the agency's analysis isn't streamlining, but rather stacking the deck against the places and species that need protection the most.”

BLM land-use planning decides the future management of hundreds of millions of acres of public lands. These plans determine where drilling, mining, roads, recreation, conservation and wildlife protections can occur – choices that can conserve a landscape or commit it to energy or other development for decades. The rule proposed today would weaken conservation tools meant to protect BLM’s most important lands and habitats. Instead of weakening these tools, BLM should use this rulemaking process to ensure that Areas of Critical Environmental Concern are protected and their designation is prioritized, not sidelined.

This rulemaking does not stand alone. Taken together with recent drastic rollbacks of wildlife policies and conservation safeguards, these changes, if adopted, will have far-reaching consequences for wildlife, habitat, and the long-term sustainability of America’s public lands.

BACKGROUND

In 1976, the Federal Land Policy and Management Act became law, establishing a broad framework for the management of U.S. public lands. Among other things, FLPMA directs BLM to develop land use plans to guide the management of individual units within the National System of Public Lands. BLM subsequently issued regulations specifying requirements for developing, revising or amending RMPs.

FLPMA established Areas of Critical Conservation Concern—a conservation designation unique to public lands designed to protect places with exceptional ecological, cultural and scenic values that are at risk—and directed BLM to prioritize their designation and protection. Despite this clear direction, BLM has consistently neglected to designate qualified places and, in places, is rescinding existing designations to enable resource extraction.

For instance, in the Rock Springs Field Office in Wyoming, BLM is revaluating a plan less than one year old to determine whether existing conservation designations, including ACECs, should be removed to facilitate increased mineral development including oil and gas leasing.

FLPMA directed BLM in 1976 to promptly develop regulations and plans for identifying and protecting ACECs. Despite this obligation, BLM went more than 50 years without issuing comprehensive ACEC regulations, until the 2024 Public Lands Rule finally remedied that gap. However, the Trump administration rescinded the Public Lands Rule just one year later once again leaving BLM without comprehensive ACEC regulations.

Despite its lackluster performance around ACECs, the ACECs that BLM has designated play an outsized role for at-risk species. Current ACECs overlap the ranges of at least 260 threatened and endangered species, as well as numerous BLM sensitive species. Some of these areas are doing an enormous amount of work for a single species. For example, 65% of the threatened Mojave desert tortoise’s designated critical habitat sits inside ACECs, the endangered Amargosa vole has 100% of its critical habitat within ACEC boundaries and the endangered Lane Mountain milk-vetch is at 99%. These aren't marginal overlaps. For a meaningful number of species, ACEC designation is doing most, if not all, of the heavy lifting for their survival.

title: A new political playbook for the green donor class | Latitude Media
authors: Catherine Boudreau, Greg Rock, Maeve Allsup, Lisa Martine Jenkins, Seyed H. Madaeni, Shayle Kann

text:
In mid-September, Bo French, the Republican candidate for an obscure agency called the Railroad Commission of Texas, went viral.

“I heard UT graduation this year looked like this,” French posted on X, alongside a photo of students, many of whom were of South Asian descent, celebrating the University of Texas at Austin’s football team’s win against Ohio State. “I didn’t believe it. The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined.”

His racism was roundly denounced by Texas GOP leaders like Sen. John Cornyn, who said they wouldn’t vote for French. And his opponents started using the comments for voter outreach and ad campaigns.

That opposition included 1.5°Climate Strategies Group, a donor network of hundreds of wealthy philanthropists, family offices, and institutional funders. The group partnered with a grassroots effort in Texas and spent $220,000 to mobilize Asian American voters through phone banking and “relational organizing” encouraging people to talk to their friends and family about the candidate’s racist remarks.

On Tuesday, French was defeated by Democrat Joe Rosenthal by a wide margin, ending the GOP’s 32-year stretch with full control over the three-member Railroad Commission of Texas. Despite its name, the commission is the state’s primary regulator of oil and gas infrastructure and gas utilities, which includes issuing drilling permits and limiting the flaring and venting of planet-warming methane emissions.

“Very few groups invested in this race. We were one of them, and we won,” Ning Mosberger-Tang, founder and president of 1.5°Climate and an early investor in Google, told Latitude Media. “I’m very excited, because this could have a huge impact, in terms of ensuring oil and gas companies are being held accountable.”

The strategy deployed by 1.5°Climate reflects how green donors, rather than making climate change itself central to their political organizing, focused on other messaging this campaign cycle: from the flaws and scandals by candidates they opposed, to energy affordability and data centers that are top of mind for Americans.

And it paid off. Up and down the ballot, groups like 1.5°Climate, Invest in Tomorrow Coalition — a clean energy-backed super PAC launched this year — the solar industry’s American Power Forward PAC, and the League of Conservation Voter’s super PAC had a string of victories in state and federal races.

1.5°Climate invested in 26 different races across states including Arizona, Georgia, Michigan, and Wisconsin, and won in all but two, according to a list shared with Latitude Media. Invest in Tomorrow Coalition won in 12 out of 17 congressional races so far, with results still too close to call in districts currently represented by Reps. Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.) and Eli Crane (R-Ariz.). All of the 12 congressional candidates the LCV’s Victory Fund put on its annual “Dirty Dozen” have been defeated, as were all the state-level targets. The PAC claimed victory in Colorado, as well, where voters shot down a ballot measure that would’ve made gas a state constitutional right. American Power Forward PAC had key victories at the Georgia Public Utilities Commission, which flipped to Democratic control for the first time in decades, as well as in Nevada and Texas where two Democratic incumbents kept their seats.

LCV’s Victory Fund dominated in these races, spending a total $125 million this cycle. Invest in Tomorrow Coalition spent $10 million, while 1.5°Climate spent about $5 million and American Power Forward PAC spent $425,000.

To be sure, these groups had a lot of factors working in their favor. President Donald Trump is widely unpopular due to his war with Iran and resulting high gasoline prices, as well as the administration’s coziness with tech billionaires advancing artificial intelligence. But after years of struggling to gain traction against the hundreds of millions of dollars spent by the oil and gas industry each election cycle, green donors now have a winning playbook with broader appeal.

“This is part of growing up as an industry,” Tom Matzzie, chair of Invest in Tomorrow Coalition and founder of CleanChoice Energy, said in reference to clean energy companies. “It’s not that we did something wrong in the past. We’ve just hit a scale where we can mature politically.”

‘The sharpest knife in the drawer’

For the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition, avoiding talk of clean energy and climate altogether is by design. The group looked for races where its spending could change the outcome in relatively cheap media markets, and where they could take on anti-clean energy candidates with baggage to exploit. Most, like Rep. Boebert, were members of the House Freedom Caucus who signed a May 2025 letter calling for the full repeal of clean energy tax credits in the Inflation Reduction Act.

“None of our ads, none of our content was about clean energy,” Matzzie said during a press call on the day after the election. “We went and found the sharpest knife in the drawer. That was the goal. How do we inflict the most damage with the money that we have available to us?”

Matzzie told Latitude Media that before the launch of Invest in Tomorrow’s PAC, the clean energy industry didn’t make any effort to hold politicians accountable for attacking it — and as a result, the industry was an easy target. That’s a dangerous place to be in Washington, he said.

“We want members of Congress to see that we’re willing to get dirty if needed,” Matzzie added. That includes exploiting a candidate’s personal flaws and conflicts of interest (such as stock trading), and in the case of Brandon Herrera — a YouTube streamer and candidate for the House from Texas — digging into the archives to use his own words against him.

Matzzie’s group made an ad compiling some of the most offensive things Herrera said or did on YouTube, called “In His Own Words,” including comments making light of veterans who commit suicide and a video depicting armed robot firing shots at cardboard cutouts of cartoon children. The group distributed the ads across streaming platforms like Hulu and YouTube, as well as the evening news.

Climate hushing

Meanwhile, the LCV’s Victory Fund took its cue from the success of Democratic governors Mikie Sherrill of New Jersey and Abigail Spanberger of Virginia, who both won their off-year races in 2025. Both campaigned on lowering utility bills and ensuring data centers neither shift costs onto ratepayers nor harm the local environment.

“Not only did Sherrill run and win on that agenda, but [she also] very quickly signed an executive order — in the middle of her inauguration speech — to build more solar and battery storage,” said Bill Holland, LCV’s vice president of state policy and advocacy. “She delivered on data center legislation this summer, with New Jersey trying to make sure data centers pay their fair share of utility costs and build clean energy.”

Many Democratic governors won on similar platforms on Thursday, including David Crowley in Wisconsin, where Democrats now have a trifecta in state government, as well as Hannah Pingree in Maine and Deb Haaland in New Mexico.

That said, very few candidates, and virtually none of the donors, emphasized concerns about the impacts of climate change. Their clean energy focus was instead on affordability and utility accountability. Asked whether this cycle showed that “climate hushing” in politics is here to stay, Holland said he’s always thought that whatever message appeals most to voters should be used.

“If an elected official leans in on clean energy, that’s awesome,” Holland said. “Our takeaway from last night is that our issues matter. Voters do care about clean energy and understand that data centers’ impacts on air pollution and the climate are significant.”

Nick Abraham, a spokesman for LCV, added that whether candidates say the word climate or not, the impacts of a warming planet were on the ballot. He cited rising insurance costs due to extreme weather, which shaped the California Insurance Commissioner’s race, won by the Democrat; water conservation issues, meanwhile, were critical to races in some Midwestern states and Utah.

“Climate is not a liability; it’s just not as punchy as affordability,” said Greg Rock, executive director of 1.5°Climate. “The fact is, clean energy is the most affordable form of electricity generation. So when you have the winning argument, most people will lead with that over a secondary or third argument.”

“I don’t think Democrats are running from climate change,” he added. “It’s just not the argument that is the most persuasive.”

Rock noted that the affordability message was especially effective in the down-ballot initiatives that 1.5°Climate mainly focuses on. They don’t have a ton of national attention or political spending, but have more of a direct impact on people’s day-to-day lives.

As for what’s next? After notching so many wins, green donors will turn their attention to ensuring their newly elected allies in PUC commissions, state houses, governors’ mansions, and Congress keep their promises.

But Matzzie has a message specifically for clean energy executives who want to keep up the political momentum. The industry is “massively underinvested” in communications and public affairs, he said, and should be spending between 1% to 2% of capex to rival the fossil fuel industry.

title: Democrats plan to challenge Trump's fossil fuel agenda and push clean energy to lower bills
description:
Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, the top Democrat on the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works, said Trump's clean energy attacks drove up prices for taxpayers.
He said Democrats will "work every angle to lower consumers' energy costs, and we will demand accountability for the massive corruption wrought by Trump's fossil-fuel donors."
American Clean Power Association CEO Jason Grumet said everybody who is trying to build clean energy "feels bolstered."

text:
Some Democrats are promising to push for more clean energy to help tackle rising energy costs when they take control of Congress in January, though President Donald Trump says he will use his veto power aggressively.

With new majorities in the House and Senate after last week's midterms, Democrats can set an agenda boosting clean energy and addressing climate change. While those are traditionally core priorities of the party, climate was not a central topic in this election cycle.

Democrats can begin investigations and hold hearings into climate policy rollbacks and elimination of green energy grants by the Republican administration, potentially trying to undo some changes and restore renewable energy incentives.

Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, the top Democrat on the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works, said Trump's clean energy attacks drove up prices for taxpayers. He said Democrats will "work every angle to lower consumers' energy costs, and we will demand accountability for the massive corruption wrought by Trump's fossil-fuel donors."

American Clean Power Association CEO Jason Grumet said everybody who is trying to build clean energy "feels bolstered."

Enacting major changes would require Republican support because Democrats will lack the numbers to override presidential vetoes. Even then, lower energy bills are not guaranteed because prices also depend on fuel costs, demand and the expense of maintaining the electric grid.

"The wins give Democrats more leverage over spending and more political power to advance a coherent agenda; the question is whether they'll use that power effectively," said Lisa Sachs, director of the Columbia Center on Sustainable Investment. "The vote was for affordability and opportunity. Democrats now need to be clear about which policies deliver them."

Trump holds veto power but thinks he and Democrats can deal

Trump said after Tuesday's election that Democrats will send over "things that are insane" and he will veto them, speaking generally about legislation. But in the comments to Fox News, he predicted that "after a couple of months of vetoes," he and Democrats will find ways to work together.

The White House said in a statement Wednesday that Trump is "committed to unleashing reliable, affordable, and secure energy sources to lower prices, strengthen our grid, and protect our national security, and is willing to work with anyone to accomplish this."

Trump promised to lower energy prices. Instead, his war with Iran and other policies increased the price of gasoline, diesel and electricity. At the same time, the administration canceled many clean energy projects and grants and slowed clean energy permitting.

Trump particularly dislikes offshore wind. Developer Orsted said Thursday that Revolution Wind, a large wind farm in federal waters off Rhode Island, has started operating commercially.

Will the president change his tune on green energy? That's doubtful, said former Sen. Byron Dorgan, D-N.D., co-chair of the government relations practice at ArentFox Schiff.

"He is likely to keep pushing his energy issues, and I think he will be forced to give some room for a new Congress to recreate a different strategy that will add clean energy," Dorgan said in an email.

Trump promotes expanding production of oil, natural gas and coal, which cause climate change, because he argues that would give the U.S. the lowest-cost electricity. Mike Sommers, CEO of the American Petroleum Institute, the oil and gas industry's top lobbying group, said that as voters have changed the balance of political power in Washington, "the affordability message is unmistakable."

Sommers said in a statement there is a real opportunity for bipartisan cooperation to reduce costs and strengthen the economy, starting with an energy permitting reform proposal announced in September. The Senate is expected to hold a procedural vote Monday on the legislation, which is aimed at shortening the timeline to get big energy projects started.

Ife Kilimanjaro, executive director of the U.S. Climate Action Network, said Democrats should reject that proposal and use their stronger position to pass legislation that actually builds out much-needed clean energy.

Reversing Trump's anti-climate policies

The administration has reshaped the Environmental Protection Agency, reversing pollution limits as it promotes fossil fuels.

Clear Street energy transition analyst Tim Moore said he expects Democrats to investigate the climate and environmental rollbacks, in an effort to block some from taking effect. Democrats could also try amending the Clean Air Act to cut carbon pollution and push back against EPA budget cuts, he added.

READ MORE: Outdated power grids a major hurdle in renewable energy transition

Rep. Sean Casten, D-Ill., said he is cautiously optimistic some Republicans will now seek to differentiate themselves from Trump and back pro-environmental policies. But without Republican support, Democrats' more ambitious bills will largely lay out their agenda for 2028, he added.

Climate is not necessarily at the top of Democrats' list of priorities. They are targeting healthcare access, trade tariffs and the Iran war.

Rep. Frank Pallone, the New Jersey Democrat who is expected to become chair of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, said the party should focus on healthcare, affordability, consumer and environmental protections, clean energy and regulating Big Tech.

A potential stalemate seen on clean energy and climate policy

David Victor, a professor of innovation and public policy at the University of California, San Diego, largely expects a stalemate at the federal level on climate and energy policy because of the divided government. He said agreement could come on some bipartisan measures such as a permitting overhaul.

Victor thinks Democratic-led investigations and hearings will center on corruption and other topics that may only touch on energy and climate. Like Casten, Victor said many of the Democratic bills likely will not become law, but will outline what Democrats could accomplish if they win the White House in 2028.

"The Democrats are going to be drafting things that the administration's not going to like. They don't have the votes to override a veto, and on top of it, the administration is going to be in turmoil because of its own electoral failures and because of all the investigations," Victor said. "This seems to me, at the federal level, largely a recipe for kind of intense chaos over the next two years."

One of the biggest wild cards is the behavior of the administration, which could use executive power to double down on rollbacks of climate and environmental rules, he said.

States could advance clean energy without waiting for Congress

Democrats scored victories in races for governor in states long controlled by Republicans, including Texas and Georgia.

Leah Stokes, a political scientist at the UC Santa Barbara, said there could be a lot of state action on climate next year because of those wins. That is where climate leadership has traditionally come from, she noted. At the federal level, Stokes is optimistic about extending clean energy tax credits since some Republicans support that.

Jay Inslee, a former Democratic governor and congressman from Washington, also expects growing momentum for clean energy in states that elected Democratic governors, particularly in states where they also won legislative majorities.

"This is a really powerful instrument for the United States to join the rest of the world and get back in a leadership position, even if we still have a climate denier that might exercise a veto on some things that we want to do federally," Inslee said. "So I hope people will pay attention to the big progress we're going to make on a state-level basis."

Associated Press writers Alexa St. John and Matthew Daly contributed to this report.

Eastern Ontario has always played a critical role as a clean energy powerhouse and nuclear innovator, which is why it’s fitting that we announce contracts across the region that will keep the economy strong."
Ontario’s nuclear industry is tariff-proof and recession-proof.
“Gillam Construction Group is incredibly proud to provide construction services to the Darlington New Nuclear Project through the delivery of its new Administration Building,” said Marcus Gillam, CEO, Gillam Construction Group.
“Mansteel Rebar Ltd. is proud to be part of the Darlington New Nuclear Project, contributing to one of Canada's most significant energy infrastructure investments.
"Companies like Gillam Construction Group and Mansteel Rebar are essential partners in delivering the G7's first small modular reactor, showcasing the strength of Ontario's world-class nuclear supply chain and skilled workforce," said Nicolle Butcher, President and CEO, OPG.
text:
These contracts will add more than $66 million to Ontario’s GDP, and represent another milestone in Ontario’s nuclear build-out, connecting local businesses to one of the province’s largest clean energy infrastructure projects and creating opportunities for Ontario workers, skilled trades and suppliers to participate in the next generation of nuclear technology.

“Ontario is taking decisive action to be a first mover in the Western World on small modular reactors to unlock generational prosperity and safeguard our energy sovereignty,” said Stephen Lecce, Minister of Energy and Mines. “As we advance construction on this nation-building project, we are creating more than 18,000 good-paying jobs and securing a world-class nuclear supply chain that builds the components for SMRs at home and around the world. Eastern Ontario has always played a critical role as a clean energy powerhouse and nuclear innovator, which is why it’s fitting that we announce contracts across the region that will keep the economy strong."

Ontario’s nuclear industry is tariff-proof and recession-proof. As global uncertainty and U.S. tariffs put pressure on the province’s key industries, the DNNP is opening new markets for tariff-impacted sectors, including steel. Today’s announcement builds on the 14 contracts awarded last week to companies in the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area (GTHA). Gillam Construction Group and Mansteel Rebar now join the over 100 Canadian companies that have already signed agreements with Ontario Power Generation (OPG) to deliver this first-of-a-kind project, establishing themselves as leaders in the growing domestic and global markets for new nuclear technologies.

“Gillam Construction Group is incredibly proud to provide construction services to the Darlington New Nuclear Project through the delivery of its new Administration Building,” said Marcus Gillam, CEO, Gillam Construction Group. “We are honoured to play a part in this generational project that will provide clean, safe and reliable energy to Ontarians for generations to come.”

As countries around the world undergo a major nuclear resurgence in search of reliable, affordable and secure electricity, Ontario’s first-mover advantage is making it the partner of choice to build the components these projects need. This advantage has secured new domestic manufacturing investment in Ontario, including Velan’s planned facility in Durham Region to build critical safety valves for SMRs in Europe, and BWXT Canada’s agreement to manufacture key SMR components in Ontario for Poland.

“Mansteel Rebar Ltd. is proud to be part of the Darlington New Nuclear Project, contributing to one of Canada's most significant energy infrastructure investments. As a Canadian-owned and operated business, sourcing all of our reinforcing steel from local Canadian based steel mills, we are proud to support Canadian jobs and manufacturing,” said Allen Piddington, General Manager, Mansteel Rebar Ltd. “With our skilled workforce currently on site and the recent award of additional work, this project represents an important opportunity to support local employment, strengthen Ontario's construction and steel industries, and contribute to the province's long-term energy needs. We look forward to continuing our role in building Ontario's nuclear future.”

Once complete, the four SMR units at the DNNP will deliver 1,200 megawatts (MW) of reliable, clean electricity, enough to power approximately 1.2 million homes. The construction, operation and maintenance of the four SMR units will add $38.5 billion to Canada’s GDP over the next 65 years. The government has worked with OPG to ensure that 80 per cent of project spending goes to Ontario companies, helping anchor the economic benefits of this generational investment in the province. The construction and operations will protect Ontario workers and jobs by sustaining an estimated 3,800 highly-skilled, good-paying jobs for the next 65 years.

"Companies like Gillam Construction Group and Mansteel Rebar are essential partners in delivering the G7's first small modular reactor, showcasing the strength of Ontario's world-class nuclear supply chain and skilled workforce," said Nicolle Butcher, President and CEO, OPG. “This complex, first-of-a-kind project will meet Ontario's growing electricity demand while strengthening the made-in-Ontario workforce, expertise, and supply chain capacity that will be essential as we advance the next generation of large-scale nuclear projects.”

title: M.Eng. students partner with Tesla on clean energy solutions | Cornell Chronicle
description:

text:
When Azhir Barodawala, M.Eng. ’18, looks at the Cornell Duffield College of Engineering today, he sees a community worth investing in.

Now a staff sales engineer at Tesla, the R.F. Smith School Master of Engineering (M.Eng.) alum worked directly with current M.Eng. students on a real-world design project focused on utility-scale battery energy storage systems, a technology increasingly central to the future of the U.S. power grid.

The collaboration pairs M.Eng. students in Cornell’s chemical and biomolecular engineering program with one of the world’s leading clean energy companies, giving students the opportunity to tackle the same technical, financial and systems-level questions facing industry today.

“This is exactly the kind of experience that defined my time in the M.Eng. program,” Barodawala said. “You’re not just solving a textbook problem. You’re working through the same tradeoffs, constraints and uncertainties you’ll face on the job. Coming back to mentor students feels like giving back, and also giving forward.”

Designing the grid of the future

The student team – Siddhant Dhende, Yi-Hsuan (Sharon) Chen, Chia-Hung (Alex) Liu, and Sreekar Mukkamala – is developing a full end-to-end plan for a 250 MW utility-scale battery energy storage system, reflecting the complexity of real infrastructure projects.

For Dhende, who came to Cornell from Mumbai with a background in chemical engineering and a focus on energy systems, the project represents exactly what drew him to the program.

“I wanted to move beyond textbook problem-solving and work on open-ended, industry-relevant challenges,” he said. “This project brings together engineering fundamentals, systems thinking, and real-world decision-making in a way that directly connects to the future of energy and my long-term goal of contributing to sustainable energy innovation.”

Under the guidance of Cornell faculty and with input from Tesla, students are evaluating everything from site selection and system sizing to cost modeling and financial feasibility. Their work addresses a central challenge in renewable energy: aligning electricity supply with demand.

“As solar and wind continue to expand, energy isn’t always available when it’s needed,” Dhende said. “Battery storage helps solve this by storing excess energy and releasing it during peak demand. Our goal is to design a system that is reliable, economically viable and capable of strengthening grid stability.”

The team is also assessing battery technologies, balance-of-system components such as inverters and transformers, and operational strategies including energy arbitrage and ancillary grid services.

Beyond technical design, students are building full financial models, calculating metrics such as net present value, internal rate of return, and levelized cost of storage – skills central to the M.Eng. program’s emphasis on translating engineering insight into deployable solutions.

“This project brings together chemical engineering fundamentals, systems thinking and financial analysis in a way that’s very true to industry practice,” said Brian Bauer, professor of practice and associate director of the Master of Engineering program at the R.F. Smith School. “Having an alum from Tesla involved elevates the experience and shows students what’s possible after Cornell.”

Learning from those who’ve been there

For students, working with a Cornell alum embedded in industry adds a powerful layer of relevance.

“It’s different when someone who once sat in your seat is now applying these tools at Tesla,” Dhende said. “You gain insight into how technical analysis, economic modeling and system design come together to influence real decisions in the energy landscape.”

Dhende said one of the most rewarding aspects of his M.Eng. experience has been applying classroom concepts, such as energy systems and process modeling, to practical engineering challenges.

“At Cornell, you see how fundamental chemical engineering principles can directly shape large-scale infrastructure and sustainability solutions,” he said.

The collaboration also highlights one of the defining strengths of Duffield Engineering’s M.Eng. programs: deep industry engagement. Alumni frequently return as project partners, mentors and guest speakers, reinforcing a culture in which professional success and community commitment go hand in hand.

Each year, industry partners work with Cornell faculty and M.Eng. student teams on projects designed to address real-world engineering and business challenges. These collaborations give companies the opportunity to explore topics relevant to their organizations while providing students with hands-on experience, professional mentorship and direct exposure to industry problem-solving. Faculty help frame project goals, while student teams deliver technical analyses, recommendations and next-step strategies informed by their work.

Giving back and forward

For Barodawala, the project reflects a belief that engineering education works best as a continuous loop between campus and industry.

“The M.Eng. program prepared me to think across technical and business dimensions,” Barodawala said. “Helping today’s students do the same is one of the most meaningful ways I can contribute.”

For students like Dhende, the experience is shaping both immediate career goals and long-term ambitions.

“My goal is to work as a process engineer in the energy sector and contribute to cleaner, more reliable energy systems,” he said. “Projects like this give you the confidence and practical skills to step into that role and make an impact on day one.”

As the team finalized its feasibility analyses and strategic recommendations for their project presentation to faculty and Borodawala at the end of their year-long M.Eng. program, the students gained technical experience and professional confidence, industry fluency and connections that extend well beyond graduation.

It’s a reminder that a Duffield Engineering education does not end with a diploma. It grows stronger as alumni return to help shape what comes next.

text:
Honda will spend $3 billion to build a next-generation plant in Ohio to manufacture hybrid-electric vehicles, with production expected to begin in 2029, the automaker announced today.

The plant, which will be Honda’s fourth manufacturing facility in Central Ohio, is expected to have capacity to produce 240,000 vehicles per year and add more than 2,000 jobs to Honda’s workforce.

“The new plant is part of a broader set of investments at Honda operations in Ohio, Alabama and Georgia that will expand and strengthen an integrated U.S. production network to boost production of hybrid-electric vehicles and the engines and systems that power them,” the company said in a press release.

Located between Honda’s East Liverpool and Marysville, Ohio, plants, the new plant is part of the company’s strategy to increase production capacity from 1.3 to 1.9 million vehicles a year in the U.S. and increase its manufacturing flexibility as consumer preferences, market conditions and electrification trends change. Honda’s Development & Manufacturing of America Facility and its L-H Battery Co. joint venture facility are also located nearby.

Honda is also investing in:

Retooling its Alabama Auto Plant for increased vehicle production and new V6 engine production

Retooling its Anna Engine Plant in Ohio to build next-generation engines and expanding its parts consolidation center there

Retooling its transmission plants in Ohio and Georgia for production of next-gen Honda hybrid systems to increase hybrid capacity by 250% over time

Updating and retooling its plant in Alliston, Ontario, for new models and reintroducing engine production there

In May, Honda announced plans for 15 new Honda and Acura hybrid models by 2030, with North America expected to be the primary market for many of those vehicles.

Honda opened its first U.S. automotive manufacturing plant in 1982 in Marysville and has well-established workforce development relationships with nearby schools, including Ohio State and Columbus State universities.

title: Electrification Can Lower Energy Bills, but Only if We Do it Right
description:
