Governments need energy systems that support growth, expand access and strengthen energy security while delivering on climate commitments.
Countries will need to build, operate, finance and price their electricity systems so that lower costs translate into affordable energy bills for people.
Governments and finance providers should help households and businesses afford investments that lower energy costs over time.
That efficiency advantage means that even if electricity costs three times as much per unit as gas, the energy cost of heating is still 10% lower.
text:
More and more of the energy that powers daily life is shifting to electricity. Commuters are replacing gas-powered cars and scooters with electric vehicles. Households are changing out gas appliances for heat pumps and electric stoves. Cities are swapping diesel-fueled buses for electrified fleets.

The UN climate summit in Antalya, Turkey (COP31) aims to accelerate the shift, urging countries to adopt a pledge to supply 35% of global final energy consumption with electricity by 2035, up from around 23% today. But how quickly the world moves toward electrification hinges on a key question: Will it actually lower rising energy bills?

The Promise of Electrification

Households need affordable heating, cooling, cooking and mobility. Industry needs competitive, reliable power to invest, create jobs and replace fossil fuels. Governments need energy systems that support growth, expand access and strengthen energy security while delivering on climate commitments.

Dramatic falls in solar, wind and battery costs have created an extraordinary opportunity to meet those needs while also reducing emissions and exposure to volatile fossil-fuel prices. Yet an awkward question persists: If renewables are so cheap, why is electricity still expensive in so many places?

The answer is that cheaper technology is just one piece of the puzzle. Countries will need to build, operate, finance and price their electricity systems so that lower costs translate into affordable energy bills for people. If upfront costs put electric products out of reach — or promised savings fail to materialize — political ambition will struggle to sustain public backing, putting the entire shift to electrification in jeopardy.

Five priorities can help governments, regulators and industry turn electrification into savings:

1) Make the switch to electricity affordable upfront.

Governments and finance providers should help households and businesses afford investments that lower energy costs over time. For the user, the decisive question is how much it costs to get the job done.

Take home heating. Electricity can deliver cheaper warmth even when it costs more per unit than gas. A heat pump moves heat rather than generating it by burning fuel, delivering three to four units of heat for every unit of electricity purchased — an effective efficiency of 300-400%. Even at the lower end of that range, a heat pump uses 70% less purchased energy than a modern gas boiler operating at 90% efficiency. That efficiency advantage means that even if electricity costs three times as much per unit as gas, the energy cost of heating is still 10% lower. In other words, a higher electricity bill need not mean higher total energy costs. A household replacing a petrol car or gas boiler buys more electricity, but far less petrol or gas.

The same is true for mobility. In India, a 2025 analysis by the Council on Energy, Environment and Water estimated that electric two-wheelers cost around 40% less to own and operate per kilometer than petrol models.

However, lower lifetime costs do not remove the upfront barrier. Equipment and installation can make switching unaffordable even where electric products would save money over their lifetime. In Britain, for example, an air-source heat pump installation costs around £12,000 ($16,000) before grants, compared with roughly £3,700 ($5,000) for a replacement gas boiler, including installation. An investment that saves money over 10 years is of little use to a family that can’t afford the sticker price this year.

Affordable loans, leasing and targeted support can help. In England and Wales, for example, eligible homeowners replacing gas heating can receive £7,500 ($10,000) towards a heat pump through the Boiler Upgrade Scheme until March 2027. Practical barriers also need addressing, including charging availability, connection costs and, for renters, permission to install equipment.

2) Reduce the financing costs for clean power.

Making the switch affordable also depends on the cost of supplying electricity. Governments and financial institutions should lower financing costs for clean generation so that cheaper technologies can deliver cheaper power.

Few energy technologies have undergone a cost transformation comparable to solar. Between 2010 and 2025, the global average lifetime cost per unit of electricity from new utility-scale solar fell by a staggering 89%. Over the same period, onshore wind costs fell 71%; offshore wind by 63%. The installed cost per unit of storage capacity for four-hour utility-scale batteries, meanwhile, dropped by 95%, including by almost 30% in 2025 alone.

These cost reductions have rewritten the economics of generating and storing electricity, putting clean power at the heart of the opportunity to build more affordable, secure energy systems.

Wind and solar also offer a crucial advantage over fossil fuels: They eliminate exposure to ongoing fuel costs that can be volatile and affected by geopolitics. Maintenance and financing still cost money, but the fuel bill stays at zero.

The value of escaping fossil fuel bills comes into sharper focus with every energy crisis. The IEA counted 13 major oil-price shocks between 1973 and 2024 — roughly one every four years. When “shocks” recur this often, we need to stop being surprised by them and recognize them for what they are: structural features of continued fossil-fuel dependence. This year’s Hormuz crisis cut global oil supply by roughly a tenth in a single month, amid what the IEA described as the largest disruption in the history of the oil market.

These crises force families to cut back on essentials, put jobs and livelihoods at risk, and pile emergency relief costs onto already stretched public finances, leaving governments with less to spend on the services people depend upon.

Investing in clean power can reduce that recurring economic vulnerability, but we need affordable finance to harness the benefits of clean power.

Much of the lifetime cost of wind and solar lies in building them, while fossil-fuel plants require continuing fuel purchases throughout their operation. The cost of financing that upfront investment therefore has a major influence on how cheaply they can generate electricity; clean power is more sensitive to financing costs because of this upfront investment. Currency risk, unstable policy and uncertainty over utility payments can make excellent renewable resources expensive to develop. This is particularly true in developing and emerging economies, where financing costs tend to be higher than in advanced economies.

Governments can lower financing costs through predictable rules, credible contracts and reliable payments to generators. Development banks can help with guarantees against non-payment, support for managing currency risk and concessional loans. Cheaper capital is therefore an affordability measure in its own right: It can mean cheaper power.

3) Prevent avoidable costs before they are locked in.

WRI’s strategic electrification work through the Clean Energy Ministerial’s 21st Century Power Partnership highlights a central choice. New demand can become either a grid constraint or a flexible resource, depending on how it is planned and managed.

Imagine 100 electric buses returning to a depot for an overnight recharge. They need to be ready for the morning route. Charging them all at full power the moment they arrive is one option, but it would create a much higher peak in power demand, potentially requiring costly grid upgrades. A better way would be to use software that can spread charging across buses’ parking window, reducing the maximum power the depot draws from the grid. Where local grid conditions allow, that can defer or avoid costly upgrades without taking a single bus out of service. With vehicle-to-grid technology, those same buses can even supply electricity back to the grid at peak times.

Electrification adds demand, but well-planned, flexible demand can put spare grid capacity and abundant renewable power to work. Spreading infrastructure costs across more consumption can then lower the average cost of each unit of electricity delivered.

Governments, utilities and major electricity users should plan supply and demand together, before sites, equipment and connections are fixed. Where demand is growing, designing new buildings, transport systems and industry for efficient, flexible electrification from the outset can avoid costly retrofits later.

4) Reward lower system costs.

In many regulatory systems, utilities earn returns on investment in physical infrastructure, but have weaker — if any — incentives to pay for services that could avoid new construction. That can favor building more infrastructure even when other options would serve users more cheaply and efficiently. Regulators should give utilities incentives and procurement tools to assess new infrastructure, storage, flexible demand and better use of existing grids on equal terms, choosing the combination that delivers reliable service at the lowest total system cost.

The potential savings are substantial. Centre for Net Zero modelling suggests that flexible electric-vehicle charging and home heating could reduce Britain’s annual electricity-system costs by £5 billion ($6.7 billion) by 2035, compared with a scenario without that household flexibility. In the US, Brattle estimates that better use of existing electricity infrastructure, including strategically locating new demand, improving efficiency and reducing peaks, could save consumers over $100 billion over the next decade.

Realizing these savings also requires flexibility that operators can count on. Households and businesses providing flexibility — for example, by adjusting vehicle charging or heating — need fair compensation and control over how their equipment is used, backed by investment in the equipment and market arrangements that make participation both reliable and attractive.

Countries will still need substantial new infrastructure, developed with consideration for communities and care for nature. The aim is to ensure that new construction and alternatives compete on their ability to meet people’s electricity needs reliably and affordably.

5) Carry savings through into prices.

Even when clean power is cheap to produce, those savings don’t always show up on bills. Two challenges stand in the way.

The first is pricing practices. For example, in Britain’s wholesale auctions, generators offer electricity at different prices. Wind and solar can bid low because they need no fuel. Gas plants must cover fuel costs, which fluctuate with international markets. Under marginal pricing models, the last — and most expensive — offer accepted to meet demand sets the price paid to all successful generators in that auction. When that offer comes from a gas plant, gas prices influence even what cheaper generators receive.

The second challenge is that electricity bills pay for far more than power production. Embedded in the cost are grid networks, policy commitments, payments under existing contracts and more. Bills can therefore still rise despite cheaper new renewables if other costs increase faster. How those costs are shared between households, industry and public budgets, however, is a policy choice.

Long-term contracts can secure electricity at agreed prices, reducing buyers’ exposure to volatile wholesale markets. Governments and regulators should enable these arrangements and ensure that lower clean-power purchasing costs are reflected in the electricity prices charged to households and businesses.

India demonstrates how procurement can turn renewable cost advantages into industrial savings. Its open-access arrangements allow eligible businesses to contract with renewable generators and pay to use the public grid, rather than buying all their electricity from the local distribution utility. Ember estimates potential savings of ₹1–4 per kilowatt-hour (roughly $0.01-$0.04) compared with utility supply, after applicable charges and depending on the state.

Turning Electrification into Lasting Benefits

The credibility of the “35x35” pledge will depend on whether governments, regulators and utilities turn these priorities into changes people can see beyond the halls of Antalya. Success means families with more to spend on essentials, businesses with greater confidence to invest and create jobs, and countries less exposed to the next fuel crisis.

It’s a bill that would make it easier to build big infrastructure projects in America – everything from fossil fuel pipelines to transmission lines that would add more clean energy to the grid. And it would roll back environmental and social protections to achieve this goal. That is why climate advocates are torn over the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs act (Baaja), which is scheduled for an initial procedural Senate vote on Monday.

Donald Trump urged all senators to vote for the 417-page bill, which is sponsored by two Republicans and two Democrats in the Senate, but after last week’s historic “blue wave” elections, some environmental and tribal advocates called on Democratic leadership to pump the brakes.

Earthjustice, Sierra Club and the ACLU have come out against the bill because it would significantly weaken environmental laws including the National Environmental Policy Act (Nepa) and accelerate the construction of gas pipelines and ICE detention centers.

Indigenous groups held a press conference on Friday calling on senators to vote against Baaja because it would weaken the federal government’s legal obligation to consult tribes on projects that affect them. “This is such an existential threat to Indian country,” said Mark Macarro, president of the National Congress of American Indians.

Protesters rallied outside Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer’s building on Friday over concerns that the bill could boost datacenters. “It would be highly ironic if, having won an election where datacenter opposition was at the front and center, the first act of Congress was to make it easier to build datacenters,” said Bill McKibben.

Democrats elected in the blue wave will not take their seats until January, so the bill’s proponents still have time to rush it through the Senate, and technically there is time for it to pass in the House before new Congress and go to Trump.

But the election success for the Democrats is dialing up the political friction. House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries, expected to be the House speaker in the new Congress, said the bill “falls short in several areas” including failing to protect tribal sovereignty, and he would not “rubber-stamp legislation without more constructive involvement with our caucus”.

On Monday, the bill’s Democratic sponsors, Senators Martin Heinrich and Sheldon Whitehouse, said they had the votes to pass the bill. Heinrich said they had made last-minute changes to ensure tribal consultation, and they believed the bill would favor renewables over fossil fuels. “If we can create an open, competitive level playing field, clean is cheap, and cheap wins in the marketplace,” Heinrich said.

Whitehouse, who wore a tie with wind turbines on it, argued that passing the bill would set the stage for Democrats to work on clean energy policies next year with majorities in the House and Senate. “People should just cool their jets and have a little faith that this is not the end of the story,” he said.

Proponents of Baaja say it is needed because it takes too long to build large projects in America and the bill shortens timelines. It simplifies federal rules for building interstate transmission lines, it narrows what gets reviewed under the National Historic Preservation Act and limits tribal consultation, it limits the use of the Clean Water Act, shortens timelines for the Endangered Species Act, limits how the executive branch can interfere with federal permitting, and makes big changes to Nepa such as changing what requires Nepa review and who has standing to sue.

Baaja would expand fossil fuels

The fossil fuel industry is backing Baaja. The American Petroleum Institute (API) hailed the bill as “a historic opportunity” and called on congress to “finish permitting reform this year”.

“It creates a very accelerated fast track for gas pipelines,” said Earthjustice Action’s president, Abbie Dillen. “The gas industry is extraordinarily excited about this because they are interested in expanding existing pipeline capacity to get more liquefied natural gas out for export, and to be feeding power-hungry datacenters with gas.”

The bill could help pave the way for the Constitution gas pipeline that Williams Companies is trying to build through New York. The state denied the project’s water quality permit in 2016, but the company has revived the project under the Trump administration. The proposed pipeline could benefit from the bill’s changes to the Clean Water Act.

Baaja could also enable construction of gas pipelines in the west. Fossil fuel advocacy group Western States and Tribal Nations wants to build gas pipelines to feed domestic datacenters and export LNG from the west coast. During a 3 November election day meeting with New York’s Sweetwater county board of commissioners, the advocacy group’s president, Andrew Browning, said he was talking to lawmakers about the bill: “The permitting bill’s a huge thing … We’re going to need that for everything we’re envisioning and building out.”

How the bill would increase clean energy

Some clean energy advocates want the bill to pass because it would connect renewables to the grid. Wind, solar and battery storage are now cheap to build, but the country lacks the necessary transmission lines to bring clean energy where it’s needed.

Interstate transmission lines can take a decade to get built, and energy projects also face a bottleneck in connecting to the grid. At the end of 2025, 2,060 GW of total generation and storage capacity were waiting in a queue to connect to the grid.

Ben King, energy and climate director at Rhodium Group, said Baaja would reform the interconnection queue process and unlock the ability to build the transmission that is needed. “We’re at a pretty low point for policy support for clean [energy],” he said, referring to Trump’s repeal of clean energy tax credits. “[Baaja] sets up the ability to build stuff more quickly for when the next wave of climate policy happens.”

Many experts have modeled what the bill would do to emissions, but there is a lot of uncertainty on that question. Rhodium Group’s analysis found that domestic emissions go down if Baaja passes. But another model by the Purdue engineering professor Kevin Kircher found it would increase domestic emissions.

Kircher said the optimistic case for Baaja is that there’s a huge amount of clean energy ready to go, and if we get rid of the long queues and regulations, “level the playing field and let it rip”, then clean energy wins on the economics. “I think that understanding is outdated,” he said.

What the bill does to emissions partly depends on what type of energy gets connected to the grid. Rhodium Group assumed, based on a report from 2025, that 85% of the capacity added to the grid would be renewables. But Kircher said some grid operators have updated their queues this year to remove redundant and speculative offers. (PJM’s queue as of 3 August looks quite gassy.)

King said the economics show an impressive decrease in the cost of renewables, while fossil fuels are not getting any cheaper. “Some of it is just a bet on what’s going to win out in the future,” he said. “Our modeling suggests that clean stuff is going to dominate energy expansion for the foreseeable future, and there might be people who have a different view on that. API might have a different perspective – they might bet that there’s more room for them to grow.”

Kircher emphasized that the various models have not had time for peer review since the bill was first introduced on 30 September. “We need to have some humility in recognizing that the process of taking that 417 pages of super dense legal text and mapping it … is extremely complicated and full of uncertainties,” he said.

What the bill would do to Nepa

The bill would significantly reduce the scope of Nepa. It would narrow the definition of a “major federal action” that would trigger Nepa review, and effectively eliminate the authority of courts to enforce Nepa compliance.

Nepa is the powerful law that attorneys used to block the Trump administration’s plans to convert 11 mega-warehouses into massive ICE detention centers. If the bill passes, it could accelerate the development of ICE detention centers, according to a letter the American Civil Liberties Union sent to senators. “As written, this bill would hamper, if not altogether thwart, critical work by the ACLU and our partners to halt ICE’s dangerous expansion of immigrant detention,” the letter said.

Baaja’s passage would be “the single biggest overhaul” of American environmental laws since the 1970s, said Dillen of Earthjustice. “There are legitimate concerns that Nepa has been weaponized to slow down important projects, but people have recognized this problem for years, and the law has been reformed, and it’s also been weakened very significantly by the supreme court. What this bill does is take the last pieces of it that are very relevant in an administration like this,” she said.

Trump has pushed a “drill, baby, drill” fossil fuel agenda, and Baaja’s weakening of environmental regulations would further embolden him, Dillen said. She pointed to Trump’s plan to allow drilling near Chaco Culture national historic park, a Unesco world heritage site. “Chaco Canyon is in the crosshairs,” she said.

“At Earthjustice, we are deeply committed to building clean energy and to do it in a time frame that is meaningful, given the threats that we face. But the way to do this, the way to build our country better and even faster, is not by running over tribes and by emboldening a president who voters have just come out in a historic turnout to push back on,” Dillen said.

text:
(Honda in America via X)

Honda Motor Co. plans to build a $3 billion factory in central Ohio to manufacture its next-generation hybrids, boosting its output capacity for the popular vehicles.

The Japanese automaker announced the new plant on Nov. 9, which is expected to start production in 2029 and expand output by 240,000 vehicles a year. Honda has been mulling over the decision for months as part of a strategic pivot earlier this year away from all-electric vehicles. It aims to introduce 15 new hybrids globally by March 2030, primarily targeting North America.

“These investments strengthen America’s role as a cornerstone of Honda’s global future,” Bob Nelson, executive vice president of the company’s U.S. business operations, said in a statement.

Honda’s U.S. sales have risen 5% in the first 10 months of the year, powered by strong demand for hybrid versions of its best-selling CR-V compact SUV, Accord midsized sedan and compact Civic sedan. Fuel-efficient hybrids, which make up about a third of the company’s total sales volume in the U.S., have caught on with cost-conscious buyers as gas prices have soared.

Honda is preparing to introduce a new system that will provide hybrid options for its larger, V6 engine-powered vehicles such as the Pilot SUV and upscale Acura MDX SUV.

The new facility will be located between two existing auto assembly plants it operates in Ohio. It will be tooled to build gas-only, hybrid and fully electric vehicles, but the company didn’t provide a powertrain mix breakdown by production volume. It also said it will make unspecified investments in a numer of other facilities in North America.

Honda also has vehicle assembly operations in Alabama and Indiana as well as in Ontario, Canada and in central Mexico. In addition, it makes key parts such as engines and transmissions in Alabama, Georgia and Ohio.

U.S. trade relations with Canada and Mexico have been complicated by President Donald Trump’s tariffs on imports and his decision in July not to renew a North America free trade accord negotiated during his first administration. Earlier this week, Trump threatened to impose 50% levies on vehicles and auto parts made in Canada as of Jan. 1.

text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Senate on Monday is set to take up bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews for data centers and other infrastructure projects, in the first major action since last week's election that soundly repudiated President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans.

The Senate convenes at 3 p.m. EST. Watch live in our video player above.

The Senate is expected to hold a procedural vote on the bill, which senators and the president have pushed as officials seek to meet growing demand for electricity and other forms of energy that now faces yearslong delays in getting to the grid.

The legislation's sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to get big energy projects started — both for clean energy and fossil fuel projects — and make sure data centers pay for the energy they use. Anger over artificial intelligence data centers and rising electricity helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the massive, energy-hungry structures.

Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News

Trump urged senators to vote for it, calling it a "BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE." in a social media post on Sunday. The bill will "ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines, and Power Plants faster than ever before, lowering Energy Costs for American Families," Trump wrote.

Major industry groups representing developers in clean energy and in the oil and gas sector also support the bill.

However, many environmental organizations have panned the deal because they say it would lock in fossil fuel development, weaken environmental safeguards and make it harder for communities to challenge energy project approvals.

READ MORE: Outdated power grids a major hurdle in renewable energy transition

While the bill has received bipartisan support, the Democrats' sweeping midterm win could complicate its passage.

Some Democrats say the party should use its stronger position in the next Congress to pass legislation that produces needed clean energy but limits expansion of oil, natural gas and mining. Some critics have said the permitting bill as proposed could lead to a vast increase in exports of liquefied natural gas and facilitate a "reckless" build-out of data centers powered by natural gas.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, a New York Democrat who is expected to become speaker in January, criticized the bill last week, with his office saying it "falls short" in a number of areas.

Major environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and National Wildlife Federation, have strongly opposed the measure in recent days, citing concerns about its limits on judicial review and changes to the landmark National Environmental Policy Act. The 1970 law requires agencies to consider a project's possible impacts and allows the public to be heard before a project is approved, but supporters of an overhaul say that causes yearslong delays in federal permitting.

READ MORE: Opposition to AI data centers in the midterms foreshadows tougher regulations ahead

The bill's four main champions — two Democrats and two Republicans — released a detailed set of amendments Saturday designed to bolster support for the legislation.

The four senators, who lead the chamber's energy and environment panels, negotiated the deal weeks before the election. Republican Sens. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah and Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island say Americans are tired of paying more in utility bills while projects that could lower costs sit stuck in the planning phase for years.

"Americans can't afford to wait for lower electricity prices. We need to pass this bill now," said Heinrich.

Trump promotes expanding production of oil, natural gas and coal and he particularly dislikes offshore wind. His administration has been paying energy companies to walk away from offshore wind projects under development. It has spent nearly $4 billion on such settlements.

Whitehouse said a provision in the permitting bill would end the buyouts, so the administration will no longer be able to use public money to pay clean energy developers to relinquish wind energy leases and oblige them to invest in fossil fuels instead.

At a press conference with Heinrich on Monday, Whitehouse said the bill is "the floor, not the ceiling, of our climate and environmental aspirations. And we look forward to working to accomplish big things with our big Democratic majorities" next year.

Heinrich said he worked hard to incorporate feedback from tribal leaders on the initial proposal, adding that the amended version requires federal agencies to consult with tribes on projects that affect important cultural sites.

Sponsors also extended the window for objections to agency reports and strengthened opportunities for states to weigh in, Heinrich said.

If passed, the bill will save households billions on electricity costs, create jobs, cut emissions and force big corporations to pay their full share for data centers instead of pushing energy costs on consumers, he said.

McDermott reported from Providence, R.I.

Honda announced another expansion to its US car building business, with a new Ohio plant set to go online in 2029.

Over the past several months, you’ve seen announcements of automakers onshoring further American manufacturing capacity. The latest to do so is Honda, which just announced a $3 billion project to further build out its manufacturing capacity near Columbus, Ohio. As part of that deal, the automaker can build up to 240,000 additional vehicles a year, while it also plans to further bolster its existing engine and transmission plants to support a larger car assembly footprint.

The main facility marked above sits between two plants Honda is already operating in Ohio. The company has been running the Marysville plant since 1982, while the East Liberty plant came along seven years later. So, while Honda already has significant capacity here, 2029 will mark one of the largest expansions of that capacity in decades.

Honda announced the investment will create another 2,000 jobs, while bolstering its overall US automotive output to 1.3 million vehicles each year. This new plant comes as the automaker invests in its American operations across the board — not just in Ohio, but in Alabama and Georgia as well.

Now, Honda did initially plan to site its ‘EV Hub’ in Ohio. That strategy has shifted dramatically over the past year or so, as Honda pulled away from such a heavy investment toward fully electric vehicles toward a hybrid-first approach. As such, all this latest investment supports its goals to build out next-generation hybrid systems, and push out more new vehicles that will have those hybrid systems onboard. The new strategy does hedge potential futures a bit more broadly, however, as Honda also said the new capacity could build internal combustion vehicles, hybrids or fully electric vehicles.

Currently, Honda builds the Accord at its Marysville plant, while it builds the CR-V and Acura MDX at the East Liberty plant.

At this point in time, it is not 100% clear which vehicles Honda will start manufacturing from this new Ohio plant. Honda just said it will be “one of the most advanced in the world”, and provide the automaker the flexibility it needs to meet increasing — and more importantly, constantly shifting — demand.

The total $3 billion investment also includes money earmarked for Honda’s Lincoln, Alabama Auto/Engine plant, which will facilitate a new hybrid V6 system, as well as to facilitate infrastructure updates on the line that currently produces the Passport. Honda will invest in its Anna Engine plant in Ohio to produce a new four-cylinder engine for its smaller hybrid vehicles, and it will also put money into its Ohio and Georgia transmission plants.

We will inevitably get more details on the new auto manufacturing plant and updates on Honda’s other retooling efforts over the next couple years.

Ewing, NJ (November 9, 2026) - Today, Congresswoman Bonnie Watson Coleman (NJ-12) and State Senator Andrew Zwicker (District 16 - Hillsborough) announced a letter to Commissioner Ed Potosnak of the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection demanding a pause on the permitting of the Sentinel Data Center in South Brunswick.

The letter highlights potential gaps in the environmental study of the project that could lead to adverse environmental and health impacts on the surrounding communities.

The letter reads, in part:

We respectfully request that DEP not issue the permit in its current form. Before any final decision, DEP must independently recalculate the Sentinel Data Center facility’s potential to emit and properly classify the facility to account for emergency operation and the full planned buildout; publish its health risk assessment inputs and its review of them; add enforceable limits on non-emergency use; and give the public an opportunity to review and comment on that information. We are not asking DEP to prejudge the application.

We are asking for a complete, transparent review that protects public health and gives residents confidence that the law will be enforced.

Congresswoman Watson Coleman introduced the Data Center Community Impact Act, legislation that would authorize a federal study on the environmental, economic, and public health impacts of data centers, with a focus on communities of color and low-income communities. Watson Coleman is also an original cosponsor of the AI Data Center Moratorium Act.

Senator Zwicker is a primary sponsor of NJ S4659, which would require the DEP to conduct a study and submit a report to the Governor and the Legislature concerning the environmental impacts of data center development in the State and prohibit the construction of new data centers until the study is complete.

Last month, State Senator Zwicker, along with Assemblymembers Frieman and Drulis, secured from the state an extension on the public comment period for the Sentinel Data Center project.

text:
Outdated power grids are a major hurdle in the transition to renewable energy, since older systems often can't absorb all the electricity from new, cleaner sources.

This threatens global efforts to curb climate change by reducing fossil fuels and switching to renewable energy such as solar and wind. At U.N. climate talks kicking off this week, co-hosts Turkey and Australia want more ambitious goals to slash fossil fuels, install renewables and upgrade grids.

Grid concerns are gaining urgency this year as nations race to improve their energy security following the Iran war. The U.N. recently launched a new initiative to rally funding for grid upgrades in Africa and Southeast Asia.

"There needs to be a massive, massive, massive scaling up of investments into grids if we are going to get close to meeting our climate, energy and development goals," Selwin Hart, special adviser to the U.N. secretary-general on climate action, said.

Climate talks address grid bottleneck

At the U.N. climate talks, hosted in the Turkish resort city of Antalya, organizers describe modern and reliable electric grids as "the backbone of the clean energy system."

But billions of dollars are needed to upgrade out-of-date grids. These steep costs could hinder further renewable energy installations.

During the U.N. General Assembly in September, the global body launched a Global Grids Accelerator to speed up international funding for electricity infrastructure in Africa and Southeast Asia.

"We're very confident that the long-term trend is an acceleration of the pace of the energy transition, but we need the infrastructure, grids and storage, to really keep pace," Hart said.

Annual investment in electricity generation, such as building new power plants, has risen by almost 70% since 2015, reaching $1 trillion a year, according to the International Energy Agency. Yet the agency noted annual grid spending has risen at less than half that pace.

To meet electricity demand through 2030, the IEA calculates annual grid investment must increase by about 50% from today's $400 billion per year. Any delays will substantially increase global emissions by prolonging reliance on fossil fuels, the IEA warns.

"Power grids have not been readied enough for the scaleup of renewable electricity generation," said Jan Rosenow, a professor of energy and climate policy at Oxford University. "We have been complacent in the past and now the grid has become a real bottleneck."

Old grids slow energy transition

Power grids deliver electricity from power plants to homes through a network of transmission and distribution lines, substations and transformers.

Originally designed around large, centralized power plants, many of today's power grids were built like one-way roads, with producers sending electricity to consumers. These older one-directional grids are being overwhelmed by demand surges and a boom in renewables.

Grids have a maximum capacity of electricity that they can safely store, transport and distribute. If a grid is already at capacity, solar and wind farms can be instructed to limit their electricity output, a process known as curtailment.

China and India, which have installed impressive amounts of renewables, can't take full advantage of the massive buildout for this reason.

China curtailed 360 terawatt-hours — close to the equivalent of the United Kingdom's annual electricity demand — of wind and solar electricity in the first half of 2026, according to Global Energy Monitor and the Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air.

READ MORE: Energy Department will spend nearly $2 billion to squeeze more electricity from the nation's aging power grid

India curtailed 11 terawatt-hours of solar generation — enough electricity to power about 10 million homes — over the course of 15 months spanning 2025 and 2026 because of insufficient transmission and storage capacity, according to the energy think tank Ember.

Curtailing solar and wind generation while fossil fuels continue to supply electricity is a blow to climate efforts, especially since China and India are among the world's largest emitters, said James Abraham, with the New Delhi-based Council on Energy, Environment and Water.

To transition away from fossil fuels, he said, "you need a grid changeover. You need a grid transformation."

Solutions exist, despite funding concerns

Upgrading existing grids to be more flexible could increase efficiency by allowing electricity flows to adjust to supply and demand. It could help areas with excess solar and wind energy send it to places with higher electricity demand and fewer energy resources.

Newer, more flexible grids could also make it easier for utility companies to exchange electricity with households that have solar panels or battery storage.

But many countries can't afford to take these steps, or at least not quickly enough, according to Abraham, who said "the need is now. It's a time tension rather than anything else."

Global energy security concerns deepen

The Iran war's energy shock built up momentum for the energy transition, especially in hard-hit regions like Southeast Asia, but investment in renewables is outpacing grid development, said Gahee Han, with the Seoul-based nonprofit Solutions for Our Climate.

"Unless we upgrade our power grid in Asia, Asia will have no choice but to rely on the conventional power plants, like gas or coal," she said. "It's nonsense to rely on those power plants, especially considering the energy crisis."

One of the solutions being promoted by the Association of Southeast Asian Nations is an interconnected power grid that would allow countries to trade power more easily, adding a safeguard against future shocks.

Interest in the ambitious plan, which is still in its infancy, is growing, according to Abdul Razib Dawood, executive director of the ASEAN Center for Energy.

"We have this crisis that will unify the region. You need your neighbors," he said. "This is an opportunity for us to really strengthen the cooperation."

text:
Envusa Energy, the joint venture between Anglo American and EDF power solutions, now has its 520MW Koruson 2 wind and solar cluster fully running, supplying Valterra Platinum and two other mining customers over Eskom’s grid.

Some R16 billion has gone into the 520MW Koruson 2 cluster on the border of the Eastern and Northern Cape, where roughly 50 wind turbines and about 420,000 solar panels now supply mining customers through Eskom’s transmission network, according to Envusa Energy, which developed it.

The Mooi Plaats solar PV plant in the Northern Cape provides 240MW of the total and two 140MW wind farms in the Eastern Cape, Umsobomvu and Hartebeesthoek, provide the other 280MW, all of them connected to the Koruson 400kV main transmission substation. Hartebeesthoek, which runs Nordex N163/5.X turbines, was the last to finish, reaching commercial operation at 130MW in August with its final 10MW due the following month, and reports at the end of October described the cluster as fully operational.

Valterra Platinum takes 461MW of the output, with 48MW going to De Beers’ Venetia mine and 11MW to Kumba Iron Ore’s Kolomela mine, each under a 20-year agreement with Envusa, a licensed electricity trader. Envusa expects the three generators to abate about 2.2 million tonnes of carbon dioxide a year, some 640,000 tonnes of it at Hartebeesthoek.

Pele Green Energy and the Winds of Change Community Trust are shareholders in the projects alongside Anglo American and EDF power solutions, and about R20 million has gone into socio-economic programmes across the cluster, with more than 200 jobs created at Hartebeesthoek during construction. The projects were awarded in October 2021 and reached commercial and financial close in February 2024.

“The completion of Koruson 2 shows that this model works,” Nicole Mason, Envusa Energy’s chief executive, said when Hartebeesthoek began operating. The joint venture already has a further 340MW of wind under way, with financial close targeted for the first quarter of 2027 and commercial operation for 2029, as part of its plan to develop 3GW to 5GW of wind, solar and battery storage across Southern Africa by 2030.

name: Texas Environment
title: What the Texas blue wave could mean for state environmental, oil and gas agencies
description:
The historic midterm elections in Texas will have wide-ranging implications for the state agencies that oversee environmental permitting and the oil and gas industry.
The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) could see at least two new commissioners appointed by Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa.
"We have a railroad commissioner... who was not the oil and gas industry's pick to win the seat," said executive director Virginia Palacios.
Palacios said she's also watching how the election of Democrat Nathan Johnson as attorney general may influence recusals on the Railroad Commission.
"In Texas, the attorney general is responsible for overseeing how recusal policies are followed at the Railroad Commission," Palacios said.
text:
The historic midterm elections in Texas will have wide-ranging implications for the state agencies that oversee environmental permitting and the oil and gas industry.

The Texas Railroad Commission has a new Democratic commissioner for the first time in over three decades, which could be a deciding vote when the two sitting Republican commissioners disagree. The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) could see at least two new commissioners appointed by Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa.

"I think the work that we've been doing to advance environmental policy in Texas has never had a greater opportunity to succeed," said Kathryn Guerra, director of Public Citizen's TCEQ watchdog campaign. "We're very optimistic about changing the leadership of the state agencies (and) directing those state agencies to work in the best interests of Texans instead of... corporations."

The three commissioners currently leading TCEQ were all appointed by Gov. Greg Abbott. Chairwoman Brooke Paup was appointed in January 2025; her term expires in August 2027, within Hinojosa's first year as governor. Commissioner Catarina Gonzales was appointed in February 2024 and her term expires in August 2029.

The newest commissioner, Tonya Miller, was appointed in October 2025; her stint expires in August 2031, past Hinojosa's first term as governor. However, Guerra said Miller was never officially confirmed by the state Senate.

"So folks are thinking... this is an opportunity for the new governor to appoint somebody who could better protect Texans from environmental harms," Guerra said. Another possibility is to ask the commissioners for their resignations. Hinojosa has not indicated she will make this move.

Environmental activists often criticize the agency for "rubber-stamping" permits they say cause pollution. A 2023 state legislative report found TCEQ needs to improve transparency and opportunities for public input. The report also suggested the agency needs to remedy its monitoring and enforcement processes.

Meanwhile, on the Texas Railroad Commission, Democratic state Rep. Jon Rosenthal won a contentious race against Republican Bo French, who has a history of hateful rhetoric and who in September made a racist social media post about South Asian students celebrating at a University of Texas football game and drew national bipartisan backlash.

"[These] results show that experience and good governance matter," Rosenthal said in a statement on social media on election night. "I am humbled and honored by the faith placed in me by the people of Texas, who have sent the message that the politics of hate and division do not win in the Lone Star State."

Commission Shift, a nonprofit watchdog group, called Rosenthal's election "historic."

"We have a railroad commissioner... who was not the oil and gas industry's pick to win the seat," said executive director Virginia Palacios. "I think this upset by Democrats could communicate to the sitting Republican... commissioners that they need to focus more on what constituents want and less on what their oil and gas industry campaign donors want."

Rosenthal, a career oilfield engineer, joins two Republican commissioners, Wayne Christian and Christi Craddick, who don't always see eye to eye. For example, Craddick voted against the agency's recent decision to eliminate public comment during open meetings while Christian voted for it.

Rosenthal's proposed policies are novel for an agency that's usually viewed as friendly to the oil and gas industry. They include ending routine gas flaring, suspending new permits for operators with chronic violations, and raising surety bonds, a financial commitment that operators will follow regulations.

Palacios said she's also watching how the election of Democrat Nathan Johnson as attorney general may influence recusals on the Railroad Commission.

"In Texas, the attorney general is responsible for overseeing how recusal policies are followed at the Railroad Commission," Palacios said. "Commission Shift previously documented cases where sitting railroad commissioners failed to recuse themselves from decisions that they had a personal financial interest in. [So now] we might see more interest in actually enforcing those policies that are on the books."

Celeste Guajardo is the Climate, Energy and Environment reporter for KERA and Grist. Got a tip? Email her at cguajardo@kera.org.

title: Report: Expanding DERs Could Avoid $600B+ in US Grid Costs, Cut Household Bills through 2050
description:
Deploying these DERs across multiple networks, such as residential, commercial and industrial customers, could help avoid an estimated $614 billion in U.S. power system costs through 2050.
In the firm’s report titled “The National Case for a More Distributed Power Grid: New Evidence on Affordability and Demand Growth,” researchers studied the rising impacts on the U.S. power system through 2050 under a nationwide scenario.
Addressing grid strain: DERs balancing historic demand Between now and 2027, U.S. electricity generation is expected to surge to historic highs.
The aging U.S. power grid is leading many states and power generators to take action and seek off-grid solutions to boost their distributed energy resources.
The Brattle study concluded that removing key policy barriers to DER deployment and technologies in its research scenario would more than quadruple U.S. DER capacity.
text:
The rise of distributed energy resource (DER) assets, such as solar, battery storage and managed EV charging, is breaking down barriers to next-generation frameworks and policies, ultimately unlocking these applications across multiple networks.

Deploying these DERs across multiple networks, such as residential, commercial and industrial customers, could help avoid an estimated $614 billion in U.S. power system costs through 2050. According to a new report by the global consulting firm The Brattle Group for The Pew Charitable Trusts, broader DER adoption across these networks nationwide could offset roughly half of projected household electricity bill increases, apart from those related to inflation.

In the firm’s report titled “The National Case for a More Distributed Power Grid: New Evidence on Affordability and Demand Growth,” researchers studied the rising impacts on the U.S. power system through 2050 under a nationwide scenario. In this scenario, DER deployment expands to levels already observed in key U.S. markets.

Addressing grid strain: DERs balancing historic demand

Between now and 2027, U.S. electricity generation is expected to surge to historic highs. According to the Energy Information Administration (EIA), the projected 2.2% increase will result in a record energy output equivalent to an average continuous grid load of 498.63 GW (4,368 BkWh). An additional 1.7% growth is anticipated next year.

The joint Pew and Brattle Group study detailed that leveraging DERs located close to electricity users is crucial to supporting energy affordability and meeting rising demand.

U.S. utilities have reportedly proposed investing $1.4 trillion through 2030 in infrastructure upgrades and DER projects. The aging U.S. power grid is leading many states and power generators to take action and seek off-grid solutions to boost their distributed energy resources.

The Platte River Power Authority, a community-owned power utility provider in Colorado, is one example of these investments at work, with expanded plans for a virtual power plant (VPP) with software company EnergyHub. The growing need for a VPP is part of efforts to provide dispatchable, on-demand power to support its increasingly renewable energy portfolio. DERs work in tandem with VPP aggregating technology to help feed excess energy back to the grid or reduce load where needed.

DER participation in programs like VPPs provides direct financial benefits for customers, not large-scale power developers, allowing them to earn direct compensation for services they provide to the grid.

Scaling grid-edge flexibility through DERMS

Expanding DER deployments would reportedly shift roughly 105 GW of storage capacity from centralized utility-scale projects to localized distributed storage managed by distributed energy resource management systems (DERMS) for grid-edge flexibility.

The Brattle study concluded that removing key policy barriers to DER deployment and technologies in its research scenario would more than quadruple U.S. DER capacity. By doing so, it reduces the risk of excessive capital expenditures and the cost of overbuilding conventional energy infrastructure driven by electricity demand uncertainty.

In this scenario where anticipated load growth falls short, greater reliance on DERs would reportedly reduce overbuilding energy infrastructure costs by $33 billion (40%) between 2030 and 2040. Addressing regulatory hurdles, the firm noted, could add over 400 GW of grid capacity by 2050—the equivalent of nearly one-third of the country’s entire existing power generation fleet today.

“Many homes and businesses already have technologies that could help the grid meet rising demand, and adoption of those technologies will continue to grow. The opportunity is to treat them as resources in utility planning rather than leave their capabilities untapped,” said Ryan Hledik, a Brattle principal and report coauthor, in a statement. “At scale, DERs could avoid or defer a portion of U.S. infrastructure investment needs, reduce pressure on household bills and give utilities more flexibility in the face of uncertain demand.”

Broader decarbonization pathways: Reducing system expenditure, CO2 emissions

The firm explains that rapid demand growth amid AI and data centers is colliding with rising infrastructure costs, long development timelines, affordability pressures and the continued need to decarbonize the power system.

To mitigate this, DER deployment could reportedly enable an annual reduction of $122 in average household electricity bills by 2050, offsetting roughly half of the projected bill increases assumed by the inflation rate.

In addition, researchers highlighted that expanding DER deployment could avoid roughly 70 GW of projected net gas additions. It would reportedly mark a 22% reduction equivalent to 175 natural gas-fired plants nationally. Decreasing carbon emissions (CO2) is highly critical in this scenario, Brattle Group adds, detailing the deployment and integration of EVs.

According to the EIA, CO2 emissions are on the rise again in the U.S. Despite two decades of intermittent but steady declines, EIA data show a 2% rise in 2025. Electricity sector growth and coal dependency are reportedly playing critical roles in this rise.

The Brattle Group noted that DERs would directly reduce cumulative power sector CO2 emissions by an estimated 3% through 2050 in its research scenario. By requiring a carbon-free generation fleet by 2050, expanded DERs could offset roughly 175 GW of utility-scale capacity and lower annual generation costs in 2050 by $45 billion (20%), making a decarbonized power system less costly.

Ambitious but feasible adoption of DERs could reportedly address these overall challenges and deliver over half a trillion dollars in cost savings to the grid and customers across multiple networks over the next 25 years.

“At a time of historic demand from data centers, new manufacturing and electrification, DERs can provide a significant new energy supply if barriers to their adoption are removed,” said Maureen Quinlan, who leads Pew’s work to decarbonize the grid. “This report underscores how pragmatic policy changes that enable DER technology can save billions, cut emissions and help build a more affordable, reliable and flexible grid that meets today’s and tomorrow’s energy needs.”

title: COP31: What is it and what's at stake? - The New Arab
description:
The COP31 summit is being held at the end of what scientists expect to the warmest year on record, as global temperatures continue to rise on the back of climate change.
A Conference of Parties (COP) summit has been held every year since 1995 to negotiate global rules to combat climate change.

text:
World leaders, diplomats and climate activists are gathering in Turkey for the next two weeks for the annual round of COP climate talks.

The COP31 summit is being held at the end of what scientists expect to the warmest year on record, as global temperatures continue to rise on the back of climate change.

What is COP31?

Officials from more than 190 countries are convening for the annual UN climate talks in Antalya between 9 and 20 November.

A Conference of Parties (COP) summit has been held every year since 1995 to negotiate global rules to combat climate change.

Though the summit is taking place in Turkey, Australia is leading the negotiations in an unusual arrangement agreed as a compromise after both countries bid to host the 2026 event.

Turkey's Environment Minister Murat Kurum has been named COP31 president, while Australian climate minister Chris Bowen is president of the negotiations.

Who's attending – and who isn't?

Almost all of the 194 countries that signed the landmark 2015 Paris Agreement on climate change will be present in Turkey.

The one glaring omission is the United States, which is not sending any representatives to the summit after President Trump withdrew from the treaty at the beginning of this year.

The heads of state and government of many other major countries will also be absent from Turkey. They include China's Xi Jinping, French President Emmanuel Macron, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, and Italy's Giorgia Meloni.

What are the main issues being discussed?

Negotiators will return to the familiar yet unresolved issues from previous COPs, including emissions reductions and climate finance.

The 1.5C climate target set at Paris has already been breached. But the UN has said that serious action to curb global emissions now could pave the way for lower temperatures by the end of the century.

But global leaders remain divided about how fast to reduce emissions and how climate-related projects should be funded.

The issue of fossil fuels has been particularly difficult to find consensus over, given oil and gas producers' long-running opposition to any curbs on their activities. The final agreement in COP28 included for the first time a commitment to transition away from fossil fuels, though this was vague and included no plan or timeframe for doing so.

Countries failed to agree on a roadmap at the two following COPs. The final agreement at COP30 in Brazil omitted the term "fossil fuels" in a move interpreted by some as a backtrack on the earlier commitment to phase them out.

Ahead of the summit, outgoing COP president Brazil published the first roadmap to reduce fossil fuel emissions by 2033 though whether this can be translated into a binding global agreement seems unlikely.

Meanwhile, developing countries will continue to push for richer countries to shoulder more of the financial burden.

They argue that, not only are they more vulnerable to the effects of climate change, but they are also less responsible for it, with advanced economies accounting for the vast majority of historic CO2 emissions.

COP29 in Baku secured an agreement for developed countries to mobilise $300 billion a year by 2035 to help developing countries reduce their emissions and adapt to the impact of climate change. A record $136.7 billion was mobilised in 2024, according to the OECD.

Why does it matter?

The COP framework is often criticised for moving at a snail's pace and achieving little to address the escalating impacts of climate change.

But it remains the only mechanism for making global climate policy and will be critical if the world is to put a lid on the rising temperatures.

COP31 is being held at the end of what scientists say will be the hottest year on record as temperatures continue to rise even higher due to rising emissions.

The record temperatures have been felt more keenly than ever this year, with escalating droughts across the world, huge wildfires across Europe, and a glacier collapse in Nepal, which left more than 1000 people dead.

text:
BATON ROUGE — Gov. Jeff Landry, alongside the governors of Alabama, Mississippi, Arkansas and Texas, is petitioning the Environmental Protection Agency to waive the Renewable Fuel Standard volume requirements for 2027, saying it will help lower gas prices.

Landry and the other governors say that the RFS requirements, which require that fuels sold in the United States contain a minimum volume of renewable fuels, are harming their states' economies. The coalition of governors says that this imposes a cost on every gallon of gas and diesel sold.

Landry and the other governors asked that the percentage standards be adjusted, asking that the relief and the waivers be granted until the economic harm is remedied.

"Meanwhile Europe pays zero for the American gas and diesel, and they export it," Landry said Monday in a post on X. "Affordability starts with lowering fuel cost for all Americans."

A letter from Landry and Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey said the rising gas prices, including record-high diesel prices, are driven by interruptions in global supplies from wars in the Middle East and Ukraine. Landry said that President Donald Trump's actions, including deferring the federal excise tax on dyed diesel, the release of 100 million barrels from European reserves, and the rejection of an export ban, all helped in response to surging prices.

Despite this, Landry says that "more regulatory relief could significantly benefit American consumers and diesel users."

"Time to put American drivers FIRST," Landry said in his X post.

text:
Japanese automaker Honda Motor will build a new $3 billion auto plant in central Ohio to make hybrid vehicles, creating 2,000 jobs, it said on Monday.

The company said the plant will be able to produce 240,000 vehicles annually and begin production in 2029. It will increase its US auto production capacity to 1.3 million vehicles annually, and North American capacity to 1.9 million.

Honda also plans additional new investments in Canada and Ohio, Georgia and Alabama.

The company announced plans in May to add 15 new Honda and Acura hybrid models worldwide by 2030. It also announced it would scrap electric vehicle sales goals, and indefinitely suspended an $11 billion Canada EV project as part of a $9 billion EV writedown.

Advt

Honda said it will invest in Alabama to build a new V6 hybrid engine, and retool its Ohio engine plant to build a new four-cylinder engine. It will also retool transmission plants in Ohio and Georgia, and plans to reintroduce engine production in Ontario.

Automakers facing US tariffs

A number of foreign automakers have announced major new investments as they face tariffs imposed by President Donald Trump's administration.

Last month, Volkswagen ​luxury unit Audi said it would build a $4 billion assembly plant near Macon, Georgia to open in the early 2030s that would produce 200,000 SUVs annually and employ 4,500 workers.

Reuters reported last month that Trump's administration had promised tariff relief to Audi to help secure the plant's future. US officials told Audi executives the government plans to offer broad relief from tariffs for automakers making significant investments in US production.

In July, Toyota Motor said it would spend $3.6 billion to build a 2.5-million-square-foot (232,000-square-metre) truck assembly line on its San Antonio, Texas manufacturing campus and shift some truck production to the US from Mexico.

The Japanese automaker said the expansion would be completed by 2030, creating 2,000 jobs.

title: Subaru and Toyota picked the perfect time to roll out affordable EVs - The Business Times
description:
“I have been watching the EV market for more than a decade,” she said.
As US auto executives cooled on electric cars this year, scrapping models and cutting production, Subaru and Toyota Motor nosed into the void.
“It’s a reset for the EV market and it is resilience,” said Stephanie Valdez Streaty, director of industry insights at Cox Automotive.
The companies’ new EVs are affordable SUVs, which is the sweet spot of the US car market, she added.
While it takes a long time to take a new car model from sketch to assembly line, scrapping one is relatively fast.
text:
[NEW YORK] Karla Fisher, a Marine and retired engineer, arguably should have bought an electric vehicle a year ago.

There were federal incentives and a crowd of options, including the Ford F-150 Lightning, Honda Prologue and Nissan Ariya – all of which have since disappeared.

But none of those vehicles quite met Fisher’s specific requirements: at least seven inches of ground clearance, more than 250 miles (402 km) of range and a price in line with – or slightly below – that of gas-burning alternatives.

The Subaru Trailseeker, a new model that hit the market early this year, checked all the boxes. Fisher bought hers in September and already has put 2,000 miles on it, driving to trailheads, fishing holes and campsites near her home on the Oregon coast.

“I have been watching the EV market for more than a decade,” she said. “Alas, no cars were produced that made sense to me as a consumer in all that time.”

The battery-powered Subaru, she attests, is now her “most favourite car of all time”.

As US auto executives cooled on electric cars this year, scrapping models and cutting production, Subaru and Toyota Motor nosed into the void. With five new models, the companies have collectively sold almost 62,000 EVs in the US in the first three quarters of 2026, more than double their year-earlier tally.

Though the brands still represent only 9 per cent of the US EV market and trail General Motors in the space, their sales are growing, while rivals have gone in reverse. In the year to date, Rivian Automotive, which also added a new truck, is the only other carmaker to post a gain in battery-powered business.

Subaru and Toyota are relatively late to the electric-car race, but their timing is propitious. While EV demand cooled when federal incentives expired in September, the market has stabilised and the ranks of electric-curious drivers are growing.

Analysts said the two brands are scooping up drivers addled by high gas prices and market share that might have otherwise gone to larger rivals who scrapped EV models.

“It’s a reset for the EV market and it is resilience,” said Stephanie Valdez Streaty, director of industry insights at Cox Automotive. “And you start to see this divergence of who’s winning the race and who’s pulling back.”

Toyota, which owns 20 per cent of Subaru, is now selling two EVs in the US to every one of Ford’s. And while Subaru is still a small player, Valdez Streaty said it is capitalising on a renaissance in EV interest. The companies’ new EVs are affordable SUVs, which is the sweet spot of the US car market, she added.

To some extent, the sales boom required as much luck as strategy. While it takes a long time to take a new car model from sketch to assembly line, scrapping one is relatively fast. When the US EV market plummeted late last year, a cluster of models was pulled from production within weeks.

Meanwhile, the new EVs from Subaru and Toyota had been in the works for years and just happened to debut as gas prices spiked, and the EV field had thinned considerably.

“There’s been so much volatility with EVs out there in terms of regulations that it’s been an interesting go,” said Timothy Tagye, vice-president of field operations for Subaru of America. “But our timing was good.”

Critically, the companies have partnered with each other in developing many of their latest EVs, sharing resources and splitting costs. While each brand put its unique stamp on external designs, underneath the metal, much of the machinery is shared.

Subaru spokesman Dominick Infante said the arrangement is the main reason sticker prices on the vehicles, including Subaru’s Trailseeker and Uncharted and Toyota’s C-HR and bZ Woodland, are relatively affordable. Priced from US$35,000 to US$45,000, all the new models are well below what the average internal-combustion car sells for in America these days.

“We do believe there’s an EV future,” Infante said.

Toyota said its plan for some time has been to avoid trying to discern whether the auto industry would be gas-powered or electric. Its new EVs are just another option, alongside hybrids and machines that run solely on petrol, according to Owen Peacock, general manager of Toyota marketing and communications.

Both brands now have a Goldilocks situation for EVs in the US: SUVs in sizes small, medium and large. Next year, they’ll each add an extra-large offering. An electric version of the three-row Toyota Highlander SUV, which Subaru will market as a new model dubbed Getaway, is expected to arrive in the spring.

“Our multi-pathway strategy is really kind of ‘let’s serve everybody’,” Peacock said, “versus, ‘Let’s move people from one to the next to the next.’” BLOOMBERG

name: American Energy
title: The AI Power Grab That Could Upend America's Electricity Industry | OilPrice.com
description:
A large US electric utility, such as Entergy or Dominion Resources, has a market capitalization of $50-60 billion.
US technology giants, mimicking the apex carnivorous predator T Rex, will do whatever they want in the domestic electric power arena.
The large gas fired combined cycle power plants favored by utilities have heat rates around 7,000 btus/kwh versus about 12,000 btus/kwh for simple cycle CTs.
Simple cycle turbines emit hot gases at about 1,000 degrees (F) while combined cycle units repurpose that waste heat to produce even more energy.
This will be a new source of competition for US electric utilities in those areas.
text:
Let’s begin with a question. “How would an average-sized human fare in a 'negotiation' with a six-ton Tyrannosaurus Rex?” Obviously, the interaction would end with the human serving as a high-protein snack. The T-Rex weighs 75 times more than the average person. With that kind of weight disparity, there is no “negotiating,” just a stomp and gulp.

Something analogous may be in store for the electric industry: a T-Rex

scenario. In negotiating with prospective data center owners, US utilities are puny in size compared to giant technology corporations. A large US electric utility, such as Entergy or Dominion Resources, has a market capitalization of $50-60 billion. Microsoft has a market capitalization of $3.8 trillion. (Nvidia is even bigger.) In fact, Microsoft by itself is more than three times larger than the entire U.S. investor-owned utility industry, which “only” has a market capitalization of $1.2 trillion. Looking at another way the S&P 500 information and technology sector comprises about 30% of the overall index. Adding in the related adjacent businesses puts overall technology at about 40% of the S&P index. Electric utilities make up 2% of the index. Our point here is simple. US technology giants, mimicking the apex carnivorous predator T Rex, will do whatever they want in the domestic electric power arena. And the utilities will be impotent to stop them. We may be witnessing an enormous, rapid expansion of non-regulated power generation to serve the exploding energy needs of the technology industry.

Consider the scale of this technology build-out. According to a recent article in American Compute, over two thousand facilities are under construction in five states: TX, VA, GA, PA, and OH. If you look at this map long enough, you begin to see why these facilities are where they are. And it’s for only one reason: cheap natural gas. Mentally erase the state lines and think in terms of resource plays: Haynesville, Utica, Marcellus, Eagle Ford etc. The main input cost for these facilities, apart from computing hardware, is electricity. American Compute says that the goal is simple. Get cheap (and dirty) electricity at a hoped-for price of about 3-5 cents kWh—way below the average industrial rate of most utilities. That’s why data center developers are salvaging old aircraft engines and repurposing them for power production.

But let’s take a step back and ask a simple question. Why don’t franchise-owning electric utilities install gas-fired combustion turbines (CTs), in many cases literally rebuilt aircraft engines, throughout their service territories to meet this huge new wave of demand for electricity? After all that’s what some data center developers are doing. Apart from the fact that these new CTs pollute heavily (both particulates and CO2), from a utility perspective these relatively small machines are inefficient at converting fuel into electricity. The state utility commission that has to approve these things would never allow it. The industry uses two measures: heat rates and thermal efficiency to compare different types of power generation. The large gas fired combined cycle power plants favored by utilities have heat rates around 7,000 btus/kwh versus about 12,000 btus/kwh for simple cycle CTs. (With heat rates, lower is better, i.e. more efficient conversion of fuel to energy.) Comparing thermal efficiency tells the same story. Simple cycle turbines emit hot gases at about 1,000 degrees (F) while combined cycle units repurpose that waste heat to produce even more energy.

In the utility business, these small-size CTs are called referred peaking units. They are used to provide energy when more efficient resources are fully deployed. In a typical year, they run about 5% of the time and remain idle most of the year. The larger, more efficient combined cycle gas plants are designed to run for almost 70% of the year. Why would anyone build out a parallel electric grid in the US using relatively inefficient peaking plants instead of far superior base-load power plants? As many of our readers already know, the answer is time. It now takes about 5-7 years to build a new large power plant from scratch. And the costs have more than doubled. Large turbines from the likes of GE Vernova, Mitsubishi Power, and Siemens are all on back order. However, a truck mounted GE LM2500 aeroderivative CT can be up and running in months. Maybe sooner. Some developers are also combining an installation of these turbines and batteries.

We’ve seen published estimates of 30 to 50 gigawatts of behind the meter power production at data centers within five years. For comparison, this would mean adding new power generation roughly the size of Southern Company’s regulated generating fleet (46 gws). And since these CTs are for powering data centers, we already know where they will be located: Texas, Virginia, Georgia, Ohio etc. If there is a meaningful downturn in the data center business, won’t these developers try to sell their excess power to the grid? This will be a new source of competition for US electric utilities in those areas. We doubt anyone is discussing this yet. However, our technology “T-Rexes” have been permitted to literally stomp on environmental regulations. If environmental concerns reassert themselves, this could impose constraints on the newly emerging parallel grid. If future environmental rules shut down the dirty generators, who will provide electricity to the AI centers? The grid? Close down the data centers or make utility customers foot the bill? Are we back to that, again?

That’s the T-Rex scenario. Robust enforcement of antitrust and environmental laws, less political deference to the AI giants, energy-efficient AI, bursting of the AI bubble, or some other unexpected event could change the picture. After all, the dinosaurs were highly successful until that meteor landed at Chicxulub and wiped them out. Almost as unlikely an event as electing a Democrat in Kansas. No prediction intended, of course. We are not prophets

text:
Honda announced on November 9 that it will invest $3 billion to build a new auto plant in Central Ohio, creating more than 2,000 new jobs. The plant will be located on land between Honda's existing East Liberty and Marysville Auto Plants and is expected to begin production in 2029, pending final government approvals, according to the company's release.

The facility has a planned capacity of 240,000 vehicles. It will be Honda's fourth auto plant in Ohio and its ninth auto-related production facility in the U.S. Together with projects at existing plants, the investment will increase Honda's U.S. auto production capacity to approximately 1.3 million vehicles a year and its North American capacity to approximately 1.9 million, Honda said.

Flexible production for hybrid demand

Honda said the plant will have the flexibility to produce multiple vehicle types and powertrains, including hybrid and gasoline-powered vehicles as well as battery-electric vehicles. The company said the added capacity will support its expanding hybrid lineup. In May 2026, Honda announced plans to introduce 15 new Honda and Acura hybrid models globally by 2030, with North America expected to be the primary market for many of them.

The new plant is part of a broader set of investments at Honda operations in Ohio, Alabama and Georgia to expand U.S. production of hybrid-electric vehicles and the engines and hybrid systems that power them. Honda said hybrid powertrain production capacity in Ohio will increase 250 percent.

Why Ohio

Honda said it selected Ohio based on factors including a highly skilled workforce, close proximity to a large concentration of its U.S. supply base, nearby vehicle development operations, existing Honda manufacturing for vehicles, engines and hybrid systems, and the L-H Battery Company joint venture facility.

Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine said Honda's leadership "could have chosen to build this plant anywhere in the world, but they chose Ohio because there are so many advantages to being here."

description:
