title: What Democrats Can, And Should, Do with Their New Majority - Legal Planet
description:
When the 120th Congress convenes on January 3, 2027, Democrats will have the biggest congressional majority in years — but not a filibuster-proof majority or veto-proof majority.
The House majority will be big enough to allow for intra-party divisions and debates rather than require party-line votes.
Given all this, what can and should Democrats do when it comes to climate, energy and the environment?
Legislation and resolutions House Democrats unarguably have a clear mandate to address affordability and Americans’ bipartisan concerns about the development of data centers.
House Democrats proposed legislation along these lines earlier this year.
text:
“Green Ideas for the New Blue Majority” is a series from UCLA Law faculty exploring legislative opportunities for the 120th Congress.

Democrats achieved a generational landslide victory in the 2026 midterm elections largely by campaigning on affordability, fighting corruption, and acting as a check on unpopular Trump policies.

To date, Democrats have won at least 253 seats in the House and 54 in the Senate. For the first time this century, Democrats won statewide in Texas — including a Senate seat and the governor’s mansion. They won a Senate seat in Kansas, which had not happened in 94 years. Democrats flipped 5 senate seats in states that voted for Trump by double digits in 2024 — including in Iowa where Josh Turek, like many, campaigned on the cost of living and a pledge to fight corruption with an additional focus on fighting high cancer rates related to environmental harms.

When the 120th Congress convenes on January 3, 2027, Democrats will have the biggest congressional majority in years — but not a filibuster-proof majority or veto-proof majority. The House majority will be big enough to allow for intra-party divisions and debates rather than require party-line votes.

Given all this, what can and should Democrats do when it comes to climate, energy and the environment? Faculty of the UCLA Emmett Institute are thinking about the various ways congressional Democrats could tackle salient voter concerns at the intersection of corruption, pollution, and the cost of living. These include oversight authority, budgetary powers, and working on legislative priorities that might find some cooperation from Republicans and even Trump.

Of particular note is a theme we call toxic corruption. “The phrase ‘polluter pays’ has taken on a new meaning in the Trump Administration,” Ann Carlson says. “It’s bad enough that the Administration has rolled back climate and air pollution regulations on cars, trucks, power plants, and landfills, but they’re also giving polluters a pass for laws that remain on the books. At least 200 industrial facilities are now allowed to spew hazardous air pollutants above legal limits with impunity; and car companies that can’t meet fuel economy standards now pay $0 in penalties for failing to comply. What are these polluters giving the Administration for their get out of jail free cards? The new Congress should use its legislative, budgetary and oversight powers to investigate why EPA isn’t enforcing toxic pollution laws; use reconciliation to reinstate CAFE penalties; and provide extra funding for EPA’s enforcement staff to go after scofflaws.”

Possible course of action include practical goals related to topics in which Democrats have a clear mandate but also more ambitious proposals that might be vetoed but set up a 2029 agenda for a possible Democratic administration. However, there is reason to exercise careful consideration around priorities and messaging. “Democrats should use the next two years to be as productive as possible,” Julia Stein says “They should be looking to make deals to preserve clean energy investment with the group of Republicans that were already opposed to Trump’s push to eliminate that investment on ideological grounds. And when they use oversight and investigatory powers, it should be directly linked to either affordability or public health — ideally both.”

Over the next two months, we’ll be sharing these ideas in greater detail for a new series called “Green Ideas for the New Blue Majority.” Here’s where we see opportunities worth exploring.

Oversight and investigations

Democrats will hold the full investigatory powers of Congress, including the ability to subpoena records for review and compel individuals to testify before lawmakers. They have already indicated that priorities here include corruption and public health. Efforts could center around cleaning up “toxic corruption” — where pollution and corruption meet.

What would this look like? For starters, they could investigate the “pay for play” free passes to polluters: Representatives around the country, including some new House members, could help shine a spotlight on polluting facilities and recent exemptions (202 in 39 states) especially by holding field hearings in local districts.

They could also investigate the corporate influence of the fossil fuel industry as it relates to the coordinated industry-federal campaign to try to preempt state-level climate lawsuits, using subpoenas, hearings and GAO reviews to document such coordination. Alejandro Camacho, who has been closely following the recent Supreme Court case related to state climate lawsuits, says oversight is just one of the ways Democrats can help preserve climate remedies from the fossil fuel industry.

Then there’s health and science: Democrats already released a report documenting how the Trump administration has undermined public health infrastructure and U.S. scientific research into chronic and deadly diseases, they could continue that investigation with a focus on HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

Other possible investigations: EPA and DOE decisions to gut climate rules and revoke the Endangerment Finding; the financial deals to kill clean energy projects, offshore wind especially; the lack of environmental review behind the final “harm” rescission from the Endangered Species Act and the risk it creates for more than 1,200 habitat conservation plans.

Budget reconciliation and appropriations

Since 60 votes are required to overcome a filibuster, Democrats can use the budget reconciliation process for passing some provisions with a simple majority. They can and should consider some options for budget reconciliation even if a presidential veto is threatened. Democrats can also add extra requirements of departments through appropriation riders, because appropriations bills are “must-pass” legislation.

Some options here include: Restoration of CAFE standards and penalties, which was previously done through reconciliation; restoration of agency funding for EPA, DOE and for underfunded wildlife agencies to carry out listing and recovery under the Endangered Species Act; fund dedicated NEPA staff, the Permitting Council and digital public tracking of project reviews.

Given all the emphasis on energy affordability and project streamlining here’s another possibility: Restore funding to the Grid Deployment Office, a Department of Energy office tasked with accelerating the regional transmission buildout that is essential to meeting growing energy demand by providing upgrades. Funding for transmission planning & permitting programs fell by roughly 90% between FY2025 and FY 2027 (proposed).

Legislation and resolutions

House Democrats unarguably have a clear mandate to address affordability and Americans’ bipartisan concerns about the development of data centers. They should include in any “New Affordability Agenda” or new federal restrictions on data centers, a broader focus on electricity affordability, utility rates, and renewable energy, among other concerns.

This could take many different forms. One option would be to pass a bill that establishes new incentives for renewable projects and to protect consumers from rising electricity costs due to grid demands from large energy users such as data centers. House Democrats proposed legislation along these lines earlier this year.

On the topic of climate liability, they could pass a bill expressly preserving state and federal statutory and common-law claims for climate-adaptation costs, forcing the President to sign it or veto it on the record. Congress could also adopt a concurrent resolution, and file amicus briefs from members, stating that the Clean Air Act preserves state common-law climate remedies.

title: Windows of Opportunity Open in the States - Legal Planet
description:
These dramatic shifts open up many exciting opportunities for climate and clean energy initiatives.
It is in the state governments where exciting opportunities exist for major policy changes.
The opportunity is biggest in states where Democrats won trifectas: Arizona, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, Michigan, Minnesota and Nevada.
That may be especially important in states like Ohio and Texas where polluters have enjoyed a free hand until now.
States are also going to have to start grappling with climate change risks that many preferred to ignore under Republican climate deniers.
text:
The most exciting new prospects for environmental progress are far outside the Beltway

Summary

In the aftermath of the 2026 election, Democrats in Congress can do a lot to hinder Trump's anti-environmental policies but much less to advance their own climate agenda. The real opportunities for progress are in the states. Consider Texas, a state that has long been under iron GOP control and also the country's biggest emitter of carbon. Democrats will now control all statewide offices and one legislative chamber. Or there's Wisconsin, where Democrats will control the governorship and the legislature. These dramatic shifts open up many exciting opportunities for climate and clean energy initiatives. We can’t foresee all the long-term effects, but we do know that in many places the winds are starting to blow in the right direction.

A small event last Thursday captures this moment of change. The Fifth Circuit heard a challenge to Texas’s 2021 anti-ESG law, which gives the Texas Comptroller sweeping powers to blacklist companies that disfavor fossil fuels. The law was vigorously defended by the state’s current Attorney General. But here’s the thing: The new Texas Attorney General will be Nathan Johnson, a Democrat who has no reason to defend the law. And the new Comptroller will be Sarah Eckhardt, another Democrat.

The new Congress will be a significant thorn in the President’s side. But Trump’s veto power will severely limit its ability to enact policies of its own. It is in the state governments where exciting opportunities exist for major policy changes.

The political configuration and policy potential vary state by state. The opportunity is biggest in states where Democrats won trifectas: Arizona, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, Michigan, Minnesota and Nevada. The last time this happened in Minnesota, the state’s clean energy policies took major steps forward.

But there have been major changes in other states too. Democrats flipped governorships in Georgia, Iowa, Texas, Ohio and Nevada, Democrats may also end up with the governor’s mansion in Alaska and Kansas. They flipped thirteen legislative chambers. Despite intense gerrymandering, Democrats will have the governor and one legislative chamber in Texas, North Carolina, and Georgia.

Given the focus on affordability right now, we may not see new cap and trade systems or bold new climate targets. But the declining costs of solar, wind, and battery storage mean that removing barriers will directly advance affordability. Support for rooftop and balcony solar is likely to be especially popular. We can also expect to see greater environmental enforcement against polluters as new governors look for ways to improve local quality of life. That may be especially important in states like Ohio and Texas where polluters have enjoyed a free hand until now. States are also going to have to start grappling with climate change risks that many preferred to ignore under Republican climate deniers.

This will be a heady time of change in many states. We can’t foresee the long-term effects, but we do know that in many places the winds are starting to blow in the right direction.

text:
Catawba County News

Catawba County joins NC C-PACE program to support business building improvements

Published: November 09, 2026

Catawba County has joined a program that opens new pathways for businesses to finance investments in energy efficiency, renewable measures, resiliency and water conservation.

The Catawba County Board of Commissioners unanimously voted to participate in North Carolina’s Commercial Property Assessed Capital Expenditure program, which allows private property owners to apply for private financing through a voluntary lien placed on property by local government. The program allows for payback periods over the life of the improvements.

The North Carolina C-PACE program was created by the N.C. General Assembly in 2024.

The program offers another financing tool for property owners to improve commercial, industrial, agricultural and multi-family properties with projects related to key areas identified by the program. This includes properties owned by nonprofit, charitable or religious organizations.

The program can help drive economic development in our community and improve properties.

Qualifying projects include:

Energy efficiency measures: projects that reduce energy use and increase efficiency.

Resiliency measures: projects that increase environmental resiliency, including storm retrofits, flood mitigation and stormwater management.

Renewable energy measures: projects that utilize renewable energy sources.

Water conservation measures: projects that decrease water consumption or demand, and that address safe drinking water.

There are no program costs for Catawba County government. C-PACE is administered by the Economic Development Partnership of North Carolina, which works with private capital providers to help interested property owners apply for C-PACE funding.

This initiative supports the Board of Commissioners’ strategic plan by promoting economic development in Catawba County through private investment and job growth.

Catawba County commissioners adopted a resolution of intent to participate in C-PACE on Oct. 19. On Nov. 2, the board held a public hearing, then adopted a final resolution to join the C-PACE program.

As such, the ones that proceed are the ones with a customer who has signed a long contract at a guaranteed minimum bill.
Lazard’s July 2026 numbers show what the credits were worth: unsubsidized utility-scale solar at $40 to $98 per megawatt-hour, with the production tax credit having pulled the low end down to $16.

text:
American utility-scale solar split into two eras on July 4, 2026. Any project that began construction by that date retains its federal tax credits under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act’s transition rule, while any that missed it must be in service by December 31, 2027, or proceed without them. For tax equity, the financing method built on those credits, this is a real ending.

What replaces it is demand: developers now hold more projects than they can build by 2030. As such, the ones that proceed are the ones with a customer who has signed a long contract at a guaranteed minimum bill.

Lazard’s July 2026 numbers show what the credits were worth: unsubsidized utility-scale solar at $40 to $98 per megawatt-hour, with the production tax credit having pulled the low end down to $16. Because that value was written into statute and the money came from the U.S. Treasury, lenders treated it as the most dependable revenue in a project, which let sponsors get by with fewer signed sales contracts for everything else.

Regulators have created a framework for that at speed: DELTa (Database of Emerging Large-Load Tariffs), the quarterly-updated public tariff database maintained by the Smart Electric Power Alliance and the North Carolina (NC) Clean Energy Technology Center, counted 14 large-load tariff approvals across the entire 2018-2024 period.

The year 2025 on its own produced 29. The first half of 2026 produced 23 in only six months, nearly the 2025 full-year total (Figure 1). Thirty-seven states now have a large-load tariff approved or pending. In addition, eligibility thresholds have moved up, with around two-thirds of the 2025 class between 50 and 150 MW.

Put the approved tariffs side by side and a rate archetype appears (Figure 2). Among the 27 approved filings in DELTa that publish both terms—22 distinct rate designs—minimum bills cluster at 80 to 85 percent of contracted demand, and initial contract terms cluster at 12 to 15 years as written, with the four- or five-year load ramp counted inside the term in some tariffs and added on top of it in others.

AEP Ohio charges 85% across an eight-year firm term on top of a four-year ramp. Dominion’s GS-5 charges 85% for distribution and transmission—60% for generation—across 14 years, its four-year ramp counted inside. Indiana Michigan charges 80% over 12 years with a five-year ramp on top. A Tri-State Generation and Transmission analysis of 11 tariffs found security averaging seven years of minimum bills and exit fees averaging five.

These terms are similar to the contracted revenue line a lender asks for: take-or-pay, an investment-grade counterparty, collateral, with a regulator’s approval behind it. The obvious objection is that these commitments run to the utility, not to any particular solar project—which is quite precisely what the next generation of tariffs changes.

A second generation of tariffs converts that contracted demand directly into new clean supply. Google’s Clean Transition Tariff with NV Energy, for example, funds a 115-MW enhanced geothermal plant and credits Google the plant’s energy and capacity value. A similar Google tariff with Xcel in Minnesota covers wind, solar, and storage, and Georgia Power’s 2025 IRP settlement created a Customer-Identified Resource option inside its CARES program. RMI groups these under bring-your-own (BYO) tariffs: the customer pays the full incremental cost of a specific new resource, the resource gets built, and other ratepayers are insulated from the risk.

For solar developers, supply in this market is already set. Wood Mackenzie counts 216 to 240 GWdc of utility-scale solar safe-harbored—begun in time to keep the credits—most of it before year-end 2025, while its base case holds annual additions flat near 43 GWdc through 2031—about five years of building at that rate, so for the next five years, the question is: which of those projects will get built?

There are three ways large-load demand can support a project: the BYO route referenced above, minimum-bill revenue supporting what the utility buys through its resource plan, or, in ERCOT, which has no tariff of this kind, power purchase agreements (PPA) signed directly with developers. Q1 2026 offtake signings ran 6.3 GWdc, up 15% year over year, led by Texas projects with data and technology buyers.

The tariffs also tend to significantly filter out demand that wasn’t real: AEP Ohio’s data-center interconnection queue fell from 30 GW to 13 GW once its tariff required real financial commitments—Enverus puts the first-year cost to a 100-MW facility near $10 million, and as a result, more than half the queue decided it would rather not. This filtering out is useful, as a load that stays and agrees to those terms is one a utility can plan new generation around.

The ITC paid per megawatt-hour, with a project earning the credit whether it had a twelve-year buyer or a term sheet and a prayer. What a large-load tariff pays for, on the other hand, is a customer who has committed to a term and a minimum bill. Those commitments are approved by state commissions rather than written into federal law, so an election changes what is left of the tax credits and does not touch them. In sum, solar developers now have more safe-harbored projects than they can build by 2030, and what increasingly decides which ones go ahead is whether a buyer has signed.

title: Honda to invest $3 billion in new vehicle assembly plant in Ohio - CNBC
description:
MARYSVILLE, Ohio — Honda Motor plans to invest $3 billion to build a new vehicle assembly plant in Ohio, the automaker announced Monday.
The plant is expected to increase Honda’s light-duty vehicle capacity to 1.3 million units annually in the U.S.
It’s the company’s first new mass production U.S. vehicle assembly plant since it opened a facility in Indiana in 2008.
It also opened a $70 million performance vehicle facility in 2016 and a multibillion-dollar joint venture battery plant earlier this year, both in Ohio.
The new Ohio plant is expected to notably boost Honda’s U.S. production and American-produced sales.
text:
MARYSVILLE, Ohio — Honda Motor plans to invest $3 billion to build a new vehicle assembly plant in Ohio, the automaker announced Monday.

Honda said the new plant, which will be near its other facilities in Marysville, Ohio, is expected to begin production in 2029, have a capacity for 240,000 vehicles annually and create more than 2,000 jobs.

The facility is expected to be capable of producing traditional vehicles with internal combustion engines, all-electric vehicles and hybrid models, which have been growing in popularity in the U.S.

The plant is expected to increase Honda’s light-duty vehicle capacity to 1.3 million units annually in the U.S. It currently has 12 manufacturing plants in United States, eight of which produce engines or light-duty vehicles for the auto industry.

It’s the company’s first new mass production U.S. vehicle assembly plant since it opened a facility in Indiana in 2008. It also opened a $70 million performance vehicle facility in 2016 and a multibillion-dollar joint venture battery plant earlier this year, both in Ohio.

“This is not simply an investment in another plant. It is an investment in the future of Honda manufacturing in America,” Bob Nelson, executive vice president of American Honda Motor, said during the announcement at the company’s U.S. heritage center in Ohio.

The auto industry has been trying to localize more production amid President Donald Trump’s tariffs and inflated logistics costs that have cut into profits.

Honda’s plans for a new plant come roughly two weeks after Volkswagen-owned luxury brand Audi announced it would invest more than $4 billion in its first U.S. manufacturing facility in Georgia.

Detroit automakers General Motors and Ford Motor and international automakers Toyota Motor and Hyundai Motor also recently said they will spend billions of dollars on new or updated U.S. facilities.

Honda’s announcement comes after the automaker in May indefinitely suspended an $11 billion investment plan to produce all-electric vehicles and batteries in Canada. It also canceled three planned EVs for the U.S. market.

The new Ohio plant is expected to notably boost Honda’s U.S. production and American-produced sales. Honda said nearly all of its vehicles sold in the U.S., including its Acura luxury brand, were produced in North America, including more than 60% in the U.S.

American Honda Motor Co. executive Jennifer Thomas recently emphasized the Japanese automaker’s commitment to the U.S. and need for additional capacity.

“In order to be competitive in this market, you’re going to need to build products here,” Thomas, senior vice president of corporate affairs, said Oct. 27 in Detroit. “We are focused on trying to maximize the existing capacity that we have, but we are at capacity, and so we’re exploring all options.”

Thomas also warned the automotive industry faces a “catastrophic” scenario if the U.S. and Canada cannot reach a new trade deal by the end of this year, when Trump has threatened to double tariffs on Canadian vehicles and parts from 25% to 50% on Jan. 1 if the two countries don’t reach a deal.

Honda said it has built more than 33 million vehicles and more than 39 million engines in the U.S. since it started auto production in the U.S. in 1982.

The Japanese automaker currently has more than 30,000 employees in the U.S.

text:
Hans Eric Melin, the founder of London-based Circular Energy Storage Research & Consulting (CES), has announced the publication of a report on recycling electric vehicle (EV) lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries and two online workshops tied to the report.

Regarding the findings of the report, “LFP recycling: Who pays for the feed,” and the state of LFP markets, the consultant says, “Recycling pays—just not where, or why, most people think.”

He says the LFP recycling market is evolving at its own pace—but faster than perceived by skeptics—similar to what occurred with lithium-ion EV batteries.

“Almost 10 years ago I spent much of my time explaining that lithium-ion batteries could be recycled, and were being recycled,” Melin says. “The common view in Europe and North America was that it didn’t work, didn’t pay, or would only happen if regulation forced it.”

He continues, “Meanwhile a large, well-developed industry was already running in China, largely unnoticed by the people making those claims.”

Melin says LFP battery recycling “is at exactly that stage now,” adding, “You hear that it isn’t worth recycling unless lithium is expensive. You hear that China only does it thanks to subsidies or shortcuts. Neither holds up.”

The consultant calls the new CES report “one of the most thorough pieces of work we have done at CES,” saying the report “goes down to how the recycling processes actually work and what they cost, and shows why the same process makes money in one part of the world and is very costly in another.”

CES is offering an online workshop on two different days in November to add additional insight and context for report purchasers.

The first workshop will be Thursday, Nov. 12, at 10 a.m. Central European Time, 5 p.m. China Time and 4 a.m. Eastern Time in the U.S.

The second edition of the workshop will be Monday, Nov. 16, at 9 a.m. Eastern Time, 3 p.m. CET and 10 p.m. China Time.

More information about purchasing the report and access to the workshop can be found on the CES website.

In part, Melin says, the report and workshop focus on two different ways of looking at recycling, with one view predominating in Asia and the other (traditionally) in Europe and North America.

While in North America and Europe, companies consider waste management and commodity markets foremost, “In China, where most batteries are made, the question has always been: How do we source our production?” Melin says.

How these viewpoints are considered and measured can affect the evolution of LFP battery recycling beyond China, Melin says.

In Europe and North America, he says, “A lot can be done in how plants are designed and run, in how recyclers, repurposers and battery owners work together, and in policy. That is why we are running a workshop alongside the report: What are the right strategies, given how the industry actually looks today?”

text:
Following Democratic election victories, North Carolina's environmental enforcement policies may see significant changes.

Democrats could strengthen PFAS enforcement by appointing new members to the state's Environmental Management Commission and revisiting discharge permits.

Environmental groups claim N.C. Republicans prioritized business interests over resident health and environmental protection.

While North Carolina Democrats digest their stunning success on Election Day that gave the party control of the N.C. House and touching distance of taking over the N.C. Senate, supporters are wondering what the changes in the state legislature will mean in practice.

One of the issues top of mind for residents, and one that became a campaign issue in the bruising race between Sen. Michael Lee, R-New Hanover, and victorious Democratic challenger Jessica Bichler, was what the changes could mean for environmental enforcement − specifically when it comes to "forever chemicals."

The StarNews first broke the story in 2017 of the chemical discharges into the Cape Fear, which serves as the primary drinking water supply for nearly 500,000 people in Southeastern North Carolina, that couldn't be filtered out by local utilities before the water reached homes and businesses. Since then, testing also has found extensive PFAS contamination in groundwater and the environment across the Cape Fear region.

Formally known as per-and poly-fluoroalkyl substances, PFAS are manmade substances used in a range of products from medical devices to nonstick cookware that don't break down quickly − hence their name forever chemicals − and have been tied to a host of health problems, including several types of cancer, immune suppression issues and organ disruptions.

The GOP-dominated General Assembly has been seen by many as dragging its feet on going after Chemours and other PFAS polluters, in effect placing business interests ahead of the health of residents and the environment.

'So far not done what's necessary'

Republicans have disputed those claims, stating that there needs to be a balanced approach to fixing the problem. They also note that the 2026 budget, authored by the GOP, includes several provisions to help local utilities and funding to continue programs to help private well owners deal with polluted water and to research and remediate PFAS contamination at fire stations.

But environmental groups and grassroots organizations, especially those downstream of Chemours' Fayetteville Works plant roughly 75 miles upstream of Wilmington, say federal and state officials have largely failed to hold the PFAS polluters' feet to the fire and force them to take responsibility for the mess they've created. They've also failed to adopt strong rules that would reduce the contamination and potential future health risks associated with the continued release of forever chemicals into the environment.

"The status quo is not and has not been acceptable," said Jean Zhuang, senior attorney with the Southern Environmental Law Center. "It's clear our state legislature has so far not done what's necessary to protect our communities."

State Rep. Deb Butler said she expects there to be renewed focus on a host of issues, including the state's environmental woes, once Democrats gain some of the levers of power in January 2027.

"People aren't satisfied, and they showed that with their votes," said the Wilmington Democrat who has served in the House for nearly a decade and is likely to have a leadership role in the new-look chamber.

'Real nasty stuff in it'

Steps Democrats in the N.C. House could take to strengthen PFAS enforcement include appointing new members to the state Environmental Management Commission, which has hobbled attempts by state regulators to adopt tougher water quality standards. Legislators also could pressure state officials to tighten discharge permits and requirements under existing rules for PFAS releases.

"Let's keep this stuff out of the environment in the first place," Butler said. "That just makes good common sense."

In a press conference Wednesday, Nov. 4, Gov. Josh Stein, a Democrat, said he was excited about moving North Carolina forward after record voter turnout and was looking forward to working with leaders from both sides of the political aisle.

“Voters across North Carolina have made their voices heard, and together, we restored common sense to the General Assembly," he said. "North Carolinians have sent a clear message: They want real action from their elected officials − leaders who are committed to serving them.

"I look forward to working on the issues that matter the most, from lowering the cost of living to keeping people safe and continuing to invest in the people who make North Carolina the best place to live, work, and raise a family."

The Stein administration in early September 2026 announced a $600 million settlement with Chemours and DuPont over contamination tied to the decades-long production of forever chemicals at Fayetteville Works.

The legal fight to get the companies to pay for clean-up and mitigation efforts has dragged on for years, frustrating residents and local officials. State regulators have been more successful in stopping new discharges from Fayetteville Works by threatening to pull the facility's permits if Chemours didn't clean up its act, but even those actions haven't moved quickly enough for many.

While the settlement represents a step in the right direction, environmental and clean water advocates have said there remains much work to be done to clean up the mess left behind by decades of unregulated dumping of manmade chemicals into North Carolina's environment.

Advocates also say other lingering water quality woes, such as 1.4-dioxane getting discharged in the Piedmont and eventually reaching the Cape Fear River basin, remain to be tackled.

"We're at the end of the river, that's just geography, and we have some real nasty stuff in it," Butler said.

Reporter Gareth McGrath can be reached at GMcGrath@usatodayco.com or @GarethMcGrathSN on X/Twitter. This story was produced with financial support from Journalism Funding Partners. The USA TODAY Network maintains full editorial control of the work.

title: Canada's Budget 2026: Commitments on charging infrastructure and energy policies
description:
Canada's latest federal Budget was tabled on 5th November, with three bodies of policy and commitment that have impact on the future of the EV and EV infrastructure industries in the country.
There are commitments to specific funding for charging infrastructure and for research into advancing charging technology.
The Budget outlines a renewal of the Greening Government Operations Fleet Programme, providing $2.2 million over five years, starting in 2027-28.
The government wants to extend the Clean Technology and Clean Electricity investment tax credits to the end of 2040 rather than 2034, an extension of six years.
Ottawa also wants to expand eligibility for the Clean Electricity investment tax credit to high-voltage intra-provincial transmission lines in each province and other renewable energy and electricity sector projects.
text:
Canada's latest federal Budget was tabled on 5th November, with three bodies of policy and commitment that have impact on the future of the EV and EV infrastructure industries in the country.

There are commitments to specific funding for charging infrastructure and for research into advancing charging technology. Consumers will see a continuation of the EV Affordability Programme, there are government plans to move its own vehicles to zero-emission models, plus there are extended tax credits and wider electricity industry mandates and targets.

Outside the EV industry but having an impact on it, Ottawa has committed to an increase in domestic production of minerals commonly used in batteries such as lithium and nickel.

The government says it will commit CA$587 million (US$415 million) to create a further 55,000 chargepoints starting in 2027-28, with some emphasis on regional targets that should help ensure additional public charging infrastructure is not confined to the most populous areas.

Coming under the climate strategy's electrification section, the continuation of the EV Affordability Programme (EVAP) has been announced, but the Budget does not detail any specific future changes in funding, eligibility or rebates. At present, the country's EVAP is a federally run point-of-sale incentive that began formally at the end of March this year. The scheme is due to run until March 31, 2031 at the latest (earlier, if allocated funds are exhausted). Incentives as they stand at present are up to $5,000 for battery-electric and fuel-cell electric vehicles, and up to $2,500 for PHEVs.

The Budget outlines a renewal of the Greening Government Operations Fleet Programme, providing $2.2 million over five years, starting in 2027-28. This is an initiative designed to ensure federal agencies move vehicle fleets to zero-emission vehicles in line with the government's broader Greening Government Strategy targets, released in December 2017.

As part of the wider National Electricity Strategy, a $50 billion electricity investment programme, clean electricity tax incentives and proposed regulatory changes provide the energy policy with regards to electrifying transportation – a remit that includes but extends well outside EVs. The government wants to extend the Clean Technology and Clean Electricity investment tax credits to the end of 2040 rather than 2034, an extension of six years. "Combined, these measures are expected to cost $2.4 billion from 2027-28 to 2030-31 and $36.1 billion from 2031-32 to 2041-42," the Budget document states.

Ottawa also wants to expand eligibility for the Clean Electricity investment tax credit to high-voltage intra-provincial transmission lines in each province and other renewable energy and electricity sector projects. Specific mention is given to a new tranche of funding for the Smart Renewables and Electrification Pathways Programme, a $4.5-billion programme launched in 2021 to fund grid modernisation, energy storage and renewable energy deployment in the country.

text:
Demand for commercial trucks has surged

US fleet operators are buying: 79% expect their fleet to grow over the next 12 months, and more than one-third project a fleet increase of 10% or more (see Figure 1). Elevated fuel prices, freight demand recovery, and aging fleets are the primary demand drivers.

The lesson from the last upcycle is that availability wins. Whichever OEMs can quote and deliver on credible lead times will take market share from competitors. To win those deals, leading OEMs must ensure post-pandemic supply chain resilience programs are fully operational so dealers can mobilize to win on the front lines.

Figure 1

TCO remains king—and has become more important than ever

When asked what matters most in a purchase decision, operators were clear: economics. Fuel efficiency (45%), reliability/uptime (42%), and TCO (37%) topped the list, consistent with prior studies. However, when asked how the relative importance of purchase criteria has changed over the last three years, TCO jumped to the top spot alongside fuel efficiency (see Figure 2).

Figure 2

“Reliability, total cost of ownership, fuel efficiency and sustainability have simply become more important.”

US fleet operator

TCO and fuel economics have become more critical as fuel costs and tariffs continue to squeeze fleet margins. Nearly half of operators report moderate or significant cost impacts over the last year due to tariffs and trade policies, while 70% cite fuel prices as their top operational challenge. In our survey, no OEM earned an “excellent” rating for fuel efficiency.

Today’s “gas math” puts every OEM’s market share at risk. Despite posting high Net Promoter Scores (NPS), more than one-third of operators say they would switch OEMs to improve their economics. Willingness to switch increases with fleet size: 41% of the largest, most sophisticated fleets say they would change OEMs.

Meanwhile, 49% of fleet operators believe electric trucks now offer superior TCO compared to diesel when certain enablers, such as charging infrastructure, are in place (see Figure 3). Infrastructure buildout takes time and TCO parity remains highly dependent on use cases—but those buffers are temporary. The industry is approaching a tipping point; as TCO becomes increasingly important, more operators’ scales will tip toward EVs for select use cases.

Figure 3

The rise of Tesla

Passenger vehicle companies famously miscalculated the Tesla threat, investing heavily in new EV platforms and pushing customers toward adoption before they were ready (with government incentives throwing fuel on the fire). In trucking, the risk is the opposite. Customers see the economic benefits of electric trucks and want to transition fast. Fleet operators tend to be more sophisticated, economically driven buyers compared to passenger vehicle customers. If the math pencils out and necessary infrastructure is in place, the market could see a meaningful shift to electric trucks in the coming years.

Roughly two-thirds of customers say they would consider a Tesla Semi, and over a quarter describe themselves as “actively interested,” with those buyers skewing toward states like California and Texas (see Figure 4).

Consideration and purchase intent are not the same—and the gap between them is typically wide. However, interest is broad enough that OEMs cannot afford to take a wait-and-see approach. Incumbents should map their customer exposure and accelerate EV programs to stay competitive, keeping in mind that Tesla’s play in the truck segment is likely to extend further than semi sales.

Figure 4

Double disruption: How autonomous and electric might travel together

Our survey found widespread interest in autonomous driving, especially among larger fleet operators that represent a significant portion of trucks on the road. Fleet operators cite safety (59%), reliability (44%), and clarity on liability (42%) as the primary barriers to adopting autonomous vehicle (AV) technology sooner (see Figure 5).

Figure 5

Many operators express interest in both electrification and autonomy (see Figure 6). This overlap is most pronounced in regions with high pilot activity, such as Texas and California, and where routes are well-matched with these technologies (e.g., return-to-base routes, shorter routes, and corridors with available charging infrastructure). This could foreshadow an integrated push into autonomous, electric fleets by a player like Tesla, forcing traditional OEM-AV partnerships to reassess their competitive positioning.

Figure 6

Based on common adoption criteria and route characteristics, the trucking industry could adopt AV technology faster than the passenger vehicle market.

Route variance

Diverse daily routes (outside of typical commutes)

Highly repeatable routes on well-known corridors

Buying decision

Emotional purchase influenced by branding and marketing

Economically driven decision based on per-mile operating cost

Asset utilization

Small percentage of total time in use, reducing the value of autonomy

High percentage of total time in use, increasing the relative value of autonomy

Operating environment

Mixed urban/rural routes with many edge cases (e.g., closed roads, animals/children)

High mix of on-highway driving with simpler, more predictable conditions

Customer base

Highly fragmented

More concentrated, professional fleets

Severity of failure

Lighter and smaller vehicles with less impact in a crash (and generally able to stop faster than trucks)

Heavy, large vehicles that travel at a higher average speed and have slower stopping times

Regulatory environment

Suitable for state-by-state regulations

Often includes intrastate travel that requires multiple state or federal approvals

Six strategic imperatives for major trucking players

1. Maximize the upswing. Leading OEMs will mobilize marketing, dealer enablement, lead-time management, and capacity planning now to protect and grow share while demand is strong.

2. Win on TCO. OEMs must aggressively reduce costs and product complexity. Fleet operators explicitly stated their willingness to switch brands for better economics, meaning cost management will drive share just as much as margin.

3. Treat Tesla as a fundamental threat. Identify which customers are most exposed to Tesla, accounting for use cases, geography, and infrastructure availability. Accelerate EV programs to match the threat and stay competitive. Traditional OEMs can also lean into existing service and dealer network advantages.

4. Don’t sleep on autonomy. AV interest is strong, but adoption is currently restrained by safety, reliability, and liability concerns. Because the economics are so compelling, these issues will eventually be resolved—making it a question of when and where adoption will accelerate first.

5. Define a flexible strategic roadmap. The dual forces of electric and AVs will drive significant disruption in the coming years. The exact timing is uncertain, so OEMs must learn how to read signposts along the adoption curve that indicate adoption is slowing down or speeding up. OEM roadmaps should account for a range of potential strategic outcomes, from slow uptake to the perfect storm of rapid, dual adoption. Winners will be ready to act once they see the green lights they’ve been watching for.

6. Fix pain points in the buying and service experiences. Prioritize pricing transparency, order visibility, and shorter lead times to improve the sales process while simultaneously investing in parts availability and repair turnaround times to protect uptime and defend core profit pools, such as telematics.

The US commercial truck market sits on the cusp of significant disruption. Is the sky falling? No—but the winds are shifting, and OEMs that fail to adapt to technological and market changes risk being left in the dust.

title: COP31 Dispatch - November 6, 2026 | Newsletter | EESI
description:
Fossil Fuel Roadmap: Early this week, the COP30 Presidency unveiled a long-awaited roadmap for transitioning away from fossil fuels (TAFF).
The TAFF roadmap also made calls for accelerated collective action on an energy transition—a TAFF Mutirão—including through future COPs and global stocktakes (GSTs).
Since the roadmap’s publication, Colombia, France, the Netherlands, Germany, and the UK have prepared national TAFF plans, with additional countries expected to make similar announcements over the course of COP31.
The IPCC has indicated that it intends to reconvene as soon as possible, but it is unclear if that will happen before the end of 2026.
EESI Podcast: Engendering Durable Climate Solutions Through a Gender-Responsive Lens at COP31
text:
Fossil Fuel Roadmap: Early this week, the COP30 Presidency unveiled a long-awaited roadmap for transitioning away from fossil fuels (TAFF). A key component of the roadmap is the Belém Readiness Approach, a tool that measures countries’ exposure to fossil fuels and their capacity to manage the energy transition, based on that country’s energy demand, energy supply, and economic dependence on fossil fuels. This assessment, which can be tailored to each country’s unique needs and capacities, will help national leaders identify strengths, opportunities, and vulnerabilities. The TAFF roadmap also made calls for accelerated collective action on an energy transition—a TAFF Mutirão—including through future COPs and global stocktakes (GSTs). Since the roadmap’s publication, Colombia, France, the Netherlands, Germany, and the UK have prepared national TAFF plans, with additional countries expected to make similar announcements over the course of COP31.

EESI Fact Sheet: Proposals to Reduce Fossil Fuel Subsidies

Context-Setting: In April 2026, representatives from 57 countries gathered in Santa Marta, Colombia, for the first International Conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels. Co-hosted by Colombia and the Netherlands, this conference was born from a promise made by the COP30 Presidency following a failure to include a fossil fuel transition roadmap in the formal negotiation agenda. Countries in attendance worked with a panel of experts to begin developing energy transition roadmaps. Next year’s conference will be held in Tuvalu and co-hosted by Ireland.

Deforestation Roadmap: The COP30 Presidency also published a roadmap for halting and reversing deforestation and forest degradation. The plan highlights conservation, sustainable forest management, reforestation, and combating deforestation and degradation as key pathways for advancing this goal, and, like the TAFF roadmap, it can be tailored to countries’ unique characteristics and challenges. The roadmap also estimates that $300 billion will be needed annually by 2030 to meet forest-related climate goals.

Checking in on NDCs: Last week, the UNFCCC secretariat released its annual synthesis report on countries’ NDCs. The report commended that, since the conclusion of the first GST, “climate action is being broadened, including through more comprehensive approaches, and more integrated into and deeply embedded across economies and societies.” At the same time, it warned that projected emission reductions continue to be “substantially off track from the reductions required by the science to keep the goal of limiting temperature rise to 1.5°C this century within reach and to keep temporary overshoot as short and shallow as possible.” As of the publication of this newsletter, 155 countries have submitted a new NDC, representing 76% of global emissions. Notable recent submissions include those from Albania, Chad, the Gambia, Grenada, Madagascar, Niger, Oman, Palestine, and the Philippines.

Missing the Mark: In September, UNEP published Limiting Overshoot: Navigating exceedance of 1.5°C and pathways towards return. The report affirms that the world will surpass the Paris Agreement’s Article 2 goal of limiting warming to 1.5°C (2.7°F) above average pre-industrial temperatures, and that, under existing conditions, global warming will instead reach 2.6°C (4.7°F) by 2100. The authors emphasize that this “overshoot” will happen in the next few years; that every fraction of a degree of warming matters, and that countries should invest in mitigation as much and as quickly as possible; and that curbing warming now necessitates net-negative—not net-zero—emissions, which will require increased investment in carbon dioxide removal technologies.

EESI Briefing: Exploring the Policy Landscape of Carbon Dioxide Removal

Mind the Gap: A month following its Overshoot report, UNEP published its annual Emissions Gap Report, designed to highlight the difference between climate commitments made and actual progress achieved. The 2026 report, titled The Point of Return, works off of the Overshoot report’s urgent calls for emission cuts, calling the exceedance of 1.5°C (2.7°F) in warming “unavoidable.” UNEP authors also found that temperature projections have only increased since the prior year’s report and that global greenhouse gas emissions in 2025 were similar to those in 2024, but that it is still possible to close the emissions gap.

AI Finds Its COP Niche: Last week, the Turkish Presidency launched the Antalya Artificial Intelligence Pledge. The pledge declares a “shared ambition to make AI part of the climate solution” and outlines voluntary commitments for signatories, such as requiring data centers to be powered by clean energy and improving monitoring and reporting on the environmental impacts of AI. It also sets a goal of reviewing progress on AI commitments next year at COP32. The COP31 president-designate will formally announce the pledge next week in Antalya, and invite countries, subnational governments, international organizations, businesses, investors, financial institutions, research institutions, and civil society to sign on. In a speech to the UN General Assembly in September, UNFCCC Executive Secretary Simon Stiell criticized AI, citing that it increases greenhouse gas emissions, household energy costs, disinformation, and wealth inequality.

EESI Briefing: Artificial Intelligence: Implications for Energy and the Environment

Biodiversity COP: The COP17 biodiversity summit in Yerevan, Armenia, concluded last week with agreement on all major negotiation texts. These talks marked the halfway point to the 2030 deadlines of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework and resulted in the first global review of the framework’s nature targets—similar to the GST process under the Paris Agreement. UN Secretary-General António Guterres launched the State of Biodiversity Action report ahead of COP17 to help inform the global review. The report detailed widespread engagement with the framework, but warned that engagement has not translated to ambition, implementation, or financing. Countries are currently falling short on 22 out of 23 targets to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030.

EESI Podcast: Polling Shows the Bipartisan Nature of Natural Climate Solutions

IPCC Scheduling Conflict: Last month, the 65th session of the IPCC failed to produce a schedule for its seventh assessment report on the state of climate change knowledge—a setback that could end up undermining the second GST, which will start at COP31. Countries gathered in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, only to suspend talks after a week of heated disagreement regarding the assessment cycle’s timeline and budget. The IPCC has indicated that it intends to reconvene as soon as possible, but it is unclear if that will happen before the end of 2026.

Girl Math: According to the secretariat’s latest gender composition report, female representation on constituted bodies (decision-making and technical bodies) under the UNFCCC currently averages 44%—up from 40% in 2025—with 7 out of 17 of those bodies achieving gender balance. In keeping with the expectations laid out in the Belém gender action plan, the report also includes gender composition data on party delegates who received funding through the trust fund for participation in the UNFCCC process.

text:
WASHINGTON, Nov 9 (Reuters) – A sweeping bipartisan energy bill has unexpectedly emerged as the US Congress’ first test of how to tackle public anger over and rising electricity costs, which helped to power Democrats to a landslide election victory last week.

The legislation, years in the making and due to come before the Senate for debate on Monday, would speed approvals for new power plants and transmission lines, while requiring large data center operators to bear more of the cost of grid upgrades needed to serve them.

Supporters say the bill may be Congress’ best near-term opportunity to address the costs of the AI infrastructure build-out. But some Democrats, who campaigned on promises to rein in data centers and whose party will control both houses of Congress next year, are skeptical of provisions they say could encourage even more construction.

The chances of passage for the bill, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, have fallen to 25% versus 40% before the election, according to investment firm TD Cowen.

But the fight may help to define the data center debate with Democrats expected to introduce a range of bills targeting AI and data center development when they take control of Congress next year. Fears of stepped-up AI scrutiny led to a steep market selloff in technology shares last week.

“Democrats ran and won on affordability and data center accountability, and BAAJA will allow us to start delivering immediately on both of those election promises,” US Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, the top Democrat on the Senate’s environment committee and one of the bill’s authors, told Reuters.

“We’d be silly not to take this win.”

The legislation would also establish protections designed to prevent households, businesses and other utility customers from being left with the bill if projects fail.

“The language that’s in BAAJA that’s focused on data centers is a good first step,” said Jeremy Harrell, chief executive of ClearPath Action, a conservative clean energy advocacy group. “Those are policies where Republicans and Democrats agree.”

President , who has endorsed the bill, highlighted its data center provisions in a social media post on Sunday while urging the Senate to pass it.

“Remember, China will take any Data Center that we don’t want, and pay lots of money for it,” Trump said.

The Data Center Coalition, an industry trade group, has not endorsed the bill. Representatives for the group did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

PASSAGE UNCERTAIN

BAAJA’s passage, however, is far from assured. It faces opposition from environmental and tribal groups who say the legislation weakens environmental reviews and undermines tribal sovereignty.

“It would be highly ironic if the first action Congress took after an election largely defined by opposition to data centers would be to make it easier to build them,” said author and environmentalist Bill McKibben.

The bill’s authors unveiled a package of amendments on Saturday that they intend to introduce to address some of those concerns, but several environmental groups, including the Sierra Club, said the changes would not resolve their objections.

Some Democrats in Congress have also expressed concerns with the bill, including House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become speaker next year. Jeffries told Politico on Friday that the bill falls short on environmental protections and needs input from House Democrats.

TD Cowen said Democrats’ resounding election victory “likely emboldens voices arguing the bill gives ⁠too many concessions to (oil and gas).”

Senator Ron Wyden, an Oregon Democrat, said on Friday that Democrats should use their leverage after the election to negotiate a different approach.

“Democrats have a unique opportunity to negotiate a deal that will reduce red tape for all new energy projects to bring down Americans’ energy costs without substantial risk of political interference,” Wyden said in a statement.

Some analyses estimate the bill could also help to reduce emissions associated with data center operations.

Rhodium Group found that BAAJA’s transmission and permitting reforms could allow more data center demand to be served through an increasingly clean electric grid rather than dedicated gas-fired power plants, reducing associated greenhouse-gas emissions by 31% to 90%, depending on the mix of power sources.

Investment bank ING said sweeping federal legislation to rein in data center construction remains unlikely while Trump is in office, since he and his administration view them as essential for the US to compete with China.

ING also cited disagreements over how much authority should reside with states versus Washington.

Joseph Majkut, who leads the energy security and climate program at the bipartisan think tank Center for Strategic and International Studies, said the measure is important for affordability and governing data center growth. “The provisions on data center costs might save the bill,” he said.

(Reporting by Valerie Volcovici and Nichola Groom; Editing by Timothy Gardner and Edmund Klamann)

U.S.-based X-Energy, which makes gas-cooled small modular reactors (SMRs), has teamed up with Fluor, an engineering and project management company, to build the former’s second nuclear power plant. The 320 MWe facility planned for Richland, Washington State, is scheduled to have X-Energy’s four Xe-100 small modular reactors.

The increasing demand for carbon-free energy is bringing back nuclear energy in a new format. Instead of building large-scale nuclear power plants, nuclear startups are working to build reactors at scale in a factory and connect modules to improve the capacity of the power plant.

The idea has been around for a while but has gathered steam in recent years, and SMRs have received approvals from the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (US NRC).

Maryland-based X-energy is one such SMR maker in the U.S.; it has not only received regulatory approval but is also close to securing a building permit for its first nuclear power plant in South Texas.

The company is now making its next big move in the northwest by deploying four of its Xe-100 SMRs at the Cascade Advanced Energy Facility in Washington State.

What is the Cascade Advanced Energy Facility?

First announced in 2024, the Cascade Advanced Energy Facility is a joint project between Amazon and X-energy near the Columbia Generating Station in Richland, Washington.

The project will feature X-energy’s Xe-100 SMRs that can generate 80 MW of energy per module and boast passive safety systems that prevent the reactor from overheating.

More from Energy

See All

At the core of the power plant is the high-temperature gas-cooled reactor, which uses helium as a coolant and TRISO fuel, which is embedded inside a graphite matrix, the size of a billiard ball.

Xe-100 reactors can be refueled while online, and four such units are planned at Richmond; they will generate 320 MW of electricity. The site will seek a license for 12 modules, meaning that after complete expansion in the future, the facility will generate 960 MW of electricity. Power utilities may purchase up to 50 percent of the energy generated at the site once it is fully operational.

Teaming up with Fluor

X-energy has teamed up with Fluor to provide engineering, design development, supply chain and other services for the Cascade Energy Facility. However, the association of the two organizations goes back to X-energy’s first power plant at Dow’s UCC Seadrift Operations in South Texas.

“The Cascade Advanced Energy Facility represents an important step forward in the deployment of next-generation nuclear energy,” said Pierre Bechelany, Fluor’s Business Group President of Energy Solutions. “Fluor is proud to bring decades of nuclear expertise and project execution experience to support X-energy and its partners in advancing this innovative project.”

“The success of our projects begins with working as one team, building on each other’s expertise to drive toward scale,” said Dragan Popovic, Global Chief Operating Officer at X-energy, in a press release.

“Repeated execution with partners of Fluor’s quality helps us build that expertise in real time, so that every lesson we carry forward supports greater efficiency in design, licensing, and construction.”

X-energy is working towards a goal of 11.5GW of commercial deployment, the equivalent of installing 144 Xe-100s. Of these, 5 GW is to be deployed by 2039, and Cascade Advanced Energy Facility is the one of the first projects in that direction.

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

RALEIGH (November 9, 2026) – With nearly 87,000 North Carolina households at risk of losing critical energy bill assistance in less than two months, the NC Justice Center, Southern Environmental Law Center, Democracy Green, and a coalition of 27 additional consumer, housing, environmental, faith, and community organizations are calling on Duke Energy to renew its Customer Assistance Program (CAP) and meet with coalition leaders before November 20 to discuss how to extend the program before it expires on December 31.

In a letter to Duke Energy State President Kendal C. Bowman, the coalition urges Duke to seek approval from the North Carolina Utilities Commission to continue CAP beyond its initial three-year pilot. The coalition also requests a meeting with Duke’s executive regulatory and customer service leadership to discuss concrete procedural pathways for extending the program, including filing for an interim extension before the end of the year.

CAP provides eligible households with a $42 monthly credit on their electric bills, along with access to weatherization assistance and other no-cost energy-efficiency programs. The program was developed through years of collaboration between Duke Energy, consumer advocates, and other stakeholders to create a sustainable approach to energy affordability. Allowing the program to expire would be a devastating loss for the households who depend on this program and for the future of energy affordability in North Carolina.

“In a time of an energy affordability crisis, it is horrifying that Duke Energy would discontinue the only recurring direct assistance program it offers to help lower electricity bills for our state’s most vulnerable customers,” said Peter Gilbert, Director of Litigation at the NC Justice Center.

“If Duke does not move quickly, tens of thousands of our struggling neighbors will face a dramatic bill increase right after the Christmas season, when power bills are often at their highest,” said David Neal, Senior Attorney at the Southern Environmental Law Center. “We should be building on the success of the Customer Assistance Program, making sure these families get access to energy-saving weatherization and energy efficiency services on top of regular bill-payment assistance.”

Democracy Green Co-Founders Prof. La’Meshia Whittington and Ms. Sanja Whittington shared the following statement:

“True energy fairness for all requires solutions that meet disaster-affected communities where they live. Duke Energy’s proposal to rely on one-time payments or restrictive weatherization leaves critical coverage gaps, excluding renters and families whose storm-damaged roofs or mold issues prevent them from qualifying for assistance. One-time emergency aid cannot resolve an ongoing affordability crisis.

“Preserving the Customer Assistance Program is essential to ensure our neighbors can maintain basic electric service. Families recovering from disaster need consistent bill relief, without eligibility barriers that put help beyond reach when they need it most.”
