text:
The fight to bring rare earth metal technologies to the United States’ shores has made its way to SMU’s campus.

What pushed it here? A $25 million dollar research grant.

Saeed Salehi, the Herman Brown Chair of Mechanical Engineering at SMU, was awarded $19.3 million in federal funding from the U.S. Department of Energy as part of the department’s Mine of the Future initiative. United States Energy Secretary Chris Wright announced the funding in a visit to the campus on Sept. 10, meeting with students and university officials to discuss the project.

Salehi will receive a combined $25 million in research funding from the government and industry partners, the largest individual research funding commitment in SMU history. SMU was one of four organizations to receive this grant.

“I think ours was one of the novel [proposals] because in the actual response to the office represented, the secretary of energy came himself,” Salehi said. “So this project was sort of a poster child of that funding, that this is what we’re trying to do.

The goal of Salehi’s project, the Well-to-Mine Proving Ground, is to take oil and gas fracking technologies and apply them to rare earth mining. In traditional oil and gas fracking, underground wells are stimulated by injecting high pressure liquid into bedrock to release trapped oil and natural gas energy. Salehi plans to apply this method to rare earth mining by developing the world’s first synthetic mine that will emulate real mining conditions to test fracking technologies.

Rare earth mining is used to obtain critical minerals and metals like copper and lithium, which are used in the production of things like cell phones, computers, and cars. The U.S. currently relies on imports from foreign countries for over half of its consumption of rare earth metals and minerals, according to the U.S. Department of Energy.

“We are under geopolitical risks that if those countries or foreign governments stopped importing those [critical minerals] to the U.S., we have to stop manufacturing a lot of these things that we have today,” Salehi said.

Salehi has been working at SMU since July 2024, and he has worked in teaching and research for 20 years, beginning his career in the energy industry.

“I have industry experience and try to come with that perspective when I teach,” Salehi said. “That’s my passion, teaching students on different aspects of what type of energies exist, what are the differences.”

The Department of Energy gave out $73 million in federal funding to four organizations in early September to develop domestic testing grounds for new mining technologies. Salehi specializes in subsurface energy, and said that the U.S. has “fallen behind” in its mining technology.

“In a nutshell, you can think of this as a matter of daily livelihood, of world dependence on these advanced technologies,” Salehi said.

Salehi’s research plans to build the synthetic mine inside of a full-scale oil and gas drilling facility in Navasota, Texas, a small town about 70 miles northwest of Houston. The mine will serve as a “digital twin” to show the capabilities of these new mining technologies and will serve as the bedrock for predictive maintenance in the mining industry.

SMU received its Carnegie Classification R1 status in 2025, which requires the university to spend at least $50 million in research and development per year. The university reported $70 million in research expenditures in 2025, but Nair expects SMU to go beyond $100 million within a year or two.

According to Nair, Salehi’s well-to-mine project is a step in the right direction.

“We need to start somewhere, but in the last four years, we had doubled our research expenditure. That’s the trajectory I’m interested in,” said Suku Nair, SMU’s vice provost for research and chief innovation officer. “Next time, when another $20 million grant happens, people think, ‘Okay, that’s usual stuff. It’s not an anomaly,’ which I guarantee is going to happen.”

The federal funding is just one of a number of investments in SMU’s energy programs. In 2025, the O’Donnell foundation donated $60 million to create a new Energy Science, Innovation and Enterprise program as well as a new honors fund at SMU. That donation was the second largest in university history.

The Well-to-Mine project will enlist multiple SMU undergraduate and PhD students to assist in the research. Salehi said he will hire at least 20 undergraduate students, and will recruit more students next semester and over the summer. The sponsoring organizations will take the next six months to review the project paperwork, and then Salehi will have three years to complete his research.

“I would say my goal is to engage as many [students] as possible,” Salehi said.

This dedication to student involvement is a common theme throughout Salehi’s research and teaching. Salehi already has around six students working on a similar project in his lab, and according to Nair, he will train over 10,000 students for workforce development over the course of the well-to-mine project.

For senior engineering student Ben McBride, Salehi’s desire for student involvement in this project comes as no surprise.

McBride first approached Salehi for research opportunities his sophomore year as he was trying to fill his resume. Salehi placed McBride and his research partner on their own project for a Canadian oil and gas company.

“When we met with Dr. Salehi, he was like, ‘All right, this is what I want y’all to do. This is going to be y’all’s research,’” McBride said. “His whole point was like, ‘I don’t want to be micromanaging y’all. Y’all need to be leaders and figure it out yourselves.’”

McBride did not work on Salehi’s current research project, but Salehi invited both McBride and McBride’s research partner, Thomas Couvillion, to be on the student panel when the U.S. Energy Secretary came to SMU in September. During the event, Secretary Wright shared how Salehi’s research will be used to advance the United States’s position as a leader in fine earth mining.

“The coolest part about being on that panel was actually being a part of a conversation that has a massive geopolitical impact,” McBride said. “I was actually seeing policy being put into action.”

Salehi recognizes the responsibility his research holds for future mining technologies, but says he is ultimately proud of his team for what they have achieved so far.

“I’m very proud of the institute, the leadership, the students team. I think we have a much larger impact than we think,” Salehi said. “Sometimes we think that maybe we are known in Texas or in DFW, but we are known nationally.”

name: Congress
title: Ten Ways Congress Could Defund War to Fund Climate Solutions
description:
Trump has requested an unprecedented $1.5 trillion war budget for FY 2027.
While the Trump administration perpetuates war and seeks oil riches in Venezuela and beyond, communities around the country are reeling from severe storms, flooding, wildfires and other climate disasters.
On top of the devastating human costs, excessive war spending worsens both the affordability and climate crises, fuels data center expansion, and empowers billionaires and oil executives who profit from endless war and climate collapse.
The National Energy Assistance Directors Association has testified that adequate spending on LIHEAP would be $7 billion in FY 2027.
Despite this, the Trump Administration has zeroed-out the budget for Conservation Technical Assistance for the second year in a row.
text:
Trump has requested an unprecedented $1.5 trillion war budget for FY 2027. The first step in achieving this record-shattering budget includes a $250 billion increase to last year’s base war budget of $900 billion, to $1.15 trillion (the rest would come from separate legislation). While the Trump administration perpetuates war and seeks oil riches in Venezuela and beyond, communities around the country are reeling from severe storms, flooding, wildfires and other climate disasters.

Congress should oppose any increase in Pentagon spending, which is fueling the immoral, illegal, and unpopular war on Iran and ongoing genocide in Gaza. On top of the devastating human costs, excessive war spending worsens both the affordability and climate crises, fuels data center expansion, and empowers billionaires and oil executives who profit from endless war and climate collapse. More money will not fix a bad foreign policy strategy; it only throws more gasoline on our already burning world. Here are ten better investments than adding $250 billion to the endless war chest:

10 Investments Totaling $250 Billion that Would Address the Affordability and Climate Crises Instead of Fuel Endless War

A $250 billion investment in solutions for working families instead of war profiteers would transform millions of lives. This isn’t just a moral imperative; investing in climate solutions results in greater economic benefits and job creation than dollar-for-dollar investment in the Pentagon. It’s also about the integrity of our democracy. Voters want Congress to invest in making life better for our families, our environment, and our futures on this planet – not bombing families abroad.

How does unaccountable military spending worsen the affordability and climate crises?

Military-related operations – from combat, to daily training, to manufacturing – are environmentally devastating. The military’s degradation and pollution of water, land, and air is a leading cause of public health crises near military sites at home and globally.

The Pentagon is the world’s largest institutional oil consumer and fossil fuel emitter. The U.S. is already a global outlier, responsible for the vast majority of greenhouse gas emissions that are warming our world – and doing the least about it. Instead of investing resources as the world’s wealthiest nation into transitioning away from oil, the Trump Administration is now using ‘national security’ as a justification to drill and burn even more climate-destroying carbon. Military-related carbon pollution will likely worsen as carbon-intensive data centers become more integrated into the U.S. national security apparatus.

The Pentagon budget eats away at investments that would make our communities less susceptible and more resilient to climate crises. In 2025, the average U.S. taxpayer paid $4,049 for weapons and war vs. just $394 for the Environmental Protection Agency, our National Parks, and Energy Efficiency and Renewable Energy programs combined. That’s 10 times more taxpayer dollars going towards endless war than to protecting our environment and ensuring a livable future for our children and the planet.

For questions, please contact Hanna Homestead (hanna@ips-dc.org). Special thanks to Basav Sen for his generous feedback. Download a PDF of this analysis here.

Sources and Methodology

Transition jobs from the war economy to a green economy: Heidi Peltier’s policy brief, De-Militarizing the Federal Budget and Recalibrating the Labor Market, lays out a $100 billion plan for a just transition for military workers and communities that invests in jobs, green energy, and public infrastructure.

Install solar panels on 3.5 million homes, boosting residential solar installation by more than 50%: We use cost benchmark data from the Department of Energy (table 2) to calculate that the average cost of installing residential solar photovoltaic (PV) systems is $23,600 per household. Given that in 2026, approximately 6 million homes have residential PV, installing 3.5 million more systems would boost overall installation by more than 50%. According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA), the residential housing sector accounts for about 20% of total U.S. carbon dioxide emissions.

Expand green affordable housing: Homelessness in the United States is at a record-high. A Climate and Community Institute (CCI) report, Green Social Housing at Scale, proposes the creation of a Green Social Housing Development Authority (Green SHDA) that would tackle housing insecurity and the climate crisis by delivering 1,390,000 affordable, climate-resilient, fossil fuel–free housing units (and creating more than 300,000 jobs). The proposal requires $30 billion in annual appropriations.

Ensure public transit remains safe by fulling-funding its maintenance budget: Functioning public transit is critical to millions of people’s lives and their ability to access workplaces and education. Investing in public transit is also essential to decarbonizing our economy. The maintenance budget for the nation’s public transit system is facing a $152 billion budget gap over the next 10 years that could lead to greater delays and unsafe conditions. An additional $15.2 billion per year would close that gap, ensuring public transit remains functional.

Fully fund the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA): Instead of slashing the EPA budget by 52%, Congress should fully fund $12 billion that advocates say the agency needs to protect our air, land, and water.

Restore electric vehicle (EV) tax credit to 500,000 people: The clean vehicle credit (CVC) was an essential mechanism to transition away from fossil-fuel based vehicles and towards cleaner, more affordable transit options. It provided a credit of up to $7,500 for individuals purchasing new electric vehicles (EVs), subject to restrictions. In 2023, 488,000 households claimed the clean vehicle credit. However, Congress allowed the program to expire in 2025, leaving individuals who would like to purchase an affordable, fossil-fuel free vehicle without assistance as gas prices continue to hit record highs. For $3.75 billion, Congress could provide the full CVC tax credit to another 500,000 people.

Fully-fund the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP): LIHEAP is an essential program that provides federally funded assistance to lower-income individuals and families to reduce the costs of home energy bills and weatherization efforts to improve energy efficiency. The program is more important than ever, as gas prices rise due to the US war on Iran, extreme weather events become more common due to climate change, and more and more people across the country fall into poverty due to increasing wealth inequality and affordability challenges. The National Energy Assistance Directors Association has testified that adequate spending on LIHEAP would be $7 billion in FY 2027. However, the Trump Administration has proposed cutting LIHEAP funding to $3.6 billion – about half of what’s needed. We proposed doubling this budget to bring spending up to where it belongs.

Restore funding for renewable energy and climate resilience projects on Tribal lands: Last year, the Trump Administration cut approximately $1.5 billion in federal funding earmarked for tribal renewable energy and climate resilience projects. We propose restoring that funding.

Fully fund land conservation assistance for farmers and rural communities: USDA conservation programs are utilized by farmers and small-landowners across the United States to adopt conservation practices that enhance water quality, increase resilience, and reduce harmful emissions. These programs are highly impactful and in high demand, with more than half of eligible recipients turned away due to lack of adequate funding. Hundreds of farm coalitions and conservation groups have advocated for fulling funding conservation assistance, which they say requires at least $1.05 billion. Despite this, the Trump Administration has zeroed-out the budget for Conservation Technical Assistance for the second year in a row. We suggest restoring it to at least the requested amount of $1.05 billion.

text:
NPCA is calling on the Senate to reject this bill and take up a more balanced approach in the next Congress.

Washington, DC – As the Senate prepares to vote on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 and its sponsors’ substitute amendment, the National Parks Conservation Association (NPCA) is urging senators to oppose the bill in its current form. The legislation trades too many protections under bedrock laws that protect our national parks and their air, water, wildlife and cultural heritage. NPCA shares the bill’s sponsors’ urgency on addressing climate change and expanding clean energy but cannot support a bill that prioritizes those goals at the expense of our national parks. NPCA is calling on the Senate to reject this bill and take up a more balanced approach in the next Congress.

Statement by Daniel Hart, Director of Energy and Climate Policy for the National Parks Conservation Association (NPCA):

“Climate change is one of the greatest threats our national parks face. Parks are already experiencing shrinking glaciers, rising seas, and longer and more intense wildfire seasons. Advancing clean energy is essential to protecting these places and all they hold. We share that goal, and we appreciate the senators who have worked hard to advance it.

“But the path to a clean energy future should not run through our national parks. The sponsors’ latest changes include welcome improvements, and we thank the senators who advocated for them. But those changes don’t go far enough. Despite the efforts of many organizations to improve it, this bill still limits the voice of the public, Tribes, and park experts in decisions affecting our most cherished places. In fact, its historic preservation provisions were written without consulting Tribal Nations. The bill also weakens safeguards against irresponsible development and creates uncertainty for our country’s most threatened and endangered species.

“NPCA stands ready to work with senators on permitting reform that advances clean energy while also protecting our parks. And we urge the next Congress to make both a priority. Our national parks deserve a better plan than this one.”

text:
Dear Senator,

Since 1919, the National Parks Conservation Association (NPCA) has been the leading voice of the American people in protecting and enhancing our National Park System. On behalf of our 1.9 million members and supporters nationwide, we urge you to oppose S. 5653, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA). While we share the sponsors’ goal of building clean energy and transmission faster, and we recognize the years of bipartisan work behind this bill and the improvements in the sponsors’ substitute amendment, the amendment does not fix the provisions that would seriously jeopardize protections for our cherished national parks. We urge you to vote no on this bill in its current form and on any procedural motions to advance it. We hope Congress can take a more balanced approach next year.

Climate change is the greatest long-term threat national parks face, from shrinking glaciers to rising seas to the loss of ancient giant sequoias. NPCA has long supported efforts to cut pollution causing record-setting wildfires, droughts and floods that are affecting every park across the country. We acknowledge that this bill could unlock clean energy projects and build out a stronger power grid. Parks benefit from such advancements. We understand how important developing more renewable energy resources and the transmission network is to bring this clean energy to communities across the country. NPCA supports the bill’s transmission title, its requirement that data centers pay their share of the new grid costs, its guidance steering offshore wind away from national park waters and its funding authorization for the Historic Preservation Fund. Clean energy and park protection can advance together, and the changes we recommend below would ensure these gains do not come at the expense of national parks.

We are also focused on helping all our special places prepare for the changes they cannot avoid. National parks do not exist in isolation. Federal projects – whether a pipeline, transmission line, mine or oil and gas drill field – impact park lands Congress and past presidents have protected for the American people. It is the impact the bill could have on the ability of parks to prepare that causes us the biggest concern. The bill’s changes could lock in permits for projects that impact parks without examining their whole impact on all park resources. Federal permits should seek to avoid impacting parks, which are visited by over 300 million people annually and preserve irreplaceable American resources. Federal decisions affecting these places should be informed by the people who know them best. Limiting engagement from the National Park Service (NPS), the public, Tribes and interested organizations may speed up the process, but it silences the people and communities most affected, ignores the knowledge they bring and will ultimately cause any progress to come at a greater cost.

National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA)

Among the many changes the bill proposes, one of our greatest concerns is Division B, Title III, which rewrites the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA). Section 106 remains the primary way the public, Tribes and state and local governments have a voice in federal projects that affect historic places. For projects reviewed under Section 106, most are cleared quickly. Of roughly 120,000 projects reviewed each year, about 98% are designed to avoid harm to historic properties. Only the most damaging come under additional scrutiny, which is appropriate to protect resources that once lost are gone forever.

Instead of reforming the existing system, Section 2301 still lets agencies end consultation at their sole discretion and limits participation including shutting out the public organizations like NPCA. It also directs agencies to largely ignore a project’s visual and audible effects on historic sites, ends review for many federally funded projects, restricts legal actions and allows the federal government to take funding away from State and Tribal Historic Preservation Offices and responsibilities away from State offices. The substitute amendment makes welcome changes, including dropping the narrower definition of places of traditional religious and cultural importance and the federal takeover of Tribal Historic Preservation Offices. But these provisions were still written without Tribal consultation.

At Minidoka National Historic Site in Idaho, where Japanese Americans were incarcerated during World War II, Section 106 consultation gave survivors’ families, local residents and the state’s preservation office a voice in a proposed wind project. The result was an approved permit in which wind turbines were moved farther from the site and were reduced in number and height to protect the historic landscape. Consultation improved the project rather than stopping it. The Department of the Interior (DOI) separately reversed the approval in 2025. NPCA welcomes a genuine effort to improve the NHPA, developed with Tribes, preservation officials and the public. This title should be removed or revised further next year.

National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA)

NPCA is also concerned with similar changes to the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) in Division A, Title I. Section 1110 would bar courts from halting a project based on NEPA claims alone and limit the remedy for an unlawful approval to sending it back to the agency while the project moves forward. NPCA has seen firsthand what this means. After a federal appeals court found in 2019 that the Army Corps of Engineers should have prepared a full environmental impact statement for transmission towers across the James River near historic Jamestown (part of Colonial National Historical Park) and the Captain John Smith Chesapeake National Historic Trail, the permit was left in place during the new review. The towers, built while the case was pending, still stand today. Under this bill, this outcome could become the norm with projects completed despite significant flaws. The bill also narrows the actions NEPA covers, allows agencies to adopt one another’s categorical exclusions and shortens the time the public has to weigh in. We welcome efforts to make environmental reviews faster and more predictable while keeping a meaningful voice for parks and the public. Section 1110 and these related provisions should be removed or substantially revised next year.

Endangered Species Act (ESA)

NPCA has serious concerns with several provisions in Division A, Title III - Endangered Species Act. Of greatest concern is Section 1304, which changes how consultation under Section 7 of the ESA is undertaken. ESA consultation evaluates the effects of agency actions on listed species and critical habitat and considers ways to minimize those effects. Currently, the federal agency involved in a project must consult with either the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) or the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS). Under this bill, the state where a federal action takes place may act as the consultant under the ESA, instead of FWS or NMFS. This change could create over 50 different programs undermining the efficiency goals of this bill. This approach runs the risk of creating conflicts and overlapping decisions, especially in areas where project decisions are being made specific to migratory species such as threatened and endangered aquatic and avian species. As a result, a decision made on a project in Florida could have a significant impact on a species Rhode Island is working to recover. Additionally, as written, no exception is made for federal actions inside national parks or other federal lands. The substitute amendment adds safeguards for poorly performing state programs but does not resolve these concerns. NPCA welcomes stronger partnerships with states on species recovery, built on the expertise of federal wildlife agencies. Section 1304 should be removed or substantially revised.

Project Certainty

NPCA had several concerns with Division A, Title IV - Project Certainty. Although the title is intended to remedy the political and arbitrary stalling and revocation of permits for energy projects, certainty is equally important for communities, landscapes and sustainable and compatible development near parks. Recent limits on public input already imposed and proposed by this administration, combined with the proposed changes in this bill to laws like NEPA, ESA, and NHPA, could grant permits or federal approvals to covered projects with little or no public or scientific review. The bill’s original language could also support legal challenges to future attempts to regulate under other laws or put conditions on the operation of infrastructure covered by this legislation. The substitute amendment improves this title, including requiring a showing of bad faith before added damages are awarded, preserving courts’ authority to grant relief and adding a new savings clause. It addresses many but not all of our concerns.

Geothermal Leasing

NPCA is also concerned that geothermal provisions in Division B, Title II, Subtitle C could put the geysers of Yellowstone National Park or geothermal features at other parks at risk. Yellowstone holds more than half of the world’s active geysers, fed by underground heat and water that extend beyond the park boundary. Since 1988, the Geothermal Steam Act has required DOI to deny geothermal leases that are reasonably likely to significantly harm thermal features in national parks. Section 2229 would exempt broad categories of geothermal drilling from NEPA entirely. Section 2225 would eliminate the federal drilling permit for many wells on non-federal land, including wells that only pass through federal geothermal resources, removing additional reviews at the permit stage to further verify whether a project threatens Yellowstone or other parks. The substitute amendment broadens these exemptions rather than narrowing them. Geothermal development has degraded or destroyed geyser fields around the world, and a geyser that stops erupting cannot be restored. These provisions should not apply to activities that may affect protected thermal features in national parks.

Agency Capacity

Lastly, none of this can be carried out without remedying the fact that the federal agencies, especially those in DOI and the Department of Agriculture, have seen steep staff losses over the last decade. NPS alone has lost 25% of its staff since 2025. Without funding and direction to hire more staff and provide adequate resources, permitting reform will still be bogged down regardless of any changes to the law. NPCA welcomes the bill’s permitting improvement fund as an important first step. Sustained funding and direction to rebuild staff at NPS and other agencies that carry out these reviews would help ensure permitting reform delivers on its promise.

Thank you for considering our views.

text:
This story is part of Flipping the Switch, KQED’s series about California’s transition to clean energy and what it means for you. What works? What doesn’t? And how much does it cost?

It took just 15 seconds of shaking for the top level of the Cypress Freeway in West Oakland to flatten with force onto the section of road below.

This structural failure was the deadliest catastrophe of the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake, killing 42 people driving in Bay Area rush hour traffic.

The breakdown was especially devastating for West Oaklanders, who’d opposed the overpass’s construction — slicing through the heart of their neighborhood — in the first place. But out of the twisted rebar and tragedy, they created an opportunity.

First, they lobbied to relocate the freeway and build a greenbelt — Mandela Parkway — in its footprint. Second, they established the Cypress Mandela Training Center for West Oakland residents to be a part of the rebuilding process and set participants on a path toward secure, well-paying jobs in construction and related trades.

With time, Cypress Mandela expanded to provide foundational training for people all over the Bay Area, for an array of trades, including the basics of working with electricity. That sector is expected to grow 15% by 2034, through an increase of roughly 12,000 electrician jobs, many of those to power California’s enormous transition away from fossil fuels.

Workforce development programs like Cypress Mandela are an essential first step on a career path to build large-scale solar projects, fix up the electrical grid, and swap gas-burning appliances like furnaces for electric alternatives, not to mention build out data centers. Training programs like it are key to bringing low-income and minority trainees — at risk of getting left behind as the state abandons fossil fuels — into the fold.

The U.S. and California have a history of leaving minorities behind during major transitions. “The patterns of disparity and inequity are basically going to be reproduced when we do anything clean energy-wise, unless we approach it differently,” said Shrayas Jatkar, who worked for the U.S. Department of Energy under the Biden Administration.

Alejandro Ramos grew interested in the trades last year after his girlfriend gifted him a new gaming system that did not fit on the desk in his room.

Ramos took the table apart in his Oakland home and reassembled it to fit his video games. As he sweated, putting the slats of wood back together, he felt accomplished in a way he often had not during high school.

“I don’t really know how to explain it – but your own work – it feels good,” Ramos said, remembering the day last year.

Ramos is smart, he said, “but I can’t sit still in a classroom. I like to be up, moving.”

Ramos’s high school advertised a five-week summer program in the trades at Cypress Mandela.

Despite some bumps at the program’s start — Ramos was late the first day, a transgression that cost him 100 push-ups — he was enthusiastic.

“The next day, I was the first one in line,” Ramos said. “It really pushes you to do better for yourself.”

He continued on past the summer, joining the center’s flagship training program: a free, four-month journey, including hands-on skill-building and classroom instruction. Participants learn the basics of construction, plumbing, carpentry, concrete and electricity. One day they’ll be working on how to climb ladders of varying sizes safely, and the next they’ll be constructing a small home.

Cohorts range from 40 to 80 people, and come from all kinds of backgrounds — some having just finished high school, others finding their footing after being incarcerated. Participants commute daily from as far as Sacramento or Salinas to the enormous warehouse in East Oakland, where the center moved a decade ago.

Cypress Mandela runs like a bootcamp. Participants don khaki uniforms and hard-toed work boots. They begin each day with an hourlong, rigorous workout, each person equidistant from their neighbor, in neat lines as they sweat through jumping jacks and crunches. If they fail to comply with the program’s high standards — a shirt is untucked, someone starts to doze in class — it’s more push-ups.

“Lines are straight. Everything is neat,” said Charles E. Simmons Jr., the center’s executive director. “We have a saying here: We don’t build suffice, we build superior. I don’t want your half, I want your best.”

The tough-love approach is intentional, to match the real-world dangers of working in the trades. Occupations the students plan to go into have some of the highest rates of injuries and fatalities of all industries in California.

“This is not a game. You’re dealing with life and death situations here,” Simmons said.

Workforce training programs like Cypress Mandela and dozens of others in the state are “really trying to create these on-ramps to registered apprenticeship and the construction trades,” Jatkar said.

Experts in the construction trades underscore the difference between what are known as “high road” jobs — offering good pay, benefits, and opportunities for growth, often found through union membership — and those that cut costs at a worker’s expense. High road jobs are more common when it comes to large-scale industrial or commercial projects than single-family residential work.

Julia Hatton, who heads a training program in the Bay Area and Central California, the Rising Sun Center for Opportunity, said some centers are focused on high-road jobs after learning hard lessons from President Barack Obama’s 2009 initiative to stimulate green jobs.

Back then, Hatton’s organization trained people to go into home solar installation and home weatherization, but the pay was low, the schedules were inconsistent, and people received no benefits. “We realized that those jobs were keeping people in poverty,” she said.

When Rising Sun saw money coming back to support more “green jobs” in recent years, they advocated for worker protections, like competitive wages for employees working on a state-funded program to cut sources of pollution from low-income homes.

For Cypress Mandela graduates interested in becoming electricians, one path forward is to enter an apprenticeship program, like that offered through the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers, Local 595. Like most union apprenticeships, it’s yearslong and “earn while you learn,” meaning apprentices work and get paid while they also attend classes.

But they’re competitive to get into. Each year, roughly 3000 people apply for IBEW Local 595’s apprenticeship program, and only 50 to 75 get in, said Jason Bates, who directs its training.

Participants who go through Cypress Mandela’s vetted workforce development program, or others like it, have a few legs up, Bates said. For one, they don’t have to take a math and reading comprehension test, because they’ve gone through an algebra and reading comprehension curriculum.

They are also trained in how to interview, another key piece of IBEW Local 595’s selection process. They take classes on it and go through mock versions of the real thing, which is hugely important for people preparing for their first professional interview.

“It’s just like riding a bike. The first time you ride a bike, you’re not very good. But when you practice riding a bike, you get better and better until your training wheels are off,” Bates said.

Connecting participants to union jobs is important. These careers come with benefits, salary increases, pensions and more.

The center also has close partnerships with PG&E, East Bay Municipal Utility District, BART and other local contractors and employers.

Programs like Cypress Mandela “play a really vital role in creating pathways to registered apprenticeship in the trades,” Jatkar said. The reason they’re able to do that is “because of the long history and relationship that they have with one another, the familiarity, the trust. They know Cypress is turning out good graduates that are going to pan out.”

Cypress Mandela’s job placement success has been one of the forces sustaining it for so long.

“It gained a lot of notoriety for getting people jobs,” Simmons said. Roughly one-third of the most recent cohort was employed before the program finished, said Crystal McDowell, the center’s office manager.

There are three main qualities that make for successful green job workforce development programs, said Jessie Hammerling, director of the Green Economy Program at the UC Berkeley Labor Center.

First, programs should teach a wide range of skills, avoiding going too deep on one kind of job that is currently in demand as California builds out its clean grid, but may fade as trends change.

Second, education should be responsive to market demands for certain jobs, tweaking curriculum to better match trends, like a surge in interest in heat pumps.

And third, training should teach students to consider job quality, union representation, and the progression of wages they can make by following certain paths, while avoiding others. In the construction sector in particular, “most of the jobs are really bifurcated,” Hammerling said, between those that lead to family-sustaining work versus jobs that barely make ends meet.

These qualities are central to Cypress Mandela, and likely one of the reasons the program born from a quick, violent jolt has had such staying power.

text:
The rapid proliferation of data centers to support the ongoing AI boom has triggered widespread public backlash in the United States and Europe, with one of the major issues being the potential for these facilities to compete with local communities for limited supplies of energy and water.

A new study underscores that concern, showing that at least 25 percent of the world’s data centers operate in places where water demand exceeds supply for part of the year. The findings provide a valuable starting point for efforts to measure and mitigate the facilities’ environmental impact.

Recent estimates suggest that the world’s data centers use between 313 and 764 billion liters of water annually for cooling. Though substantial, this volume is dwarfed by other sources of water demand, according to Stanford University engineer and hydrologist Lorenzo Rosa, who led the research team. “Irrigation is almost 1,000 times more, so, globally, it’s very small,” he said.

And while not all data centers are big guzzlers, every drop matters in arid or drought-prone regions, where an individual facility’s needs could trigger fierce competition for water in the surrounding area when supply runs short.

To identify such water-stressed sites, Rosa and colleagues utilized a database of 9,347 data centers around the world - one of the largest inventories available, though probably not a complete list, the researchers noted.

They then deployed a supercomputer to determine the local water supply and demand by existing communities as well as agricultural and industrial users in 50-kilometer-by-50-kilometer map “pixels” encompassing those data centers. (The hydrologic measurements, based on extensively validated data from 2001 to 2010, may represent an underestimate of water stress, given the steady march of climate change.)

The team determined that a quarter of these data centers sit within areas experiencing a shortfall of water supply for at least one month annually but that a small though sizable number are in far drier locales. “Globally, 6 percent of data centers are located in regions that face nine to 12 months of scarcity,” Rosa said.

The researchers also projected how rising global temperatures might influence water stress by replicating their model in a world that has warmed by 3 degrees Celsius - a possible outcome in many models if greenhouse gas emissions are not brought under control. In that scenario, one-third of all existing data centers would be in areas experiencing water shortfalls for at least one month every year.

“Now we have a really rigorous study that tells us … the water-stress levels of the specific locations where those data centers are located,” said Eric Masanet, an engineer specializing in sustainable technology at the University of California at Santa Barbara. He was not involved in the work.

The study, published in Environmental Science & Technology, does not directly link data centers to water shortages, and their impact on water-stressed regions depends heavily on how water is used in the facilities’ cooling process.

“There are data centers that can use very little or no water,” Masanet said, whereas others use evaporative cooling that consumes water pulled from municipal or natural sources. Unfortunately, he added, the companies constructing and operating these facilities remain close-lipped about their design and capacity. “There’s not a lot of transparency.”

Rosa wants to drill deeper into localized use at specific locations where water stress and shortages might become particularly problematic, findings that he hopes might provide guidance for companies looking to build out their processing capacity in a more sustainable manner. “They have the capital to do that, but sometimes they don’t know how to do it,” he said.

Masanet pointed out that existing data centers can be upgraded to improve their water-use footprint, with the Rosa team’s study providing the foundation for the development of evidence-based regulations and incentives to ensure sustainable planning and operation.

“We need to think about this as an enabling set of research that’s going to help us maybe start solving these problems,” he said.

description:

text:
As attention turns toward COP31, the 31st edition of the annual United Nations climate conference, the pace of the global energy transition will increasingly depend on what happens in emerging markets and developing economies (EMDEs). These markets account for most of the world’s population, a growing share of electricity demand and an increasing proportion of new clean-energy investment. Yet progress remains highly uneven across markets and technologies. This Factbook examines where transition activity is accelerating in emerging markets, the different forces shaping deployment, and how investment, infrastructure, policy and industrial and transport development are influencing the pace and form of the transition.

Renewable investment reached a new high last year, but it remains concentrated. Emerging markets attracted a record $176 billion of new-build renewable investment in 2025, equivalent to a decade-high 25% of the global total. Asia Pacific accounted for almost half of EMDE investment and nearly 90% of the net increase since 2023, although a relatively small group of markets continues to dominate flows.

Distributed solar is opening new routes to clean-power growth. Small-scale solar additions accelerated sharply across emerging markets in 2025, led by India with 16.9 gigawatts, Pakistan with 13.2GW and Brazil with 12.7GW. Falling equipment costs, high grid tariffs and unreliable electricity supply can all drive deployment even where utility-scale pipelines remains limited.

As renewables penetration rises, grids and flexibility are becoming more important constraints. Across emerging markets, low-carbon technologies accounted for 45% of total installed capacity in 2025, up from around 32% in 2016. Yet intermittent generation comes with its own challenges. Battery deployment and grid investment are both beginning to scale in response. In several markets, however, low-carbon investment is already running ahead of grid spending, increasing the risk of connection delays, congestion and curtailment.

Industrial decarbonization is advancing, but economics and trade exposure will determine the pace. EMDEs are building pipelines of lower-emissions steel and renewable PPAs, while the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism is increasing pressure on exporters to reduce and verify embedded emissions. Yet cleaner industrial projects remain small relative to planned coal-based capacity.

Electric vehicle adoption is broadening beyond established markets. Passenger EV sales in emerging markets jumped 67% in 2025 and are expected to account for 18% of global EV sales by 2035. Tax policy, local manufacturing, model availability and fuel economics are all boosting adoption, and several emerging markets are already electrifying faster than the global average.

EMDEs remain a small part of global clean-technology manufacturing, and localization strategies are producing mixed results. Manufacturing capacity is concentrated in a few markets and technologies. India and Southeast Asia lead emerging-market solar manufacturing, while trade barriers, local-content rules and proximity to demand increasingly influence where factories are built.

Approach: This report brings together contributions from more than 10 BNEF analysts across regional and sector teams, combining market-level expertise with BNEF’s proprietary datasets, forecasts, models and primary-source research.

DELHI, La. & STERLINGTON, La.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Nov 9, 2026--

Veolia, the world’s leading provider of water and wastewater products and services, has expanded its wastewater treatment scope by entering new partnerships with two fast-growing communities in northern Louisiana that need to ensure their environmental security and protect their water resources amid rapid development.

Veolia now operates wastewater treatment plants in Delhi and Sterlington with a combined capacity of more than two million gallons of wastewater each day. They draw on Veolia’s resources in the region that include a 30-year partnership with the nearby City of Bastrop, 34 years of providing wastewater operations for the Sewerage and Water Board of New Orleans and multiple nearby communities in Mississippi.

“ Communities turn to Veolia when they need an experienced and well-resourced partner to help manage rapid growth, modernize existing infrastructure and adopt digital solutions – all while maintaining high levels of service, meeting every regulatory requirement and protecting public health ,” said Joseph Tackett, CEO of North America Municipal Services for Veolia . “ We’re dedicated to serving the needs of our partners, providing them environmental security they need to confidently welcome new residents and businesses, and we’re thrilled to join Delhi and Sterlington in meeting these challenges .”

New commitments strengthen municipal operations

Both Delhi and Sterlington are managing the impacts of rapid regional development and welcomed Veolia to ensure they could provide reliable wastewater management services. A major data center under construction nearby has brought many new workers and supporting businesses to the area, and focused the Town of Delhi’s attention on achieving its sustainability goals to support a strong quality of life alongside economic vitality. Sterlington’s booming residential development has helped it become one of the fastest-growing towns in the state, creating new pressure to build and improve wastewater infrastructure to serve new homes as they are constructed.

Both towns recognized they needed professional expertise to meet those goals. The Town of Delhi partnered with Veolia to operate and maintain its wastewater treatment plants, 15 lift stations and composting sites for four years, with the option to renew for two additional two-year terms if both parties agree. The Town of Sterlington partnered with Veolia to operate and maintain its wastewater treatment plant and 24 lift stations for six years.

Delhi Mayor Jesse Washington said, “ I am excited to welcome Veolia to the Town of Delhi. This nationally recognized company offers the hands-on technical assistance and direction we need right now. As our city continues to grow, the demands on our water facilities will remain a top priority. This partnership is a necessary step to ensure compliance and to make our systems efficient and top quality. ”

Sterlington Mayor Matt Talbert said, “ The Town of Sterlington is proud to partner with Veolia, a global leader in water and wastewater management. This partnership strengthens our operations by ensuring a dedicated team of experienced professionals is available to operate, maintain and continually improve our wastewater system . Together, we are committed to delivering reliable, efficient and environmentally responsible services while positioning Sterlington’s infrastructure to meet the needs of our growing community well into the next millennium .”

Veolia’s service to Delhi and Sterlington is an example of its GreenUp strategy to lead the ecological transformation of the planet by accelerating improvements in water quality, ensuring proper hazardous waste treatment and disposal, driving decarbonization and encouraging technological innovation.

Milestone follows secured power capacity and positive expansion study as HyProMag USA advances domestic rare earth magnet manufacturing

VANCOUVER, BC / ACCESS Newswire / November 9, 2026 / CoTec Holdings Corp. CTHCTHCF ("CoTec" or the "Company") notes the press release issued today by its joint venture, HyProMag USA LLC ("HyProMag USA"), announcing the delivery of the first major process equipment to its rare earth magnet recycling and manufacturing facility in Northlake, Texas (the "Northlake Texas Facility" or the "Project"), marking an important milestone as the Project advances toward financing, commissioning and operations.

Key Highlights

First major process equipment delivered: The first major process equipment has arrived at the Northlake Texas Facility, reflecting continued progress in detailed engineering and procurement.

Site secured in Dallas-Fort Worth: In December 2025, HyProMag USA secured a long-term lease for the Northlake Texas Facility at Ironhead Commerce Center, Building 1, Denton County, Texas, near critical infrastructure, including the BNSF intermodal rail link and Alliance Airport.i

Development advancing: Electrical power capacity secured through Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC, permitting progressing with Weston Solutions, Inc., and contractor selection underway.ii

Phased timeline: Initial magnet cutting and finishing operations targeted for the first half of 2027, followed by commissioning of Phase 1 integrated recycling and manufacturing operations in mid-2028.

Production and jobs: The Northlake Texas Facility targets approximately 1,526 metric tons per year of total payable production upon completion of Phase 2iii and is expected to create approximately 100 direct jobs.

Expansion potential: The Expansion Pre-Feasibility Study ("Expansion PFS") announced on October 27, 2026iv targets approximately 4,192 metric tons per year of neodymium iron boron ("NdFeB") magnet production and approximately 6,000 metric tons per year of total salable materials by 2034 across four plants.

Julian Treger, Chief Executive Officer of CoTec, commented: "The delivery of the first process equipment to the Northlake Texas Facility marks an important milestone for HyProMag USA as we advance toward commercial operations. The Project is expected to create around 100 direct jobs and support workforce training and skills development, helping build the skilled workforce required for advanced manufacturing in the United States. By establishing a domestic source of recycled rare earth magnets, HyProMag USA will strengthen U.S. manufacturing capacity and contribute to a more secure and resilient rare earth magnet supply chain."

Equipment Delivery and Site

The arrival of the equipment reflects continued progress in detailed engineering and procurement as HyProMag USA develops a secure, sustainable and domestic source of recycled rare earth permanent magnets in the United States. In December 2025, HyProMag USA secured a long-term lease agreement for the Northlake Texas Facility, located at Ironhead Commerce Center, Building 1, Dallas-Fort Worth, Denton County, Texas. The Project site is strategically located near critical infrastructure, including the BNSF intermodal rail link and Alliance Airport.

Project Development and Timeline

The Northlake Texas Facility is expected to become one of the first commercial-scale integrated rare earth magnet recycling and magnet manufacturing operations in the United States. Project development continues to advance, with electrical power capacity secured through Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC, permitting progressing with Weston Solutions, Inc., and contractor selection underway. HyProMag USA is targeting initial magnet cutting and finishing operations in the first half of 2027, followed by commissioning of Phase 1 integrated recycling and manufacturing operations in mid-2028.

The milestone follows the successful completion of the Expansion PFS as announced on October 27, 2026, which confirmed the potential to significantly increase HyProMag USA's production capacity while maintaining robust project economics. The Expansion PFS highlighted the opportunity to establish one of the largest rare earth magnet recycling and manufacturing platforms in the United States, targeting approximately 4,192 metric tons per year of NdFeB magnet production and approximately 6,000 metric tons per year of total salable materials by 2034 across four plants.

The Northlake Texas Facility is expected to create approximately 100 direct jobs and play an important role in supporting the development of a secure, resilient and sustainable domestic rare earth magnet supply chain. By recovering valuable magnetic materials from end-of-life products and manufacturing scrap, HyProMag USA aims to transform waste streams into a domestic resource for new magnet production, reducing reliance on imported rare earth materials and supporting U.S. manufacturing.

About HyProMag USA

HyProMag USA is developing advanced rare earth magnet recycling and manufacturing operations to establish a secure domestic U.S. supply chain for NdFeB magnets, essential components for AI infrastructure, medical systems, robotics, electric vehicles, and advanced electronics. Leveraging the revolutionary Hydrogen Processing of Magnet Scrap ("HPMS") technology, developed over 15 years with over US$100 million in R&D investment, HyProMag USA is designed to deliver faster magnet-to-magnet short-loop recycling that uses 88% less energy and reduces carbon emissions by 85% compared to conventional methods. HPMS accepts a wide range of magnet-bearing feedstocks - including end-of-life EV motors, data-center and industrial equipment, consumer electronics, and manufacturing scrap - enabling recovery of magnet-grade material without chemical processing.

Ownership

HyProMag USA LLC is owned 50:50 by CoTec and HyProMag Limited. HyProMag Limited is 100% owned by Maginito Limited, which is owned 79.4% by Mkango Magnetic Materials Limited (AIM/TSX-V: MKA) and 20.6% by CoTec.

For more information on HyProMag USA, please visit www.hypromagusa.com

About CoTec

CoTec Holdings Corp. CTHCTHCF is redefining the future of resource extraction and recycling. Focused on rare earth magnets and strategic materials, CoTec integrates breakthrough technologies with strategic assets to unlock secure, sustainable, and low-cost supply chains.

CoTec's mission is clear: accelerate the energy transition while strengthening strategic mineral supply chains for the countries we operate in. By investing in and deploying disruptive technologies, the Company delivers capital-efficient, scalable solutions that transform marginal assets, tailings, waste streams, and recycled products into high-value critical minerals.

title: Ford Tested 36,000 Mustang Mach-E Batteries. Here's How They Held Up After 100,000 Miles
description:
Ford collected battery health data from around 36,000 Mustang Mach-E electric SUVs and shared the results.
Even Mach-Es with 100,000 or 200,000 miles on the odometer retained most of their original range.
More On Battery Degradation Nearly 10,000 EVs Were Tested For Battery Degradation.
Ford says the 30-plus cars in its dataset that had covered more than 200,000 miles showed 88% battery health.
After 150,000 kilometers (around 93,000 miles), most models studied showed between 90% and 94% health.
text:
Battery degradation is one of the top concerns among potential EV buyers. New data from Ford shows you probably shouldn't worry much.

Ford collected battery health data from around 36,000 Mustang Mach-E electric SUVs and shared the results.

Battery degradation is one of the top concerns from car buyers, but Ford's data shows that there isn't much to worry about.

Even Mach-Es with 100,000 or 200,000 miles on the odometer retained most of their original range.

It's one of the top questions I get about EVs: "How long will the battery last?" Understandably, people want to know that their car will go the distance before dropping tens of thousands of dollars on a new car with new-to-them technology.

A growing body of research shows that modern electric cars hold up just fine over years of normal use. And a huge study of Ford Mustang Mach-E SUVs further proves the point.

The Detroit automaker collected battery-health data from 36,000 Mach-E SUVs from the 2021 model year that were sold in the U.S. and Canada. The results, released Monday, should help quiet fears that EVs degrade like smartphones, which struggle to hold a charge after a few years of daily use.

On average, the cars had traveled 55,000 miles over 5.2 years and retained 92% of their usable battery capacity. That means a top-trim 2021 Mustang Mach-E with 305 miles of EPA range would in theory be rated for around 280 miles today. All the cars in the study have nickel-cobalt-manganese (NCM) battery packs, since Ford didn't introduce a lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) battery for the Mach-E starting until the 2023 model year.

The 2021 Mustang Mach-Es Ford studied retained 92% of their battery health on average after five years on the road.Photo by: Ford

Ford physically tests cells in the lab and tries to predict battery degradation using computer models before a model launches, Kevin Vander Laan, the automaker's technical leader of high-voltage battery cells and systems, told me in an interview. But the real test comes after a car spends years on the road.

"Our report card slowly trickles in over time," he said. "So here we are with a five-year report card, and it looks great."

Interestingly enough, putting on twice as many miles as average in the same time period barely impacted overall battery health. Ford says the over 2,000 SUVs with more than 100,000 miles on the odometer retained more than 91% of their battery capacity.

More On Battery Degradation

Nearly 10,000 EVs Were Tested For Battery Degradation. These 2 Models Won Out.

What Ultra-High-Mileage EVs Teach Us About Battery Degradation

Those few drivers who put some 40,000 miles on their Mach-Es each year still had strong battery health after five years. Ford says the 30-plus cars in its dataset that had covered more than 200,000 miles showed 88% battery health.

Of course, these are just averages. So your results may vary depending on lots of factors. EVs that spend their lives in the hot American Southwest tend to age more rapidly than those driven in more temperate climates. Likewise, EV batteries that are frequently fast-charged to 100% and drained to near-empty typically wear out faster than those that are kept in the happy zone of 20% to 80%.

Still, Ford says the distribution of results is encouraging for its battery engineers: It says 95% of the 36,000 cars fell between 87% and 97%.

The results are in line with what other research has uncovered about how EVs age. Some early EVs (notably the first-gen Nissan Leaf) had less sophisticated battery thermal management and saw steep degradation as a result. But modern EVs tend to age far more gracefully.

According to Recurrent, a firm that tracks range retention in used EVs that opt in, the average EV retains 97% of its original observed range after three years and 95% after five years.

In September, battery-health startup Aviloo released the results of 500,000 EV battery tests. After 150,000 kilometers (around 93,000 miles), most models studied showed between 90% and 94% health. The Hyundai Ioniq 5, BMW i4, and Mercedes EQA stood out with readings near the top end of that range. The Mustang Mach-E did just about as well as Ford's own data show: 92.5% battery health. The Tesla Model 3 and Model Y came in at 88.9% and 90.3%, respectively.

Ford makes some familiar recommendations to drivers looking to make sure their EVs last as long as possible. The company says to manage temperature extremes by parking in the shade on scorching days and preconditioning the cabin while the vehicle is plugged in. It also recommends relying on Level 2 charging for daily driving, and using Level 3 DC fast chargers sparingly.

Vander Laan says the learnings from this crop of EVs and how they perform contribute to the development process for Ford's next-generation electric cars, like the sub-$30,000 Fathom pickup coming next year.

"It's really continuous learning," he said. "We have a design that we deeply understand, the data is flowing in, we're learning learning from that, and feeding that to the engineering teams in the company here."

text:
NEW ORLEANS — A community garden in Hollygrove is getting solar power, cooling fans and a more accessible entrance, with young New Orleans workers helping bring the improvements to life. Groundwork New Orleans is expanding the Hollygrove Community Stormwater Garden into a gathering place where residents can find relief from the heat, connect with neighbors and, eventually, have access to a neighborhood resource during power outages.

The improvements bring new uses to a garden in one of New Orleans’ low-lying neighborhoods, where stormwater runoff and drainage challenges have long contributed to flooding concerns. Along with helping manage rainwater, the garden is being developed as a place where residents can spend time outdoors while young workers gain experience building and maintaining green infrastructure.

Two 450-watt solar panels, with a combined rated generating capacity of 900 watts, are being installed to help power outdoor cooling fans and other small electrical needs. The system will also have connection ports for additional panels, allowing Groundwork New Orleans to expand its solar capacity in the future.

Groundwork New Orleans intends for the solar system to help the garden serve as a neighborhood resource during power outages.

Community Improvements and Workforce Training

Beneath the garden’s shade structure, new outdoor fans are being installed to make hot New Orleans days more comfortable for residents, volunteers and visitors. Workers are also building an ADA-accessible entrance ramp to make the space easier for more people to enjoy.

The work is being carried out by the Groundwork New Orleans Ground CREW (Creating a Resilient Environmental Workforce), a paid workforce development program for young adults ages 19 to 25. As they improve the garden, participants are putting their training to work in solar infrastructure, electrical installation support, carpentry and sustainable construction, gaining experience that can help prepare them for jobs in those fields.

“We are not training in a classroom, we are training on actual green infrastructure, solar and reforestation projects. We’re leaving assets in communities,” said Todd Reynolds, executive director of Groundwork New Orleans. “We’re basically training folks to be able to be at the forefront of the Green movement and to be able to earn high-wage, real employment. Not only training them, but helping them develop as young men and young women.”

Rather than focusing on short-term certification programs, Ground CREW emphasizes sustained employment and hands-on training, allowing participants to build their resumes while developing infrastructure that benefits local neighborhoods.

Groundwork New Orleans also works closely with community organizations and is working with the Hollygrove Neighbors Association on these resiliency improvements.

“Our biggest strength is our partnerships with our community folks. I can be called in, but they really know the history of their neighborhood and what’s going on in their communities,” Reynolds said.

The Hollygrove project is nearing completion but Groundwork New Orleans as not announced a specific completion date.

Previous Groundwork New Orleans Projects

The Hollygrove improvements follow a similar effort on North Claiborne Avenue, where Groundwork New Orleans opened the Vision 2 Reality Stormwater Management Park in September 2025. The organization invested more than $400,000 to develop a green space with a bioswale, solar-powered charging stations, cooling fans and other amenities. Ground CREW members completed 99% of the construction work, giving participants a direct role in building a neighborhood resource.

Groundwork New Orleans is also working on a Touro Street project that will incorporate a solar-powered gazebo, native plantings and bioswales designed to capture stormwater and help reduce neighborhood flooding.

Groundwork New Orleans received a $10,000 grant from the Greater New Orleans Foundation’s Racial Equity Fund in August 2026 to support its youth development, environmental improvement and neighborhood resilience programs.

Founded in 2006, Groundwork New Orleans is part of the national Groundwork USA network, which supports community-based environmental improvements and workforce development.

title: San Diego's congressional delegation is all Democrats. What's next? - inewsource
description:
San Diego County’s five-member congressional delegation will consist entirely of Democrats next year after a landslide midterm election that left the Democratic Party in control of the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate.
That shift threatened more than $40 million a year in grants to San Diego County.
A COVID-era voucher program ran out of money years early for 650 San Diego families before a September spending bill gave them a reprieve.
A University of San Diego Nonprofit Institute survey found local groups laid off nearly 500 employees in the first weeks of Trump’s second term.
That policy came months after Trump’s tariffs whipsawed import prices for San Diego businesses.
text:
San Diego County’s five-member congressional delegation will consist entirely of Democrats next year after a landslide midterm election that left the Democratic Party in control of the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate.

Local experts told inewsource they hope the election results will motivate Congress to address recent federal policy changes that have left people scrambling in San Diego and elsewhere.

Among other priorities, they’re monitoring housing aid, nonprofit funding, nutrition and farm subsidies, and the future of President Donald Trump’s divisive tariffs. Here’s a brief overview.

Housing aid

The Trump administration has spent the past year trying to shift federal homelessness funds away from “Housing First” model programs like permanent housing and toward “Treatment First” programs that require participants to meet goals like getting sober before receiving housing.

That shift threatened more than $40 million a year in grants to San Diego County.

Courts blocked the government’s first attempt, but the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) tried again this year. HUD can now choose this year’s grantees under its new priorities while an appeal plays out, with awards due Dec. 1.

The city and county closed their section 8 waitlists — with 76,000 and 124,000 people on them, respectively — because rising housing costs outpaced stagnant federal funding. A COVID-era voucher program ran out of money years early for 650 San Diego families before a September spending bill gave them a reprieve.

Congress also passed the biggest housing bill in decades, which became law in July without Trump’s signature, though local experts said it wouldn’t bring renters immediate relief.

So what might be expected next year with a Republican president and a Democratic Congress?

Stephen Russell, CEO of the San Diego Housing Federation, wants Congress to reverse the cuts in Trump’s signature spending bill, H.R 1, to expand housing vouchers and to change HUD rules so mixed-status households can get housing benefits.

“I actually remain very optimistic that given the scale of the turnover in the Congress, that we can get veto-proof direction from Congress to do these things,” he said.

Despite his optimism, he is counting on the state housing bond voters approved — Proposition 1 — that authorizes $11.25 billion for affordable housing. Russell said he thinks the measure will usher in the construction of thousands of new affordable housing units locally — the kind of building San Diego hasn’t seen in two decades.

Russell said between the housing bond and the services that will be provided via San Diego County’s Measure B voters showed that they want California to “seize its own destiny.”

“We cannot always be relying on the federal government,” he said. “Affordable housing does not finance itself. It does not pay for itself.”

Nonprofit funding

San Diego nonprofit leaders declared a state of emergency in June 2025, six months into federal grant cancellations that pulled money from libraries, museums, environmental projects and Rady Children’s Hospital. A University of San Diego Nonprofit Institute survey found local groups laid off nearly 500 employees in the first weeks of Trump’s second term.

Laura Deitrick, the institute’s executive director, told inewsource that an upcoming, updated survey expected to be released in January shows that the strain hasn’t eased.

One in four San Diego nonprofits described their financial health as weak or very weak this fall, according to that survey by USD’s Nonprofit Institute. About a third said they had cut staff positions or hours, and just as many had cut programs or services.

Fewer nonprofit staff means “less health care appointments, fewer child care options, less capacity to help families,” Deitrick said.

The demand continues to outpace what nonprofits can provide, she said, and private donors “cannot come even close to the full cost of lost government funding.”

She added that “at a certain point in time, it becomes impossible to fully deliver on your mission.”

Her hope for the incoming Congress is that its members listen to nonprofit organizations to learn what they are going through and create a more predictable policy environment.

Casa Familiar, for example, lost a $12.7 million grant from the Environmental Protection Agency for clean transportation and air purifiers, and another $500,000 grant after the Trump administration cut funding for programs related to environmental justice.

Casa Familiar President and CEO Lisa Cuestas said that the lost grants caused them to restructure and layoff staff.

“Do I think that I’m going to see those dollars come back to me?” Cuestas asked. “No, because those dollars have been spent somewhere else.”

She said she doesn’t expect funding priorities to change overnight when the new Congress gets sworn in because the staff at grant-making agencies won’t change with Congress “and those seats are not elected.”

Despite setbacks, she said Casa Familiar’s work continues.

“We didn’t stop,” she said. “We just paused.”

Nutrition and farm subsidies

Trump’s signature spending law H.R.1 cut the federal Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), known as CalFresh in California, and Medicaid, known as Medi-Cal.

At the time, county officials estimated 400,000 people would face new work requirements.

Starting in October 2027, California could owe about $2 billion a year for CalFresh benefits the federal government used to cover, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office. Medi-Cal work requirements begin Jan. 1, days before Democrats take control of Congress.

Gina Plata-Nino, the SNAP director at the Food Research & Action Center, a national anti-hunger group, said that states can’t afford to wait for the new Congress to get sworn in.

Most states finish their budgets by June and need to know now whether they’ll have to pay for part of SNAP benefits.

“This is the reason why we need this to happen during the lame duck session, as Congress comes back,” she said. “States need to be able to plan.”

While Plata-Nino is advocating for all H.R.1 cuts to be reversed, she is hoping that Congress might more quickly implement a two-year delay for the provisions to take effect.

“Rural America and farm country was really vocal about what the policies have done and really turned and gave a strong rebuke to the administration,” she said, adding that “the new Congress is coming, but the time to act is now.”

Plata-Nino said that if Congress doesn’t delay the onset of H.R.1 cuts, it will let down “millions of Americans who will continue to go hungry and farmers who need farm relief.”

President Trump’s tariffs

When President Trump ended the so-called “de minimis” exemption in August 2025, which let goods worth under $800 enter the country duty-free, border business leaders warned it would hit Tijuana warehouses that shipped directly to U.S. shoppers and the Otay Mesa companies that serve them.

Eduardo Acosta said then that “millions of square feet in Tijuana” would have to downsize.

He’s the international business affairs chair for the San Diego Chamber of Commerce and vice president of RL Jones, a customs brokerage founded in Calexico that works along the U.S. Mexico border.

That policy came months after Trump’s tariffs whipsawed import prices for San Diego businesses. Duties of 50% on steel, aluminum and copper stayed in place even for many Mexican-made goods that otherwise cross duty-free under the North American trade deal known as the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement or the USMCA.

The U.S. Supreme Court struck down many of Trump’s tariffs in February, but the steel and aluminum tariffs that hit Mexican factories remain in effect, and so does the end of de minimis.

Now, Acosta said, it’s those duties on steel and aluminum that are creating the most pain for cross-border manufacturing.

“In my industry, people are laying people off, warehouses are downsizing,” Acosta said. “And then you’ve got to pay more gas.”

On top of that, a federal rule will require customs brokers to vet foreign companies that import goods into the U.S., starting in January. That puts the burden on brokers like Acosta.

He doesn’t expect Congress to pursue immediate relief on trade given competing priorities.

“We’re going to be in a lame duck session, but we understand the duck is going to be very upset,” he said.

Initially, all he’s banking on is a return to normal politics and good manners like “dealing with the government, knowing what you’re getting into. No knee jerk reaction to a guy from Canada pissing off the president and now tariffs on Canada.”

Eventually, he said he hopes that anger over the rising costs at gas stations and grocery stores that helped Democrats wrest control of Congress from Republicans move all lawmakers to bring down tariffs.

text:
Dover Corporation, a diversified industrial manufacturer headquartered in Downers Grove, Illinois, has completed its previously announced acquisition of Leistung Engineering Pvt. Ltd. The acquired business will become part of OPW Fluid Transfer Solutions within Dover’s Clean Energy & Fueling operating segment.

The transaction expands Dover’s industrial technology portfolio through the addition of Leistung Engineering, supporting its broader strategy of developing specialized manufacturing and equipment businesses.

OPW Fluid Transfer Solutions provides equipment and related technologies within Dover’s Clean Energy & Fueling segment.

By incorporating Leistung Engineering into that business, Dover is adding an operating company to its established industrial platform.

The announcement confirms the completion of the acquisition and the planned organizational placement of the acquired company.

Dover has developed a diversified portfolio of industrial businesses serving customers across a range of manufacturing, energy, infrastructure, and technology markets.

Its products include engineered equipment, components, consumable supplies, aftermarket parts, digital solutions, and related support services.

The company operates through five reporting segments: Engineered Products, Clean Energy & Fueling, Imaging & Identification, Pumps & Process Solutions, and Climate & Sustainability Technologies.

These segments serve different customer needs while sharing Dover’s broader operating approach centered on specialized products and industrial applications.

The Clean Energy & Fueling segment encompasses technologies associated with the movement, handling, and management of fuels and other industrial fluids.

Leistung Engineering will be integrated into OPW Fluid Transfer Solutions as Dover continues developing this portion of its business.

Dover generates more than $8 billion in annual revenue and employs approximately 24,000 people.

The company has operated for more than 70 years, combining a global industrial presence with business units focused on specialized customer requirements.

Its acquisition strategy supports the development of its operating businesses through complementary technology, manufacturing capabilities, and market opportunities.

Dover’s broader portfolio includes products used in industrial processes, energy applications, environmental systems, and equipment maintenance.

The acquisition of Leistung Engineering represents another transaction within that strategy.

Although Dover confirmed completion, its announcement did not provide detailed information about the acquired company’s revenue, workforce, customer base, or expected financial contribution.

The transaction nevertheless establishes Leistung Engineering as part of Dover’s Clean Energy & Fueling business and expands the collection of specialized industrial companies operating within the group.

description:

This achievement highlights the industrial innovation fostered through the EU Horizon Programme and demonstrates the readiness of recycled battery materials for commercial-scale manufacturing.
