text:
Potential U.S. Policy Shifts Could Benefit ESS, Hydrogen and Solar Businesses, Though Legislative Hurdles Remain

Democratic gains in both chambers of the U.S. Congress following the midterm elections could bring greater scrutiny of President Donald Trump's fossil fuel-focused energy policies. The results have also raised the possibility that Democrats will seek to restore clean energy tax credits and other industry support measures, drawing attention to the North American business prospects of South Korean companies in energy storage systems (ESS), hydrogen and solar power.

Financial and industry sources expect the election results to prompt a reassessment of policy uncertainty across the clean energy sector. South Korea's battery industry, in particular, is looking to North American ESS operations as a potential growth driver. According to market research firm SNE Research, LG Energy Solution and Samsung SDI together held approximately 20.9% of the North American ESS market in the first three quarters of 2026, up from 13.4% in the same period last year. The increase reflects a growing market presence for the two companies, rather than the combined share of all three major Korean battery makers.

The Democrats' support for strengthening battery supply chains outside China could create opportunities for South Korean suppliers. The country's major battery makers, including LG Energy Solution, Samsung SDI and SK On, are working with domestic materials companies such as POSCO Future M and L&F, which produce lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cathode materials, as they seek to diversify their raw material supply chains. Lee An-na, an analyst at Yuanta Securities Korea, projected in a research report that North American-made battery cells could gain a cost advantage of more than 40% over Chinese-made products when tariffs and subsidies are taken into account, potentially helping local suppliers expand their market share.

In the solar sector, Hanwha Qcells and OCI Holdings are seen as potential beneficiaries because of their production facilities and supply chains outside China. Hanwha Qcells began producing solar cells at its facility in Cartersville, Georgia, in July 2026, while OCI Holdings has established a non-Chinese polysilicon supply chain through its Malaysian subsidiary. Equipment manufacturers such as GnBS Eco could also benefit if investment in U.S. solar manufacturing facilities picks up.

However, a change in congressional control is unlikely to lead to sweeping policy shifts immediately. Although Democrats won majorities in both chambers, they do not hold the two-thirds majorities in both the House and Senate needed to override a presidential veto. An industry official said major changes to laws and policies could therefore be limited, while negotiations with the administration could still lead to gradual adjustments.

Potentially tighter oversight of data centers is another factor for the industry. If lawmakers introduce stricter requirements for AI-related infrastructure and data center electricity use, some new projects could face additional constraints. On the other hand, requiring large power consumers to bear more of the costs of grid upgrades could increase demand for alternative power solutions and related equipment. The extent to which companies such as Enchem, Doosan Fuel Cell and mPLUS benefit will depend on their ability to secure specific projects and convert orders into revenue.

Ultimately, South Korean companies' prospects will depend not only on policy developments but also on their ability to win orders and establish competitive local production bases. While the election results have changed the policy outlook, the timing and scale of any impact on individual companies will vary according to customers' investment schedules and facility ramp-up plans.

title: China goes Detroit with full-size family SUV EVs that roads can't bear - Notebookcheck
authors: Daniel Zlatev, Daniel went, from the infinite scroll, move of our existence
description:
The reasons that the Chinese automakers in the world's largest car market are doing it are the same that Detroit does it for: demand and profit.
In other words, the typical new Chinese EV is now the kind of vehicle one would expect to see in a Texas parking lot.
The US is also noticing the impact of the heavier electric vehicles on road surfaces.
According to some studies, electric cars are damaging road infrastructure much more than ICE vehicles, as they are heavier.
That is why states are increasingly mulling or implementing an EV road tax that is often higher than the one for gas vehicles.
text:
Chinese carmakers used to be known for compact, city-friendly EVs. That reputation is fading fast. According to the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA), SUVs measuring 5 to 5.5 meters (16.4 to 18 feet) made up 56% of all new SUV launches in the first ten months of 2026. In 2024, that figure sat at just 17%, as the market share of full-size damily SUVs more than tripled in size in the span of just two years.

The reasons that the Chinese automakers in the world's largest car market are doing it are the same that Detroit does it for: demand and profit. CPCA chief Cui Dongshu blames fierce price competition, with large SUVs and MPVs serving as a showcase for technology and a way to protect margins. The end of subsidies and rising costs have also hurt small car development.

It's not just SUVs, as the newly announced BYD Altior limo can attest. Among new energy vehicle launches, the share of models longer than 5 meters has climbed from 34% to 58% in two years, while the 4.5 to 5 meter class has shrunk from 55% to 40%. In other words, the typical new Chinese EV is now the kind of vehicle one would expect to see in a Texas parking lot.

Bigger bodies mean bigger batteries, and that’s where the trouble starts. Nio CEO William Li recently pointed out that some models carry packs of up to 120 kWh weighing 700 to 800 kg (1,543 to 1,764 lbs). By his math, a car that is 1.2 times heavier does roughly 2.07 times the damage to the road. That comes from the "fourth-power law" of pavement engineering, in which damage scales with axle load raised to the fourth power.

Nio is practicing what Li preaches, as its packs typically weigh 400 to 500 kg (882 to 1,102 lbs), which means accepting smaller capacity and making up for the lost range with more efficient drivetrains. He admits he doesn’t know whether the market will reward that. Each extra kilogram (2.2 lbs) also needs his personal sign-off in terms of added value.

Local regulators are starting to react, too. A new mandatory energy-consumption standard that took effect in January ties limits to curb weight, and authorities are reportedly studying a weight-based tax. Cui has also suggested standards for economy cars and support for micro EVs. In the meantime, China's EV industry is making the same bet Detroit once did with upsizing.

The US is also noticing the impact of the heavier electric vehicles on road surfaces. According to some studies, electric cars are damaging road infrastructure much more than ICE vehicles, as they are heavier. The Highway Trust Fund that is responsible for their maintenance, however, faces a funding shortfall just as EV adoption increases. That is why states are increasingly mulling or implementing an EV road tax that is often higher than the one for gas vehicles.

text:
THE British government is expected to cut its electric vehicle sales target for 2030 by about a quarter to around 60%, the Guardian said on Sunday, citing government sources.

The 2024 mandate requires carmakers to ensure zero-emission vehicles (ZEVs) contribute a rising share of annual sales, with the 2026 target of 33%, rising to 80% in 2030 and 100% by 2035.

Louise Haigh, the de facto deputy prime minister, is expected to finalise the plan after a meeting in Downing Street on Wednesday, the newspaper said.

Haigh will probably approve a 2030 target of about 60% and extend flexibility until 2034, it added.

"The government is united in its commitment to the ZEV mandate, and no decisions have been taken," a government spokesperson told Reuters, reaffirming commitment to the 2030 phase-out of all new cars with only petrol and diesel engines.

The mandate consultation would not alter the zero-emissions target for all new car and van sales by 2035, the spokesperson added.

Options set out in August by Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government could ease pressure on carmakers to switch new sales to zero-emission vehicles, with existing targets under review.

Carmakers say supply chain disruptions and poor consumer demand make it tough to comply with the mandate.

Battery-electric vehicles made up 26.6% of new car sales year to date, off the 33% target for 2026, the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders said last week, urging "substantive" target changes to pull them closer to demand. - Reuters

title: Lessons from Apex: How Community Perspectives Can Shape Better Data Center Policy
description:
Apex and Public Opinion about Data Centers Taking a step back, the concerns raised by Apex residents are largely emblematic of public opinion on local data center development generally.
Data centers are currently facing considerable pushback across the country, with high-profile community mobilizations happening in Tucson, Northern Virginia (the “Data Center Alley”), and Memphis.
A Roadmap for Local Governments As demonstrated in Apex, local governments, residents, and community organizers often don’t see eye to eye on what a new data center means to the community.
Instead, existing framework incentivizes data center development through aggressive tax exemptions, including sales-and-use tax breaks on construction, equipment, and electricity.
[8] Our findings underscore the need for the North Carolina state government to critically assess its data center development policies.
text:
The rise of AI and cloud services over the past decade has brought a rapid buildout of data centers to meet surging compute demands. As a global leader in AI, the United States hosts approximately 5,400 of the world’s 12,000 global data centers—a number that is projected to grow 10 percent annually through 2030.[1]

North Carolina has emerged as a key destination in this national expansion. The state currently hosts at least 97 data centers.[2] That number is expected to roughly double over the next decade as firms like Amazon and Apple continue to invest in large-scale data center infrastructure in the state. Companies are drawn to North Carolina by its affordable land, robust energy grid, strategic East Coast location, and favorable tax incentives.

However, this rapid development raises critical questions about localized impacts on the communities in which data centers are built. Residents increasingly worry about surging utility rates, water and energy consumption, and environmental and health risks like air and noise pollution. These concerns have sparked community pushback against proposed developments across the state and country. Examining local perspectives is critical to ensuring residents do not bear the costs of technological development.

Study Background

A team of graduate student researchers from Duke University collaborated with the Benton Institute for Broadband & Society to study community perspectives on new data center development in North Carolina. The Benton Institute was interested in this research for several reasons, including its work with the Blue Ridge Broadband Alliance in Western North Carolina, and the emerging national conversation around AI adoption, data centers, and their relationships with broadband. The research team’s goal was to understand the benefits and challenges identified by communities when data centers come to town, and how these perspectives can help shape policies that mitigate harms and expand local benefits.

A real-world case of community engagement with a data center project emerged during project design, so the study specifically focused on Apex, North Carolina, where the New Hill Digital Campus was proposed in September 2025. If built, the Digital Campus would have spanned 190 acres and consumed 300 megawatts at peak capacity.[3]

When plans for the Digital Campus became public, tensions quickly emerged between Apex residents, local policymakers, and the developer, Natelli Investments. Concerned residents organized to voice their concerns and urge the town to reject the proposal. Natelli tried to address questions and frame the Digital Campus as a critical source of tax revenue for the town. Town officials, caught in the middle, attempted to weigh the potential economic benefits of the Digital Campus with the environmental and social harms to make a decision on whether or not to allow the development. These tensions made Apex a great case study to understand how community voices can shape smarter, more proactive infrastructure policies.

Research Findings

The research team interviewed eight Apex community members and five subject matter experts to identify what issues were most salient and pressing in the community. Five core themes emerged from these conversations: transparency of the plan, pollution, financial investment, governance and regulation, and resource use and extraction.

1. Transparency of the Plan

Community members overwhelmingly felt that Natelli Investments was not transparent about its plan for Digital Campus’s operations. They raised numerous transparency concerns including the misrepresentation of megawatt usage, failure to address questions about utility prices, and lack of disclosure around the project’s evaporative water-cooling process. Participants were also frustrated that negotiations between Natelli and local policymakers were held behind closed doors and with minimal community input. Notably, community members didn’t know which technology company would be occupying the Digital Campus.

2. Pollution

Community members and experts were afraid that the New Hill Digital Campus would pollute the town’s air, water, and soundscape, putting residents at risk of environmental health hazards. Participants were primarily concerned about water and noise pollution. They feared that polishing and aerosolization during the evaporative cooling process would leave contaminants in local water sources and deposit corrosive minerals on nearby homes and cars, resulting in damaged property and negative health outcomes for the community. Many also voiced worries about the persistent, low-frequency hum associated with data centers, which could disrupt the lives and sleep of residents, particularly children and neurodivergent individuals.

3. Financial Investment

Community members were skeptical that the Digital Campus would create the financial benefit promised by Natelli Investments—namely job creation, tax revenue, and economic development. Some participants also worried that benefits would not be distributed to the local community, but would instead be received by landowners, developers, out-of-town workers, and consumers of digital services. While some participants acknowledged short-term economic benefits like temporary construction jobs, they anticipated limited meaningful impacts in the long run.

4. Governance and Regulation

Community members felt that local policies and governments failed to protect the community from the potential adverse impacts of data centers. Notably, some participants worked in the technology sector and were deeply familiar with AI and data center infrastructure, with multiple sharing that they were not against AI. However, they were frustrated with the lack of adequate regulation to curb the pace of development and mitigate specific harms to health, the environment, and the local community. Some participants pointed to specific legislation that they supported—such as North Carolina House Bill 1002, which would protect residents from utility rate increases caused by data centers. Notably, multiple community members shared appreciation for Apex officials that they felt were taking the Digital Campus seriously and listening to the community’s concerns.

5. Resource Use and Extraction

Community members were concerned that the Digital Campus would lead to the overuse and overextraction of finite local resources—such as water, land, electricity, and fuel—resulting in a lower quality of life for Apex residents. These concerns were closely tied with the scale and intensity of the project.

Concerns about electricity were especially prominent. Many North Carolina residents experienced blackouts amid the back-to-back winter storms and prolonged freezing temperatures that hit the South in recent winters. As a result, they did not trust the local power grid to deliver consistent service once the new data center went online. In addition, community members worried that the data center would result in surging utility prices.

Apex and Public Opinion about Data Centers

Taking a step back, the concerns raised by Apex residents are largely emblematic of public opinion on local data center development generally. Data centers are currently facing considerable pushback across the country, with high-profile community mobilizations happening in Tucson, Northern Virginia (the “Data Center Alley”), and Memphis.[4] According to a Gallup poll conducted in March, 2026, 7 in 10 Americans oppose local construction of AI data centers.[5]

As in Apex, Americans are also mixed on data center impacts in different areas. A Pew Research poll conducted in January found that Americans generally view data centers as being negative in terms of environmental impacts, home energy costs, and local quality of life, but are more likely to anticipate positive economic impacts.[6] This reflects the mood in Apex: while environmental harms and utility costs sparked widespread alarm, residents viewed the project’s economic promises with mild skepticism rather than major concern.

A Roadmap for Local Governments

As demonstrated in Apex, local governments, residents, and community organizers often don’t see eye to eye on what a new data center means to the community. While government officials may view these projects as an economic boon, many community members and activists fear that they’ll strain local infrastructure, put residents’ health at risk, deteriorate the beauty and of the community, and fall short on promises to grow the local economy.

To confront these tensions, local governments should establish mechanisms or procedures for accountability with or for the community. The research team’s analysis of the case study and review of guidance for host communities suggests that local governments incorporate both independent expertise and systematic community input when considering data center projects. We propose the following five-step roadmap that local governments can adopt to align infrastructure decisions with local priorities and context.

Step 1: Engage Independent Expertise at the Start of Negotiations

At the beginning stages of negotiations for a large digital infrastructure project, local governments should consult with independent, unbiased experts who can assess the technical, environmental, and economic impacts. This may require maintaining pre-approved consultant lists or establishing accountability mechanisms for developers. In the Apex case, this step may have reduced concern that the developer was misrepresenting the energy use associated with the facility by providing a trusted evaluation for all stakeholders to review.

Step 2: Inform the Community and Gather Their Priorities Early

Local governments should establish formal processes for gathering community input on the proposed data center infrastructure, such as through public forums. Community engagement should begin as early as possible—ideally before plans are officially filed—and continue consistently and transparently throughout all stages of zoning and approval. We also recommend that local leaders proactively seek input on the areas of resource use, pollution, financial investments, transparency, and governance. Current practices that shroud data center negotiations in secrecy produce distrust in the community; opening the process to the community offers greater opportunity for residents’ participation and to gain buy-in.

Step 3: Consider the Full Range of Policy Tools

Local governments should evaluate multiple policy mechanisms, drawing from existing toolkits and best practices like MediaJustice’s Site Fight Guide.[7] Policy interventions include but are not limited to community benefits agreements (CBAs), moratoriums, conditional use permits, zoning ordinances, and strict water and energy use regulations. There is not necessarily one solution for all communities when it comes to data centers: consider those protections that assuage community concerns. While the Apex case ended in a withdrawn proposal, a set of policy interventions may have created conditions that residents could live with.

Step 4: Tailor Policy Tools to Local Context

Once a policy choice is identified, the choice should then be carefully tailored to reflect the specific priorities identified through community engagement. Any regulatory framework should directly incorporate local preferences into concrete demands and requirements. This step was not part of the Apex case, where it would have allowed local officials to bridge the gap between abstract community feedback and enforceable zoning regulations.

Step 5: Use Community Priorities to Evaluate and Choose From Policy Options

Local governments should make their ultimate decision by evaluating all policy options in the context of the community’s biggest priorities. This can be done by referring back to each of the top priorities identified in Step 2 and deciding—such as through explicit criteria—whether they are reflected by the policy. Where feasible, governments can conduct a full cost-benefit analysis that reflects the local harms and benefits to the community. In the Apex Case, this approach would have provided a structured mechanism to weigh the project’s projected economic benefits against the community’s concerns.

Lessons for North Carolina State Government and Advocates

Listening to residents leads to better infrastructure decisions

The study identified key takeaways for state governments and advocates. Specifically, participants noted that North Carolina lacks statewide policies to protect residents. Instead, existing framework incentivizes data center development through aggressive tax exemptions, including sales-and-use tax breaks on construction, equipment, and electricity.[8]

Our findings underscore the need for the North Carolina state government to critically assess its data center development policies. Specifically, the resident perspectives gathered in this study justify a formal review of existing tax incentives to ensure these corporate benefits do not overshadow community priorities. While the state recently repealed the electricity tax exemption in its July budget, incentives for support equipment, software, and business property remain active.[9] These localized insights signal that expanding statewide policies is a necessary step to safeguard the long-term interests of residents. The state can also look to expand policies to protect the priorities and interests of their residents. North Carolina can also direct its AI Leadership Council—which is tasked with driving innovation and advancing trustworthy AI—to integrate community engagement into its research into the impacts of new data centers on residents.[10]

For advocacy groups, the findings highlight a clear path forward: mobilize early to force community perspectives into local infrastructure decisions. When a community faces risks from a proposed data center, proactive intervention is critical. Initiating dialogue with local governments and developers during the earliest planning phases ensures that resident concerns are factored into the project before agreements are finalized. Additionally, advocates can take steps to assist local governments in following the proposed roadmap. For example, advocacy groups can curate lists of independent experts that the government can consult with, and direct governments to existing resources.

As data centers continue to expand across North Carolina and the country, Apex highlights an important lesson: listening to residents leads to better infrastructure decisions. After Natelli Investments pulled its application due to community pushback, the town heard its residents and took an encouraging first step—placing a 12-month moratorium on new data center projects in order to research local impacts. By continuing down this road and centering community perspectives, Apex can set a bold example for how to design infrastructure policy that works for the people—not against them.

To learn more about the findings and takeaways from this research, read the full report.

Muniba Khan is a Master of Public Policy candidate at Duke University's Sanford School of Public Policy, concentrating in technology policy. Her work examines the community impacts of emerging technologies, technology governance, and digital equity.

title: This Midwest farm once raised thousands of hogs. Why is it growing mushrooms instead?
description:

text:
Want more news about agriculture and the environment? Sign up for the Harvest newsletter for our latest reporting, plus behind-the-scenes exclusives.

Inside a long, dimly-lit building, Tyler Faaborg slipped into a “fruiting room” cordoned off by what looked like plastic curtains. Fog rolled over shelves of sprouting mushrooms. A bulbous fungi called lion’s mane still had another week before harvest, he explained.

“You can see they’re sort of, a little bit pinkish,” Faaborg said. “When they get mature, they’re going to be almost all the way white.”

Tyler Faaborg, along with his parents and brother, grow specialty mushrooms on their family farm in central Iowa and sell them as tinctures, coffee blends and flavored salt.

They call their operation 1100 Farm, which is a nod to the number of hogs each of their two buildings held for decades. The Faaborg family recently transitioned from pigs to mushrooms with technical and financial support from The Transfarmation Project, which is part of the charity Mercy for Animals.

“We primarily work with industrial animal farmers to help them transition out of that way of farming and into sustainable practices, and that can be growing mushrooms, growing diversified vegetables, incorporating trees and agroecology,” said the organization’s director Katherine Jernigan.

Along with resources online and a network of experts to help farmers grow new crops and start a small business, Transfarmation provides open-source blueprints for converting industrial pig, poultry and dairy barns.

“That’s really what makes Transfarmation unique,” Jernigan said. “We’re finding ways to repurpose the infrastructure that the farmers already have.”

The Faaborg family farm was once a concentrated animal feeding operation, or CAFO. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency defines CAFOs as operations that meet certain animal number thresholds and confine them in an area without vegetation for at least 45 days out of the year.

There are more than 20,000 medium and large-sized CAFOs across the U.S., according to the most recent data available from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. Iowa led with 3,938 such operations in 2024. Minnesota, Nebraska and Texas also had high numbers.

The Faaborgs finished converting half of one 200-foot-long hog barn this summer. They say the retrofitted space will allow them to scale up their mushroom production after a successful pilot project. It’s also meant to be a resource for other farmers as Transfarmation’s second demonstration hub in the U.S. The first is a former chicken farm in North Carolina.

“The reason we established this as a demonstration hub is very much so the doors can be opened, so people can come and see firsthand,” Jernigan said. “They can ask questions, and also, importantly, we’re collecting data from this hub with the whole transition, as well as their production.”

The data include the Faaborgs’ costs, hours of labor and product margins, along with lessons learned along the way. A Transfarmation spokesperson said the Faaborgs are being compensated $216,000 through a four-year contract for tracking and sharing their information.

Jernigan said other farms enrolled in the Transfarmation program have shown it’s possible to be profitable switching from concentrated animal feeding operations to specialty crops. Transfarmation’s website includes estimated budgets for strawberries, tomatoes and microgreens.

But having more test cases and being transparent about both the challenges and opportunities could help other farmers make the leap, she said.

Tanner Faaborg, the one who brought the vision of 1100 Farm to the family several years ago, wants their mushroom operation to be another “proof of concept.”

“It just takes someone doing something a little different to help folks realize that it is possible,” he said.

How it started

Tanner Faaborg said his parents, Rand and Tammy, bought their 25-acre farm in the 1980s with the dream of a homesteading lifestyle. The family of seven harvested and preserved produce from their garden and fruit trees. They had a wood burning stove and chickens for eggs.

Rand Faaborg said he tried raising a few market hogs for “pocket money” to supplement his income as a welder. But it didn’t work out.

“I lost money,” Faaborg said. “And then I saw in the paper this advertisement of contract feeding and called a guy.”

Under this setup, a company provides the animals and pays for the feed while the farmer contributes the labor and covers the costs of the infrastructure. Rand Faaborg said contract feeding seemed like a good opportunity at the time.

Rand Faaborg did not put up new buildings for the enterprise at first. He retrofitted existing buildings on the farm to raise 2,000 hogs at a time. He said it was “very profitable” but required more work than he expected on top of his day job.

“I was working 16 hour days, sometimes 24 hour days, going to work without even sleeping,” he said. “That was hard. We did that for a few years, and then [the company] came out with this program where they would finance these buildings.”

The new hog barns, designed for efficiency, had automatic feeder lines and systems to move the manure out to an open air holding pit. Rand Faaborg said the total cost for both barns was over $400,000.

“Fortunately, we could make cash flow until we got the buildings paid off,” he said, explaining it took 12 years to get out of debt.

But raising hogs was physically demanding work and became less profitable for the family over time, he said.

“In my day job, my pay over 35 years increased tenfold, and my pay raising hogs dropped by two-thirds,” Rand Faaborg said.

As livestock production has shifted toward large-scale industrial operations in recent decades, dozens of research studies have documented negative health impacts on workers as well as surrounding communities. These operations also generate large amounts of nutrient-rich manure, which can pollute surrounding waterways and ecosystems.

Rand and Tammy Faaborg decided several years ago they were ready to exit the hog business. He said they didn’t have a deep love for raising pigs, but they had poured so much money and time into the buildings that they didn’t want to see them fall into disrepair, only to be bulldozed.

They asked their family if they had ideas to use the buildings for something else. That’s when their son, Tanner, began to lay out his vision.

“We have this infrastructure. We could retrofit it, change it, and do something that is a lot healthier on us, healthier for the planet, and actually is profitable, that’ll be a job creator for the family, but for the community, as well,” Tanner Faaborg said.

Converging two worlds

Tanner Faaborg said he developed a passion for sustainability and climate change mitigation in college. After traveling abroad for several years, he returned to Iowa and joined Urban Ambassadors, a volunteer-driven nonprofit that promotes sustainability in the Des Moines area. He represented the group as part of the steering committee for the city’s climate action and adaptation plan.

But his work in Iowa’s capital felt out of line with other parts of his life.

“I would come back [to the farm] and help out with pig chores, kind of living a double life that I felt terrible about,” he recalled.

The Faaborgs raised around 8,000 hogs each year, producing roughly a million gallons of liquid manure. They stored it in an open pit until they could find row-crop farmers to haul it off to spread on their fields during tight windows in the spring and fall.

While manure can provide essential crop nutrients, it also contributes to climate change.

Manure stored in pits and lagoons release methane, which is “28 times as potent as carbon dioxide at trapping heat in the atmosphere,” according to the EPA. And excess manure in fields can increase nitrous oxide emissions and pollute waterbodies by flushing out with rain and eroded soil.

Tanner Faaborg said he was also bothered by the reshaping of rural Iowa from industrial agriculture. Down the road from his childhood home, he pointed to long buildings surrounded by corn fields.

“There used to be a house over there. Now, instead, there’s turkey barns,” he said. “There used to be a house over there, and now it’s hog barns.”

Where Tanner Faaborg saw an opportunity for change, his brother Tyler needed more convincing. Tyler Faaborg said he marketed around 200,000 hogs a year across three counties when he decided to try something different with his family.

“I had a good job. I got paid well,” he said. “But I did it for 25 years. It’s really hard on your body, and Tanner just kept talking to me about it.”

The Faaborgs began working with Transfarmation in 2021 and sold the last herd of hogs a year later. With a $15,000 grant from the program in 2023, they experimented with growing mushrooms and developing products as a year-long pilot project. The Faaborgs reported site preparations in one of their outbuildings, supplies, branding and website development cost roughly $35,000.

As the business grows and expands with the new demonstration hub, Tyler Faaborg said the family would like to sell fresh mushrooms to a few companies. Eventually, 1100 Farm could convert the second hog barn. But Tanner Faaborg said it would be used for something else, possibly microgreens.

The Faaborgs said the transition from CAFO to specialty mushrooms has not always been easy, and they have a long road ahead. But there have been rewards along the way, like the conversion of a manure pit into a freshwater pond.

A U.S. Department of Agriculture Natural Resources Conservation Service grant program partially funded the remediation, Tanner Faaborg said. Instead of being an eyesore, he said it’s become a haven for frogs, ducks and other wildlife.

“It just shows that if you create the right environment, that rewilding can happen faster than you think,” he said.

Rand Faaborg said the manure pit was a significant source of anxiety when he raised hogs. He watched the level rise and hoped farmers would take it away before it reached capacity. Sometimes people said they would take it but not show up, he added.

“That part of my life is gone and in exchange is just this little pond. My grandkids catch frogs. It’s just been great,” Rand Faaborg said. “That’s probably been my favorite part of it all.”

The Faaborgs have also planted native grasses and wildflowers to support pollinators. They’re expanding their orchard and adding hundreds of trees and shrubs next to the creek that cuts across their farm to support wildlife habitat and better water quality.

Standing next to an empty grain silo, Tanner Faaborg said he’d like to turn it into a space for visitors to stay overnight and wake up the next morning with a view of the farm while sipping lion’s mane coffee.

The list of projects are enough to fill his lifetime. But Tanner Faaborg hopes the impact of 1100 Farm extends well beyond that.

The original story was produced and published by Iowa Public Radio.

text:
The Turkish city of Antalya is hosting the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31), with 197 countries expected to negotiate ways to accelerate the implementation of the 2015 Paris Agreement and expand funding to address the consequences of climate change.

The conference will run from 9 to 20 November under the slogan "Together for a Cleaner Future", bringing together world leaders and government delegations to discuss the implementation of existing climate commitments and the development of new environmental policies.

Since 1995, annual UN climate conferences have helped shape the future of the planet through environmental legislation and commitments. They have produced significant decisions, including the agreement reached at the Paris conference to limit global warming. COP31 is expected to help steer international environmental policies in a new direction.

Antalya's selection as host was not accidental. Its location in the Mediterranean basin makes it particularly relevant to discussions about climate change, given the region's exposure to drought, wildfires and other climate-related risks.

Australia is leading the negotiations under an unusual arrangement that resolved a dispute over which country would host the conference during COP30, held in the Brazilian Amazon city of Belém in November 2025.

Around 100,000 people are expected to visit the UN-managed Blue Zone, alongside official country delegations, while the Green Zone, managed by the host country, is expected to receive 1.5 million visitors.

According to organisers, participants will include 91 heads of state, more than 300 ministers, as well as officials from the European Union and the United Nations Development Programme. More than 45,000 volunteer applications have been received from 154 countries, while around 2,000 non-governmental organisations have announced their participation.

Organisers have also approved 160 applications for exhibition pavilions and 90 for offices. The leaders' summit will take place on 11 or 12 November, unlike previous COP conferences, where world leaders generally attended only the opening sessions. The new arrangement is intended to involve them directly in technical negotiations.

The 12-day conference will focus on the "Zero Waste" and "Resilient Cities" initiatives, alongside discussions on binding carbon emissions commitments, the green transition in energy policies, climate financing and its distribution, and sustainable development models.

The agenda will prioritise implementing previous pledges before introducing new rules, particularly in food and agriculture, health, green manufacturing and clean energy.

COP30 concluded in Brazil with an agreement calling for a threefold increase in funding for developing countries to protect their populations from the worsening effects of the climate crisis and strengthen support for communities transitioning to clean energy.

COP31 is expected to advance previous commitments through three main priorities: implementing emissions reduction targets under the Paris Agreement; financing responses to climate change through the achievement of the collective quantified climate finance goal set for developing countries at COP29; and adaptation, by increasing the resilience of countries and communities most exposed to climate risks.

The conference will also promote the deployment of low-carbon and climate-resilient technologies, strengthen international cooperation and knowledge-sharing, and support policies that improve the ability of vulnerable communities, ecosystems and economies to withstand climate threats.

Another priority is accelerating climate solutions and investment through structured cooperation between governments and private-sector institutions, and supporting scalable climate solutions with tangible results.

Clean energy, waste and resilient cities

Sustainable cooling, electricity supply and the production of clean, safe and accessible energy will feature prominently in discussions. The agenda includes transforming energy sector infrastructure and supporting access to biotechnology.

According to UN figures, approximately 730 million people worldwide lack access to electricity, while two billion still rely on polluting cooking methods, contributing to 3.7 million premature deaths annually.

COP31 aims to increase electricity's share of final energy consumption to 35 percent by 2035.

Waste management is another major focus, with delegates expected to explore how climate action can unlock the potential of scalable circular economy solutions.

The waste sector is the third-largest source of human-caused methane emissions and has been responsible for 30 percent of global warming since the beginning of the Industrial Revolution. Global waste production is also expected to increase by 50 percent by 2050, according to the UN.

The Antalya conference aims to expand circular economy initiatives that prevent emissions at source, including measures to reduce food waste and incorporate methane emissions into countries' nationally determined contributions (NDCs).

Discussions will also address the development of cities capable of withstanding climate change. Cities account for approximately 70 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions and face some of the most severe consequences of climate change. Meanwhile, 15 percent of major cities worldwide are exposed to the risk of severe flooding or drought.

COP31 aims to reduce energy intensity in the construction sector by 25 percent by 2035.

Green manufacturing will also feature prominently. Industry accounts for around 25 percent of global emissions, while sectors where emissions are difficult to reduce face complex decarbonisation pathways. Many developing countries also need support to establish the foundations of green industry from scratch.

Youth participation, implementation challenges

COP31 has also dedicated space to young people, recognising that they are not merely the generation inheriting climate risks but also potential builders of solutions.

People aged between 10 and 24 account for 1.8 billion of the global population and will experience the consequences of climate change over a longer period. Despite this, their participation in decision-making remains limited.

The conference will seek to raise climate awareness and encourage knowledge-sharing between generations.

A further priority will be identifying ways to implement existing climate protection commitments and bridge the gap between priorities, investment and action. The UN has emphasised the need to accelerate the translation of climate pledges into tangible results.

Although many countries have established ambitious climate targets through their NDCs, adaptation action plans and long-term strategies, implementation continues to face obstacles. These include limited institutional capacity, fragmented investment opportunities and insufficient alignment between policy priorities and financing solutions.

The annual Conference of the Parties is the most important international forum for climate negotiations. It is held under the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, adopted in 1992, and serves as the main platform for negotiations, international cooperation, assessing global progress and coordinating responses to climate change.

Among its key functions is reviewing national communications on greenhouse gas emissions and assessing the impact of measures adopted by individual countries.

The 1992 convention was the first comprehensive global agreement aimed at combating climate change. Subsequent conferences helped shape international climate policy, including the Kyoto Protocol, adopted in 1997 and entering into force in 2005, and the Paris Agreement of 2015.

Meanwhile, a US congressional delegation is heading to Turkey to attend COP31 following the Democratic Party's sweeping victory in the midterm elections.

The United States will not participate in the official negotiations after President Donald Trump withdrew from the Paris climate agreement for a second time following his return to the White House.

text:
North Carolina's coast is more than a popular getaway. It's home to fishing, aquaculture, and research that could grow into what's known as a blue economy.

RTI (Research Triangle Institute) International, based in Research Triangle Park, recently produced a study with NC EcoTech that looks at ways to create new opportunities for coastal businesses. It recommends adopting new technologies, developing a statewide plan, and removing regulatory hurdles that will allow businesses to test new ideas.

WUNC News' Bradley George spoke with two researchers who worked on the report: Jessica Wilkinson, a economic development researcher at RTI, and Adams Bailey, a research economist.

This conversation has been lightly edited for clarity and brevity.

What is a blue economy?

Jessica Wilkinson: The blue economy is all types of economic activity that's tied to oceans, coasts, marine ecosystems. So you can think about fish and shellfish farming, anything from boat building, commercial fishing, shipping, coastal resilience at all falls under the blue economy.

There's already a lot of economic activity on North Carolina's coast. Of course, it's a popular tourist destination. Lots of people are moving there. Where does this idea of a blue economy fit into the economic activity that's already happening along the coast?

JW: One thing we talk about in this report in particular is that North Carolina's got a lot of heritage in the blue economy and a lot of diverse assets. But one of the things that we realized when we were working in this area is that a lot of it's disconnected. So we, of course, we have tourism. We didn't talk about that too much, and sometimes that can be kind of at heads with aquaculture, so I think that's something you know that people probably have heard of before. But we have a long history of fishing and aquaculture and fish farming and fin fish farming across the state from the west to the coast.

Adams Bailey: At one point, I would add is North Carolina is really unique in just how many miles of coastline we have, protecting those from erosion is maintaining habitats. If you're building in resilient coastline, you're building in cleaner habitats and are just overall good for sustainability in the environment of our state.

Jessica, you mentioned seafood. Most of what we eat in the U.S. is imported. What are some of the recommendations you came up with to encourage more seafood production in North Carolina?

JW: One thing we talk about is just the big importance of introducing these new technologies that are coming online every day, and helping to make sure that current farmers and future farmers and fishermen are aware and able to access these technologies. So, of course, AI is a huge one. Remote sensing is a huge one. Another one are some of these recirculating aquaculture systems we talk about, making sure that they're accessible.

Adams, are there examples of other states in the U.S. or even other places around the world that have adopted these blue economy strategies and have seen benefits from them?

AB: Absolutely. So, one of the companies we're really excited about is Hima Seafood in Norway. Has been adopting RAS (recirculating aquaculture systems) to farm fish in Norway. They've been considering a North Carolina investment. They still haven't made an announcement on where that investment could be, but if they did come here, it would be a major economic win for our state, both in terms of jobs created and value created, but also in you know adopting advanced systems here that are producing fish in a clean and sustainable way, and create a lot of jobs and allow us to eat seafood that was grown locally.

You've produced this report, so what are the next steps?

JW: This project, the NC EcoTech project, ended about a year ago. And some of this work was catalyzed by these federal investments I mentioned through the National Science Foundation. A lot of the federal funding landscape has changed, and some of these efforts that were time limited have ended. And so, part of this report was like a call to action as well for who could step in with some of this federal support. And then other calls to action were about the regulatory environment. We had spoken to many people who said that the regulatory environment is perceived as acting in kind of a case by case basis, and there were some bottlenecks, and it could kind of slow down the implementation of new technologies that come online.

text:
UN Climate Change News, Antalya, Türkiye, 9 November 2026 – As world leaders gather for COP31, the Yearbook of Global Climate Action 2026 shows climate solutions scaling across sectors – from energy and transport to nature and food – while highlighting where implementation must go further and faster.

Produced by the Climate High-Level Champions and UN Climate Change, this tenth edition tracks progress, gaps and practical approaches to implementing the Paris Agreement.

“Behind every number in this Yearbook is a family, a farmer or a city. Even as floods, heatwaves and droughts intensify, climate action is building resilience and driving innovative, tangible solutions. Now we must scale these solutions, so the benefits reach every community, everywhere,” said Samed Ağırbaş, COP31 Climate High-Level Champion.

Where progress is being made

Among the strongest climate action success stories:

Clean power is scaling: Renewable capacity grew 17 per cent to 5,149 GW in 2025, a record 108 GW of battery storage was added, and renewables overtook coal in electricity generation (33.8 compared to 33.0 per cent).

Transport is electrifying: Electric vehicles made up a quarter of light-duty sales in 2025, public charging points passed seven million, and zero-emission trucks rose from 1.8 to nine per cent of heavy goods vehicle sales.

Explicit Fossil fuel subsidies are falling: These subsidies fell from USD 1.4 trillion in 2022 to USD 725 billion in 2024.

Forest and ocean protection are gaining ground: Deforestation fell by nearly 14 per cent in 2025, 11.8 million hectares are under active restoration (up from 10.6 million in 2024), and marine protected areas more than doubled in a decade, from 4.1 to 10 per cent of the ocean.

Food security is improving: Undernourishment fell from 9.1 to 7.8 per cent (2023–2025), and the share of people unable to afford a healthy diet fell from 37.4 to 32.7 per cent (2021–2025).

Cities and resilience planning are advancing: National climate plans with strong urban content doubled from 52 to 104 (2024–2026), countries with multi-hazard early warning systems rose from 108 to 119, and developing countries with updated National Adaptation Plans rose from 59 to 81.

Finance and jobs are growing: Climate finance passed USD 2 trillion in 2024, and renewable energy jobs reached 16.6 million.

text:
Environmental advocates are focused on efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, and are pointing their efforts on industrial agriculture's impact.

That was the focus of a recent webinar led by the Minnesota Center for Environmental Advocacy in late October.

The conversation was led by MCEA’s Chief Impact Officer Leigh Currie. It centered around “industrial agriculture’s role in Minnesota’s accelerating climate crisis and what it will take to create change.”

She made the point that the topic of a climate crisis cannot be discussed without also talking about industrial ag.

“In Minnesota today, agriculture is the second biggest climate-polluting sector of our economy,” Currie said. “It trails just slightly behind transportation, and it is historically and notoriously hard to regulate.”

She added that agriculture has become very polarized and thus has been difficult to make change from a political standpoint.

Currie shared that sustainable agriculture practices are out there, but that state lawmakers need to make sure large-scale agricultural operators are using those practices.

Talking on the subject were Matthew Sheets, a policy organizer for Land Stewardship Project, Jay Eidness, supervising attorney at MCEA, and Laura Fox, a clinical lecturer and research scholar at Yale Law School.

Prompted by Currie, Sheets spoke about Minnesota’s shift toward industrial agriculture, specifically from his view from Morris, Minnesota, where he has helped organize against the permitting of the largest feedlot in the state, the recently approved Riverview LLP West River Dairy expansion, which is set to become the state’s largest dairy with around 19,000 head permitted.

Environmental groups continue to challenge that project's future.

Sheets used that dairy as an example, saying that when he first got started with Land Stewardship Project, they were using dairy data from 2018, when there were around 5,000 dairies in the state. He said that number fell off a cliff and now includes about 1,600 dairies.

“So we’re losing farms at an incredibly fast rate,” Sheets said.

At the same time, the number of dairy cows in the state is nearly unchanged. Sheets explained that what he sees happening is the majority of the economic power is going to fewer hands, and the livestock are more concentrated than ever.

“It's a really important topic for us to be talking about like this, because it is having massive impacts on the land, the people and just the economy of our area,” Sheets said.

Eidness touched on how he saw industrial agriculture contributing to the climate crisis.

“Agriculture emits about a quarter of our state's greenhouse gases,” he said. That means agriculture emits more than it takes to generate all the electricity needed to power every home and business in Minnesota.

This is more than just cow gas. Eidness broke it down further, explaining how livestock emit gases through the digestive process, but there are also greenhouse gas emissions associated with raising the crops to feed the livestock. Another area of concern is when land is cleared for farming or peat grounds are drained for farming to occur.

“When we drain land, we expose a lot of the carbon sequestering ability of the landscape to oxygen, which then releases the greenhouse gas emissions,” Eidness said. “When we cut down trees to make way for arable land that too will lose the tree's ability to sequester the carbon and will create more greenhouse gases in that way,” Eidness said.

While Eidness sees the agriculture industry failing to lower emissions, he said sectors like transportation have made significant drops.

“And I don’t find that to be surprising because we really don’t have any measures in place to intentionally focus efforts to bring those greenhouse gas emissions down,” Eidness said.

Fox said the big concern is that without change, the world is headed toward warming by 3 degrees Celsius this century. She warned that now is not a time to surrender to the warming.

“The higher temperatures climb even by a fraction of a degree, the greater risk of extreme heat, flooding, drought, ecosystem collapse,” Fox said.

Fox pointed at animal agriculture’s methane production as a major contributor of greenhouse gases, and reducing that methane is one of the most effective opportunities to reduce warming in the near term.

While she considered methane reduction similar to “pulling the emergency brake on the climate crisis,” she explained that pulling that brake faces stiff opposition from a political standpoint.

“One of the recurring findings is that industrial animal agriculture has largely escaped from climate accountability, even environmental accountability more broadly,” she said.

While her research has shown increased scrutiny on fossil fuels, power plants, and transportation systems, the same scrutiny has not yet been applied to large industrial agriculture.

Eidness said change needs to start from legislatively mandated greenhouse gas emission reduction goals. Fox said methods to control greenhouse gas emissions are already in place for other sectors and those same measures should be placed on animal agriculture, too.

“We can't effectively regulate pollution that we're not adequately measuring,” Fox said. “And you know, large industrial livestock operations should be required to quantify and report their greenhouse gas emissions. And we need to account for their full climate footprint. Not just emissions, right, from the animals and manure but also emissions associated with growing feed, energy use, you know, other activities throughout the supply chain and lost carbon sequestration opportunities from land use changes, right?”

Fox mentioned that this must be an approach taken by states. She gave California as an example of a state that has set a goal of reducing methane emissions by 40% by 2030. She said, in that case, incentives are in place to help producers achieve the goal.

Fox gave another example of giving farmers pathways to help them transition.

“We shouldn't be simply demanding farmers change practices, right, without creating viable economic pathways for them to do so,” she said. “And states can be helpful in providing those resources and incentivizing through the procurement it undertakes itself.”

The entire conversation is available at youtube.com/watch?v=DyFlsxgWZh0.

text:
US sodium-ion developer Mana Battery has appointed former BMW battery technology lead Frederik Morgenstern as vice-president of cell engineering.

Morgenstern joins the Broomfield, Colorado-based start-up after more than 15 years working on battery and vehicle technology. Most recently, he was senior technology and innovation lead for batteries at BMW of North America.

At BMW AG in Munich, Morgenstern led an interdisciplinary team developing the company’s sixth-generation cylindrical cell and module technology from initial concept towards series production, according to Mana.

Since moving to California in 2022, he has managed BMW’s North American battery partnership portfolio. This included more than 30 projects with start-ups and national laboratories and an annual research and development budget of up to $10 million.

His work covered fast charging, lithium-metal and silicon anodes and lower-cost cathode chemistries including lithium manganese-rich, lithium nickel manganese oxide and lithium manganese iron phosphate.

At Mana, Morgenstern will be responsible for advancing the company’s anode-free sodium-ion technology towards customer qualification and commercial production.

The architecture removes the conventional hard-carbon anode used in most sodium-ion cells. Instead, sodium supplied by the cathode is deposited directly onto a current collector during charging and stripped away during discharge.

Removing the permanent anode material can reduce cell weight, volume and material costs. However, commercialisation depends on controlling sodium deposition and achieving sufficiently high coulombic efficiency to prevent the limited sodium inventory being consumed over repeated cycles.

Mana is developing proprietary liquid electrolytes

Mana is developing proprietary liquid electrolytes intended to support this deposition process while improving cell stability and safety. The company claims its cells could exceed LFP energy density while offering faster charging, better cold-weather performance and lower projected costs. It did not provide independently verified comparative performance or cycle-life figures with the appointment announcement.

Mana chief executive Tyler Evans said: “Frederik has done what few people in this industry have: taken a new cell from a blank page to a global automaker’s production line. His experience with OEMs and cell suppliers will help us move our technology into customers’ hands faster.”

Morgenstern said Mana was close to combining technical performance with the cost needed to compete against established Asian battery manufacturers.

He said: “Mana is on the verge of doing that. Its sodium-ion cells outperform LFP on energy density, cold-weather performance and charging speed, at a projected price below today’s cost leader. That mix of innovation and cost leadership is why I joined.”

The company was founded in 2023 as a spin-out from the University of Colorado Boulder. Its target markets include defence, grid storage, data centres and electric vehicles.

Saft and Mana signed a joint development agreement in August to develop and validate anode-free sodium-ion cells for defence and critical-infrastructure applications.

text:
BMW is expanding its global electric vehicle battery supply network by adding Samsung SDI in Europe and LG Energy Solution in the United States as new suppliers of next-generation battery cells. The move is part of the German automaker’s strategy to strengthen regional production, diversify its supply chain and secure a reliable supply of batteries for its upcoming electric vehicles.

The two battery manufacturers will supply BMW with cells for its sixth-generation (Gen6) high-voltage batteries from their existing regional production facilities starting in the late 2020s. The partnerships further strengthen BMW’s commitment to its “local for local” approach, which prioritizes sourcing components close to vehicle production sites.

Battery cells are among the most important components of an electric vehicle, directly influencing driving range, charging performance and overall efficiency. Securing a reliable supply of advanced battery technology is therefore essential as BMW prepares to expand its next generation of electric vehicles.

Under its latest supplier agreements, BMW will source battery cells produced in Europe from CATL, EVE Energy and Samsung SDI. In the United States, LG Energy Solution will become another key supplier.

By working with several leading battery manufacturers across different regions, BMW aims to reduce its dependence on individual suppliers while improving the flexibility and resilience of its global production network.

The company says this diversified approach will also help strengthen industrial value creation in Europe and North America, supporting local manufacturing and shortening transportation distances between battery suppliers and vehicle assembly plants.

Nicolai Martin, BMW AG’s Board Member responsible for Purchasing and Supplier Network, said the company is committed to developing regional supply chains while taking advantage of global procurement opportunities.

The strategy is intended to keep BMW competitive across international markets while building stronger partnerships with battery manufacturers in key production regions.

Five New Battery Assembly Facilities Support BMW’s Gen6 Strategy

BMW’s local-for-local approach extends beyond battery cell sourcing. The automaker is also establishing battery assembly operations close to its vehicle production facilities around the world.

For its sixth-generation high-voltage batteries, BMW has built five new battery assembly facilities in strategically important locations:

– Irlbach-Straßkirchen, Germany: Supporting BMW’s battery production network in Europe.

– Debrecen, Hungary: Serving the company’s expanding European manufacturing operations.

– Shenyang, China: Strengthening BMW’s production presence in the Chinese market.

– Woodruff, United States: Supporting regional battery manufacturing in North America.

– San Luis Potosí, Mexico: Expanding the company’s battery production capabilities in Mexico.

Locating battery assembly facilities close to vehicle factories helps reduce logistics costs, shorten delivery times and improve production flexibility.

It also supports regional industrial infrastructure and employment while reducing the risks associated with long-distance transportation and disruptions to international supply chains.

Building Local Battery Supply Chains Is a Long-Term Challenge

Establishing competitive battery production in different regions is not a straightforward process. Battery cell manufacturing requires substantial investment, advanced technology, specialized infrastructure and reliable partnerships with experienced suppliers.

BMW believes that developing comprehensive regional battery ecosystems will be essential to the long-term competitiveness of the electric vehicle industry.

However, attracting battery manufacturers and establishing local production capacity also depends on favorable economic conditions, suitable industrial infrastructure and predictable government regulations.

The company is therefore pursuing a long-term strategy that combines established global battery suppliers with localized manufacturing operations.

Rather than relying on a single geographical production hub, BMW is spreading its battery supply network across major automotive markets to improve its ability to respond to changing market conditions.

BMW Expands In-House Battery Technology and Recycling Expertise

Alongside its partnerships with external battery manufacturers, BMW continues to invest in its own battery research, development and recycling capabilities.

The company operates several specialized competence centers in Bavaria, Germany, focusing on different stages of battery technology development.

The Battery Cell Competence Center (BCCC) in Munich focuses on researching and developing new battery cell technologies for future electric vehicles.

Meanwhile, the Cell Manufacturing Competence Center (CMCC) in Parsdorf investigates how these cells can be manufactured at industrial scale while maintaining high quality and resource efficiency. The facility also produces and tests near-series battery cells.

BMW is also expanding its work on battery recycling through the Cell Recycling Competence Center (CRCC) in Salching.

The facility focuses on recovering valuable raw materials from used battery cells through an innovative direct recycling process developed by BMW. The recovered materials can then be reintegrated into the battery production process.

Although Encory GmbH will build and operate the recycling competence center, BMW retains ownership of the intellectual property behind the recycling technology.

This approach reflects the company’s broader ambition to develop a more sustainable battery ecosystem, covering everything from cell development and manufacturing to material recovery and reuse.
