The crux, as summarized by The Verge, is that while the legislation, if passed, "could be a catalyst for lots of clean energy, it could also speed up polluting projects and limit oversight of new data centers."

Green groups in the days leading up to Monday have intensified their opposition, even as lawmakers have introduced changes to make the bill more palatable. On Saturday, the Senate Democratic Caucus met in Washington, DC to discuss the bill and offer "manager's amendments" in hopes of garnering enough votes for passage.

According to Elizabeth Bast, executive director of Oil Change International, however, “No amount of last-minute tinkering can disguise that this bill is a massive giveaway to fossil fuel companies and Big Tech at the expense of communities, the climate, and people’s energy bills."

The bill, Bast added, "is exactly what the fossil fuel industry has been asking for years" and called on all lawmakers to vote against it.

Earthworks, one of the hundreds of advocacy groups lining up against BAAJA, warns that the legislation would give the public and Tribes less say in major energy projects, creating conditions that are a giveaway to the mining, data center, and fossil fuel industries.

"The bill would expand the 1872 Mining Law so companies could claim nearly unlimited public land for waste dumps, roads, pipelines and power lines," Earthworks said in a statement. "The demand for minerals for the energy transition is real, but it is no excuse to let mining companies take more public land with fewer safeguards, under a law that already prioritizes mining ahead of other land use."

The group's policy director, Lauren Pagel, said, “We need a fast, fair transition to clean energy, but not one built on the backs of communities that live next to mines and pipelines. These communities are the ones drinking the water and breathing the air, and this bill gives them fewer protections."

Veteran climate organizer Bill McKibben, writing about the legislation on Saturday, also pointed out the fundamental problem with legislation that treats permitting reform for clean energy projects and dirty energy projects as an equal endeavor.

While acknowledging that currently it remains "too hard to build stuff we badly need—housing, transit, energy," when it comes to building energy infrastructure, "there’s a problem, and that problem (as so often) is climate change. Building more housing produces…more housing. But if you take climate change seriously, you have to build more clean energy and less dirty energy, or otherwise you don’t get anywhere."

It's a similar argument made by groups like Public Citizen, who said Friday that while some of the bill's provisions—like those related to transmission lines and ratepayer protections from data centers—are "strong and sorely needed," the problem remains that "the bill’s drawbacks are greater, more immediate, and more certain."

Whatever benefits the legislation might secure, explained David Arkush, director of Public Citizen’s Climate Program, the downsides will be far worse, undercutting existing laws designed to protect public lands, endangered species, and the nation's natural resources, including clean air and water.

BAAJA, said Arkush, "seriously weakens the Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act and guts the National Environmental Policy Act and the National Historic Preservation Act. It fast-tracks the permitting of all manner of projects, then makes it virtually impossible to regulate or arguably even enforce existing rules against them, without an act of Congress."

"Among other effects," he continued, "the bill will open the door to a vast increase in exports of liquefied natural gas and facilitate a hasty and reckless buildout of data centers powered by fossil gas. And the bill would make it significantly more difficult to moderate, regulate, or alter these actions later, regardless of what public health, climate destruction, or public sentiment demand."

As far as McKibben is concerned, "I think that if this deal had been made 30 years ago, it might have made sense—we’d be reaping the benefits now. But the fossil fuel industry made sure we didn’t. And this bill, which they’re backing with great enthusiasm, seems an awful lot like a hedge to make sure they can string their business model out for a few more decades—a way to lock in the fruits of their decades of political obstructionism."

With Democrats soon returning to power, opponents of the permitting reform bill said it makes no sense to bend to Republicans now to pass a bill that falls short in such fundamental ways.

“In the November 3 elections, voters across the country resoundingly rejected data centers," said Arkush. "This is not the time to pass a bill that enables Big Tech to charge forward with them, powered by fossil fuels, over the objection of local communities."

Come January, he said, "the makeup of Congress will change substantially," making it likely that a significantly "better deal can be reached then—one that enacts the laudable and important provisions in this bill, and more, without so many sacrifices."

In October, veteran Democratic operator John Podesta warned that providing legislation like BAAJA to the Trump administration would be like giving the president and his party a "loaded howitzer" with which to attack environmental protections.

With Trump's appointment on Friday of Stephen Miller to be his new White House chief of staff, McKibben connected that choice of the "single most vile character I've ever seen on our national scene" with Podesta's comments and offered this guidance: "Handing Stephen Miller a loaded howitzer is not something any senator should even contemplate. Period."

Gaza’s Government Media Office on Saturday, holding Israel wholly responsible for the disaster, said initial losses from flooded and destroyed tents were estimated at $3 million and that dozens of walls of homes had collapsed, resulting in injuries, while the threat of broader building collapse remained a serious risk.

In a statement, Palestinian Health Minister Dr. Majed Abu Ramadan said, “What is happening in Gaza is not a passing winter crisis. I urgently call on the international community, the United Nations, and health, humanitarian, and relief organizations to intervene immediately to save the lives of hundreds of thousands of displaced people in the Gaza Strip, following the flooding of thousands of tents with rainwater and the absence of basic safe shelter conditions."

Al-Jazeera reports:

According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), about 950,000 displaced people in Gaza are living in areas exposed to flooding. Low-lying locations and sites near the coast are particularly vulnerable, with more than 400,000 people living in areas considered at high risk of flooding.

About 44,000 Palestinians are living in structurally unsafe buildings, while more than 4,000 buildings across the territory are estimated to require full or partial demolition due to damage caused by Israeli air strikes. About 294,250 families need shelter assistance ahead of winter, but the available supplies cover only 18 percent of their needs.

Ramadan further warned of "a catastrophic deterioration in health and environmental conditions, alongside growing risks of the spread of diseases and epidemics" if an emergency response was not rapidly and comprehensively deployed.

Video footage and eyewitness accounts offered a heartbreaking picture of those hit by the floods.

“We woke up and found ourselves surrounded by water," a man named Mansour al-Sakni, 33, told the Middle East Eye. "The children were crying. I did not know what to do, and I started crying too."

“We stood inside the tarpaulin shelter waiting for the rain to stop so we could try to push the water out of the room,” he said. “We are poor people in Gaza. We want to live. We do not want to die from the bombing or the cold. Enough. Have mercy on us.”

According to NBC News:

The territory’s civil defence service said it had received 1,500 distress calls from displaced residents. Three abandoned houses collapsed without causing injuries, it added.

At a tent encampment in Gaza City, some people tried to repair their tents, ⁠while others used sand to reinforce them and prevent water from entering. ⁠Some were busy getting their children out of flooded tents.

Olfat Magdoub, a Gaza resident, tried in vain to sweep water away from her tent.

“This is the first day of rain, and of course ⁠we are already flooded. What will happen if it rains again the next day? This is only the first day and ⁠we’re already overwhelmed,” said the woman.

“Two weeks ago when it rained, I swear to God, I spent four days sleeping on blankets spread on the floor because the rainwater had flooded the bedding. Same now, the mattresses are wet so we sleep on the ground.”

While the flooding devastated the people and families trapped by the blockade of life-saving aid and shelter, fresh ire was pointed at the US government for refusing to rebuke the Israeli government for its wanton disregard for human life and suffering.

On the ground in Gaza, the anguish of Palestinians, including children, was on display in videos of the devastation and ongoing catastrophe posted to social media:

"How long are we supposed to live like this?" declares the young boy featured in the video. "I swear I don't know what to do. Have mercy on us for God's sake! For the sake of God, have mercy on us!"

Rain is worsening the suffering of Gaza’s children as water pours into homes damaged by Israeli bombardment, soaking bedding and clothes. With no shelter repair materials or tarpaulins available, families are left unable to protect their children from the flooding. https://t.co/OzVMGHzssI

"For the fourth consecutive year," Abdul added, "Gaza remains under a suffocating Israeli siege that prevents even the recovery of victims’ bodies from beneath the rubble."

While the final totals are not yet established, Democrats emerged from Tuesday's elections with at least 254 seats in the next Congress, reclaiming the majority from the Republicans, who currently can count on just 162 seats when new members are sworn in come January.

While Jeffries is clearly the presumptive choice for Democrats, and he formally put himself in the running on Wednesday with a letter to all members, outside progressives have voiced serious opposition given his failure to embrace many of the positions—including backing Medicare for All, taking on entrenched corporate power, and restricting military assistance to Israel over its genocide in Gaza—that have animated voters nationwide this election cycle.

According to the petition:

We believe the Speaker should represent the Democratic voters, not just the Democratic establishment.

The Speaker has enormous influence over the House's direction, including its legislative priorities and agenda. Before casting their votes, representatives should closely examine Jeffries's public record, policy positions, campaign donor record, and leadership...and listen to constituents who do not want him elevated to Speaker.

This is not a foregone conclusion. There is still time for other Democratic members of the House to step forward and seek the nomination for Speaker, someone whose priorities more closely reflect the voters who hope to elect the Democratic majority.

We are calling on every member of the incoming 120th Congress to vote against Hakeem Jeffries for Speaker in January 2027 and choose a different candidate.

Axios reported Friday that members of Congress have been "inundated" with calls urging them not to elect Jeffries and suggested that some of the hesitations are not just among progressives.

The outlet reported, interviewing "nearly a half-dozen incoming House Democrats in deeply red seats Thursday who declined to state a firm position one way or another on voting for him."

As Corbin Trent, the former top aide to Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) who now runs a progressive organizing outfit called A Fight Worth Having, wrote in a column published at Common Dreams on Friday, "the Democratic leadership we have today is completely ill-suited for this moment. They do not have the vision for what it’s going to take to rebuild the trust the American people have lost in their government, their institutions, and the Democratic Party itself."

"Democrats have spoken loudly and clearly that they want new leadership," Trent said of the election. "Unfortunately, too many of the people in Washington aren’t listening."

While the large Democratic majority in the House makes it easier for Jeffries to maneuver leading up to the leadership vote, and given that no challenger has stepped forward to take him on directly, the betting money is still safe that Jeffries will be the next Speaker of the House.

But the public push denouncing him as the wrong choice of leadership at a moment when Democratic voters are clearly demanding—and expecting—a much bolder agenda may still affect his calculations.

"If he wants to pass Trumpcare-for-All, I'm ok with it. He seems to like to put his name on things," said El-Sayed.

"That's a pretty good compromise—that's bipartisan," Hasan quipped. "You'll offer him the name, and everyone gets healthcare?"

"Yeah," responded El-Sayed. "Donald, if you're watching, we'll put your name on it. You get to be the American president who finally guaranteed health care for every single American—met the unmet promise of America. You get to be that guy, so let's talk about it."

“If he wants to pass Trumpcare-for-All, I'm ok with it.. Donald, if you're watching, we'll put your name on it. You get to be the American president who finally guaranteed health care for every single American."@AbdulElSayed to me today, lol.Full intv: https://t.co/W8g8V0efSF https://t.co/m4QC14saNE

— Mehdi Hasan (@mehdirhasan) November 7, 2026

In Sanders' remarks Thursday, which he made on MS-NOW with Chris Hayes, the Independent Senator from Vermont interrupted when Hayes said the chances of Trump ever signing Medicare for All into law were extremely low.

"Hold it, hold it, hooooold it," Sanders said, waving his hand. "Two points. Trump has the constitutional right to veto—if he wants to. But we have the constitutional right to represent the American people and to pass the damn thing and to show the American people that we are sick and tired of maintaining a broken [healthcare] system."

Hayes on Medicare for All: "The odds of Donald Trump signing that into law, pretty small--"Sen. Sanders: "Hold it, hold it, hold it... Our job is to produce it. He wants to veto it, Republicans want to sustain that veto, that is their responsibility, the American people will see it."

— NewsNewsNews (@RealCrookedNews) November 6, 2026

"Number two," Sanders continued. "Donald Trump may be a bit crazy, but he is not stupid. And he is a good politician. I mean this guy looks out all over the country, and he says, 'Everyone knows this system is broken. You know what, what do I gotta lose?' So I am not absolutely certain that Trump wouldn't sign it. But whether he would or not, our job is to produce it. He wants to veto it, and Republicans want to sustain that veto—that is their responsibility and the American people will see it."

Poll after poll have shown that Medicare for All—which would cover everyone in the country for less money overall than the current system dominated by for-profit insurers—is incredibly popular, not just among Democrats but also independents and increasing numbers of those who identify as Republican or conservative.

Many social media users applauded the idea. "I just had this discussion with someone," said one user in response to comments separate Sanders made about the subject earlier in the week. "Call it Trumpcare-for-All, who cares as long as we get it. People around him have been taking advantage of his narcissism for years; he doesn't have any real beliefs himself, it's worth a shot."

In response to El-Sayed's strategic idea of renaming "Medicare for All" to "Trumpcare-for-All," Hasan admitted that while he thought it was a "good move," he'd have a hard time seeking care if it meant invoking Trump's name at the doctor's office.

"I just want people to have healthcare," said El-Sayed.

According to the report, the administration is seeking to use a little-known provision in the federal tax code to strip nonprofits of their status without going through the normal Internal Revenue Service investigation and appeals process.

The law, signed in 2003 by then-President George W. Bush, allows the president to identify an organization in an executive order as supporting or engaging in terrorism. The law also prevents organizations from challenging designation or suspension in proceedings concerning federal tax liability.

It’s not clear yet which groups will be targeted, but the administration and its allies in Congress have already signaled their intent to go after left-leaning groups like George Soros’ Open Society Foundations, the Southern Poverty Law Center (SPLC), and the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR).

The latter was forced to cease operations in Florida Thursday following a state-level "terrorism" designation by Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis.

In September 2025, weeks after the assassination of right-wing activist Charlie Kirk, Trump signed National Security Presidential Memorandum 7 (NSPM-7), which identified “anti-capitalism,” “anti-Christianity,” “extremism on migration, race, and gender,” and “hostility towards those who hold traditional American views on family, religion, and morality” as ideological characteristics associated with “domestic terrorism.”

The memo directed the IRS and other federal agencies to investigate nonprofits and their funders for alleged connections to political violence.

Shanna Singh Hughey, a policy strategist at the anti-authoritarian watchdog group Protect Democracy, said in September that the memo's vague and subjective language gave the administration expansive powers to target the nonprofits of its political foes.

“It goes way beyond that to the organizations that are connected to the folks who might be accused [of violence], including board members and staff, as long as that organization is accused of either funding or facilitating the violence done by the target," she told Inside Philanthropy.

“This is exactly what we expect to see when authoritarians attempt to consolidate and hold power,” she said. “There are entities that seek to hold the government accountable, and so the government uses the tools in its toolkit to try to silence them.”

Then-White House Deputy Chief of Staff and Homeland Security Advisor Stephen Miller speaks during an event with US President Donald Trump in the Oval Office of the White House on August 6, 2026, in Washington, DC. (Photo by Alex Wong/Getty Images)

Trump's reported plan to attack nonprofits comes on the same day that he named Stephen Miller, the chief architect of NSPM-7, as his new White House chief of staff.

Weeks before the memo was signed, Miller vowed to "dismantle and take on the radical left organizations in this country that are fomenting violence." He has said that descriptions of Trump and his immigration policies as "authoritarian" or "fascist" were examples of language that "incites" violence.

He has also referred to the Democratic Party itself as "not a political party," but "a domestic extremist organization."

During a State Department ministerial on terrorism in July, Miller said that under NSPM-7, the administration was empowered to “disrupt, identify, defund, debank, arrest, and prosecute” what it called terrorist organizations.

In the same speech, he claimed that left-wing extremists invoke "civil liberties" disingenuously to evade criminal punishment.

Describing leftists as the "enemies of civilization," he said, "It is essential that we are wise enough and strong enough to understand that these appeals must fall on deaf ears."

Vance was initially unsupportive of Trump's decision to go to war, but has been one of the administration's staunchest defenders of the United States' actions in Iran—declaring that the US "never targets civilians" despite multiple bombings of schools; writing another verbose social media post falsely claiming that the decision to go to war lies only with the president—not Congress; and denying in September that the conflict that has killed more than 3,400 Iranians, 13 US service members, and thousands of people across the Middle East, is a war at all.

On Thursday, Mamdani expressed disbelief that Vance, thought to be the likely heir to Trump's MAGA movement and a potential 2028 presidential contender, would attempt to distance himself from the war the US is waging while still serving as one of the highest-ranking political officials in the country.

Holy shit! I 'd like to report a murder. https://t.co/pqABCoLTS9

— Bill Madden (@maddenifico) November 5, 2026

"I find it quite ironic to read a post from the vice president as if he's describing the actions of a different administration," said Mamdani. "He's the vice president of the United States of America. He is not just some commentator online. And there has to be a reckoning of the fact that this is a war that they started."

"It's a war they can end," continued the democratic socialist mayor, who since entering the mayoral race in a long-shot bid early last year has rapidly become one of the most influential and popular Democratic politicians in the country. "If they think it was a part of their political demise, then why don't they actually start to take some action to reflect that?"

Vance said in his post that Republicans must focus on ending the Iran War, bringing down the cost of living, putting "America First," and changing the US relationship with Israel, which the administration has said pushed it to launch its attacks on Iran.

Vance's comments were taken by some as an initial attempt to begin distancing himself from the actions of an increasingly unpopular administration, in preparation to run for president.

Mamdani's response, said Jacobin writer Branko Marchetich, offered a "preview of the struggles" that the vice president will face in doing so.

"He's done his best to leak stories that he opposed it and thread the needle in public," said Marchetich. "But end of the day it's his administration too, so he owns it."

Although some races haven't yet been called, "Democratic voters, independent voters, and even some Republican voters spoke loudly and clearly: They want this country to go in a different direction," wrote Trent, a former communications director for Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) and two-time presidential campaign staffer for Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.).

Trent, who also co-founded Justice Democrats and now runs the super political action committee A Fight Worth Having, stressed that "this is an amazing, unprecedented moment in my lifetime. I'm 46 years old, and this is the most hopeful political moment I've ever experienced."

"Democrats have spoken loudly and clearly that they want new leadership. Unfortunately, too many of the people in Washington aren't listening," he added. While Trent and his group are far from alone in calling for new Democratic leadership when the party takes over Congress in January, Schumer and Jeffries are expected to become majority leader and speaker, respectively.

"Do you expect to face any kind of challenge in the election for Senate majority leader?" Michael Barbaro, who hosts The New York Times' podcast The Daily asked Chuck Schumer on Friday. He simply responded, "No."

Schumer ultimately added that "our caucus is focused on moving forward. Everyone's very happy with what we all did. But this is just the beginning. As I said before, and I'll say it again and again to my caucus, to the country, to everybody: If we don't deliver, all this will go away. This is just the first step. But I think we're united together to do that."

He delivered a similar message of unity during a Thursday night appearance on MS NOW, telling host Lawrence O'Donnell that the victorious Democrats—so far the party has 54 seats in the Senate and 253 in the House of Representatives, but those numbers could rise—were "all running on the same basic themes: costs, chaos, corruption."

As both majority and minority leader in recent years, Schumer has faced criticism from the party's left flank—and, as Al Jazeera noted Thursday, at least seven Democratic senators-elect have signaled or outright said they will not support him: Abdul El-Sayed (Mich.), Peggy Flanagan (Minn.), Adam Hamilton (Kan.), Chris Pappas (NH), Juliana Stratton (Ill.), and James Talarico (Texas).

However, as Fox News chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram explained Friday, basic math and a lack of clear challengers suggest Schumer will win: "The selection of Senate majority leader is not a vote which plays out on the floor. The concept of 'Senate majority leader' has only been around since the early 20th Century and is not mentioned in the Constitution."

"Let's say Democrats do win Mississippi and Alaska, giving them 56 senators who caucus with the Democrats. All Schumer needs is 29 Democrats to support him in caucus, and he's the next majority leader," Pergram wrote on social media.

He noted that other possible contenders are Democratic Sens. Brian Schatz (Hawaii) and Chris Van Hollen (Md.), but the former is running to succeed retiring Senate Minority Whip Dick Durbin (D-Ill.) and the latter reportedly isn't seeking the post—though Van Hollen has said publicly that Democrats should demand an ambitious progressive agenda before backing Schumer or anyone else.

"Progressives are flipping Republican seats and winning critical battlegrounds where pundits told us our politics could never compete. Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan. Troy Jackson in Maine. James Talarico in Texas. Sam Forstag in Montana. Randy Villegas in California. Bob Brooks in Pennsylvania," said Joseph Geevarghese, executive director of Our Revolution, which grew out of Sanders' 2016 presidential run. "We gave people something to vote FOR, and they showed up."

"The progressive movement drove this victory. We spent a decade building the infrastructure, developing leaders, and making the argument that brought us here... This is a vindication of our politics and our theory of change: Organized people can beat organized money when we advance an anti-corporate, working-class agenda," he stressed, recalling when "the talking heads, academics, and party establishment scoffed at Bernie Sanders and our movement for talking about oligarchy."

The organizer said that "this was the corruption election. Affordability was central, but people were also asking why life keeps getting more expensive and who keeps cashing in. From AI and data centers to healthcare, Big Pharma, crypto, oil, and the war industry, people want a say over decisions being made at their expense. Corporate control of government is making their lives harder."

The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC)—which notably congratulated Jeffries and Schumer, who wasn't even on the ballot this cycle, by name on Wednesday—along with GOP megadonor Elon Musk "and other billionaires and corporate interests have poured money into shaping our politics," Geevarghese continued. "Our victories show that their money does not make their agenda inevitable. People can organize, fight back, and win."

In the wake of these victories "powered by a progressive wave," Geevarghese called on Democrats to "use every committee, hearing, and budget negotiation. Follow the contracts and conflicts of interest. Put executives and administration officials under oath. Fight for concrete gains and make Trump answer for what he blocks."

"People need to see Democrats using every bit of power they have to fight for them," he said. "That requires leadership ready to meet the moment. Chuck Schumer should step aside. Bernie Sanders has provided the clarity and urgency a real opposition party needs. Leadership must match that ambition, including by investing in candidates and communities too often written off."

Aru Shiney-Ajay, executive director of the youth-led climate group Sunrise Movement, similarly said in a statement after the midterms that "young people voted for change. We deserve a Senate majority leader who will end the filibuster so we can stop the Iran Oil War, end corporate control of our government, and create good green jobs, not more data centers."

"Young people won't get that with the same old Democratic leadership. Schumer, it's time to put the American people first–commit to ending the filibuster or step aside," Shiney-Ajay added, referring to controversial chamber rules that effectively block legislation unless at least 60 of the 100 senators support advancing it to a final vote.

As for Jeffries, he got "the majority of his dreams," as Axios put it earlier this week. The outlet reported:

The left's strategy is "going to look different from what it would have been with a smaller margin," one incoming House progressive told Axios, noting that "leaders have more flexibility when they have big majorities.

Progressives "can't really extract much now [with this] colossal majority," a progressive strategist acknowledged, adding that "we don't have to do this high-stakes Jeffries fight."

Although Jeffries is on track to secure the role, there are calls for him to not be the next speaker. Nearly 900,000 people have signed a related Change.org petition, Nicole Whitted, an author and social media creator who receives compensation in connection with the effort.

"After historic wins on Tuesday, I believe the Democratic Party and our country as a whole is at a crossroads," Whitted told Newsweek. "My opposition to Hakeem Jeffries is about more than any single policy disagreement. It's about real leadership that aligns with today's Democratic voter, real accountability, and whether the party is genuinely listening to the voters demanding change."

In anticipation of Jeffries serving as speaker, the outlet Sludge examined his "financial backing from executives at Anduril and Palantir, cryptocurrency industry interests, and major Wall Street investors—business interests with a stake in how aggressively the new majority pursues corporate beneficiaries of Trump's presidency."

In response to that reporting, Melanie D'Arrigo, executive director of the pro-single-payer Campaign for New York Health, said that "you can't lead the opposition party while being bankrolled by the opposition. This should not be a controversial take."

Those dots pretty much invariably connect back to clean energy sources that cost less, deploy faster, deliver better in a local emergency, support energy democracy, and reduce emissions when used as directed.

• As part of its post-election roundup, Canary Media tracked three states where voters approved ballot initiatives to promote clean energy and utility accountability.
Mitchell Beer traces his background in renewable energy and energy efficiency back to 1977, in climate change to 1997.
Now he and the rest of the Energy Mix team scan 1,200 news headlines a week to pull together The Energy Mix and The Energy Mix Weekender.
text:
When you’re right in the midst of the kind of transformative change we may have seen in this week’s midterm elections in the United States, it’s hard to fully grasp what you’re witnessing, impossible to fully predict where it will land.

This is almost certainly a moment as profound as the one so many of us still remember from 11½ years ago, when Donald Trump’s ride down that ridiculous escalator dropped us into a lost decade of dread and destruction, division and disinformation. But even so, it’s just one important part of a bigger picture.

That’s because, astonishingly, the top-to-bottom sweep that Democrats carried off in the midterms was just the biggest of four major stories we were following last week. The profound challenge to the rogue MAGA regime in the White House came alongside:

• The latest in a series of analyses, this one from the International Energy Agency (IEA), showing a surge of clean energy options that are transforming global energy markets that the fossil industry will never again be able to take for granted;

• A federal budget in Canada that channelled the Carney government’s continuing fascination with fossil fuel megaprojects but also contained the seeds of faster, deeper carbon cuts, in what climate policy veteran Dan Woynillowicz called “Canada’s first true energy transition budget”;

• The existential urgency of a global climate emergency that is overshooting the 1.5°C limit on global warming as it spirals out of control, with former UN human rights commissioner Mary Robinson stressing the need get on with the job of phasing out fossil fuels, reforming international climate finance, and getting funds in place for climate adaptation.

All of that in the space of three days, with just a few days more before this year’s United Nations climate summit, COP31, convenes in Antalya, Türkiye.

If your head is spinning, you’re not alone. But when we look back, we may also see this as one of those moments we’ve been training for all our lives. Taken as a whole, this week’s news menu signals both the overwhelming need and a shining opportunity to get on with the job of delivering faster, deeper carbon cuts that leave no one else behind.

So Many Buried Ledes

In journalism-speak, “burying the lede” is one of the cardinal sins. It’s what happens when the opening or “lead” paragraph of a story misses the main point and forces readers to troll through for the news that matters most. (We purposely misspell “lede” as an homage to “leads”, the thin strips of metal that used to separate lines of type in a newspaper column before the advent of computer typesetting.)

But what do you do when you have a story with four legitimate, compelling ledes? (Apart from, y’know, publishing a full news digest to give each piece of the puzzle its due?) There’s so much to say about the midterms, and we’ll get there. But the context matters, too.

• Although Trump has made it one of his singular missions to delay and destroy the energy transition after shaking down fossil fuel interests for a “breathtakingly corrupt” $219 million in campaign contributions, no one country—not the U.S., not China—will be able to get the job done on its own. That’s why it matters when the IEA documents an accelerating transition, with “faster deployment of renewable power across India, Southeast Asia, Africa, and the Middle East.”

For better and for worse, the shift is not driven by a sudden uptick in concern about climate change, but by something even more immediate in the minds of most national governments—the need for geopolitically secure energy supplies that people can afford, and that countries can control rather than relying on volatile imports. Those dots pretty much invariably connect back to clean energy sources that cost less, deploy faster, deliver better in a local emergency, support energy democracy, and reduce emissions when used as directed.

• Canada’s federal budget was a predictable mix of old announcements and new, good news and bad. The government is still looking ahead to decades of strong demand for oil and gas exports to many of the same countries that—as the IEA has just told us, again—are decarbonizing at warp speed. At the same time, the budget emphasizes energy efficiency and mostly clean electrification, beginning with $50 billion to support a National Electricity Strategy that aims for major emission reductions in the country’s biggest energy-consuming sectors.

• And still, always, the urgency. The UN Environment Programme reported that we’re now on track to inevitably overshoot the 1.5°C endpoint of the 2015 Paris agreement. Oil Change International warned that fossil fuel projects already under way will exceed the remaining carbon budget for a 1.5°C future seven times over.

And then Mary Robinson arrived in Ottawa to deliver a keynote address to GreenPAC’s annual Breakfast on the Hill. In a feature interview with The Energy Mix, she called for Canada and other countries to develop roadmaps to phase out fossil fuels, just as Brazil has done in the lead-up to COP31. And she warned that international trust will break down fast if rich countries don’t keep their promises to finance climate adaptation in the world’s most vulnerable countries and develop new ways of mobilizing funds to confront the climate emergency.

Each of these buried ledes, on their own and all together, make the U.S. election result matter even more.

The Victory Lap…Now With Dinosaurs

The morning after the midterms, with the top-line outcome assured but many of the votes still being counted, a hastily-called media conference dug into how deeply and totally U.S. voters had repudiated Trump, how wide and important a win this was for the rest of us.

“I’m awake, barely,” said Rep. Sean Casten (D-IL), a former clean energy entrepreneur first elected to Congress in 2019. “I think we’re all still processing the victory from last night.” Casten said legislation to lower energy bills and speed up permitting for clean energy projects will likely be one of the top 10 priorities when Democrats regain control of the U.S. Congress in early January.

“The American people made their voices heard at the polls by resoundingly rejecting the destructive, corrupt actions of the Trump administration, including the war in Iran, the attacks on clean energy that have driven up costs for everyday people, and while they’re doing this, they’re boosting the profits of fossil fuel polluters,” said Gretchen Goldman, president of the Union of Concerned Scientists.

Heatmap says early priorities for Democrats in Congress will include restoring federal tax credits for renewable energy and investigating Trump’s funding cuts to the U.S. Department of Energy. Although with Trump vowing to spend the next two years playing “Mr. Veto”, it isn’t clear how much of that activity will be anything more than a marker leading up to the 2028 presidential election.

Still with the theme of victory laps, there’s so much to say about how thoroughly Americans defeated Trump. Proving definitively that we live in weird times, term-limited Gov. Ron DeSantis (R-FL) actually got the quote of the night, describing the political drubbing as “the political equivalent of a meteor strike” and an “extinction-level event” for his party. So yes, of course we all get to go there—the self-styled creationists who’ve worked so long and hard to deny science and dismantle the U.S. education system are acknowledging now that a meteor took out the dinosaurs?

Setting High Expectations

After any election, the only way to judge any group of politicians is by their results, not their party label or platform. And we already know that not every partisan win will be an advance for emission reductions or the energy transition—in New Jersey, a Republican incumbent who opposed offshore wind development lost his seat to a Democrat who holds much the same position.

But this was one campaign in which most or all of the winning Democratic candidates ran on a dual platform of cutting energy costs and adopting solutions that will also reduce climate pollution, former Washington State governor Jay Inslee told the Nov. 4 media briefing. So the overall shift opens up possibilities that haven’t been imaginable over the last two years, or much of the last decade—for the U.S. to rejoin the climate fight and the energy transition, and for U.S. voices to show up more constructively in international climate talks, beginning with COP31 this week and next.

So now, back to buried ledes…because the big-picture storyline was made up of so many local victories, big and small.

• As of Sunday morning, Democrats were leading or elected in 259 House of Representatives seats—41 more than they would need for a simple majority—compared to 176 for the Republicans.

• Democrats held 54 out of 100 Senate seats, with two still to be decided, compared to 44 Republicans.

• To win the Senate, Democrats had to flip at least four seats previously held by Republicans—a feat that pundits considered virtually impossible going into the election. They’ve got seven so far: Iowa, Kansas, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina, and Texas. Each of those wins was its own kind of milestone that would have ranged from unlikely to unimaginable in past electoral cycles. In Kansas, megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton became the state’s first Democratic senator since the 1930s. In Texas, former middle school teacher James Talarico became the state’s first since the 1980s.

• Democrats also successfully held their ground in states like Michigan, where public health physician Abdul El-Sayed brought a message of hope and humanity to a bruising campaign. In Minnesota, outgoing lieutenant-governor Peggy Flanagan, a citizen of the White Earth Nation, became the first Native-American woman to enter the U.S. Senate.

• Flanagan may soon be joined by Rep. Mary Peltola, a woman of Yup’ik Indigenous descent, who is so far on track to win the Senate seat in Alaska. In Mississippi, district attorney Scott Colom is now 2,500 votes ahead of the Republican incumbent with 97% of the votes counted, putting him within reach of becoming the state’s first African-American senator since the period following the U.S. Civil War in the 1860s.

• Governors-Elect Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia, Deb Haaland in New Mexico, and Gina Hinojosa in Texas are the country’s first African-American, Native-American, and Latina women, respectively, to win their positions.

• In Michigan, Sunrise Movement co-founder Will Lawrence flipped a Republican-held seat in a campaign that channelled local rage over data centre development, while also drawing support from opponents of large-scale solar and battery projects. The common thread, as reported by Grist: “Most communities have little say over whether a data centre or a solar farm gets built near them, and they don’t have any reason to believe that these projects are good for them.”

• In Florida, a longstanding renewable energy advocate in the U.S. House, Rep. Kathy Castor, withstood a partisan gerrymander to retain her seat in Hillsborough County near Tampa.

• In Texas, long a stronghold of a U.S. fossil industry now facing calls for a windfall tax on its war profits, Democrats swept the full slate of statewide offices, electing the governor, lieutenant-governor, attorney-general, and more. They even secured the 14+ seats they needed to flip the state house. Democrats also swept in Arizona, Georgia, Nevada, and Wisconsin. For the first time in a couple of decades, 30 of the country’s 50 state governors are Democrats, and “every single one of them are engines of clean energy development,” Inslee said.

• In states like Texas, Georgia, and Arizona, Democrats took control or gained seats on some of the key regulatory bodies with power to either obstruct or advance the energy transition. They seized majority control of the Georgia Public Service Commission for the first time in decades and grabbed two open seats on the Arizona Corporation Commission, in a campaign driven partly by a nearly universal, bipartisan backlash against local data centres. Those votes mattered, Casten told media Wednesday morning, because utility commission and state races “in many cases have a bigger impact on the actual deployment of clean energy in the United States than the federal level does, much to my chagrin.”

• With 22 states now represented by Democratic “trifectas”—the same party holding house and senate majorities as well as the governor’s chair—the election results will “change the course of America and allow us again to assume a leadership role in developing a clean energy economy, for us and the rest of the world,” Inslee told media. In a post-election news release, Minneapolis-based Common Charge called on state governors to meet voters’ demand for action on the cost of living by expanding local community power.

• As part of its post-election roundup, Canary Media tracked three states where voters approved ballot initiatives to promote clean energy and utility accountability. Smart Cities Dive pointed to US$24.7 billion in successful ballot initiatives to support public transit systems. And the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition, last seen defeating Republican primary incumbents who’d voted against renewable energy development, declared wins in races in Indiana and Colorado and vowed to be back for the next round of congressional elections in 2028.

• Stock markets were quick to respond to the election results, with renewable energy companies like Ørsted, First Solar, and NextEra gaining ground while AI data centre and nuclear stocks slid. “While it’s too early to call this a turning point for U.S. offshore wind, the outcome lowers the risk of further regulatory disruption and provides a more stable backdrop for projects already under way,” Morningstar senior equity analyst Tancrede Fulop told The Financial Times.

For Canada, Some Things Don’t Change

A win is a win. And just once in a while, isn’t it nice when “the world as it is” begins to align somewhat with “a world we wish to be”?

And yet—it takes nothing away from what the U.S. has achieved to say that nothing fundamental has changed for Canada.

Even with the U.S. Congress in nominally sane hands, Trump will still be sitting in the Oval Office for the next 26 months, and his response to the midterms does not bode well. In addition to his standard default—blaming everyone but himself for whatever goes wrong—he has elevated one of his top loyalists, “Chief Bigot” Stephen Miller, to chief of staff. Miller, the architect of the Trump administration’s most viciously vindictive policies, is so far outside the U.S. mainstream that most of his extended family has reportedly disowned him, with one cousin describing him as the “face of evil” on social media.

“The president’s choice sent a clear signal about the posture he intends to strike in his final two years in office and how little he intends to alter his approach in response to the most decisive political rout in half a century,” the New York Times writes. “He also put on centre stage a figure who had already been a galvanizing target for Democrats intent on using their new powers in Congress to check the administration.”

So that makes things a bit more complicated. We can see that so much has changed, but so much will not, at least not for the foreseeable future. Which means that, as much as extending a hand with gratitude and support to our U.S. friends and allies is absolutely the right answer, we still have to stay united with our #ElbowsUp against their federal government and the threat it represents.

As communicator and commentator Tod Maffin writes:

There is hope. This week was a good result for our American friends. The adults in the room are starting to come back.

But don’t ease up, Canada… Keep buying the Canadian cereal… holidaying in Tofino or Charlottetown… find a small business hit by the tariffs that you can buy from this holiday season.

Somebody will tell you this week the storm has passed. It hasn’t. And the forecast says so.

Even as we cheer on our friends and family and colleagues in the U.S., so many of whom have been fighting Trump’s brand of neo-fascism from within, we must also recognize that the shared interests between two countries will never be a perfect match.

For Canada and the United States, we can hope that the Venn diagram overlap will be a good deal wider as a result of the midterms. It would be a decent start and a start toward decency if their commerce secretary stopped threatening to invade us by sundown, and for bonus points, if their malignant Ambassador to Canada would just shut up and go away. But after all the effort and care we’ve put in to secure our sovereignty and diversify our trade, the reimagined travel plans and the checkout counter boycotts, and the 19 major international partnerships the Carney government has pursued or completed in the last 16 months, there’s no going back to the way things were.

China's Three Gorges Dam, begun in 1994 and becoming fully operational in 2012, appears to be a major win in the battle against climate change while also reducing the chances of catastrophic flooding that have claimed so many lives in the past.

"The Mass Mortality Event was devastating. In a few short weeks, something strange wiped out more than 60% of the species’ global population"

Chernobyl Exclusion Zone: When humans fled the worst nuclear incident in history, animals moved in. This is what happened next

And yet, the story of the mighty Three Gorges Dam is not one of pure good news. Indeed, its construction and subsequent operation have had a massive impact on human communities and have altered the nature of the river to such an extent that a number of species have either gone extinct or are on the verge of vanishing from Earth.

Rising in the mountains of China's Qinghai province on the Tibetan plateau, the Yangtze flows for 6300km to each the East China Sea at Shanghai. Some 400 million people live within the river's catchment and it provides about half of all the fish eaten in China and two-thirds of its rice. Industries and farming along the Yangtze contribute about 40% of China's economy.

Its raw power has long been harnessed for energy, the water being channelled through dams to drive electricity generating turbines. Since 1950 more than 50,000 dams have been built within the river's mighty basin. But there is nothing to compare with the Three Gorges Dam, which was constructed at a cost of over $30 billion.

It stretched a humongous 250km and blocked a mighty American river for 900 years. Then humans destroyed it, unleashing a disaster

At 2.3km long and 180m high it is the world's largest hydroelectric gravity dam, and the reservoir that formed behind it is 600km long and comprises 39 billion tonnes of water. The hydroelectric power plant has a stated generating capacity of 22.5 gigawatts of electricity, enough power for 4.5 million people and dwarfing the output of a typical modern nuclear power plant.

The three gorges in the dam's name are the Qutang, Wu and Xiling gorges, and they lie upstream. Plans to construction a dam here had been mooted as early as 1919. There were several false starts but major disasters, such as the 1931 and 1954 floods that killed tens and possibly hundreds of thousands of people, encouraged further interest and then definitive plans for a dam.

As well as producing power, the proposed dam would moderate the river's flow in monsoon season and drastically reduce the chances of serious flooding. And to a greater degree, the completed dam has achieved these aims, and given the Chinese economy a gigantic boost in the process.

But this progress has come at a cost. The creation of the dam and reservoir meant that 100,000 hectares of farmland and hundreds of villages, towns and even cities were submerged under the rising water. An estimated 1.4 million people were forced to relocate to higher ground and though new accommodation was provided, much of it was poor quality and close-knit communities were uprooted and broken apart.

The dam has also had a huge, and largely negative impact on the wild ecosystems along the river, particularly downstream of the dam. There are regular landslides both above and below the dam that affect human and wildlife communities. The dam has caused major changes to water flows that have removed important habitats, especially breeding areas, for many fish species.

The example of the Yangtze sturgeon is typical. This ancient fish, whose ancestors would have swum when the dinosaurs roamed the land, is now blocked from reaching its spawning grounds. And while the authorities herald a massive restocking project for the species, many experts believe none of these fish are able to breed and the species is living on borrowed time.

According to Yangtze River Fisheries Research Institute, fish populations of four species of carp – a crucial food fish - have declined by close to 90% due to changes in river flows. Many more fish species are under threat and it is already too late for the endemic Chinese paddlefish of the Yangtze and Yellow rivers. This huge fish with its strange snout was last seen in 2003 and has now been officially declared extinct.

Gone too is the Chinese river dolphin, also known as the baiji. It's thought that, coupled with overfishing, the massive increase in ship traffic due to the dam making the river more navigable has doomed the species.

River dolphins on the brink: Where the enigmatic river dolphins live, why they are at risk of extinction - and the battle to save them

The noise of the ships is extremely disruptive to the aquatic mammals' ability to hunt and find mates. A similar fate may await the Yangtze finless river porpoise whose numbers have plummeted since the dam was built.

Reptiles and amphibians have fared little better. The Yangtze giant softshell turtle is now extinct while the Chinese alligator and the Chinese giant salamander face uncertain futures, again due to how the dam has changed water flows and altered the river's interaction with flood plains and other riverine habitats crucial for these species.

On the positive side, there are some signs that the authorities, including the Chinese Three Gorges Corporation, have begun acknowledging and attempting to mitigate the impact of the dam, including stocking, and improving “environmental flows”.

Most astonishing still, at face value at least, is the notion that the creation of the dam and the elevation of such a huge amount of water, has slowed the Earth's rotation and even changed the planet's rotational axis. According to NASA calculations, however, the change is completely negligible, harmless, and too small to affect daily life, navigation, or standard timekeeping. Thank goodness for that, at least!

Hawaiʻi Gov. Josh Green recently announced designation of 25 census tracts throughout the islands under the federal Opportunity Zones 2.0 program.

These include tracts on Oʻahu, Hawaiʻi Island and Maui, including Lahaina’s Front Street census tract. No census tracts on Kauaʻi were eligible for designation, nor was census-level data available to seek an appeal.

Opportunity Zones 2.0 designations on Hawaiʻi Island

The tracts were not originally eligible; however, the state secured these designations through an appeal to the U.S. Department of the Treasury.

The Opportunity Zones 2.0 program offers federal tax incentives to investors who put long-term capital into designated low-income communities, with additional benefits for eligible rural areas, unlocking hundreds of millions of dollars in private investment throughout the state in economically depressed neighborhoods.

“As a physician, I’ve spent my career in places where resources were scarce,” said Green. “What I learned is that when you invest early and in the right places, you prevent a lot of pain down the road. That’s as true for our communities as it is for our patients. These designations will catalyze investments to build a healthier and more affordable Hawaiʻi.”

The designations follow months of engagement with county leadership, federal partners, national experts, community stakeholders and the private sector, led in partnership through the Office of the Governor as well as Hawaiʻi Department of Business, Economic Development and Tourism and Hawaiʻi Office of Planning and Sustainable Development.

“Opportunity Zones 2.0 puts Hawaiʻi on the map for investors looking to make a lasting difference,” said Hawaiʻi Department of Business, Economic Development and Tourism Director James Kunane Tokioka. “From housing and health care to film and agriculture, these designations will funnel capital into projects that build lasting value.”

The state selected tracts based on three key priorities:

Housing: Housing is the most pressing need in every county. Opportunity Zones 2.0 gives the state a new tool to attract private capital to build homes local families can afford.

Clean energy: Hawaiʻi pays some of the highest energy costs in the nation; a burden on families and drag on the economy. The designations can bring private capital into energy projects that lower costs, create local jobs and advance the state’s clean energy goals.

More resilient economy: The state aims to strengthen and diversify Hawaiʻi’s economy through investment in health care, tourism, advanced manufacturing, agriculture, broadband and film.

“Our kids shouldn’t have to leave Hawaiʻi to find a good job or an affordable place to live,” said Green. “Opportunity Zones 2.0 will help us build a stronger, more diverse economy so our people can stay, work and thrive right here at home.”

reshaped the Environmental Protection Agency
, reversing pollution limits as it promotes fossil fuels.
Clear Street energy transition analyst Tim Moore said he expects Democrats to investigate the climate and environmental rollbacks, in an effort to block some from taking effect. Democrats could also try amending the Clean Air Act to cut carbon pollution and push back against EPA budget cuts, he added.
Rep. Sean Casten, D-Ill., said he is cautiously optimistic some Republicans will now seek to differentiate themselves from Trump and back pro-environmental policies. But without Republican support, Democrats’ more ambitious bills will largely lay out their agenda for 2028, he added.
Climate is not necessarily at the top of Democrats’ list of priorities. They are targeting healthcare access, trade tariffs and the Iran war.
Rep. Frank Pallone, the New Jersey Democrat who is expected to become chair of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, said the party should focus on healthcare, affordability, consumer and environmental protections, clean energy and regulating Big Tech.

David Victor, a professor of innovation and public policy at the University of California, San Diego, largely expects a stalemate at the federal level on climate and energy policy because of the divided government. He said agreement could come on some bipartisan measures such as a permitting overhaul.
Victor thinks Democratic-led investigations and hearings will center on corruption and other topics that may only touch on energy and climate. Like Casten, Victor said many of the Democratic bills likely will not become law, but will outline what Democrats could accomplish if they win the White House in 2028.
“The Democrats are going to be drafting things that the administration’s not going to like. They don’t have the votes to override a veto, and on top of it, the administration is going to be in turmoil because of its own electoral failures and because of all the investigations,” Victor said. “This seems to me, at the federal level, largely a recipe for kind of intense chaos over the next two years.”
One of the biggest wild cards is the behavior of the administration, which could use executive power to double down on rollbacks of climate and environmental rules, he said.

Democrats scored victories in races for governor
in states long controlled by Republicans, including Texas and Georgia.
Leah Stokes, a political scientist at the UC Santa Barbara, said there could be a lot of state action on climate next year because of those wins. That is where climate leadership has traditionally come from, she noted. At the federal level, Stokes is optimistic about extending clean energy tax credits since some Republicans support that.

text:
District heating has been around for almost 150 years, with the first commercial system established in New York in 1877, yet it is still not widely used. The original systems used steam produced by a central fossil-fuel boiler. However, systems have evolved over time, and modern heating networks have more flexible infrastructure that can connect multiple energy and storage solutions to supply both heating and cooling.

At present, district heating supplies approximately 10 per cent of global building heat demand, with most networks concentrated in Northern and Eastern Europe and China. Other parts of the world have also recently begun to adopt district heating, including Canada and Ireland. District heating is particularly useful in dense urban areas as it can be developed efficiently in terms of space and can recover waste heat and reduce local air pollution, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA).

Roughly 90 per cent of the global district heating supply is produced using fossil fuels at present. However, there is significant potential to shift reliance from fossil fuels to renewable alternatives to power district heating systems, such as bioenergy, solar thermal, geothermal energy, and nuclear energy.

In the U.S. state of New York, the UpgradeNY coalition of clean energy, environmental, and labour groups has been calling for regulators to adopt clean electric heating by replacing gas pipelines with thermal networks. UpgradeNY says that by using heat pumps and tapping into sources of waste heat, such as underground and industrial or municipal systems, the region could reduce its dependence on fossil fuels.

ADVERTISEMENT

In October, the New York Public Service Commission approved two utility thermal energy network (UTEN) plans, which are expected to cost a combined $111.5 million to develop. However, it rejected nine other UTEN projects, including several in New York City. The projects will be developed in the Hudson Valley town of Haverstraw and in the city of Buffalo and, if successful, could provide blueprints for projects in other parts of the United States. The financing comes from a $150 million commitment to thermal energy networks, helping ensure costs are not shifted to consumers.

Thermal energy networks rely on wells and pipes to circulate water or other fluids that capture the ambient temperatures hundreds of feet under the Earth’s surface, as well as waste heat from sewer systems, industrial facilities, and data centres. The steady heat exchange helps to improve the efficiency of electric-powered heat pumps, which are used instead of gas-powered boilers and furnaces. The development of the new systems is expected to create several jobs in the region during construction.

Massachusetts has already developed a UTEN project that provides heating and cooling to about 140 customers. Meanwhile, California, Colorado, Minnesota, and Washington are all exploring the potential for UTEN development. However, there are still uncertainties about the costs of installing and operating these systems, as most existing projects are small-scale and do not provide a clear picture of what commercial deployment might look like.

The New York Public Service Commission plans to invest $50 million in developing the Haverstraw thermal energy network to connect up to 30 structures, including single- and multifamily residences, commercial and government buildings, and an elementary school. The network is designed to tap into ambient heat from bore fields drilled on municipal land, as well as wastewater in the city’s sewer network.

Meanwhile, the Buffalo project will use an existing steam heat system. The utility National Fuel Gas will shift away from using natural gas for heating in the area by combining water from boreholes and a wastewater heat recovery system, with plans to provide clean heat and cooling to low-income multifamily housing.

In August, the Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA) announced plans to assess whether a UTEN could help reduce temperatures on subway platforms in Lower Manhattan while transferring excess heat to nearby municipal buildings. The $800,000 feasibility study focuses specifically on the Brooklyn Bridge-City Hall 4, 5, 6 and Chambers Street J Z station complex. If implemented, it would be the first UTEN project to be installed in a U.S. public transport system.

ADVERTISEMENT

Brooklyn Bridge-City Hall recorded average platform temperatures of 35.6°C in the summer of 2025, making it one of the hottest stations in the city’s subway system. The proposed network would use radiant cooling to absorb heat from the platform and transfer it through pipes to geothermal boreholes beneath an abandoned centre platform at Chambers Street, where it would be stored underground and retrieved during colder weather to supply heat to nearby municipal buildings.

District heating has been around for over a century, but most systems continue to rely heavily on natural gas for heating and cooling. Several areas of the world are now assessing the potential to adapt systems to tap into waste heat, which is particularly common in densely populated areas and industrial operations, and transfer it to nearby buildings. This could reduce dependence on fossil fuels and provide cleaner heating and cooling systems.

text:
Vermont shares grid and costs with New England

Consider the New England Clean Energy Connect (NECEC), a line built to bring clean Canadian hydropower into the region. Years of lawsuits and political fights in Maine and New Hampshire held it up, and Massachusetts regulators estimated the delays added more than $500 million to its cost.

A power line should not cost that much in the first place (and that cost gets passed on to all of us) which is why I am concerned Attorney General Charity Clark signed a letter objecting to the newly introduced Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA).

The bill, introduced by a bipartisan group of senators, tackles our biggest clean energy bottleneck by expanding grid transmission capacity by 30%. It would end the kind of limbo that keeps efficient, cheaper clean energy stuck in gridlock and imposes clear deadlines. Challenges would need to be filed promptly and decided quickly, so a good project can’t be held hostage for years.

Independent modeling from Resources for the Future shows permitting reform will unlock a massive wave of clean energy, cutting nearly 3 billion tons of power sector carbon pollution through 2050 while saving ratepayers $350 billion. Right now, delays in building clean energy and transmission keeps legacy fossil fuel polluters online by trapping zero-emission power in administrative limbo. The resulting climate change exacerbates extreme weather, including the catastrophic floods that have devastated towns and cities in Vermont and caused millions of dollars in damage. The longer we wait to get clean energy on the grid, the longer vulnerable communities elsewhere in New England have to endure the pollution of dirty fossil fuel plants.

The bill also protects households from the growing risk of data centers, ensuring they cover the full cost of the transmission they need.

Senators Sanders and Welch both care about working families’ wallets and about climate change. I hope they vote yes on BAAJA this month and I hope Attorney General Clark gives this bill a second look.

The bill’s long-term effect is clean, low-cost power which can outcompete fossil fuels and reduce climate pollution.

Jennifer Durgin, White River Junction

Jennifer Durgin is the Vermont state coordinator for Citizens’ Climate Lobby, a nonpartisan, grassroots advocacy organization that empowers everyday people to work together on climate policy.

text:
Voters on Saturday rejected a measure that would have weakened California’s landmark environmental law by fast-tracking reviews for some projects.

With about 76% of votes counted, voters rejected Prop. 45 by 55.7% to 44.3%.

The vote maintains the status quo under the state’s Environmental Quality Act, which since 1970 has required public agencies to review project developments that could have harmful environmental impacts, and mitigate those harms.

“Californians have sent a clear message to corporate developers, utilities and data center builders that they will not stand for a broad assault at the ballot box on state law protecting our air, water and natural resources,” No on 45’s Woody Little said. “We were outspent but not outgunned.”

Supporters had said the changes would reduce building costs. The California Chamber of Commerce sponsored Proposition 45, the Building an Affordable California Act, which would limit the length of environmental reviews for projects deemed “essential” to 365 business days and require courts to resolve litigation in 270 calendar days. Those projects include housing, water, broadband and transit developments.

Proponents said the savings from building more quickly would pass to consumers and spent $41 million campaigning for the measure. The Building a Better California political action committee was the largest donor, giving $10 million to the campaign. The organization is funded partly by current and former Google executives Sergey Brin and Eric Schmidt. Two of the largest investor-owned utilities, Pacific Gas & Electric Company and Southern California Edison, together donated $4.4 million.

Environmental groups argued the measure would go too far in weakening a law meant to protect people from environmental harms. Opponents, including a coalition of environmental, health and union organizations, spent $30 million trying to stop it. Wendy Schmidt, a Democratic philanthropist, was the largest donor, giving $10 million to the campaign. The political action committee Clean and Healthy California Sponsored by Environmental Organizations contributed $7 million.

The California Democratic Party opposed the measure. The California Republican Party supported it, while county Republican groups were split.

Deborah Sivas, an environmental law professor at Stanford University, said Prop. 45 would radically change current law. It would shift power “away from local governments and to developers by giving them some new tools … and limiting what courts can do in terms of reviewing decisions that agencies and local governments make,” she said.

CEQA and housing

California’s environmental review law, signed in 1970, requires agencies to assess the environmental impacts of developments and help mitigate them.

Over decades, developers have raised concerns about the process, arguing litigation and bureaucracy slow down construction.

State legislators have tried to fix the problem by passing laws that exempt or streamline certain projects from environmental review. In 2025, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed laws that exempt many urban housing projects from the full review process.

But some supporters of Prop. 45, including the California Building Industry Association and the California Council for Affordable Housing, say those changes don’t go far enough.

“It’s an important piece of the puzzle, but (that type of housing) does not produce quickly or at scale,” said Jennifer Hernandez, an attorney who helped write the measure. “We need quicker, at scale, affordable housing.”

Supporters say Prop. 45 would help California redevelop large, unused sites like malls and parking lots into housing and make it easier to build away from urban areas.

Pro-housing groups, public agencies divided

Pro-housing and local government groups usually support CEQA reform, but Prop. 45 has divided many of them.

Housing advocates in the Bay Area, including East Bay for Everyone and the Greenbelt Alliance, oppose the measure. Other Yes in My Backyard groups are neutral, including Abundant Housing Los Angeles and both California YIMBY and YIMBY Action — the movement’s two flagship advocacy groups.

The split between pro-housing groups lies in whether California should keep building outward onto undeveloped land or promote construction in urban centers. Some supporters, including Oakland Democratic Assemblymember Buffy Wicks, have said the state needs all types of housing.

Others say building away from urban centers would make it harder to address climate change.

“We believe we can (and must) solve the housing and climate crises simultaneously. That means building communities with denser housing and alternatives to automobile dependence,” wrote Max Dubler of California YIMBY in a blog post explaining the group’s neutral stance on Prop. 45.

Public agencies and local governments that could benefit from the building rules were also divided.

The California Municipal Utilities Association opposes the measure. But most other groups representing local governments, including the League of California Cities and California State Association of Counties, remained neutral.

Financial impacts for Prop. 45

Prop. 45 supporters argued that streamlining development would make life more affordable for Californians, but the long-term financial benefits are unclear.

An analysis by Blue Sky Consulting Group, commissioned by the California Chamber of Commerce, estimated the measure would produce $1.5 billion in savings and additional revenues for public agencies over 10 years that would reduce overall housing costs.

But the measure would initially cost local governments and public agencies more as they adjust to the measure’s rules, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, a nonpartisan adviser to the Legislature.

Democrats have done well in recent elections when they win young voters by a margin of at least 20 points. On Tuesday, they carried Gen Z — those under 30 — by nearly 50 points, according to exit polling.

It's a stunning shift from 2024, when the party lost critical ground with young people. Long seen as a part of the Democratic base, voters under 30 shifted right towards Donald Trump, motivated by his pledge to better their economic prospects.

But this week, the youngest generation of voters issued a strong rebuke of Republicans, taking another chance on Democrats and their change-focused message at a moment when many of them feel as though the American Dream is out of reach.

How young voters powered Democrats to victory

Americans ages 18-29 have a history of turning out at lower rates than older voters, and this year was no exception. Gen Z made up 11% of the total vote on Tuesday.

However, where young Americans may have made the greatest difference is on the margins in House and Senate races where Democrats flipped seats.

The Texas Senate race is a key example. Democrat James Talarico won the state by 12 percentage points; however, when looking at just Gen Z, he won it by 60 points.

Explaining the massive shift from 2024

When assessing gains more broadly, Democrats argue the party's strong slate of candidates helped drum up increased enthusiasm.

But another motivating factor remains strong opposition to Trump. Throughout his second term, Gen Z increasingly soured on the president, with some arguing he failed to make good on a number of core campaign promises — from pledging to lower prices and repeatedly vowing "no new wars," to calling for a crackdown on federal corruption and the release of the Epstein files.

Much of that disappointment was reflected in exit polling. Economic issues were the top concern for a plurality of 18- to 29-year-olds, at 43%, and these voters expressed broad frustrations with Trump's handling of the issue. More than eight in 10 said that Trump's policies have worsened economic conditions, with similar shares opposing his tariff strategy and the decision to go to war with Iran.

The young voters Trump lost

Early analysis from CIRCLE indicates that 15% of young people who backed Trump in 2024 voted for a Democratic House candidate in this year's midterms.

Democrats made gains with some young voters who backed Trump two years ago, including white men and Latino men, two blocs that narrowly voted Republican in 2024 and then voted blue on Tuesday by double digits. Democratic candidates also narrowed the margins with young rural voters and people without college degrees.

Some of those gains may have been helped by young Trump voters who chose to sit this election out, but it's unclear how many of them there were.

How the election results broke down by age

The midterm results underscore how neither of the two major parties owns Gen Z, according to John Della Volpe, a left-leaning pollster who's extensively studied the politics of young Americans.

"The cohort of younger people in this cycle had a different set of experiences than the cohort of people two years ago, or four years before that," he said. "Every candidate, every party has to earn their votes."

Della Volpe, who runs the Harvard Youth Poll, notes that in the latest survey, released in October, there was a sizable enthusiasm gap between young Democrat and young Republican respondents. While half of Democrats said they definitely planned to vote, just a third of Republicans and less than a quarter of Independents said the same.

"I also think we shouldn't overread what's happened," he added. "Clearly a significant historic rebuke on the party in office — that's obvious — however, I think we need to more fully, kind of understand, the contour of the electorate, who showed up and who didn't show up."

By 2028, Gen Z and millennial voters will make up more than half of the electorate, a demographic shift with huge implications for Democrats and the GOP.

"Young adults can make a difference," said Elizabeth Matto, who serves as the director of the Center for Youth Political Participation at Rutgers University.

"They do care about politics. They can sway the outcome of elections. And they're a voting bloc worth paying attention to."
